In vain she tried to quiet herself by saying, “I do not care a straw for him, and he will soon get over his infatuation on discovering the truth.”

But she had a lesson to learn as well as he, for as we have intimated, unrecognized as yet, there was a process going on in her mind that in time would make strange havoc in her cold philosophy. Her heart’s long winter was slowly breaking up; her girlish passion, intense as it was foolish, proved that she had a heart. Everything had been against her. Everything in her experience and education, and especially in her father’s strong character and prejudices, had combined to deaden and to chill her; and had these influences continued, she would undoubtedly have become as cold and hard as some whom we find in advanced life with natures like the poles, where the ice gathers year after year, but never melts.

But in Dennis Fleet she met a nature as positive as she was becoming negative. He was so warm and earnest that when she commenced to fan his love into a stronger flame for purely artistic purposes, as she vowed to herself, some sparks of the sacred fire fell on the cold altar of her own heart and slowly began to kindle.

But this awakening would not now be that of a child, but of a *woman*. Therefore, Mr. Ludolph, beware!

But she had yet much to learn in the hard, strange school of experience before she would truly know herself or her own needs.

Success in art, however, was still her ruling passion. And though strange misgivings annoyed and perplexed her, though her respect for Dennis daily increased, and at times a sudden pity and softness made her little hands hesitate before giving an additional wrench to the rack of uncertainty upon which she kept him; still, she would not for the world have abandoned her purpose, and such compunctions were as yet but the little back eddies of the strong current.

===Chinese===
他每周来宅邸两三次，如此持续了将近一个月，克里斯蒂娜觉得自己已为最后那一幕做好了准备，可心头却又生出几分畏怯——她在这上面押下的希望实在太重了。更令她恼火的是，她发现自己竟然真的有些怕他。他的性情是那样刚毅而赤诚，以至于她越来越深切地感到玩弄这份真心实属不义。她徒劳地试图宽慰自己：“我根本毫不在乎他，等他看清真相，很快就会从这阵痴迷中清醒过来的。”

然而，正如他需要上一课一样，她同样也有一课要学；因为诚如我们先前所暗示的，一股她尚未察觉的潜流正在她心底涌动，假以时日，必将把她那套冷酷的处世哲学搅得天翻地覆。她心头漫长的寒冬正悄然消融；她少女时代那场既炽烈又愚痴的恋情，早已证明她并非无心之人。只是过往的一切都与她为敌。她所经历和受过的一切教育，尤其是她父亲那刚愎的性格与根深蒂固的偏见，共同将她的心性磨得麻木而冰冷；倘若这些影响一直持续下去，她毫无疑问会变得像我们在世间所见的某些垂暮之人那般冷酷僵硬，性情宛如南北两极，年复一年积起厚冰，永不消融。

可在丹尼斯·弗利特身上，她偏偏遇上了一个如太阳般积极炽热、恰与她日渐消极冷漠的心性截然相反的人。他是那样的温暖而笃诚，以至于当她起初暗自发誓纯粹为了艺术而将他的爱火扇得愈燃愈旺时，几星神圣火焰的余烬却悄然落在了她自己那冰冷的心坛之上，缓缓燃起了微光。

而且这一次的苏醒，不再是孩童懵懂的悸动，而是*成熟女子*的觉醒。因此，卢多尔夫先生，且当心了！

不过，在她真正认清自己以及自己内心真正的渴求之前，她还得在人生这所严酷而奇特的学校里吃上不少苦头、学上许多功课。

然而，在艺术上取得成功依然是她心中压倒一切的执念。尽管莫名的疑惧令她心烦意乱、困惑不已，尽管她对丹尼斯的敬重日渐加深，甚至有时一阵突如其来的怜悯与柔情，会让她那双纤巧的手在把悬而未决的刑架再拧紧一圈时微微迟疑；可即便如此，她也绝不肯为了天下任何东西而放弃自己的筹谋，这般愧疚在此时还不过是滚滚洪流边缘几朵微不足道的回旋漩涡罢了。

===Original===
One day, in the latter part of August, Christine felt herself in the mood to give the finishing touch to the principal figure in her picture. The day was somewhat hazy, the light subdued and favorable for artistic work. Though she had prolonged Dennis’s labors, to his secret delight and great encouragement, she could not keep him employed much longer.

She sent for him to come over in the afternoon. “Some brackets, carvings, and pictures had come for her studio, and she wished him to put them up,” she said, coolly, as he entered.

He had come glowing with hope and almost assurance, for, the last time they had parted, she had dismissed him with unusual kindness. But here was one of those capricious changes again that he could not understand.

She took her seat at her easel, saying, with a nod and a smile, “I can direct you here, for I am in a mood for work this afternoon.”

He bowed quietly and went on with his task. Her rather cool reception oppressed him, and the tormenting question presented itself, for the hundredth time, “Can she in any degree feel as I do?” He longed to settle the matter by plain, straightforward action.

===Chinese===
八月下旬的一天，克里斯蒂娜觉得自己兴致盎然，正是为画中主角添上画龙点睛最后一笔的好时机。那天天气微带薄雾，光线柔和而内敛，极利于作画。尽管她特意拖长了丹尼斯的活计——这曾令他暗自欣喜、备受鼓舞——可她终究也留不了他干活太久了。

她差人叫他下午过来。“画室里新到了些托架、木雕和画作，想请他帮忙安放悬挂起来，”他一进门，她便冷淡地说道。

他原本是怀着满腔希望与几近笃定的欣喜赶来的，因为上回临别时，她送他离开的态度格外和蔼温存。可如今，她却又一次毫无征兆地冷了下来，教他捉摸不透。

她在画架前坐下，微微颔首一笑，说道：“我坐在这里指点你便好，今天下午我正有兴致作画呢。”

他安静地躬身一礼，随即动手干起活来。她那略显冷淡的接待令他心头沉甸甸的，那个折磨人的问题第一百次浮上他的脑海：“她心里究竟有几分与我相同的感受？”他迫切渴望用坦诚直率的方式，将这桩事彻底挑明定夺。

===Original===
Her maid knocked at the door, saying, “The mail, mademoiselle.”

A dainty note was handed her, which seemed decidedly pleasing, and Dennis noticed as she read it that she wore on her finger a solitaire diamond that he had not seen before. His latent jealousy was aroused. She saw that her spell was working, and smiled. Soon she said: “Mr. Fleet, you seem very grave. What is the matter?”

He answered, curtly, “Nothing.”

She looked at him with a pretty, pained surprise. At the same time her heart smote her. His face was so pale and thin, and indicated such real suffering, that she pitied him more than ever. But she would have suffered much herself for the sake of success, and she was not one to hesitate long over the suffering of another. She compressed her lips as she said, mentally: “Art is first, and these transient feelings are secondary. There is little in the world but that has cost someone deeply.” She did not know how profound a truth this was.

After a few moments Dennis said, in a tone that had a jealous tinge, “Miss Ludolph, your correspondent seems to interest you deeply.”

“And you also, I think,” she replied, with an arch smile; “and you will be interested still more when you have read this;” and she offered him the note.

===Chinese===
这时，女仆敲门进来，禀道：“小姐，您的信。”

递到她手中的是一封精致的短笺，信中的内容似乎颇合她意；丹尼斯留意到，她读信时手指上戴着一枚他从未见过的独粒钻戒。他潜藏的嫉妒心顿时被勾了起来。她瞧出自己的法术正在见效，不由得微微一笑。过了一会儿，她开口道：“弗利特先生，你看起来神色好生凝重。怎么了？”

他简短生硬地答道：“没什么。”

她露出又娇俏又委屈的惊讶神情望向他。可与此同时，她的心却猛地一揪。他的脸庞那样苍白消瘦，流露出如此真切的煎熬，教她比以往任何时候都更怜惜他。然而，为了成功她连自己也甘愿吃尽苦头，自然不会为了旁人的痛苦而犹豫太久。她抿紧双唇，在心底暗自念道：“艺术至上，这等一时的情绪算不得什么。世间万事，哪一样不曾叫某个人付出过惨痛的代价？”她却不知，这句念头背后竟藏着何等深沉残酷的真理。

沉默了片刻，丹尼斯用带着几分酸意的语调说道：“卢多尔夫小姐，给您写信的人似乎令您很是倾心啊。”

“我看你也很感兴趣呢，”她带着一抹狡黠娇俏的微笑答道，“等你看过这封信，怕是会更感兴趣；”说着，她将短笺递向他。

===Original===
“I have no right—do not think me prying,” said he, flushing.

“I give the right. You know a lady can give many rights—if she chooses,” she added, significantly.

He looked at her eagerly.

Her eyes fell consciously, and her cheeks glowed with excitement, for she felt that the critical moment had come. But instantly her proud, resolute nature aroused as never before, and she determined to make the most of the occasion, let the consequences be what they might. Therefore she worked eagerly and watched him closely. Never had she been so conscious of power. She felt inspired, capable of placing on the canvas anything she chose. If in this mood she could succeed in bringing into his face just the expression she desired, she could catch it and fix it forever, and with it make a laurel (not a hymeneal) wreath for her own brow. But what could Dennis know of all this? To him the glowing cheek and eyes so lustrous told a different tale; and hope—sweet, exquisite, almost assured—sprang up in his heart.

And he meant that it should be assured. He would speak that day if it were possible, and *know* his happiness, instead of fondly believing and hoping that all was sure. Then he would be as prudent and patient as she desired. Thus Christine was destined to have her wish fulfilled.

===Chinese===
“我无权过问——请别以为我有窥探之意，”他涨红了脸说道。

“我准许你有这个权利。你应当知道，一位女士只要愿意——大可以赋予人许多权利的。”她意味深长地补了一句。

他热切地凝望着她。

她故作羞怯地垂下眼帘，双颊因激动而泛起红晕，因为她预感到紧要关头终于来临了。可转瞬之间，她那骄傲而果决的天性便前所未有地振奋起来，决意不管后果如何，都要把眼前这桩良机利用到极致。于是她兴致勃勃地挥动画笔，一边紧盯着他的动静。她平生从未如此真切地感受到自己手握大权。她只觉文思泉涌，仿佛只要自己想画，世间万物皆可跃然布上。倘若乘着这股灵感，能成功激发出他脸上梦寐以求的那一抹神情，她便能将它一举捕捉、永留画端，借此为自己的额头编织一顶月桂荣冠（绝非新婚的花冠）。可丹尼斯又怎会知晓这一切背后的玄机？在他眼里，那泛红的脸颊与盈盈闪耀的眼眸分明诉说着截然不同的心意；于是希望——甜美、细腻、几近十拿九稳的希望——在他心田猛然生发。

而他打定主意，今日定要让这份希望尘埃落定。只要有可能，他今天就要开口倾诉，亲口*确认*自己的幸福，而不再只是痴痴地以为、盼着一切稳操胜券。待心意挑明之后，他自然会如她所愿那般审慎忍耐。如此一来，克里斯蒂娜的心愿注定要如愿以偿了。

===Original===
She continued: “The note is from a special friend of yours; indeed I think you form a little mutual-admiration society, and you are spoken of, so I think you had better read it.”

“I shall not read the note,” said Dennis; “but you may tell me, if you choose, what you think the writer will have no objection to my knowing.”

“And do you mean to suggest that you do not know who wrote the note? I can inform you that you are to be invited to a moonlight sail and musicale on the water. Is not that a chance for romance?”

“And will *you* go?” asked Dennis, eagerly.

“Yes, if *you* will,” she said, in a low tone, giving him a sidelong glance.

This was too much for Dennis, the manner more than the words, and taken together they would have led any earnest man to committal. He was about to speak eagerly, but she was not quite ready.

===Chinese===
她接着说道：“这封信是你的一位特别好友寄来的；说实在的，我觉得你们俩倒像是结成了一个互相吹捧的小圈子，信里还提到了你，所以我劝你还是看看为好。”

“这信我是不会看的，”丹尼斯说，“不过您若是愿意，大可以把您觉得写信人不介意我知道的内容告诉我。”

“难道你是想说，你连写信人是谁都猜不出来吗？不妨告诉你，有人要请你去参加一场月夜水上泛舟音乐会呢。这岂不是桩极富浪漫情调的雅事？”

“那*您*去吗？”丹尼斯急切地问道。

“只要*你*去，我就去。”她压低声音说道，眼波斜睨着他。

这句话简直叫丹尼斯把持不住——那副神态比话语本身更撩人心弦，两者相合，换作任何一个真挚的男子都会就此倾吐肺腑。他正要急切地开口，她却觉得火候还差那么一分。

===Original===
“Moreover,” she continued, quickly, while Dennis stood before her with cheeks alternately hot and pale, “this special friend who invites you will be there. Now don’t pretend ignorance of her name.”

“I suppose you mean Miss Winthrop,” said Dennis, flushing.

“Ah, you blush, do you? Well, it is my turn to ask pardon for seeming curiosity.”

He drew a few steps nearer to her, and the expression she had so longed to see came into his face. She looked at him earnestly with her whole soul in her eyes. She would photograph him on memory, if possible. For a moment or two he hesitated, embarrassed by her steady gaze, and seemingly at a loss for words. Then, in a low, deep tone he said, “You, better than anyone, know that I have no cause to blush at the mention of Miss Winthrop’s name.”

She did not answer, but was painting rapidly. He thought this was due to natural excitement expressing itself in nervous action. But she did not discourage him, and this he felt was everything. With his heart in his eyes and tones, he said: “Oh, Christine, what is the use of wearing this transparent mask any longer? Your quick woman’s eye has seen for weeks the devoted love I cherish for you. I have heard much of woman’s intuitions. Perhaps you saw my love before I recognized it myself, since your grace and beauty caused it to grow unconsciously while I was your humble attendant. But, Christine, believe me, if you will but utter in words what I fondly believe I have read in your kindly glances and manner, though so delicately veiled—if you will give me the strength and rest which come of assured hope—I know that not far in the future I shall be able to place at your feet more than mere wealth. I, too, hope to be an artist, and you have been my chief inspiration. I could show you a picture now that would tell more of what I mean than can my poor words. There is a richer and happier world than you have yet known, and oh, how I have prayed that I might lead you into it!” and in words of burning eloquence he proceeded to tell the story of his love.

===Chinese===
“况且，”她赶忙接道——此时丹尼斯站在她面前，双颊一阵滚烫、一阵惨白——“邀请你的这位特别好友也会到场。这下可别再假装不知她芳名何许了吧。”

“我想您指的是温思罗普小姐吧。”丹尼斯脸一红，答道。

“哟，你脸红了，是不是？好吧，这回该轮到我为自己这副探人隐私的模样向你赔罪了。”

他朝她走近了几步，而她日思夜想盼着见到的那抹神情，终于浮上了他的面庞。她全神贯注地凝视着他，仿佛将整个灵魂都聚在了眼里。若能做到，她恨不得把他的容颜直接印刻进记忆的底片里。起初一两瞬，他被她那直勾勾的目光看得有些局促，迟疑着似乎一时语塞。随后，他用低沉而浑厚的嗓音说道：“您比任何人都清楚，提起温思罗普小姐的名字，我并没有任何值得脸红的缘由。”

她没有搭腔，只是手底飞快地作着画。他以为这是她心绪激动之下的自然反应，化作了手头慌乱的动作。既然她并未出言阻拦，在他看来这便已胜过千言万语。他把一颗心全倾注在眼神与嗓音里，说道：“啊，克里斯蒂娜，何必再戴着这副一望即穿的面具呢？这几周来，凭您女子敏锐的双眼，早就看穿了我对您矢志不渝的爱慕。我早听说过女人的直觉何等灵验。兴许在我自己尚未察觉之前，您就已经看透了我的爱意——因为正是您的优雅与绝色，在我还是您卑微侍从的时候，便教这份爱在不知不觉中悄然滋长。可是，克里斯蒂娜，请相信我，只要您肯亲口说出我自以为从您含蓄婉转的顾盼与举止中所读到的心意——只要您肯赐予我一份确切希望所带来的力量与安宁——我知道，不用等太久，我就能捧出远比区区财富更珍贵的礼物，献在您的脚下。我也立志成为一名画家，而您正是我最主要的灵感源泉。我现在就能拿出一幅画来，比我这番拙劣的言辞更能诉尽我的心迹。在您迄今所知的世界之外，还有一个更为丰盈、更为幸福的天地，啊，我曾多少次虔诚祈祷，盼能亲手引领您步入其中！”说罢，他便用炽热而动人的言辞，倾诉起自己的一腔深情。

===Original===
She heard him as in a dream. She understood his words, remembered them afterward, but so intent was she on her darling purpose that she heeded them not. His voice sounded far away, and every power of mind and body was concentrated to transfer his expression to the canvas before her. Even he, blinded as he was by his emotions, occupied by the long pent-up torrent of feeling that he was pouring into her unheeding ear, wondered at her strange, dazzling beauty and peculiar manner.

After speaking a moment or two, the blur over his eyes and the confusion of his mind began to pass away, and he was perplexed beyond measure at the way she was receiving the open declaration of his love. She was painting through it all, not with the nervous, random stroke of one who sought to hide excitement and embarrassment in occupation. She was working earnestly, consciously, with precision, and, what was strangest of all, she seemed so intent upon his face that his words, which would have been such music to any woman that loved, were apparently unheard. He stopped, but the break in his passionate flow of language was unnoted.

“Christine, listen to me!” he cried, in an agony of fear and perplexity. The tone of his appeal might have stirred a marble bosom to pity, but she only raised her left hand deprecatingly as if warding off an interruption, while she worked with intense eagerness with her right.

“Christine!” a frown contracted her brow for a second, but she worked on.

He looked at her as if fearing she had lost her reason, but there was no madness in her swift, intelligent strokes. Then like a flash the thought came to him: “It is my face, not myself, that she wants! This, then, has been the secret of her new hope as an artist. She would not feel, as I told her she must, but she would call out and copy my emotion; and this scene, which means life or death to me, is to her but a lesson in art, and I am no more than the human subject under the surgeon’s knife. But surely no anatomist is so cruel as to put in his lancet before the man is dead.”

===Chinese===
她听着他的话，宛如置身梦境。她听懂了他的字字句句，事后也都记得清清楚楚，可此刻她全副心思都扑在自己心爱的画作上，竟完全无暇顾及他话里的深意。他的声音仿佛是从遥远的天边飘来的，而她身心所有的气力都凝聚在一点上——将他此刻的神情原原本本地移到眼前的画布上去。就连他这个已被情感蒙蔽双眼、正把压抑已久的满腔热忱一股脑倾泻进她充耳不闻的耳畔的人，也不由得暗自惊诧于她那奇异耀眼的容光与古怪反常的举止。

倾诉了片刻之后，蒙在他眼前的迷雾与脑海中的昏眩渐渐散去，他看到她回应自己这番坦诚告白的方式，不由得困惑到了极点。她自始至终都在画画，落笔却丝毫不是那种为了借忙碌来掩饰激动与羞窘的慌乱涂抹。她画得全神贯注、清醒沉着、精准无比；而最令他感到匪夷所思的是，她的注意力似乎完全锁死在他的面容上，以至于他那番换作任何动情女子听来都如天籁般的肺腑之言，在她这里竟仿佛置若罔闻。他停住了话头，可这股激情话语的骤然中断，她却连察觉都未曾察觉。

“克里斯蒂娜，听我说！”他怀着一阵惊恐与迷惘的剧痛喊道。他呼唤的语调本足以令大理石雕就的心肠也动容生怜，可她只是略带嗔怪地抬起左手，仿佛在挡开旁人的打扰，右手却依旧极其急切地挥笔不止。

“克里斯蒂娜！”她的双眉倏然蹙了一下，手底却仍未停歇。

他凝视着她，仿佛生怕她失了神智，可她那迅捷而灵巧的笔触间却丝毫没有疯狂的迹象。刹那间，一个念头如闪电般劈过他的心头：“她要的不是我这个人，而是我这张脸！原来这便是她身为画家重燃希望的秘密。她不愿像我嘱咐的那样去真切感受情感，却要生生逼出我的深情来照样临摹；这一幕对我而言攸关生死，在她眼中却不过是一堂绘画习作课，而我，也不过是外科大夫手术刀下的一具人体标本罢了。可世上再冷血的解剖师，总也不至于在人还未断气前就狠心下刀吧。”

===Original===
Every particle of color receded from his face, and he watched her manner for the confirmation of his thought.

Her face was indeed a study. A beautiful smile parted her lips, her eyes glowed with the exultation of assured and almost accomplished success, and she looked like an inspired priestess at a Greek oracle.

But a bitterness beyond words was filling his heart.

A few more skilful strokes, and she threw down her brush, crying in ecstatic tones, “Eureka! Eureka!” as she stood before the painting in rapt admiration. In an instant he stood by her side. With all the pride of triumph she pointed to the picture, and said: “Criticise that, if you can! Deny that there is soul, life, feeling there, if you dare! Is that painting but a ‘beautiful corpse’?”

Dennis saw a figure and features suggesting his own, pleading with all the eloquence of true love before the averted face of the maiden in the picture. It was indeed a triumph, having all the power of the reality.

He passed his hand quickly across his forehead, as if to repel some terrible delusion, while yet he whispered its reality to himself, in silent, despairing confession: “Ah, my God! How cold she must be when she can see anyone look like that, and yet copy the expression as from a painted face upon the wall!”

===Chinese===
他脸上的最后一丝血色也褪尽了，死死盯着她的一举一动，只待印证自己方才的猜测。

她的神态当真耐人寻味。一抹绝美的笑意令她双唇微启，明眸中闪耀着胜券在握、大功即将告成的狂喜光芒，整个人宛若古希腊神谕所里灵思迸发的女祭司。

然而，一股难以言喻的酸楚与苦涩，却正渐渐涨满他的胸膛。

又添了几下精妙的笔触，她猛地掷下画笔，用狂喜的声调高呼：“尤里卡（Eureka）！尤里卡！”随即站在画前沉醉地端详起来。眨眼工夫，丹尼斯已站到她身侧。她满怀胜利的骄傲指着画作说道：“你若能挑出毛病，尽管品评好了！你若敢否认里面有灵魂、有生命、有情感，尽管开口便是！这幅画难道也不过是一具‘美丽躯壳’吗？”

丹尼斯定睛望去，画中那个身形面貌酷似自己的男子，正满怀真爱的深沉感染力，在画里那位微偏着脸的少女面前苦苦恳求。这确是一场了不起的胜利，画中竟蕴含着宛如真人现世般的全部震撼力。

他飞快地抬手拂过额头，仿佛想挥去一场可怕的幻觉，嘴里却仍在一声绝望的默叹中向自己低语着这冰冷的现实：“天啊！眼见一个人露出那般神情，她竟能像临摹墙上一张彩绘面孔似的将它画下来，她的心肠究竟得有多冷硬啊！”

===Original===
Then, his own pride and indignation rising, he determined at once to know the truth; whether he held any place in her heart, or whether the picture was all, and he nothing.

Drawing a step nearer, as if to examine more closely, he seized a brush of paint and drew it over the face that had cost both him and Christine so much, and then turned and looked at her.

For a moment she stood paralyzed, so great seemed the disaster. Then she turned on him in fury. “How dare you!” she exclaimed.

Only equal anger, and the consciousness of right, could have sustained any man under the lightning of her eyes.

“Rather, let me ask, how dare you?” he replied, in the deep, concentrated voice of passion; and lover and lady stood before the ruined picture with blazing eyes. In the same low, stern voice he continued, “I see the secret of your artistic hope now, Miss Ludolph, but permit me to say that you have made your first and last success, and there in that black stain, most appropriately black, is the result.”

She looked as if she could have torn him to atoms.

===Chinese===
紧接着，他心头的自尊与愤慨一齐涌了上来，他决意立刻探明真相——自己在她心里究竟还占不占一丝一毫的分量，还是说那幅画便是一切，而他自己什么也不是。

他朝前走近一步，佯装要凑近细看，猛地抓起一支蘸满颜料的画笔，顺着那张耗尽了他与克里斯蒂娜无数心血的画中面庞狠狠一抹，随后转过身来，直直盯住她。

有那么一瞬，她像被雷击中般僵立在原地，这突如其来的灾难实在太过骇人。随即她暴怒地转向他，厉声喝道：“你竟敢！”

面对她双眼中迸射出的电闪雷鸣般的怒火，世上唯有同等炽烈的义愤与理直气壮的底气，才能撑得住任何一个男子不致退缩。

“我倒想反问一句，您竟敢如此？”他用低沉而凝聚着激情的嗓音回敬道；求爱者与千金小姐站在那幅被毁的画前，彼此双目喷火。他用同样冷峻低沉的语调接着说道：“卢多尔夫小姐，如今我算看透了您艺术希望背后的秘密，但请恕我直言，这既是您的头一次成功，也是您最后一次成功；而那一抹漆黑的污渍——再相称不过的漆黑——便是它的下场。”

看她那副神情，简直恨不能将他生生撕成碎片。

===Original===
“You have been false,” he continued. “You have acted a lie before me for weeks. You have deceived in that which is most sacred, and with sacrilegious hands have trifled with that which every true man regards as holy.”

She trembled beneath his stern, accusing words. Conscience echoed them, anger and courage were fast deserting her in the presence of the aroused and more powerful spirit of her wronged lover. But she said, petulantly, “Nonsense! You know well that half the ladies of the city would have flirted with you from mere vanity and love of power; my motive was infinitely beyond this.”

Until now this had almost seemed sufficient reason to excuse her action, but she distrusted it even to loathing as she saw the look of scorn come out on his noble face.

“And is that your best plea for falsehood? A moment since I loved you with a devotion that you will never receive again. But now I despise you.”

“Sir!” she cried, her face scarlet with shame and anger, “leave this room!”

===Chinese===
“您一直虚情假意，”他继续痛斥道，“您一连几个星期都在我面前演戏作假。您在人间最神圣的情感上行欺骗之事，用渎神的双手玩弄了每一个正直男子视为神圣无上的东西。”

在他严厉的指控声中，她浑身瑟瑟发抖。良心在心底与他的话语字字呼应；面对这位被激怒的、精神力量远胜于她的受害情人，她的怒气与勇气正迅速瓦解。可她还是恼羞成怒地顶撞了一句：“一派胡言！你自己心里清楚，全城至少有一半的淑女都会只凭一己虚荣和卖弄风情的欲望去挑逗你；我的动机可比那高尚不知多少倍！”

直至方才，这套说辞在她自己看来几乎还足以替她的所作所为开脱；然而此刻，眼见他那高贵的面庞上浮现出一抹鄙夷之色，她自己也开始怀疑这套借口，甚至生出几分厌恶来。

“这就是您为自己的欺骗所作的最好辩解吗？就在片刻之前，我还怀着一份您此生再也不会遇上的赤诚深情爱着您。但现在，我鄙视您。”

“先生！”她羞愤交加，整张脸涨得通红，尖声喊道，“请您立刻离开这间屋子！”

===Original===
“Yes, in a moment, and never again to enter it while Christine Ludolph is as false in character as she is beautiful in person. But before I go, you, in your pride and luxury, shall hear the truth for once. Not only have you been false, but you have been what no true woman ever can be—cruel as death. Your pencil has been a stiletto with which you have slowly felt for my heart. You have dipped your brush in human suffering as if it were common paint. Giotto stabbed a man and mercifully took him off by a few quick pangs, that he might paint his dying look. You, more cruel, accomplish your purpose by slow, remorseless torture. Merciful Heaven only knows what I have suffered since you smiled and frowned on me by turns, but I felt that if I could only win your love I would gladly endure all. You falsely made me believe that I had won it, and yet all the while you were dissecting my heart, as a surgeon might a living subject. And now what have you to offer to solace the bitterness of coming years? Do you not know that such deeds make men bad, faithless, devilish? Never dream of success till you are changed utterly. Only the noble in deed and in truth can reach high and noble art.”

She sat before the disfigured picture with her face bowed in her hands.

She thought he was gone, but still remained motionless like one doomed. A few moments passed and she was startled by hearing his voice again. It was no longer harsh and stern, but sad, grave, and pitiful. “Miss Ludolph, may God forgive you.”

She trembled. Pride and better feeling were contending for the mastery. After a few moments she sprang up and reached out her hands; but he was gone now in very truth.

===Chinese===
“是的，我这就走；只要克里斯蒂娜·卢多尔夫一日依然像她容貌这般美艳却又性情这般虚伪，我便一日不再踏入此室半步。不过在临走之前，养尊处优、傲慢无礼的您，总算也该听一回真话了。您不仅虚伪，而且做出了任何真正女性绝不会做出的行径——冷酷得宛如死神。您的笔锋宛如一柄细刃短剑，一寸寸探刺着我的心脏。您将画笔蘸入人间的苦痛，视同寻常颜料。当年乔托（Giotto）为了描摹人临终时的神情，挥刀刺死一名男子，好歹还怜悯地让他只受几下短促的剧痛便了结了性命。而您却更为狠毒，靠着缓慢而铁石心肠的凌迟来达成目的。打从您对我时而笑脸相迎、时而冷面相对起，唯有仁慈的上天知道我经受了怎样的煎熬，可我当时总想着，只要能赢得您的芳心，吃尽万般苦楚我也甘之如饴。您虚情假意地哄得我信以为真，仿佛我已赢得了您的爱，暗地里却一直像外科大夫活体解剖般剖开我的心扉。如今，面对往后漫长岁月的凄苦，您又能拿出什么来抚慰呢？您难道不知道，这等行径会教人堕落、猜忌、心性如魔鬼般扭曲吗？在您彻头彻尾改过自新之前，休想奢望什么成功。唯有品行与内心皆高尚纯真之人，方能攀登崇高而伟大的艺术殿堂。”

她坐在那幅面目全非的画作前，双手掩面，颓然垂首。

她以为他已经走了，却依旧像个被判了死刑的人一样僵坐不动。过了片刻，他的声音竟再次响起，把她吓了一跳。那声音不再严厉冷峻，而是充满了悲怆、沉重与怜悯：“卢多尔夫小姐，愿上帝宽恕您。”

她浑身颤抖了一下。骄傲与良善的天性正在她胸中激烈交锋、争夺上风。过了片刻，她猛地站起身来，朝前伸出双手——然而这一次，他是真真切切地走了。

## XII Blue Blood / 第十二章 蓝血贵族

===Original===
Dennis’s mind was a chaos of conflicting feelings. The picture had deeply interested him, and so did the beautiful girl that it by strange coincidence so strongly resembled. It could not be otherwise with one of his beauty-loving nature. And yet the impression made by the face in the painting﻿—of something wrong, discordant﻿—was felt more decidedly in respect to the living face.

But before he had time to realize what had just passed the lady and her father appeared at the door of the office, and he heard the latter say: “I know you are right, my dear. It’s all wrong. The arrangement of the store is as stiff and methodical as if we were engaged in selling mathematical instruments. But I have not time to attend to the matter, and there is not one in the store that has the least idea of artistic combination, unless it is Fleet. I have noticed some encouraging symptoms in him.”

“What! he of the duster and mop? I fear our case is desperate, then, if he is our best hope.”

Dennis’s cheeks were burning again; but, turning his back, he rubbed away harder than ever at a Greek god that he was polishing. But they gave him no thought. Speaking with a sudden animation the young lady said, “Father, I have a great mind to try it myself﻿—that is, if you are willing.”

===Chinese===
丹尼斯的心里乱成一团，各种相互冲突的思绪交织翻涌。那幅画深深吸引了他，而因着某种奇异的巧合与画中人酷似的那位美丽少女，同样令他心生兴味。以他这般热爱美貌的天性，原也是情理之中的事。然而，画中那张面孔带给他的印象——某种隐约的不对劲与不和谐——在面对这张活生生的脸庞时，却显得愈发分明。

可还没等他回过神来琢磨方才那一幕，那位小姐和她的父亲便已出现在办公室门口，他听见后者说道：“我知道你说得对，亲爱的。确实全都不妥。店里的陈设死板又机械，简直像咱们是在卖数学仪器似的。可我实在抽不出工夫去照管这事，店里又没有半个人懂得哪怕一点点艺术搭配的门道，除非是弗利特。我倒在他身上瞧出过几分颇有起色的苗头。”

“什么！就是那个整天拿鸡毛掸子和拖把的家伙？倘若连他都算咱们最大的指望，那我看这事儿怕是没救了。”

丹尼斯的双颊又一次火辣辣地烧了起来；但他转过背去，比先前更卖力地擦拭起手里正打磨着的一尊希腊神像。不过父女俩压根儿没把他放在心上。只听那位年轻小姐忽然兴致勃勃地说道：“父亲，我倒很有兴致亲自试一试——当然，得您首肯才行。”

===Original===
“But, my daughter, I could not permit you to be engaged in any such employment before our customers.”

“Certainly not! I would come early in the morning, before art-customers are stirring. I really should enjoy the task greatly, if I had anyone to help me who could in some faint degree comprehend the effects I wished to produce. The long spring mornings soon to come would be just the time for it. To what better use could I put my taste and knowledge of art than in helping you and furthering our plan for life?”

Mr. Ludolph hesitated between his pride and his strong desire to gain the advantages which the acceptance of this offer would secure. Finally he said: “We will think about it. I am expecting a great many new and beautiful things early in the spring, and no doubt it would be well then to rearrange the store completely, and break up the rigid system into which we have fallen. In the meantime I appreciate your offer, and thank you warmly.”

Dennis’s heart leaped within him at the thought of instruction from such a teacher, and he longed to offer his services. But he rightly judged that the proposal would be regarded as an impertinence at that time. The successor of Pat Murphy was not expected to know anything of art, or have any appreciation of it. So he bent his head lower, but gave Jupiter Olympus such a rubbing down as the god had deserved long ago. In a moment more Miss Ludolph passed him on her way out of the store, noticing him no more than she did his dust-brush.

---

===Chinese===
“可是，我的女儿，我怎么能容许你在顾客面前干这种差事呢。”

“那自然不会！我可以一清早过来，赶在那些艺术品主顾还没起身之前动手。只要能有个多少领会一点我想要营造的效果的人在一旁搭把手，我准会十分乐在其中的。眼看春日渐长，清晨时光正合做这事。我这点艺术眼光和学识，又能派上什么比帮您一把、推进咱们人生大计更有意义的用场呢？”

卢多尔夫先生在自己的体面矜持与强烈的功利心之间权衡踌躇——毕竟答应这个提议所能带来的好处实在诱人。末了，他说道：“这事咱们再斟酌斟酌。开春伊始我正等着一大批精美的新货到店，届时把店面彻底重新布置一番，打破咱们如今陷进去的这套僵化格局，想来确是大有裨益的。眼下我很领你的这份心意，由衷地谢谢你。”

一想到能得这样一位高人指点，丹尼斯的心在胸腔里雀跃起来，恨不得立刻毛遂自荐。但他转念一想，便清醒地断定，眼下提出这番请求只会被视作不知天高地厚的冒犯。接替帕特·墨菲差事的人，在旁人眼里原是不配懂得什么艺术，更谈不上有什么鉴赏力的。于是他把头埋得更低，却把那尊奥林匹斯主神朱庇特（Jupiter Olympus）从头到脚狠狠擦了个通透——那神像早该受这一顿好擦了。片刻之后，卢多尔夫小姐从他身旁走过，径直出了店门，连眼角都没扫他一下，仿佛他与他手里的掸子并无二致。

---

===Original===
Mr. Ludolph was the younger son of a noble but impoverished German family, and was intensely proud of his patrician blood. His parents, knowing that he would have to make his own way in the world, had sent him, while a mere boy, to this country, and placed him in charge of a distant relative, who was engaged in the picture-trade in New York. He had here learned to speak English in his youth with the fluency and accuracy of a native, but had never become Americanized, so much family pride had he inherited, and so strongly did he cling to the traditions of his own land.

He showed great business ability in his chosen calling, especially displaying remarkable judgment in the selection of works of art. So unusual was his skill in this direction, that when twenty-one years old he was sent abroad to purchase pictures. For several years he travelled through Europe. He became quite cosmopolitan in character, and for a time enjoyed life abundantly. His very business brought him in contact with artists and men of culture, while his taste and love of beauty were daily gratified. He had abundant means, and money could open many doors of pleasure to one who, like him, was in vigorous health and untroubled by a conscience. Moreover, he was able to spend much time in his beloved Germany, and while there the great ambition of his life entered his heart. His elder brother, who was living inexclusive pride and narrow economy on the ancient but diminished ancestral estate, ever received him graciously. This brother had married, but had not been blessed or cursed with children, for the German baron, with his limited finances, could never decide in what light to regard them. Too poor to mingle with his equals, too proud to stoop to those whom he regarded as inferiors, he had lived much alone, and grown narrower and more bigoted in his family pride day by day. Indeed, that he was Baron Ludolph, was the one great fact of his life. He spent hours in conning over yellow, musty records of the ancient grandeur of his house, and would gloat over heroic deeds of ancestors he never thought of imitating. In brief, he was like a small barnacle on an old and waterlogged ship, that once had made many a gallant and prosperous voyage richly freighted, but now had drifted into shallow water and was falling to decay. He made a suggestion, however, to his younger brother, that wakened the ambition of the latter’s stronger nature, and set him about what became his controlling purpose, his lifework.

“Make a fortune in America,” said his brother, “and come back and restore the ancient wealth and glory of your family.”

The seed fell into receptive soil, and from that day the art and pleasure loving citizen of the world became an earnest man with a purpose. But as he chose his purpose mainly from selfish motives it did not become an ennobling one. He now gave double attention to business and practical economy. He at once formed the project of starting in business for himself, and of putting the large profits resulting from his judicious selection of pictures into his own pocket. He made the most careful arrangements, and secured agencies that he could trust in the purchase of pictures after he should return to the United States.

===Chinese===
卢多尔夫先生出身于一个门第显赫却已家道中落的德国贵族之家，在家中排行幼子，对自己的名门血统引以为豪到了极点。他的父母深知这个小儿子日后须得独自在世上闯出一条生路，便在他尚且年少时将他送到了美国，托付给一位在纽约（New York）经营画作生意的远房亲戚照管。他自幼便在这里学会了一口如土生土长的本地人般流利精准的英语，却从未真正美国化——他骨子里承袭了太浓重的家族傲气，对故土的传统也抱守得太过顽固。

他在自己投身的这一行里展现出过人的商业才干，尤以甄选艺术品的眼光独到著称。他在这方面的本领着实出众，年方二十一岁便被派往海外采买画作。此后数年间，他游历了欧洲各地，性情也随之变得颇具世界派头，着实过了好一阵纵情享乐的日子。单是这门营生本身便让他得以频频结交艺术家与名流雅士，而他那挑剔的品味与爱美之心亦日日得偿所愿。他手头阔绰，而对于他这样一个体魄强健又全无良心羁绊的人来说，金钱自能敲开无数寻欢作乐之门。更何况，他还能在自己心爱的德国盘桓良久，正是在逗留故国期间，他平生最大的野心悄然萌生。他的兄长孤傲而拮据地守着古老却已日渐凋零的祖产庄园过活，每次见他归来，总是礼数周全、殷勤款待。这位兄长虽已成婚，膝下却无儿无女——至于这究竟算福气还是灾祸，手头捉襟见肘的德国男爵自己也一直拿捏不准。他穷得无力同身份相当的贵族往来，又骄傲得不屑屈尊结交自己眼中的下等人，长年深居简出，家族门第的傲慢偏见便日复一日地愈发狭隘顽固。事实上，他身为卢多尔夫男爵这一点，便是他整个人生中唯一了不得的大事。他常常一连数小时埋首研读那些泛黄发霉的家族旧档，追怀往昔荣光，对先祖们的丰功伟绩津津乐道，却从未想过自己也要去效法一二。简言之，他就像附着在一艘浸满积水的老朽巨轮上的小小藤壶——这艘船从前也曾满载珍宝、意气风发地远航万里，如今却搁浅在浅滩上日渐朽坏。然而，正是这位兄长向弟弟提出的一个建言，唤醒了弟弟那更为刚强性情中的雄心壮志，促使他从此确立了支配自己一生的宏愿与毕生大业。

“去美国发一笔大财，”他兄长说道，“然后再回来，重振咱们家族昔日的财富与荣耀。”

这颗种子落进了沃土之中，打那天起，这位原本只知鉴赏艺术、及时行乐的世界浪子，摇身一变成了一个笃志实干、目标明确的人。然而，既然他立此志向的初衷大半出于自私的念头，这番抱负也就谈不上高尚。他开始加倍留心商务与精打细算，当即便谋划着自立门户，好把自己凭借独到眼光挑画所挣来的丰厚利润悉数揣进自己腰包。他做了极为周密的筹划，并在当地物色妥当了几家信得过的代理商号，以便日后返回美国后继续代为采办画作。

===Original===
During his stay in Paris, on his way back, an event occurred that had a most untoward influence on his plans and hopes. He fell desperately in love with a beautiful French woman. Like himself, she was poor, but of patrician blood, and was very fascinating. She attracted him by her extreme beauty and brilliancy. She was very shrewd, and could seem anything she chose, being a perfect actress in the false, hollow life of the world. In accordance with Parisian ideas, she wanted a husband to pay her bills, to be a sort of protector and base of general operations. Here was a man who promised well, fine-looking, and, if not rich, capable of making large sums of money.

She insinuated herself into his confidence, and appeared to share his enthusiasm for the darling project of his life. He felt that, with such a beautiful and sympathetic woman to spur him on and share his success, earth would be a Paradise indeed; and she assured him, in many delicate and bewitching ways, that it would. In brief, he married her; and then learned, in bitterness, anger, and disgust, that she had totally deceived him. To his passionate love she returned indifference; to his desire for economy, unbounded extravagance, contracting debts which he must pay to avoid disgrace. She showed an utter unwillingness to leave the gayety of Paris, laughing in his face at his plan of life, and assuring him that she would never live in so stupid a place as Germany. His love died hard. He made every appeal to her that affection prompted. He tried entreaty, tenderness, coldness, anger, but all in vain. Selfish to the core, loving him not, utterly unscrupulous, she trod upon his quivering heart as recklessly as upon the stones of the street. Soon he saw that, in spite of his vigilance, he was in danger of being betrayed in all respects. Then he grew hard and fierce. The whole of his strong German nature was aroused. In a tone and manner that startled and frightened her, he said: “*We* sail for New York in three days. Be ready. If you prove unfaithful to me﻿—if you seek to desert me, I will *kill* you. I swear it﻿—not by God, for I don’t believe in Him. If He existed, such creatures as you would not. But I swear it by my family pride and name, which are dearer to me than life, if you leave a stain upon them you shall *die*. You need not seek to escape me. I would follow you through the world. I would kill you on the crowded street﻿—anywhere, even though I died myself the next moment. And now look well to your steps.”

The glitter of his eye was as cold and remorseless as the sheen of steel. She saw that he meant and would do just what he said.

The woman had one good point﻿—at least, it turned out to be such in this case. She was a coward naturally, and her bad life made her dread nothing so much as death. Her former flippant indifference to his remonstrances now changed into abject fear. He saw her weak side, learned his power, and from that time forward kept her within bounds by a judicious system of terrorism.

===Chinese===
归途之中，他在巴黎（Paris）暂留期间，发生了一桩对他的计划与期许产生了极其不利影响的变故。他无可救药地爱上了一位美丽的法国女子。她与他一样家境清贫，却同样流着贵族的血统，魅力十足。她那倾城的美貌与耀眼的才情深深迷住了他。此人极有心计，想装成什么模样就能演得惟妙惟肖，堪称这虚伪空洞的尘世舞台上一名炉火纯青的演员。按照巴黎人的盘算，她需要找个丈夫来替她付账单，充当她的某种庇护伞和行事大后方。眼前这个男人前程似锦，相貌堂堂，眼下虽不算大富大贵，却极具生财之道。

她巧言令色地博得了他的信任，表面上装出对他平生最珍视的大业同样满腔热忱的模样。他原以为，有这样一位美貌而又体己的女子激励他前行、与他共享成功，尘世必将成为真正的天堂；而她也用种种细腻迷人的手段向他保证，事实必将如此。长话短说，他娶了她；随后便在痛苦、盛怒与嫌恶中发觉，自己彻头彻尾被她骗了。面对他炽热的爱意，她报以冷漠；面对他节俭持家的意愿，她偏要毫无节制地挥霍，欠下大笔债款，逼得他为免丢脸只得替她偿清。她丝毫不愿离开巴黎的繁华欢场，当面嘲笑他的人生大计，还斩钉截铁地说自己绝不会去德国那种沉闷无聊的地方过日子。他的爱意虽死得艰难，却也渐渐消磨殆尽。出于情意，他曾千方百计地试图感化她——哀求、温存、冷淡、发怒，样样试遍，却全无用处。她自私透顶，根本不爱他，且毫无底线，将他那颗颤抖的心踩在脚下，肆意践踏得如同街头石板一般。没过多久，他便看出，尽管自己严加防备，仍随时可能在方方面面遭到她的背叛。于是他变得冷酷而暴烈。他骨子里那股强悍的德意志血性被彻底激起。他用一种令她毛骨悚然的口吻和神态说道：“*我们*三天后启程乘船去纽约。准备好了。你若敢对我不忠——你若胆敢抛下我逃跑，我就*杀了*你。我在此发誓——不是指着上帝发誓，因为我不信他。这世上真若有上帝，绝不会容你这种东西存在。但我以我那比性命还贵重的家族荣耀与姓氏起誓，你若敢往上面抹半点污点，你就必*死*无疑。你别指望逃出我的手心。哪怕追遍天涯海角，我也不会放过你。就算在人潮拥挤的大街上——无论在什么地方，哪怕我下一刻就陪你一起死，我也要结果了你。从今往后，给我走好你的每一步。”

他眼中闪烁的寒光犹如利刃出鞘，冰冷而毫不留情。她看得出他是认真的，而且说到做到。

这女人倒也有一桩长处——至少在这件事上显得如此。她生性怯懦，再加上一贯荒唐度日，平生最怕的莫过于死。先前面对他的规劝时那副轻佻冷漠的派头，如今一变而为卑怯的恐惧。他看穿了她的软肋，摸清了自己的威慑力，打那以后便靠着一套拿捏得当的铁腕高压手段，牢牢把她管束在规矩之内。

===Original===
He took her to New York and commanded her to appear the charming woman she could if she chose. She obeyed, and rather enjoyed the excitement and deceit. His friends were delighted with her, but he received their congratulations with a grim, quiet smile. At times, though, when she was entertaining them with all grace, beauty, and sweetness, the thought of what she was seemed only a horrid dream. But he had merely to catch her eye, with its gleam of fear and hate, to know the truth.

He felt that he could not trust to the continuance of her good behavior, and was anxious to get away among strangers as soon as possible. He therefore closed his business relations in New York. Though she had crippled him greatly by her extravagance, he had been able to bring out a fair stock of good pictures, and a large number of articles of virtue, selected with his usual taste. The old firm, finding that they could not keep him, offered all the goods he wanted on commission. So in a few weeks he started for Chicago, the most promising city of the West, as he believed, and established himself there in a modest way. Still the chances were even against him, for he had involved himself heavily, and drawn to the utmost on his credit in starting. If he could not sell largely the first year, he was a broken man. For months the balance wavered, and he lived with financial ruin on one side, and domestic ruin on the other. But, with a heart of ice and nerves of steel, he kept his hand on the helm.

His beautiful collection, though in an unpretentious store, at last attracted attention, and after some little time it became *the* thing in the fashionable world to go there, and from that time forward his fortune was made.

When his wife became a mother, there was a faint hope in Mr. Ludolph’s heart that this event might awaken the woman within her, if aught of the true woman existed. He tried to treat her with more kindness, but found it would not answer. She mistook it for weakness on his part. From first to last she acted in the most heartless manner, and treated the child with shameless neglect. This banished from her husband even the shadow of regard, and he cursed her to her face. Thenceforth will and ambition controlled his life and hers, and with an iron hand he held her in check. She saw that she was in the power of a desperate man, who would sacrifice her in a moment if she thwarted him. Through cowardly fear she remained his reluctant but abject slave, pricking him with the pins and needles of petty annoyances, when she would have pierced him to the heart had she dared. This monstrous state of affairs could not last forever, and, had not death terminated the unnatural relation, some terrible catastrophe would no doubt have occurred. Having contracted a western fever, she soon became delirious, and passed away in this unconscious state, to the intense joy and relief of her husband.

===Chinese===
他将她带回纽约，命她只要在人前就须得摆出她拿手的迷人姿态。她乖乖照办了，反倒颇为享受这种刺激与做戏的把戏。他的朋友们对她赞不绝口，而面对众人的道贺，他只是报以一抹阴冷沉静的微笑。不过有时，见她举止优雅、容光焕发、温柔可人地款待宾客，他几乎以为她真正的为人不过是一场噩梦罢了。然而，他只要捕捉到她眼底那一闪而过的恐惧与怨毒，便立刻清醒了。

他觉得这女人的一时收敛终究靠不住，迫不及待想尽快带着她远走他乡，置身于陌生人之中。于是他结束了在纽约的商务往来。尽管她的挥霍无度着实令他元气大伤，他还是设法凑齐了一批数量可观的上乘画作，以及大批他凭着一贯的好眼光挑出来的艺术珍玩。老东家见挽留不住他，便提出凡是他所需的货物，尽可按代销方式提供给他。于是几周之后，他便动身前往芝加哥——在他看来，那是美国西部最具前途的城市——在那里起初只是小本经营、立足安身。即便如此，胜算也未必在他这一边，因为他创业伊始便已背负重债，把自己的信用额度透支到了极限。倘若头一年不能大宗出货，他就彻底完蛋了。一连数月，局势始终摇摆不定，他一侧悬着破产倾覆的深渊，另一侧则是家宅不宁的祸端。然而，凭着一副冷如坚冰的心肠与钢铁般的神经，他死死把住了舵盘。

他店面虽不起眼，那批精美的藏品却终于引起了人们的注意；没过多久，上他店里逛逛竟成了时髦圈子里*最*时兴的事儿，从此他便时来运转、财源滚滚了。

妻子初为人母时，卢多尔夫先生心头也曾闪过一丝微弱的希望，盼着这件事能唤醒她体内那份女人的天性——倘若她身上真还有半分女人味的话。他试着对她和善些，却发现根本行不通。她反倒误以为这是他软弱可欺。自始至终，她都表现得铁石心肠，对亲生骨肉更是恬不知耻地冷落疏忽。这终于磨灭了丈夫心中对她最后一丝情分，他当面咒骂了她一顿。打那以后，钢铁般的意志与野心主宰了他和她的生活，他用铁腕死死压制着她。她明白自己落在一个亡命之徒手里，只要敢违逆他半步，他眨眼间就会把她牺牲掉。出于卑怯的畏惧，她只得甘心做他满怀怨怼却俯首帖耳的奴隶——倘若胆子够大，她恨不得一刀刺穿他的心脏，如今不敢，便只能用鸡毛蒜皮的琐事如针尖般时不时刺他几下。这种畸形荒唐的日子终究不能长久，倘若不是死神替这段反常的关系画上了句号，迟早无疑会酿成一场惨剧。后来她染上了西部热病，很快便神志昏迷，就在这浑浑噩噩的状态下撒手人寰，这着实令她的丈夫大喜过望、如释重负。

===Original===
But the child lived, thrived, and developed into the graceful girl whose beauty surpassed, as we have seen, even the painter’s ideal. Her father at first cared little for the infant, but secured it every attention. As it developed into a pretty girl, however, with winning ways, and rich promise, he gradually associated her with his hopes and plans, till at last she became an essential part of his ambition.

His plan now was briefly this: He would entangle himself with no alliances or intimate associations in America, nor would he permit his daughter to do so. His only object in staying here was the accumulation of a large fortune, and to this for a few years he would bend every energy of mind and body. As soon as he felt that he had sufficient means to live in such style as befitted the ancient and honorable name of his family, he would return to Germany, buy all he could of the ancestral estate that from time to time had been parted with, and restore his house to its former grandeur. He himself would then seek a marriage connection that would strengthen his social position, while his daughter also should make a brilliant alliance with some member of the nobility. Mr. Ludolph was a handsome, well-preserved man; he had been most successful in business, and was now more rapidly than ever accumulating that which is truly a power with Europeans of blue blood, as with democratic Americans. Moreover, his daughter’s beauty promised to be such that, when enhanced by every worldly advantage, it might well command attention in the highest circles. He sought with scrupulous care to give her just the education that would enable her to shine as a star among the highborn. Art, music, and knowledge of literature, especially the German, were the main things to which her attention was directed, and in her father, with his richly stored mind, faultless taste, and cultured voice, she had an instructor such as rarely falls to the lot of the most favored.

When Christine Ludolph was about sixteen years of age, events occurred which might have greatly marred her father’s plans. She secretly formed a most unfortunate attachment, which came near resulting in a clandestine marriage. Although the world would have judged her harshly, and the marriage could only have been exceedingly disastrous to her future life, the motherless girl was not very much to blame. Even among the mature there is a proverbial blindness in these matters. She was immature, misled by her imagination, and the victim of uncurbed romantic fancies. But, after all, the chief incentive to her folly was a natural craving for the love and sympathy which she had never found in her own home. To her chilled young heart these gifts were so sweet and satisfying that she was in no mood to criticise the donor, even had her knowledge of the world enabled her to do so. Thus far, in his care of Christine, Mr. Ludolph had conformed to the foreign ideas of seclusion and repression, and the poor girl, unguided, unguarded by kind womanly counsel, was utterly unsophisticated, and she might have easily become the prey of the unscrupulous man whose chief incentive had been her father’s wealth. Mr. Ludolph fortunately discovered the state of affairs in time to prevent gossip. Under his remorseless logic, bitter satire, and ridicule her young dream was torn to shreds. The man whom she had surrounded with a halo of romance was shown to be worthless and commonplace. Her idol had chiefly been a creature of the imagination, and when the bald, repulsive truth concerning him had been proved to her in such a way that she could not escape conviction, she was equally disgusted with him and herself.

For some weeks Mr. Ludolph treated his daughter with cold distrust. “She will be like her mother, I suppose,” he thought. “Already she has begun to deceive me and to imperil everything by her folly;” and his heart was full of bitterness toward his child. Thus the poor girl dwelt in a chilled and blighting atmosphere at a time when she most sorely needed kindness and wise guidance.

===Chinese===
然而那孩子却活了下来，茁壮成长，出落成了一位仪态万方的少女——正如我们所见，她的美貌甚至胜过了画家笔下的理想佳人。起初，父亲对这襁褓中的婴儿并不怎么上心，但也请人妥帖照料，一应俱全。可随着她渐渐长成一个娇俏可爱、举止动人、大有可造之才的小姑娘，他便慢慢把她纳入了自己的期许与谋划之中，直到最后，她竟成了他毕生抱负里不可或缺的一部分。

简而言之，他如今的盘算是这样的：自己绝不在美国缔结任何姻亲或深交，也绝不准许女儿这样做。他留在这里的唯一目的就是聚敛巨额财富，为此他愿在几年之内倾注全部身心精力。一旦自认积攒了足够的资财，足以过上配得上家族古老尊荣的体面生活，他便立刻动身回德国，尽其所能买回历年来陆续典卖出去的祖传田产，重振门楣往日的辉煌。届时他自己再寻一门能巩固社会地位的亲事，女儿也自当风光嫁入某个贵族豪门。卢多尔夫先生生得相貌英俊、保养得宜，生意上又大获成功，眼下正以前所未有的速度聚敛着财富——要知道，金钱无论在标榜民主的美国人眼中，还是在流着蓝血的欧洲贵族眼里，都同样是实打实的权势。更何况，女儿容貌出众、前程不可限量，倘若再添上世间一切优越条件的衬托，势必能在最高雅的社交圈里惹人瞩目。他煞费苦心地按着能令她在名门望族之中宛如明星般熠熠生辉的标准来栽培她。美术、音乐、文学修养——尤其是德意志文学——成了她着力研习的主课；而她父亲本人学识渊博、品味无可挑剔、嗓音儒雅动听，由他亲自充当良师，即便是天之骄女也难得有此造化。

克里斯蒂娜·卢多尔夫大约十六岁那年，出了一桩险些大大坏了她父亲全盘大计的变故。她暗地里陷入了一段极不相宜的恋情，险些酿成私奔秘婚。虽说世人对此免不了会苛责于她，而那桩婚事于她的后半生也只会是一场彻头彻尾的灾难，但这个自幼失恃的少女其实并没有多少过错。在这类事情上，即便是历练老成的成年人也往往盲目得人尽皆知。她当时心智未熟，受了幻想的蒙蔽，成了毫无节制的浪漫遐思的牺牲品。然而归根结底，驱使她做出这番糊涂事的最大动因，乃是一种发自天性的渴望——她渴望得到在自己家中从未尝过的关爱与温情。对于她那颗冰冷寂寞的少女之心而言，这份馈赠是那样甘美而令人心满意足，即便她当时的阅历足以看清对方，也绝无心思去挑剔那施与情意之人。迄今为止，卢多尔夫先生管教克里斯蒂娜一直沿袭着欧洲旧俗，一味将她深闺幽闭、严加束缚；这可怜的姑娘既无仁厚女性长辈的温和指点与护佑，又涉世未深、天真烂漫，极易沦为那个无良之徒的猎物——那人看中的，无非是她父亲的万贯家财罢了。所幸卢多尔夫先生及时察觉了实情，才没闹出满城风雨。在他冷酷无情的逻辑剖析、辛辣讽刺与百般嘲弄之下，她那场少女美梦被撕得粉碎。那个曾被她镀上一层浪漫光环的男子，原形毕露，不过是个一文不值的平庸之辈。她的偶像本大半出自她自己的臆想，如今关于那人的赤裸而又令人作呕的真相如此确凿地摆在眼前，容不得她有半点抵赖，她顿觉既厌恶那人，也同样厌恶自己。

接连好几个星期，卢多尔夫先生待女儿始终冷若冰霜、满腹猜疑。“我料她早晚会像她母亲一个德行，”他暗想，“年纪轻轻便已学会欺瞒于我，差点因她的愚蠢断送了一切。”他心里对亲生骨肉充满了怨怼。于是，在这位可怜的姑娘最迫切需要慈爱与明智引导的年岁里，她反倒活在一片令人心寒摧折的森冷气氛之中。

===Original===
She was very unhappy, for she saw that her father had lost all confidence in her. She fairly turned sick when she thought of the past. She had lived in the world of romance and mystery; she had loved with all her girlish power; and, however wrongly and unjustly, by the inevitable laws of association she connected the words “love” and “romance” with one whom she now detested and loathed. Within a week after her miserable experience she became as utter a sceptic in regard to human love, and happiness flowing from it, as her father had taught her to be respecting God and the joy of believing. Though seemingly a fair young girl, her father had made her worse than a pagan. She believed in nothing save art and her father’s wisdom. He seemed to embody the culture and worldly philosophy that now became, in her judgment, the only things worth living for. To gain his confidence became her great desire. But this had received a severe shock. Mr. Ludolph had lost all faith in everything save money and his own will. Religion was to him a gross superstition, and woman’s virtue and truth, poetic fictions.

He watched Christine narrowly, and said just enough to draw out the workings of her mind. He then decided to tell his plan for life, and give her strong additional motives for doing his will. The picture he portrayed of the future dazzled her proud, ambitious spirit, and opened to her fancy what then seemed the only path to happiness. She entered into his projects with honest enthusiasm, and bound herself by the most solemn promises to aid in carrying them out. But in bitterness he remembered one who had promised with seeming enthusiasm before, and he distrusted his daughter, watching her with lynx-eyed vigilance.

But gradually he began to believe in her somewhat, as he saw her looking forward with increasing eagerness to the heaven of German fashionable life, wherein she, rich, admired, allied by marriage to some powerful noble family, should shine a queen in the world of art.

“I have joined her aspirations to mine,” he said, in self-gratulation. “I have blended our ambitions and sources of hope and enjoyment, and that is better than all her promises.”

===Chinese===
她心里苦闷极了，因为她看得出父亲已对她彻底丧失了信任。一想起过去那段经历，她便恶心欲呕。她曾沉浸在浪漫与神秘的幻想天地里，也曾拿出少女全部的真心去爱过；因而，哪怕有失公允甚至大谬不然，循着心理联想那不可抗拒的规律，她还是把“爱情”与“浪漫”这两个词同那个如今令她深恶痛绝的人死死捆在了一起。经此惨痛一劫，不过一周工夫，她对于人间真爱以及由此生发的幸福，便变得彻头彻尾地怀疑不信了，正如她父亲向来教导她怀疑上帝与信仰之喜乐那般彻底。她外表虽仍是个楚楚动人的年轻姑娘，她父亲却已把她调教得比异教徒还要荒芜冷漠。除了艺术与父亲的智慧之外，她再不信奉任何事物。在她看来，父亲身上仿佛凝聚着高雅的修养与世故的人生哲学——而这二者的确成了她如今眼中世上唯一值得追寻的东西。重新赢回父亲的信任成了她最大的渴望。然而这份信任业已遭受重创。卢多尔夫先生除了金钱和自己的意志之外，早已对世间万物绝了信心。在他眼里，宗教不过是粗鄙的迷信，而女子的贞洁与诚挚，无非是诗人们编造出来的虚言。

他不动声色地暗中察看克里斯蒂娜，说话只点到为止，意在试探她心底的真实念头。随后，他决定向她和盘托出自己的人生大计，好给她添足动力，使她甘心顺从他的旨意。他所勾勒出的那幅未来蓝图，令她那颗骄傲而富有野心的灵魂目眩神迷，在她的幻想中铺展出了一条当时看来唯一通往幸福的康庄大道。她满怀真诚的热忱投入了父亲的谋划之中，并立下最庄严的誓言，决心鼎力相助、共成大业。然而，他苦涩地记起了从前另一个曾佯装满腔热忱立下誓言的女人，因而不敢轻信亲女，依旧睁着山猫般锐利警觉的双眼暗暗盯着她。

不过，眼见她对德国上流社会那片锦绣天堂越来越心驰神往——在那里，她将坐拥巨富、备受钦慕，与某个显赫的贵族世家联姻，在艺术界宛如女皇般大放异彩——他这才渐渐对她生出几分信任。

“我把她的志向与我的捆在了一起，”他颇为得意地自语道，“我把咱们俩的野心、指望与乐事都融作一处，这可比她一万句誓言都管用多了。”

===Original===
When Dennis saw first the face that was so beautiful and yet so marred by pride and selfishness, Christine was about nineteen years old, and yet as mature in some respects as a woman of thirty. She had the perfect self-possession that familiarity with the best society gives. Mr. Ludolph was now too shrewd to seek safety in seclusion. He went with his daughter into the highest circles of the city, and Christine had crowds of admirers and many offers. All this she enjoyed, but took it coolly as her right, with the air of a Greek goddess accepting the incense that rose in her temple. She was too proud and refined to flirt in the ordinary sense of the word, and no one could complain that she gave much encouragement. But this state of things was all the more stimulating, and each one believed, with confidence in his peculiar attractions, that he might succeed where all others had failed. Miss Ludolph’s admirers were unaware that they had a rival in some as yet unknown German nobleman. At last it passed into a proverb that the beautiful and brilliant girl who was so free and courtly in society was as cold and unsusceptible as one of her father’s statues.

Thus it would seem that when circumstances brought the threads of these two lives near each other, Dennis’s and Christine’s, the most impassable barriers rose between them, and that the threads could never be woven together, or the lives blended. She was the daughter of the wealthy, aristocratic Mr. Ludolph; he was her father’s porter.

Next to the love of art, pride and worldly ambition were her strongest characteristics. She was an unbeliever in God and religion, not from conviction, but from training. She knew very little about either, and what light she had came to her through false mediums. She did not even believe in that which in many young hearts is religion’s shadow, love and romance, nor did her father take a more worldly and practical view of life than she.

===Chinese===
当丹尼斯头一回见到那张美艳动人却又因傲慢与自私而黯然失色的脸庞时，克里斯蒂娜约莫十九岁光景，然而在某些方面，老练得已然像个三十岁的妇人。常年周旋于最顶尖的社交圈，赋予了她一种无懈可击的从容镇定。卢多尔夫先生如今精明得很，再不会妄想靠深闺幽闭来保平安。他带着女儿出入城里最高贵的社交场合，克里斯蒂娜身边顿时蜂拥着大群爱慕者，求婚之人更是络绎不绝。这一切她倒也受用，却只是淡然处之、视作理所当然，宛如一位希腊女神冷眼领受着神庙中袅袅升起的香火。她骨子里太过矜持高雅，不屑像寻常女子那般卖弄风情，因而谁也怨不得她曾给过多少暧昧暗示。可偏偏是这副光景愈发勾人心痒，人人都自恃风流倜傥，笃信旁人折戟之处唯独自己能抱得美人归。卢多尔夫小姐的这群倾慕者浑然不知，他们真正的情敌，乃是一位尚在云山雾罩之中的德国贵族。到头来，圈子里甚至流传起一句俗话：那位在交际场上落落大方、雍容优雅的美貌才女，一颗心却冷硬如铁、毫无情愫，简直就像她父亲店里的一尊雕像。

如此看来，当命运将丹尼斯与克里斯蒂娜这两条原本平行的人生丝线拉近到一处时，他们之间却横亘着世上最难以逾越的重重屏障，这两根线似乎绝无可能交织到一处，两段人生也绝无可能水乳交融。她是豪富显贵、流着贵族血脉的卢多尔夫先生的千金；而他，不过是她父亲店里的一个搬运工。

在她的性情之中，除了对艺术的热爱，最根深蒂固的便是傲慢与尘世野心。她不信上帝，也不信宗教，这并非出于深思熟虑的笃信，而是自幼耳濡目染的熏陶使然。她对上帝和宗教都所知甚少，所能窥见的一星半点微光，也全是从歪曲的棱镜里折射过来的。在许多年轻人的心田里，爱情与浪漫原可视作宗教的影子，可她就连这也一概不信；哪怕是她父亲本人，看待人生也未见得比她更世故、更讲求实际。

===Original===
In marked contrast we have seen the character of Dennis Fleet, drawing its inspiration from such different sources.

Could two human beings be more widely separated﻿—separated in that which divides more surely than continents and seas?

Could Dennis have seen her warped, deformed moral nature, as clearly as her beautiful face and form, he would have shrunk from her; but while recognizing defects, he shared the common delusion, that the lovely outward form and face must enshrine much that is noble and ready to blossom into good, if the right motives can be presented.

As for Christine, she had one chance for life, one chance for heaven. She was *young*. Her nature had not so hardened and crystallized in evil as to be beyond new and happier influences.

===Chinese===
与此形成鲜明对照的，则是我们先前见识过的丹尼斯·弗利特的品格——他生命的源泉汲取自截然不同的所在。

世间还能有两个比他们相隔得更遥远的人吗——隔绝他们二人的，是比千山万水更能彻底阻断彼此的鸿沟？

倘若丹尼斯能像看清她秀美绝伦的容颜与身姿那样，一眼望穿她那扭曲畸形的道德天性，他定会避之唯恐不及；然而，尽管他也隐约察觉到她身上的瑕疵，却仍犯了世人常犯的糊涂，总以为如此玲珑剔透的外表与容颜之内，必定蕴藏着许多高贵的品质，只消动之以恰当的机缘，便随时能绽放出良善的花朵。

至于克里斯蒂娜，她尚有一线生机，尚有一线得救入天国的指望。因为她还*年轻*。她的天性尚未在恶念中彻底僵化凝结，还未到无可挽回、再也容不下更美好的新风吹拂的地步。

## XLIII “Christine, Awake! For Your Life!” / 第四十三章 “克里斯蒂娜，快醒醒！逃命要紧！”

===Original===
Dennis was too much stunned and bewildered to do more than instinctively work his way to the windward as the only point of safety, but the fire was now becoming so broad in its sweep that to do this was difficult. The awful event he had witnessed seemed partially to paralyze him; for he knew that the oath, hot as the scorching flames, was scarcely uttered before Mr. Ludolph’s lips were closed forever. He and his ambitious dream perished in a moment, and he was summoned to the other world to learn what his proud reason scoffed at in this.

For a block or more Dennis was passively borne alone by the rushing mob. Suddenly a voice seemed to shout almost in his ear, “The north side is burning!” and he started as from a dream. The thought of Christine flashed upon him, perishing perhaps in the flames. He remembered that now she had no protector, and that he for the moment had forgotten her; though in truth he had never imagined that she could be imperilled by the burning of the north side.

In an agony of fear and anxiety he put forth every effort of which he was capable, and tore through the crowd as if mad. There was no way of getting across the river now save by the La Salle Street tunnel. Into this dark passage he plunged with multitudes of others. It was indeed as near Pandemonium as any earthly condition could be. Driven forward by the swiftly pursuing flames, hemmed in on every side, a shrieking, frenzied, terror-stricken throng rushed into the black cavern. Every moral grade was represented there. Those who led abandoned lives were plainly recognizable, their guilty consciences finding expression in their livid faces. These jostled the refined and delicate lady, who, in the awful democracy of the hour, brushed against thief and harlot. Little children wailed for their lost parents, and many were trampled underfoot. Parents cried for their children, women shrieked for their husbands, some praying, many cursing with oaths as hot as the flames that crackled near. Multitudes were in no other costumes than those in which they had sprung from their beds. Altogether it was a strange, incongruous, writhing mass of humanity, such as the world had never looked upon, pouring into what might seem, in its horrors, the mouth of hell.

As Dennis entered the utter darkness, a confused roar smote his ear that might have appalled the stoutest heart, but he was now oblivious to everything save Christine’s danger. With set teeth he put his shoulder against the living mass and pushed with the strongest till he emerged into the glare of the north side. Here, escaping somewhat from the throng, he made his way rapidly to the Ludolph mansion, which to his joy he found was still considerably to the windward of the fire. But he saw that from the southwest another line of flame was bearing down upon it.

===Chinese===
丹尼斯惊骇呆立，神思恍惚，除了本能地朝上风向这唯一的生路挣扎挪动外，几乎什么也做不了；可火势横扫的范围越来越广，就连这一点也极难办到。方才目睹的那一幕惨剧仿佛让他半边身子都麻木了——他心知肚明，那句如同炽焰般灼人的咒骂刚一出口，卢多尔夫先生的双唇便已永远阖上。他连同他野心勃勃的美梦都在转瞬之间灰飞烟灭，被召往另一个世界，去领教他在这世上曾凭傲慢理性百般嗤笑的一切了。

一连走过一个多街区，丹尼斯都身不由己地被奔涌的人潮裹挟着往前推去。忽然，仿佛有个声音就在他耳边大吼：“北区烧起来了！”他如梦初醒，猛地一震。克里斯蒂娜的念头骤然闪过脑海——此刻她兴许正要葬身火海！他这才猛然想起，她如今已失去了庇护之人，而自己刚才竟一时把她忘了；尽管说句实在话，他先前压根儿没料到北区起火也会危及她的安危。

恐惧与焦灼如刀绞般攥紧了他的心，他使出浑身解数，疯了似的在人群中硬生生撕开一条道往前冲。眼下想过河，唯有走拉萨尔街隧道（La Salle Street tunnel）这一条路。他随同成千上万的人一头扎进了这条漆黑的通道。人世间再没有哪种境况，比这更酷似地狱的万魔殿（Pandemonium）了。身后是紧追不舍的烈焰，四周挤得水泄不通，尖叫、癫狂、魂飞魄散的人流一股脑儿涌进这黑洞洞的隧洞。形形色色、品行各异的人全都混杂其中。平日放浪形骸之徒一眼便能认出，亏心事写在了他们铁青骇人的脸上；可他们此刻却和斯文娇贵的贵妇人摩肩接踵——在这生死攸关、众生平等的酷烈时刻，名门淑媛也不得不与窃贼娼妓擦身而过。幼童哭喊着寻找走散的爹娘，不少人被生生踩在脚下；父母嘶声呼唤着儿女，妇人尖叫着寻找丈夫；有人跪地祈祷，更多的人则破口大骂，口中的咒诅比近旁噼啪作响的火舌还要滚烫。无数人身上只穿着从床上跳起来时那一身寝衣。放眼望去，这真是世间前所未见的一股怪诞、杂乱、扭曲蠕动的人潮，汹涌灌入这骇人宛若地狱之口的深渊。

丹尼斯踏入一片伸手不见五指的漆黑之中，耳畔顿时轰然响起一阵杂乱震耳的咆哮，哪怕世上胆子最大的人听了也要胆寒；可他此刻除了克里斯蒂娜面临的险境，对周围的一切早已浑然不觉。他咬紧牙关，拿肩膀顶住这堵血肉之墙，凭着一身蛮力硬往外挤，直到终于冲出隧道，置身于北区耀眼的火光之中。到了这儿，他总算略微摆脱了拥堵的人群，飞步赶往卢多尔夫宅邸。令他欣喜的是，那座宅子眼下还落在火场上风向颇远的地方；可他随即望见，西南方向另有一条火龙正滚滚扑来。

===Original===
The front door was locked, and the house utterly dark. He rang the bell furiously, but there was no response. He walked around under the window and shouted, but the place remained as dark and silent as a tomb. He pounded on the door, but its massive thickness scarcely admitted of a reverberation.

“They must have escaped,” he said; “but, merciful heaven! there must be no uncertainty in this case. What shall I do?”

The windows of the lower story were all strongly guarded and hopeless, but one opening on the balcony of Christine’s studio seemed practicable if it could be reached. A half-grown elm swayed its graceful branches over the balcony, and Dennis knew the tough and fibrous nature of this tree. In the New England woods of his early home he had learned to climb for nuts like a squirrel, and so with no great difficulty he mounted the trunk and dropped from an overhanging branch to the point he sought. The window was down at the top, but the lower sash was fastened. He could see the catch by the light of the fire. He broke the pane of glass nearest it, hoping that the crash might awaken Christine, if she were still there. But after the clatter died away there was no sound. He then noisily raised the sash and stepped in.

What a rush of memories came over him as he looked around the familiar place! There was the spot on which he had stood and asked for the love that he had valued more than life. There stood the easel on which, through Christine’s gifted touch, his painted face had pleaded with scarcely less eloquence, till he blotted it out with his own hand. In memory of it all his heart again failed him, and he sighed, “She will never love me.”

But there was no time for sentiment. He called loudly: “Miss Ludolph, awake! awake! for your life!”

===Chinese===
正门紧锁，整幢屋子黑漆漆的。他使劲猛按门铃，里头却毫无动静。他绕到窗下大声呼喊，屋里依然黑暗死寂得宛如一座坟墓。他又用力擂门，可那扇大门厚重无比，捶上去几乎连一点儿回响都激不起。

“他们准是已经逃走了，”他自言自语道，“可是，仁慈的上天啊！这种事决不能含糊猜度。我该怎么办？”

底楼的窗户全都加了坚固的护栏，无从下手；唯有通往克里斯蒂娜画室阳台的那扇窗，只要爬得上去，倒还有希望进入。一株长成半大的榆树正将婀娜的枝条摇曳在阳台上空，丹尼斯深知这种树木枝干坚韧耐折。打小在新英格兰（New England）故乡的林子里，他就练就了像松鼠一样爬树摘坚果的本事，于是没费多大周折便攀上树干，顺着悬在阳台上的枝丫纵身落到了想去的地方。那扇窗的上半扇降着，下半扇却上了插销。借着火光，他看清了插销的位置。他砸碎了离插销最近的一块玻璃，指望这声响能把或许仍在屋里的克里斯蒂娜惊醒。然而碎玻璃的哗啦声散尽之后，里头依旧悄无声息。于是他哗啦一声推起下窗扇，跨进了屋里。

环顾这间熟悉无比的画室，千般往事刹那间涌上心头！他就曾站在那块地方，向她恳求过那份他看得比性命还珍重的爱情。那儿还立着那架画架——当年克里斯蒂娜凭着一双妙手，将他的面庞绘于其上，画中人的深情诉说丝毫不逊于他本人，直到他亲手将它涂抹毁去。追忆及此，他的心头不由得又是一沉，轻轻叹了口气：“她永远也不会爱我的。”

可眼下容不得半点儿女情长。他放声大喊：“卢多尔夫小姐，快醒醒！快醒醒！逃命要紧！”

===Original===
There was no answer. “She must be gone,” he said. The front room, facing toward the west, he knew to be her sleeping-apartment. Going through the passage, he knocked loudly, and called again; but in the silence that followed he heard his own watch tick, and his heart beat. He pushed the door open with the feeling of one profaning a shrine, and looked timidly in. Even in that thrilling hour of peril and anxiety, his eye was enraptured by the beauty of the room. Not only was it furnished with the utmost luxuriance, but everything spoke of a quaint and cultured taste, from the curious marble clock and bronze on the mantel, even to the pattern of the Turkey carpet on which the glare of the fire, as it glinted through the shutters, played faintly. One of the most marked features, however, was an exquisite life-size statue of Diana at the foot of the bed, grasping her bow with one hand, and in the act of seizing an arrow with the other, as if aroused to self-defence. When Dennis first saw it, he was so startled by its lifelike attitude that he stepped back into the passage. But, with all the beauty of the room, it was utterly pagan; not a single thing suggested Christian faith or a knowledge of the true God. With the exception of its modern air, it might just as well have been the resting-place of a Greek or Roman maiden of rank.

Reassured, he timidly advanced again, and then for the first time, between the two marble statuettes holding back the curtains of the bed, saw Christine, but looking more white and deathlike than the marble itself.

She lay with her face toward him. Her hair of gold, unconfined, streamed over the pillow; one fair round arm, from which her night-robe had slipped back, was clasped around her head, and a flickering ray of light, finding access at the window, played upon her face and neck with the strangest and most weird effect.

So deep was her slumber that she seemed dead, and Dennis, in his overwrought state, thought that she was. For a moment his heart stood still, and his tongue was paralyzed. A distant explosion aroused him. Approaching softly he said, in an awed whisper (he seemed powerless to speak louder), “Miss Ludolph!﻿—Christine!”

But the light of the coming fire played and flickered over the still, white face, that never before had seemed so strangely beautiful.

===Chinese===
依然无人应声。“她肯定是走了。”他说道。他知道朝西的前屋便是她的卧室。他穿过走廊，使劲敲了敲门，又喊了一声；可随后笼罩下来的寂静里，他只听得见自己怀表的滴答声和胸膛里的心跳声。他怀着仿佛亵渎圣殿般的惶恐推开房门，怯怯地朝里望去。哪怕是在这千钧一发、心急如焚的险刻，他的目光仍不由被这间闺房的华美所慑服。屋里不但陈设奢华到了极点，而且件件物事都流露出奇雅深厚的修养与品位——从壁炉架上精致别致的大理石座钟与青铜摆件，直到那块土耳其地毯的花纹；百叶窗缝隙透进的火光，此刻正微弱地在那地毯上闪烁游移。然而最惹人注目的，却是床尾那尊真人大小的精美狄安娜（Diana）雕像：女神一手握弓，另一手作势欲抽箭矢，宛若惊觉有变、正欲自卫。丹尼斯乍一瞧见，被那栩栩如生的姿态吓了一跳，竟不由自主退回到了走廊里。只是，这房间虽美轮美奂，却彻头彻尾透着异教气息；屋里没有半件器物暗示着基督教信仰或对真神的敬畏。若撇开那股现代气象不谈，这简直就像一位古希腊或古罗马名门闺秀的寝宫。

稳住心神后，他再次怯步走上前去，这才头一回透过两尊挽起床幔的小型大理石雕像之间，看见了克里斯蒂娜——可她看上去却比大理石本身还要苍白，还要死气沉沉。

她侧着脸朝他躺着。一头散开的金发流泻在枕畔；夜衣的袖口滑落下来，露出一只白皙圆润的手臂曲枕在头边；一缕摇曳的光线从窗口钻进来，在她脸庞与脖颈间投下说不出的奇诡光影。

她睡得沉极了，活像已经死了一般；丹尼斯神经本已绷紧到了极点，一时间真以为她已香消玉殒。刹那间，他的心跳骤停，舌头也僵住了。远处传来一声爆炸，这才将他惊醒。他轻手轻脚走近床边，压低声音，带着几分敬畏低唤道——仿佛再也发不出更大的声音：“卢多尔夫小姐！——克里斯蒂娜！”

然而逼近的大火投下的光亮，只顾在那张沉静雪白的俏脸上明灭闪烁；那张容颜，似乎从不曾像此刻这般美得奇异动人。

===Original===
“Miss Ludolph!﻿—Oh, Christine, awake!” cried Dennis, louder.

To his wonder and unbounded perplexity, he saw the hitherto motionless lips wreathe themselves into a lovely smile, but otherwise there was no response, and the ghostly light played and flickered on, dancing on temple, brow, and snowy throat, and clasping the white arm in wavy circlets of gold. It was all so weird and strange that he was growing superstitious, and losing faith in his own senses. He could not know that she was under the influence of an opiate, and that his voice of all others could, like a faint echo, find access to her mind so deeply sunk in lethargy.

But a louder and nearer explosion, like a warning voice, made him wholly desperate; and he roughly seized her hand, determining to dispel the illusion, and learn the truth at once.

Christine’s blue eyes opened wide with a bewildered stare; a look of the wildest terror came into them, and she started up and shrieked, “Father! father!”

Then turning toward the as yet unknown invader, she cried, piteously: “Oh, spare my life! Take everything; I will give you anything you ask, only spare my life.”

She evidently thought herself addressing a ruthless robber.

===Chinese===
“卢多尔夫小姐！——哦，克里斯蒂娜，醒醒！”丹尼斯放大了声音喊道。

令他大为惊异又百思不得其解的是，他瞧见那双原本一动不动的嘴唇缓缓绽出一抹动人的微笑，可除此之外再无半点反应；那幽灵般的火光依旧在明灭跳动，舞过她的鬓角、额际与雪白的咽喉，又化作道道起伏的金环缠绕着她雪白的玉臂。眼前的一切如此诡谲离奇，连他自己都快生出迷信的念头，几乎不敢相信自己的感官了。他哪里知道，她是服了安神麻醉药剂才昏睡至此，而在世上千百个声音当中，唯有他的呼唤能化作一缕微弱的回音，悄然渗入她深深沉沦在昏睡中的神思。

可就在这时，一声更响、更近的爆炸轰然炸开，宛如上天降下的警钟，逼得他彻底豁出去了；他猛地一把攥住她的手，下定决心要击碎这重幻象，立刻弄个水落石出。

克里斯蒂娜那双蓝眼睛蓦地睁大，茫然直视着前方；紧接着，极度的惊恐涌上眼眸，她霍然坐起身，尖叫道：“爸爸！爸爸！”

随后她转向这个尚未认清面目的闯入者，凄声哀求道：“啊，饶我一命吧！什么东西你们都拿去；不管要什么我都给你们，只求饶我一命！”

显然，她把眼前人当成了一个心狠手辣的强盗。

===Original===
Dennis retreated toward the door the moment she awakened; and this somewhat reassured her.

In the firm, quiet tone that always calms excitement he replied, “I only ask you to give me your confidence, Miss Ludolph, and to join with me, Dennis Fleet, in my effort to save your life.”

“Dennis Fleet! Dennis Fleet! save my life! Oh, ye gods, what does it all mean?” and she passed her hand in bewilderment across her brow, as if to brush away the wild fancies of a dream.

“Miss Ludolph, as you love your life arouse yourself and escape! The city is burning!”

“I don’t believe it!” she cried, in an agony of terror and anger. “Leave the room! How dare you! You are not Dennis Fleet; he is a white man, and you are black! You are an impostor! Leave quick, or my father will come and take your life! Father! father!”

Dennis without a word stepped to the window, tore aside the curtain, threw open the shutters, and the fire filled the room with the glare of noonday. At that moment an explosion occurred which shook the very earth. Everything rattled, and a beautiful porcelain vase fell crashing to the floor.

Christine shrieked and covered her face with her hands.

===Chinese===
克里斯蒂娜刚一苏醒，丹尼斯便立刻退到了门边；这一举动叫她心神稍安了些。

他用那向来能平息人焦躁情绪的沉稳、轻柔的语调答道：“卢多尔夫小姐，我只求您信任我，配合我——丹尼斯·弗利特，让我竭力救您出险。”

“丹尼斯·弗利特！丹尼斯·弗利特！救我的命！天哪，这到底是怎么回事？”她茫然地抬手抚过额头，仿佛想挥去梦中荒诞纷乱的幻象。

“卢多尔夫小姐，您若珍爱自己的性命，就赶紧振作起来逃命吧！整座城都烧起来了！”

“我不信！”她又惊又怒，痛苦地喊道，“滚出这间屋子！你好大的胆子！你不是丹尼斯·弗利特，他是白人，而你是个黑人！你是个冒牌货！快滚出去，不然我父亲回来就要你的命！爸爸！爸爸！”

丹尼斯一言不发，大步走到窗前，一把扯开窗帘，推开百叶窗，屋外的烈火登时将整间卧室照得亮如正午。恰在此时，一声撼天动地的巨响炸开，连大地都为之震颤。屋里所有器物叮当作响，一只精美的瓷花瓶摔落在地，碎裂作一片狼藉。

克里斯蒂娜发出一声尖叫，用双手掩住了脸庞。

===Original===
Dennis approached the bedside, and said in a gentle, firm tone that she knew to be his: “Miss Ludolph, I *am* Mr. Fleet. My face is blackened through smoke and dust, as is everyone’s out in the streets tonight. You know something of me, and I think you know nothing dishonorable. Can you not trust me? Indeed you must; your life depends upon it!”

“Oh, pardon me, Mr. Fleet!” she cried, eagerly. “I am not worthy of this, but now that I know you, I do trust you from the depth of my soul!”

“Prove it then by doing just as I bid you,” he replied, in a voice so firm and prompt that it seemed almost stern. Retreating to the door, he continued: “I give you just five minutes in which to make your toilet and gather a light bundle of your choicest valuables. Dress in woollen throughout, and dress warmly. I will see that the servants are aroused. Your father is on the south side, and cannot reach you. You must trust in God and what I can do for you.”

“I must trust to you *alone*,” she said. “Please send my maid to me.”

===Chinese===
丹尼斯走近床边，用她听得真切、专属于他的温和却坚定的声音说道：“卢多尔夫小姐，我确确实实就是弗利特先生。我这副脸是被烟尘熏黑的——今晚走在大街上的每一个人全都是这副模样。您对我也有几分了解，想来从不曾听说过我有什么不光彩的劣迹。难道您还不能信我吗？眼下您非信不可，您的性命全系于此啊！”

“啊，请原谅我，弗利特先生！”她急切地喊道，“我实在当不起您这番厚待，可如今既然认出了您，我便从灵魂深处全心信赖您！”

“那就照我的吩咐去做，证明给我看，”他答道，嗓音果决干脆，几乎显得有些严厉。他退到门口，接着交代道，“我只给您五分钟时间梳洗穿衣，再收拾一小包您最珍爱的贵重物件。从里到外全穿羊毛衣裳，务必穿暖和些。我去看看仆人们都叫醒了没有。您父亲在南区，赶不过来接应您。此刻您唯有仰赖上帝，还有我能为您做到的一切了。”

“我眼下只能单单仰仗您一个人了，”她说道，“请把我的贴身女仆叫来吧。”

===Original===
Mr. Ludolph had sipped his wine during the evening, and his servants had sipped, in no dainty way, something stronger, and therefore had not awakened readily. But the uproar in the streets had aroused them, and Dennis found them scuttling down the upper stairs in a half-clad state, each bearing a large bundle, which had been made up without regard to *meum* and *tuum*.

“Och, murther! is the world burning up?” cried the cook.

“Be still, ye howlin’ fool,” said the cool and travelled maid. “It’s only von big fire!”

“Go to your mistress and help her, quick!” cried Dennis.

“Go to my meestress! I go to de street and save my life.”

“Oh, Janette!” cried Christine. “Come and help me!”

“I am meeserable zat I cannot. I must bid mademoiselle quick adieu,” said the heartless creature, still keeping up the veneer of French politeness.

===Chinese===
傍晚时分，卢多尔夫先生曾小酌葡萄酒，他手下的仆人们可就不那么讲究斯文了，偷偷喝了些更烈的酒，因此睡得死沉，很不容易醒。不过街上的鼎沸喧嚣到底把他们吵醒了；丹尼斯找到他们时，这帮人正衣衫不整地顺着楼上楼梯仓皇往下窜，每人怀里都抱着一大包东西，收拾得可全然不顾究竟归谁所有。

“哎哟我的老天爷啊！这世界是要烧光了吗？”厨娘哭喊道。

“闭嘴，你这鬼哭狼嚎的蠢货，”那位见多识广、镇定自若的贴身女仆冷冷说道，“不过是一场大火罢了！”

“快去照应你们女主人，帮她一把！”丹尼斯厉声喊道。

“去照应我的女主人？我自己还要上街保命去呢。”

“哦，珍妮特（Janette）！”克里斯蒂娜呼喊道，“快来帮帮我！”

“真是万分遗憾，我实在抽不出身。我只得赶忙向小姐告辞了。”这个冷酷无情的女人说道，嘴上却依然维持着那层法式客套的虚饰。

===Original===
Dennis looked through the upper rooms and was satisfied that they were empty. Suddenly a piercing shriek from Christine sent him flying to her room. As he ran he heard her cry, “Oh, Mr. Fleet! come! help!”

To go back a little (for on that awful night events marched as rapidly as the flames, and the experience of years was crowded into hours, and that of hours into moments), Christine had sought as best she could to obey Dennis’s directions, but she was sadly helpless, having been trained to a foolish dependence on her maid. She had accomplished but little when she heard a heavy step in the room. Looking up, she saw a strange man regarding her with an evil eye.

“What do you want?” she faltered.

“You, for one thing, and all you have got, for another,” was the brutal reply.

“Leave this room!” she cried, in a voice she vainly tried to render firm.

“Not just yet,” he answered, with a satanic grin. She sought to escape by him with the loud cry that Dennis heard, but the ruffian planted his big grimy hand in the delicate frill of her night-robe where it clasped her throat, and with a coarse laugh said: “Not so fast, my dainty!”

===Chinese===
丹尼斯把楼上各间屋子察看了一遍，确认已无他人。忽然，克里斯蒂娜发出一声撕心裂肺的尖叫，惊得他飞奔回她的卧室。一边狂奔，他一边听见她哭喊着：“啊，弗利特先生！快来！救命啊！”

话分两头，略微倒回片刻来说——毕竟在那个可怕的夜晚，变故来得与火势一般迅疾，数年的经历被浓缩进了短短几小时，几小时的波折又挤进了转瞬之间——克里斯蒂娜本已竭尽所能想遵从丹尼斯的嘱咐，无奈她自幼被娇养得蠢笨无能，事事都要仰仗女仆，此刻显得可怜又无助。她才刚收拾妥当没几样东西，忽听屋里响起沉重的脚步声。抬头一看，只见一个陌生男人正用一双贼忒兮兮的恶眼直勾勾盯着她。

“你想干什么？”她声音打颤地问道。

“一要你的人，二要你手头全部的值钱家当。”对方粗野地答道。

“滚出这间屋子！”她喊道，竭力想让声音听起来镇定些，却终究徒劳。

“还不急着走呢。”那人咧嘴露出一丝恶魔般的狞笑答道。她发出一声凄厉的喊叫——正是丹尼斯听见的那一声——企图从他身旁夺路逃走，可那歹徒却伸出一只又大又脏的黑手，一把揪住她夜衣紧扣在咽喉处的精致蕾丝花边，粗声狂笑道：“别急着跑呀，我的小美人儿！”

===Original===
Trembling and half fainting (for she had no physical courage), she cried for Dennis, and never did knightly heart respond with more brave and loving throb to the cry of helpless woman than his. He came with almost the impetus of a thunderbolt, and the man, startled, looked around, and catching a glimpse of Dennis’s blazing eyes, dropped his hold on Christine, and shrank and cowered from the blow he could not avert. Before his hand could instinctively reach the pistol it sought, there was a thud, and he fell like a log to the floor. Then, springing upon him, Dennis took away his weapons, and, seizing him by the collar of his coat, dragged him backward downstairs and thrust him into the street. Pointing his own pistol at him, he said, “If you trouble us again, I will shoot you like a dog!”

The villain slunk off, and finding some kindred spirits sacking a liquor-store not far off, he joined the orgy, seeking to drown his rage in rum, and he succeeded so effectually that he lay in the gutter soon after. The escaping multitude trampled over him, and soon the fire blotted out his miserable existence, as it did that of so many who rendered themselves powerless by drink.

When Dennis returned he found Christine panting helplessly on a chair.

“Oh, dress! dress!” he cried. “We have not a moment to spare.”

The sparks and cinders were falling about the house, a perfect storm of fire. The roof was already blazing, and smoke was pouring down the stairs.

===Chinese===
她浑身筛糠似的直抖，几乎快要昏厥过去——她向来没有半点应对危急的胆气——只得拼命呼喊丹尼斯；而世上也绝没有哪颗骑士般高洁的心，能比他更英勇、更深情地回应一位无助女子的呼救了。他几乎挟着雷霆万钧之势疾冲而至；那男人吃了一惊，回过头去，猛然瞥见丹尼斯那双怒火熊熊的双眸，吓得松开抓着克里斯蒂娜的手，畏缩着身子想躲开这避无可避的一击。他的手本能地去摸腰间手枪，还没等摸着，只听“砰”的一声闷响，他已像一段木头般直挺挺栽倒在地。丹尼斯随即扑上前去夺下他的武器，一把拎住他的外套领子，倒拖着拽下楼梯，狠狠甩到了大街上。他用夺来的手枪指着那厮喝道：“你要是敢再来招惹我们，我就像打死一条野狗一样一枪崩了你！”

那恶徒灰溜溜地逃窜了，没走多远便撞见几个臭味相投的流氓正在洗劫一家酒铺，于是立时混进那场狂欢暴行里，想借朗姆酒浇灭一肚子窝囊怒火；他灌得实在太有效了，没过多久便烂醉如泥地瘫倒在阴沟里。逃难的人潮从他身上踩踏而过，转眼间，烈火便彻底抹去了他这条贱命，正如它吞噬了无数因醉酒而丧失自救之力的男女一般。

丹尼斯折返回屋时，只见克里斯蒂娜瘫坐在一把椅子上，无助地大口喘着气。

“快啊，穿衣服！快穿衣服！”他喊道，“我们一秒钟也耽搁不起了！”

漫天火星和余烬正铺天盖地砸在宅子四周，简直下起了一场烈火暴雨。屋顶已经熊熊燃起，浓烟正顺着楼梯滚滚灌了下来。

===Original===
At his suggestion she had at first laid out a heavy woollen dress and Scotch plaid shawl. She nervously sought to put on the dress, but her trembling fingers could not fasten it over her wildly throbbing bosom. Dennis saw that in the terrible emergency he must act the part of a brother or husband, and springing forward he assisted her with the dexterity he had learned in childhood.

Just then a blazing piece of roof, borne on the wings of the gale, crashed through the window, and in a moment the apartment, that had seemed like a beautiful casket for a still more exquisite jewel, was in flames.

Hastily wrapping Christine in the blanket shawl, he snatched her, crying and wringing her hands, into the street.

Holding his hand she ran two or three blocks with all the speed her wild terror prompted; then her strength began to fail, and she pantingly cried that she could run no longer. But this rapid rush carried them out of immediate peril, and brought them into the flying throng pressing their way northward and westward. Wedged into the multitude they could only move on with it in the desperate struggle forward. But fire was falling about them like a meteoric shower.

Suddenly Christine uttered a sharp cry of pain. She had stepped on a burning cinder, and then realized for the first time, in her excitement, that her feet were bare.

===Chinese===
先前听他叮嘱时，她原已挑出了一件厚重的羊毛长裙和一条苏格兰格纹披肩摆在一旁。此刻她慌慌张张地试图把裙子套上身，可那双直打哆嗦的手指却怎么也扣不上胸前剧烈起伏的衣襟。丹尼斯眼见情势火烧眉毛，自己非得担起兄长或丈夫般的照拂之责不可，当即箭步上前，凭着童年时练熟的灵巧手脚替她扣好了衣扣。

就在这当口，一块燃烧的屋顶残片乘着狂风呼啸而来，哗啦一声砸破窗户；转眼之间，这间原本宛如华美锦匣般盛放着更稀世珍宝的闺房，便已陷入了一片火海。

他匆忙用那条厚绒毯披肩裹紧克里斯蒂娜，一把抱起一路哭泣、绞着双手的她，冲出了大街。

她拉着他的手，在极度惊恐的驱使下卯足全力狂奔了两三个街区；随后气力渐竭，气喘吁吁地喊着再也跑不动了。好在这一阵急奔已带他们冲出了眼皮底下的绝境，汇入了正拼命向北、向西突围的逃难人流。两人被死死挤在人海当中，只能身不由己地随着大伙儿绝望地往前挪动。然而漫天火星却宛如流星雨般纷纷扬扬砸落在他们头顶四周。

突然，克里斯蒂娜发出一声尖锐的痛呼。她一脚踩在了一块滚烫的炭烬上——直到这一刻，慌乱之中她才猛然察觉自己竟光着两只脚丫。

===Original===
“Oh, what shall I do?” she cried piteously, limping and leaning heavily on Dennis’s arm.

“Indeed, Miss Ludolph, from my heart I pity you.”

“Can you save me? Oh, do you think you can save me?” she moaned, in an agony of fear.

“Yes, I feel sure I can. At any rate I shall not leave you;” and taking her a little out of the jostling crowd he kneeled and bound up the burned foot with his handkerchief. A little further on they came to a shoe-store with doors open and owners gone. Almost carrying Christine into it, for her other foot was cut and bleeding, he snatched down a pair of boy’s stout gaiters, and wiping with another handkerchief the blood and dust from her tender little feet, he made the handkerchiefs answer for stockings, and drew the shoes on over them.

In the brief moment so occupied, Christine said, with tears in her eyes: “Mr. Fleet, how kind you are! How little I deserve all this!”

He looked up with a happy smile, and she little knew that her few words amply repaid him.

===Chinese===
“啊，这可怎么办才好？”她一瘸一拐地走着，把半边身子沉沉倚在丹尼斯手臂上，可怜巴巴地哭喊道。

“卢多尔夫小姐，我打心眼里为您心疼。”

“您能救得了我吗？啊，您觉得真能救我出去吗？”她吓得魂不守舍，痛苦地呻吟道。

“能的，我十拿九稳能救您出去。无论如何，我绝不会丢下您不管。”说罢，他搀着她略微避开推搡拥挤的人群，单膝跪下，掏出自己的手帕替她包扎好烫伤的那只脚。再往前走了不远，两人经过一家店门敞开、店主早已逃走不见的鞋店。克里斯蒂娜的另一只脚也已划破流血，他几乎是半抱半扶地把她带进店里，顺手抓下一双结实的男童高帮鞋，又取出另一方手帕擦去她娇嫩小脚上的血渍与尘土，索性拿手帕权充袜子裹好双脚，再替她把鞋子穿了上去。

就在这匆匆忙忙的片刻功夫里，克里斯蒂娜含着泪说道：“弗利特先生，您真是太仁厚了！我何德何能，哪里配得上您这般相待！”

他抬起头来，露出一抹欣慰的笑容；她哪里知道，光凭她这寥寥数语，便已足够报偿他的一切了。

===Original===
There was a crash in the direction of the fire. With a cry of fear, Christine put out her hands and clung to him.

“Oh, we shall perish! Are you not afraid?”

“I tremble for you, Miss Ludolph.”

“Not for yourself?”

“No! why should I? I am safe. Heaven and mother are just beyond this tempest.”

“I would give worlds for your belief.”

===Chinese===
火势蔓延的方向传来一阵轰隆塌响。克里斯蒂娜惊叫一声，伸出双手死死攀住了他。

“啊，我们怕是要葬身于此了！您难道一点儿也不害怕吗？”

“卢多尔夫小姐，我唯独为您担惊受怕。”

“您不为自己担心吗？”

“不！我有什么好担心的？我是安稳无虞的。只要穿过这场烈火风暴，彼岸便是天国与我的母亲。”

“若是能拥有您这份信念，叫我拿全天下去换我都愿意。”

===Original===
“Come, quick!” cried he, and they joined the fugitives, and for a half-hour pressed forward as fast as was possible through the choked streets, Dennis merely saying an encouraging word now and then. Suddenly she felt herself carried to one side, and falling to the ground with him. In a moment he lifted her up, and she saw with sickening terror an infuriated dray-horse plunging through the crowd, striking down men, women, and children.

“Are you hurt?” he asked, gently, passing his arm around her and helping her forward, that they might not lose a single step.

“Awful! Awful!” she said, in a low, shuddering tone.

The dreadful scenes and the danger were beginning to overpower her.

A little further on they reached an avenue to the northwest through which Dennis hoped to escape. But they could make but little headway through the dense masses of drays, carriages, and human beings, and at last everything came to a deadlock. Their only hope was to stand in their place till the living mass moved on again.

===Chinese===
“快走，跟紧了！”他喊道。两人重新汇入逃难的人群，在半个钟头里顺着水泄不通的街道拼命往前赶，一路上丹尼斯只不时轻声安慰鼓励她几句。陡然间，她只觉自己被他一把抱起扯向一侧，随即便和他双双跌倒在地。他转瞬将她扶起，她定睛一看，吓得胃里一阵翻江倒海——一匹受惊发狂的拉货大马正横冲直撞地闯过人群，把沿途的男女老少一个个撞翻踩倒。

“您伤着没有？”他轻声问道，一边伸臂揽住她的腰，搀着她继续往前赶，生怕耽误了哪怕一步脚程。

“太可怕了！真是太可怕了！”她声音低微、浑身战栗地说道。

一路所见的惨象与重重险境，渐渐快把她压垮了。

再往前走了一段，他们来到一条通往西北方的大道，丹尼斯原指望能顺着这条路突围脱险。可面对密密麻麻堵成一团的运货平板马车、四轮马车和逃难人群，他们寸步难移，到最后整条街道竟彻底卡死，纹丝不动。眼下唯一的指望，只能是原地站着苦等这片人山车海重新往前挪动。

===Original===
Strange, grotesque, and sad beyond measure were the scenes by which they were surrounded. By the side of the aristocratic Christine, now Baroness Ludolph, stood a stout Irishwoman, hugging a grunting, squealing pig to her breast. A little in advance a hook-nosed spinster carried in a cage a hook nosed parrot that kept discordantly crying, “Polly want a cracker.” At Dennis’s left a delicate lady of the highest social standing clasped to her bare bosom a babe that slept as peacefully as in the luxurious nursery at home. At her side was a little girl carrying as tenderly a large wax doll. A diamond necklace sparkled like a circlet of fire around the lady’s neck. Her husband had gone to the south side, and she had had but time to snatch this and her children. A crowd of obscene and profane rowdies stood just behind them, and with brutal jest and coarse laughter they passed around a whiskey-bottle. One of these roughs caught a glimpse of the diamond necklace, and was putting forth his blackened hand to grasp it, when Dennis pointed the captured pistol at him and said, “This is law now!”

The fellow slunk back.

Just before them was a dray with a corpse half covered with a blanket. The family sat around crying and wringing their hands, and the driver stood in his seat, cursing and gesticulating for those in advance to move on. Some moments passed, but there was no progress. Dennis became very anxious, for the fire was rapidly approaching, and the sparks were falling like hail. Every few moments some woman’s dress was ablaze, or someone was struck by the flying brands, and shrieks for help were heard on every side. Christine, being clad in woollen, escaped this peril in part. She stood at Dennis’s side trembling like a leaf, with her hands over her face to shut out the terrible sights.

At last the driver, fearing for his life, jumped off his dray and left all to their fate. But a figure took his place that thrilled Dennis’s heart with horror.

===Chinese===
围拢在他们周遭的景象荒诞离奇、古怪荒唐，又凄凉得令人心碎。在出身贵族、如今已成卢多尔夫女男爵（Baroness Ludolph）的克里斯蒂娜身旁，站着一位膀大腰圆的爱尔兰妇人，怀里死死搂着一头哼哼唧唧、尖声嚎叫的小猪。稍微靠前些，一位鹰钩鼻的老姑娘手里提着鸟笼，笼里关着一只同样长着钩嘴的鹦鹉，正扯着难听的破锣嗓子不停嚷嚷：“波莉要吃饼干！波莉要吃饼干！”丹尼斯左手边，一位身份显赫、养尊处优的纤弱贵妇光着胸口，将一名婴孩紧抱在怀中；那孩子睡得竟和在自家豪奢的育儿室里一般安详香甜。贵妇身旁的小女孩，则同样珍爱万分地抱着一个大蜡娃娃。贵妇脖子上戴着一串钻石项链，宛如一圈火焰般闪耀生辉——她丈夫先前去了南区，逃生时她只来得及一把抓起这串项链和几个孩子。就在她们正后方，站着一伙满嘴污言秽语的地痞无赖，一边说着下流荤话、发出粗野狂笑，一边轮流传递着一只威士忌酒瓶。其中一名恶棍瞄见了那串钻石项链，正伸出乌黑的脏手抓过去，却见丹尼斯举起缴获的手枪对准了他，冷冷喝道：“眼下这就是王法！”

那家伙顿时缩了回去。

紧挨着他们前头，停着一辆运货平板马车，车上搁着一具半盖着毯子的尸首。死者的一家老小围坐在尸旁号啕大哭，不住绞扭双手；车夫站在驾驶座上破口大骂，挥舞着手臂催促前头的人赶紧挪步。过了好一会儿，队伍依旧纹丝不动。丹尼斯心中焦急万分，因为火势正在飞速逼近，火星如冰雹般劈头盖脸砸落下来。每隔片刻，便有某个妇人的裙裾着了火，或是有人被半空飞来的燃烧木块砸中，四面八方惨叫呼救声此起彼伏。克里斯蒂娜因一身皆着羊毛衣料，倒免去了几分引火烧身的险情。她站在丹尼斯身侧，如风中落叶般抖个不停，双手死死捂住脸，不忍直视四周的惨状。

末了，那车夫到底惜命，纵身跳下平板马车，抛下车上众人听天由命去了。可紧接着爬上车夫空座的那道身影，却让丹尼斯惊骇得心胆俱裂。

===Original===
There on the high seat stood Susie Winthrop﻿—rather Mrs. Leonard. The light of insanity glowed in her eyes; her long hair swept away to the north, and turning toward the fiery tempest she bent forward as if looking for someone. But after a moment she sadly shook her head, as if she had sought in vain. Suddenly she reached out her white arms toward the fire, and sang, clear and sweet above the horrid din:

> “O burning flakes of fiery snow,
 

 Bury me too, bury me deep;
 

 My lover sleeps thy banks below;
 

 Fall on me, that I may sleep!”

At this moment a blazing brand fell upon the horses’ heads; they startled forward, and the crazed lady fell over on the corpse below. The animals being thoroughly terrified turned sharp around on the sidewalk, and tore their way right toward the fire, trampling down those in their track, and so vanished with their strangely assorted load.

===Chinese===
只见高高的车座上立着的，竟是苏茜·温思罗普——或者更确切地说，如今已是伦纳德太太。她眼中闪烁着疯癫痴狂的幽光；一头长发被风吹得朝北狂舞，她面向那场烈火风暴微微俯身，仿佛正在人海火影中苦苦搜寻着谁。可片刻之后，她凄然摇了摇头，似乎终究寻觅无果。突然间，她朝着熊熊大火伸出那双雪白的手臂，在一片震耳欲聋的恐怖喧嚣之上，清越而甜美地高声唱了起来：

> “哦，炽焰化作漫天飞雪，
> 也把我掩埋吧，深深掩埋；
> 我的爱人长眠在你堆叠的雪岸之下；
> 飘落到我身上吧，好让我也沉沉睡去！”

说时迟那时快，一块燃烧的火把般木块恰巧砸在马头上；马匹受惊猛往前蹿，那位神智失常的妇人顿时仰面跌倒在下方那具尸首上。两匹马彻底吓疯了，沿着人行道猛地调转方向，径直朝大火深处狂奔而去，将挡道的人群一通踩踏碾过，就这样拖着那一车诡异凑合的亡人与活人，转眼消失在了火光之中。

===Original===
Dennis, fearing to stay any longer where he was, determined to follow in their wake and find a street leading to the north less choked, even though it might be nearer the fire, and so with his trembling companion he pressed forward again.

Two blocks below he found one comparatively clear, but in terrible proximity to the conflagration. Indeed, the houses were burning on each side, but the street seemed clear of flame. He thought that by swiftly running they could get through. But Christine’s strength was fast failing her, and just as they reached the middle of the block a tall brick building fell across the street before them! Thus their only path of escape was blocked by a blazing mass of ruins that it would have been death to cross.

They seemed hemmed in on every side, and Dennis groaned in agony.
