So try to be as calm as possible, and cooperate with every effort to baffle and banish disease. After all it may be nothing more than a severe cold.”

So then in very truth this world was all. In bitterness and dread she realized how slight was her hold upon it. To her healthful body pain was a rare experience, but now her head and every bone ached, and the slightest movement caused increased suffering. But her mental trouble was by far the greatest. Often she murmured to herself, “Oh, that I had been trained to the grossest superstitions, so that I might not look down into this black bottomless gulf that unbelief opens at my feet!” and she tossed and moaned most piteously.

Mr. Ludolph returned to the store in an exceedingly worried and anxious state. As he entered he caught Dennis’s eager, questioning gaze, and a thought struck him: “Perhaps this young fellow, through his mission school, may know of some good, trustworthy woman who would act as nurse;” and coming to Dennis he explained the situation, and then asked if he knew of anyone, or could find a suitable person.

===Chinese===
“休说胡话，”卢多尔夫先生斩钉截铁地说道，“你唯一的生路就是把病治好。自欺欺人毫无用处。我已经请来了医术最高明的大夫，定会确保你得到最周全的照料。所以你务必尽可能稳住心神，配合一切医治手段，把病魔击退驱除。说到底，没准儿真的只是一场重风寒罢了。”

原来归根结底，这尘世当真是全部所在了。怀着苦楚与骇惧，她这才看清自己抓在这世上的根基是何等微薄脆弱。她向来体格强健，极少尝过病痛滋味，可此刻却头痛欲裂、浑身骨节酸痛，稍一挪动便痛楚加剧。然而比起肉体的折磨，心头的煎熬更甚百倍。她常常喃喃自语道：“哎，但愿我从小受的是最愚昧粗鄙的迷信熏陶倒好，好歹不必低头直面这由不信在脚下劈开的无底黑渊！”说罢便在床上凄楚地翻来覆去，呻吟不止。

卢多尔夫先生回到画店时，心绪焦虑烦躁到了极点。刚一进门，他便撞见丹尼斯投来的那道焦急探询的目光，心中忽地一动：“或许这小伙子通过他那所布道学校，能认识一两位品行端正、靠得住的妇人，肯来当看护呢。”于是他走到丹尼斯面前，说明了眼下的处境，随即问他是否认识这样的人，或者能否帮忙物色一位合适的人选。

===Original===
Dennis listened eagerly, thought a moment, and then said, with a flushed face and in a low tone: “I think my mother would be willing to come. She has had the smallpox and would not be afraid.”

“But would she be willing?”

“I think I could persuade her,” said Dennis.

Mr. Ludolph thought a moment, then said: “I think she would be the one of all others, for she must be very much of a lady, and I would not like to put my daughter in charge of a common, coarse woman. You may rest assured that I would reward her liberally.”

===Chinese===
丹尼斯凝神听罢，沉吟了片刻，随后面颊微红、低声说道：“我想我母亲兴许愿意去。她从前出过天花，不会害怕传染。”

“可她真会愿意吗？”

“我想我能说服她。”丹尼斯答道。

卢多尔夫先生思忖了片刻，说道：“再没有比她更合适的人选了，她必定是位极有教养的淑女，我本就不愿把女儿托付给粗俗平庸的妇人照料。你只管放心，我定会重重酬谢她的。”

===Original===
“She would not come for money, sir.”

“What then?”

Dennis flushed how more deeply than before. He had been speaking for his mother from his own point of view, and now he hardly knew what to say, for he was not good at evasion. But he told the truth, if not all the truth. “We feel very grateful to you for the means of support, and a chance in life when the world was very dark. You have since promoted me﻿—”

“Nonsense!” said Mr. Ludolph, somewhat touched, though; “you have earned every dollar you have received, and your coming has been of advantage to me also. But if your mother will meet this need, should it occur, neither of you will have cause to regret it;” and he passed on to his office, but soon after went away again and did not return that day.

===Chinese===
“先生，她去不是为了钱。”

“那是为了什么？”

丹尼斯这回脸红得比方才更深了。他方才原是按自己的心思替母亲做主应承，眼下骤然被问住，一时竟不知如何作答，因为他生来不善支吾掩饰。不过他说出口的虽非全部实情，却也句句属实：“我们母子十分感激您在世道一片漆黑之际赐予我们糊口的生计与安身立命之机。后来您又提拔了我——”

“胡说！”卢多尔夫先生嘴上这么说着，神色却多少有些动容，“你领去的每一块钱都是你凭本事挣来的，你的到来于我也同样大有益处。不过，万一真到了这一步，令堂若肯伸出援手解此燃眉之急，你们母子俩绝不会后悔的。”说罢他便走进了办公室，但没过多久又再度出门，当天再也没有回来。

===Original===
To Dennis the hours dragged on like years, full of suspense and mental tumult. At times he would bow his head behind his counter, and pray in tearful fervor for the object of his constant thought. The day was rainy, and the store empty of customers, for which he was most thankful, as he would have made the poorest of salesmen. At last the hour for closing arrived, and he was left to himself. In the solitude of his own room he once more looked the situation fairly in the face. With his head bowed in his hands he reflected: “Last night I *thought* to tear this love from my heart, but tonight I find that this would be to tear out my heart itself. I cannot do it. It is my strongest conviction that I can no more stop loving her than I can stop living. Unconsciously this love has grown until now it is my master, and it is folly to make any more resolves, only to be as weak as water when I least expect it. What shall I do?”

Motionless, unconscious of the lapse of time, he remained hour after hour absorbed in painful thought. Circumstances, reason, the Bible, all seemed to frown upon his love; but, though it appeared to be hopeless, his whole nature revolted against the idea of its being wrong.

“It cannot be wrong to love, purely and unselfishly,” he muttered. “Such love as mine seems to carry its own conviction of right with it﻿—an inner consciousness that seems so strong and certain as to be beyond argument﻿—beyond everything; and yet if God’s Word is against it I must be wrong, and my heart is misleading me.”

Again in unbroken silence an hour passed away. Then the thought struck him: “It is not contrary to God’s action! He so loved the world﻿—unbelievers and all﻿—as to give His best and dearest! Can it be wrong to be Godlike?”

===Chinese===
于丹尼斯而言，这一天寸阴如年，满是焦灼悬念与心潮翻涌。有时他会在柜台后垂下头去，热泪盈眶、虔诚迫切地为那位时刻盘踞在心头的姑娘祷告。那天窗外阴雨绵绵，店里门可罗雀，他为此暗暗庆幸不已，若真来了客人，他眼下这副神魂颠倒的模样定是最笨拙不过的伙计。终于熬到了打烊时分，他总算得以独自待着了。回到静谧的卧室，他再一次坦然正视眼下的处境。他双手抱头，低首沉思：“昨晚我*以为*能把这份爱意从心底连根拔去，可到了今晚才发觉，这无异于要把我整颗心硬生生剜出来。我办不到。我打心底里再清楚不过，我不能停止爱她，就像我不能停止呼吸一样。不知不觉间，这份爱意已然滋长到彻底主宰了我；再去立什么誓言、下什么决心，都不过是徒劳的蠢事——每逢最措手不及的当口，那些决心总会变得软弱如水。我究竟该如何是好？”

他一动不动地坐着，浑然不觉光阴流逝，一连几个钟头沉溺在苦痛的思索之中。现实处境、冷静理智乃至《圣经》经训，似乎全都对他的这份爱意投以严厉的责难；然而，纵使这段情愫看似渺茫无望，他骨子里的全部天性却本能地抗拒着“这爱是错的”这一念头。

“纯洁而无私地去爱一个人，怎么可能是错的呢？”他喃喃自语，“像我这般的爱意，本身似乎就带着一股问心无愧的正气——那是一种深植内心的明证，那样笃定有力，超越了一切辩驳——超越了一切世俗道理。可话说回来，倘若上帝的圣言反对这份爱，那便定是我错了，是我的心在将我引入歧途。”

万籁俱寂之中，又是一个钟头过去了。忽地，一个念头如闪电般劈入脑海：“这并不违背上帝的作为！祂竟如此深爱世人——连不信之人也一并爱在其中——甚至将自己至善至爱的独生子也赐予了他们！效法神明之爱，难道也能算是罪过吗？”

===Original===
“It is not wise, it is not safe,” prudence whispered, “to give a worldly, unbelieving spirit the power to influence you that she will have who is first in your heart. What true congeniality can there be? What fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel? As the most intimate friend and companion in life, you should seek one who truly can be *one* with you in all things, and most assuredly so in this vital respect.”

“Ah,” thought Dennis, “that would have been very good advice to give awhile ago. If from the first I could have understood my feelings and danger, I might have steeled my heart against the influences that have brought me to this. But the mischief is done. The words that now, in spite of myself, continually run in my mind, are, ‘What God hath joined together let not man put asunder.’ It seems as if some resistless power had joined my soul to hers, and I find no strength within myself to break the bond. I am not usually irresolute; I think I have principle; and yet I feel that I should not dare make the most solemn vow against this love. I should be all the more weak because conscience does not condemn me. It seems to have a light that reason and knowledge know not of. And yet I wish I could be more sure. I wish I could say to myself, I may be loving hopelessly, but not sinfully. I would take the risk. Indeed I cannot help taking it. Oh, that I could find light, clear and unmistakable!”

He rose, turned up his light, and opened the Pauline precepts. These words struck his eyes, “Art thou bound unto a wife? Seek not to be loosed.” Then, above, the words, “How knowest thou, O man, whether thou shalt save thy wife, even though she be an unbeliever?”

“Am I not bound﻿—bound by that which is God’s link in the chain? It does not seem as if the legal contract could change or strengthen my feelings materially, and while honoring the inviolable rite of marriage, which is God’s law and society’s safety, I know that nothing can more surely bind me to her, so that the spirit, the vital part of the passage, applies to me. Then if through this love I could save her﻿—if by prayer and effort I could bring her feet into the paths of life﻿—I should feel repaid for all that I could possibly suffer. She may slight my human love with its human consummation, but God will not let a life of prayer and true love be wasted, and she may learn here, or know hereafter, that though the world laid many rich gifts at her feet I brought the best of all.”

===Chinese===
“这既不明智，也不稳妥，”审慎之声在耳畔低语，“一个在你心中高居首位的女子，定能左右你的心志，你岂可把这等权柄交给一个贪恋尘世、不信上帝的灵魂？你们之间能有什么真正的心意相通？‘义和不义有什么相交呢？信主的和不信主的有什么相干呢？’作为人生中最亲密的知己与伴侣，你应当寻找一位在凡事上——尤其在这性命攸关的信仰大事上——真正能与你*合而为一*的人。”

“唉，”丹尼斯暗自叹息，“这番忠告若是早些时候说给我听，那确是金玉良言。倘若打一开始我就能看清自己的心意与眼前的险境，或许我还能铁下心肠，抵挡住那股将我引至今日田地的吸引力。然而事已至此，木已成舟。如今不由自主地总在我脑海里回响的，却是那句：‘神配合的，人不可分开。’仿佛有一股不可抗拒的大能，早已将我的灵魂与她的灵魂系在了一处，我在自己身上寻不到半点力量能挣断这重羁绊。我向来并非优柔寡断之人；自问也算是个讲究原则的人；可如今我却觉得，面对这份爱，我连最庄严的绝情誓言都不敢发下。正因为良心并未定我的罪，我才越发软弱无力。这心意里似乎自有某种理智与学识所不曾识得的光明。可我多希望能再笃定些！多希望能对自己说：我的爱或许毫无指望，却决无罪愆。我愿担下这重风险。其实，我也身不由己，非担不可了。哦，但愿我能寻到一道清晰无疑的明光！”

他起身拧亮了灯光，翻开保罗书信的训诲（Pauline precepts）。几行字句骤然映入眼帘：“你有妻子缠着呢，就不要求脱离。”紧接着，再往上看，又是这一句：“你这作丈夫的，怎么知道不能救你的妻子呢——哪怕她是个不信之人？”

“我岂不是也已被系住了吗——被上帝亲手锻造的那一环锁链牢牢系住了吗？一纸世俗的婚约，似乎并不会在实质上改变或加重我的情感；我固然敬重那神圣不可侵犯的婚姻盟礼，深知它是上帝的律法、社会的根基，然而我也明白，再没有什么能比此刻更牢不可破地将我系在她身上——可见这段经文的精神与真髓，正应验在我身上。再者，倘若借着这份爱，我竟能拯救她的灵魂——倘若借着祷告与努力，我能引领她的双足踏上永生之道——那么无论让我吃尽多少苦头，我也觉得值回一切了。她兴许会轻蔑我这凡俗的爱意以及尘世的圆满归宿，但上帝断不会任凭一颗终生祷告、真诚去爱的心白白虚掷；总有一天，无论是在今生知晓，还是在来世顿悟，她终会明白，纵使这世界曾将无数丰厚珍贵的礼物捧到她脚下，惟有我献上的，才是其中至宝。”

===Original===
He looked out, and saw that the early spring dawn was tingeing the horizon.

“A good omen,” he said aloud. “Perhaps the night of this trouble is past, and the dawn is coming. I am convinced that it is not wrong; and I am resolved to make the almost desperate attempt. A mysterious hope, coming from I know not where or what, seems to beckon and encourage me forward.”

Dennis was young.

===Chinese===
他抬眼望向窗外，只见早春的曙光已然染红了天际。

“好兆头，”他朗声说道，“兴许这场苦难的长夜已经过去，黎明正在到来。我深信这并无过错；我已决意放手一搏，去做这番近乎绝望的尝试。一股不知从何而来的神秘希望，仿佛正朝我频频招手，鼓舞着我勇往直前。”

丹尼斯毕竟还年轻。

===Original===
This book 

 is reverently dedicated to the memory of 

 **my mother**

===Chinese===
本书

谨此虔诚敬献，以缅怀

**我的母亲**

## XXIX Dennis’s Love Put to Practical Use / 第二十九章 丹尼斯的爱派上了实际用场

===Original===
The day following his unlucky criticism of the pictures was one of great despondency to Dennis. He had read in Christine’s face that he had wounded her sorely; and, though she knew it to be unintentional, would it not prejudice her mind against him, and snap the slender thread by which he hoped to draw across the gulf between them the cord, and then the cable, that might in time unite their lives?

In the evening his restless, troubled spirit drove him, in spite of the rain, to seek to be at least nearer to her. He felt sure that in the dusk and wrapped in his greatcoat he would not be noticed, but was mistaken, as we have seen. He was rewarded, for he heard her sing as never before, as he did not believe she could sing. For the first time her rich, thoroughly trained voice had the sweetness and power of feeling. To Dennis her song seemed like an appeal, a cry for help, and his heart responded in the deepest sympathy. As he walked homeward he said to himself: “She could be a true artist, perhaps a great one, for she can feel. She has a heart. She has a taste and skill in touch that few can surpass. I can scarcely believe the beautiful coloring and faultless lines of that picture are her work.” He long for a chance to speak with her and explain. He felt that he had so much to say, and in a thousand imaginary ways introduced the subject of her painting. He hoped he might find her sketching in some of the rooms again. He thought that he knew her better for having heard her sing, and that he could speak to her quite frankly.

The next day she came to the store, but passed him without the slightest notice. He hoped she had not seen him, and, as she passed out, so placed himself that she must see him, and secured for his pains only a slight, cold inclination of the head.

“It is as I feared,” he said, bitterly. “She detests me for having spoiled her triumph. She is not just,” he added, angrily. “She has no sense of justice, or she would not blame me. What a mean-spirited craven I should have been had I shrunk away under her taunts yesterday. Well, I can be proud too.”

===Chinese===
对画作失言批评后的第二天，丹尼斯整日陷入深深的沮丧之中。他从克里斯蒂娜的脸上已然看出自己深深刺痛了她；纵使她明知他并非有意，这难道不会让她在心里对他生出成见，从而扯断那根纤细的丝线么？——他原本指望着先借这根丝线渡过两人之间的鸿沟，再牵引出绳索，继而拉起粗缆，假以时日将两人的生命紧紧相连。

傍晚时分，那颗焦灼烦乱的心驱使着他不顾风雨，只求能离她近些，哪怕只是近上几分也好。他原以为暮色苍茫，自己又裹着厚大衣，定不会被人察觉，却不料还是看错了眼，正像我们在前文见到的那样。好在他此行也算得了报偿，因为他听见了她前所未有的歌声——他压根儿不曾料到她竟能唱出这等水准。那副饱满圆润、受过严格训练的歌喉，头一次饱含着真情实感带来的甜美与力量。在丹尼斯听来，她的歌声宛如一声祈求、一声呼救，他的心顿时生出最深切的共鸣，遥相呼应。走在归途上，他暗自思忖：“她本可以成为一名真正的艺术家，甚至是一位伟大的艺术家，因为她懂得动情。她是有心的。她那份鉴赏力与笔下功夫，世上少有人能及。我几乎不敢相信那幅画里绝美的设色和无瑕的线条竟出自她手。”他热切盼望着能有机会同她交谈，把话说开。他觉得自己有千言万语要倾吐，在脑海里设想了无数种引出她画作话题的法子。他期盼着还能在某间屋子里撞见她写生。他觉得既已听过她那番歌声，自己对她便又了解了几分，定能同她坦诚相谈。

次日，她来到店里，却从他身旁径直走过，连正眼也不曾瞧他一下。他还心存侥幸，盼着她只是没看见自己；待她出门时，他便特意站到她必得看见的地方，可一番苦心换来的，却只是她冷淡地微微颔首。

“果然不出我所料，”他苦涩地自语道，“我扫了她的兴，砸了她的得意之举，她便恨上我了。她实在有失公允，”他又气恼地补了一句，“她毫无公道之心，否则也不会怪罪到我头上。昨日若我在她的冷嘲热讽面前畏缩退让，岂不成了个卑怯的小人？好吧，我也是有骨气的。”

===Original===
When she came in again he did not raise his eyes, and when she passed out he was in a distant part of the store. Christine saw no tall muffled figure under her window again, though she had the curiosity to look. That even this humble admirer, for whom she cared not a jot, should show such independence rather nettled and annoyed her for a moment. But she paid no more heed to him than to the other clerks.

But what was the merest jar to Christine’s vanity cost Dennis a desperate struggle. It required no effort on her part to pass him by without a glance. To him it was torture. In a few days she ceased to think about him at all, and only remembered him in connection with her disappointment. But she was restless, could settle down to no work, and had lost her zest in her old pleasures. She tried to act as usual, for she saw her father’s eye was on her. He had not much indulgence for anyone’s weaknesses save his own, and often by a little cold satire would sting her to the very quick. On the other hand, his admiration, openly expressed in a certain courtly gallantry, nourished her pride but not her heart. Though she tried to keep up her usual routine, her manner was forced before him and languid when alone. But he said, “All this will pass away like a cold snap in spring, and the old zest will come again in a few days.”

It did, but from a cause which he could not understand, and which his daughter with consummate skill and care concealed. He thought it was only the old enthusiasm rallying after a sharp frost of disappointment.

Dennis’s pride gave way before her cool and unstudied indifference. It was clearly evident to him that he had no hold upon her life whatever, and how to gain any he did not see. He became more and more dejected.

“She must have a heart, or I could not love her so; but it is so encased in ice I fear I can never reach it.”

===Chinese===
待她再度进店时，丹尼斯便再未抬眼；等她出去时，他早已避去了店堂的另一头。克里斯蒂娜尽管出于好奇朝窗外张望过，却再未瞧见那个裹着大衣的高大身影站在窗下。这么一个她压根儿不放在眼里的卑微倾慕者，竟也敢摆出这般傲骨，一时间着实令她有些恼火和不快。不过很快，她便将他视若寻常店员一般，再不理会。

然而，在克里斯蒂娜不过是虚荣心受了些微触动，于丹尼斯却是一场拼尽全力的苦熬。她从他身旁掠过而不屑一顾，全然不费吹灰之力；于他而言，却无异于凌迟之苦。没过几天，她便将他忘到九霄云外，只有想起自己那桩挫折时，才会顺带记起他来。只是她心里终究躁动不安，什么活计也沉不下心去做，对往日那些消遣也提不起兴致了。她极力装作一切如常，因为她察觉父亲的目光正时刻盯着自己。卢多尔夫先生对旁人的软弱向来没什么宽容——除了他自己——动辄便用几句冷峻的讽刺直戳她的痛处。可另一方面，他以某种近乎宫廷骑士般的殷勤风度流露出的赞赏，又只滋养了她的骄傲，却喂不饱她的心灵。尽管她勉力维持着平日的作息，在父亲面前举止却总显得勉强，独处时更是倦怠乏力。他却只道：“这些不过像春寒料峭一般，过几日便散了，老劲头很快就会回来的。”

果真如此，只是这背后的缘由连他自己也猜不透，而他的女儿亦以老练的心机与谨慎将其深藏不露。他还以为这不过是女儿经历了失望的严霜之后，旧日的热忱又重新振作起来罢了。

丹尼斯那点孤傲，在她这般冷漠而毫不做作的淡然面前终究土崩瓦解。他清清楚楚地意识到，自己在她的生活里根本抓不住半点立足之地，至于该如何去争取，他也茫然无计。他愈发消沉沮丧起来。

“她一定是有心的，不然我也不会如此深爱她；只是那颗心被厚冰封得太死，我只怕自己永远也触碰不到。”

===Original===
That something was wrong with Dennis any friend who cared for him at all might see. The Bruders did, and, with the quick intuitions of woman, Mrs. Bruder half guessed the cause. Mr. Bruder, seeing preoccupation and sometimes weary apathy in Dennis’s face, would say, “Mr. Fleet is not well.”

Then, as even this slight notice of his different appearance seemed to give pain, Mr. Bruder was patiently and kindly blind to his pupil’s inattention.

Dennis faithfully kept up all his duties on Sunday as during the week; but all was now hard work. Some little time after the unlucky morning which he could never think of without an expression of pain, he went to his mission class as usual. He heard his boys recite their lessons, said a few poor lame words in explanation, and then leaned his head listlessly and wearily on his hand. He was startled by hearing a sweet voice say, “Well, Mr. Fleet, are you not going to welcome a new laborer into your corner of the vineyard?”

With a deep flush he saw that Miss Winthrop was in charge of the class next to him, and that he had been oblivious to her presence nearly an hour. He tried to apologize. But she interrupted him, saying: “Mr. Fleet, you are not well. Anyone can see that.”

Then Dennis blushed as if he had a raging fever, and she was perplexed.

===Chinese===
凡是稍稍关心丹尼斯的朋友，都能看出他有些不对劲。布鲁德一家便看出来了；凭着女人敏锐的直觉，布鲁德太太甚至猜到了几分缘由。布鲁德先生见丹尼斯脸上常带着心神不属、有时甚至是倦怠木然的神色，便会说上一句：“弗利特先生身子不适。”

后来他发觉，就连这样略微点破他神态异样，似乎也会令丹尼斯难受，于是这位厚道仁慈的先生便耐心而又体贴地假装看不见门生的失神。

无论平日还是礼拜天，丹尼斯依旧一丝不苟地履行着自己的一切职责，只是眼下桩桩件件都成了苦差。在那个令他一想起来便面露痛楚的不幸清晨过去没多久，他又如常去布道学校教他的布道班。他听男孩们背完功课，敷衍地讲解了几句苍白无力的话，便百无聊赖、疲惫不堪地用手支住头。忽然，一个甜美的声音传来，惊得他猛然回神：“怎么，弗利特先生，您的葡萄园这一角添了个新做工的，您也不打算欢迎一声吗？”

丹尼斯顿时满脸涨红，这才发觉温思罗普小姐正带着紧挨着他的那一班，而自己竟在将近一个钟头里对她的存在浑然不觉。他连忙想要致歉，她却打断道：“弗利特先生，您病了。任谁都看得出来。”

丹尼斯登时红透了脸，仿佛发起了高烧一般，反倒叫温思罗普小姐一头雾水。

===Original===
The closing exercises of the school now occupied them and then they walked out together.

“Mr. Fleet,” she said, “you never accepted my invitation. We have not seen you at our house. But perhaps your circle of friends is so large that you do not wish to add to it.”

Dennis could not forbear a smile at the suggestion, but he said, in apology, “I do not visit anyone, save a gentleman from whom I am taking lessons.”

“Do you mean to say that you have no friends at all in this great city?”

“Well, I suppose that is nearly the truth; that is, in the sense you use the term. My teacher and his wife﻿—”

===Chinese===
这时学堂散学的仪式牵住了他们的心思，随后两人便一同走了出来。

“弗利特先生，”她开口道，“我的邀请您一直没有应允。我们家里始终没见着您的身影。莫非您的朋友圈子太大，实在不愿再添新友了？”

听她这么一说，丹尼斯忍不住微微一笑，致歉道：“除了教我学画的那位先生，我平日从不登门拜访任何人。”

“您的意思是，您在这座大城里竟然一个朋友也没有吗？”

“嗯，这话大抵不差；至少按您说的那种‘朋友’来看是如此。我的老师和他的太太——”

===Original===
“Nonsense! I mean friends of one’s own age, people of the same culture and status as yourself. I think we require such society, as truly as we need food and air. I did not mean those whom business or duty brought you in contact with, or who are friendly or grateful as a matter of course.”

“I have made no progress since my introduction to society at Miss Brown’s,” said Dennis.

“But you had the sincere and cordial offer of introduction,” said Miss Winthrop, looking a little hurt.

“I feel hardly fit for society,” said Dennis, all out of sorts with himself. “It seems that I can only blunder and give pain. But I am indeed grateful for your kindness.”

Miss Winthrop looked into his worn, pale face, and instinctively knew that something was wrong, and she felt real sympathy for the lonely young man, isolated among thousands. She said, gently but decidedly: “I did mean my invitation kindly, and I truly wished you to come. The only proof you can give that you appreciate my courtesy is to accept an invitation for tomorrow evening. I intend having a little musical entertainment.”

===Chinese===
“胡说！我说的是年纪相仿、教养与身份都跟您相当的朋友。依我看，人离不开这样的交往，就像离不开食物和空气一样。我指的可不是因公事、本分而有来往的人，也不是那些按常理本就该与您交好或心怀感激的人。”

“自从在布朗小姐家初次步入社交场之后，我便再无半点长进了。”丹尼斯说。

“可您当时明明得到过诚心实意的引荐之邀呀。”温思罗普小姐说道，神情略显委屈。

“我觉得自己实在不配跻身社交界，”丹尼斯浑身不自在地说道，“我似乎只会笨手笨脚地出丑，还会惹人伤心。不过，您的美意我实在是感激不尽。”

温思罗普小姐凝视着他那张憔悴苍白的脸庞，本能地察觉出一定出了什么事，对这个身处芸芸众生之中却形单影只的年轻人油然而生真切的同情。她语气柔和却颇为坚定地说道：“我那番邀请确是一片诚意，也真心盼着您来。您若想证明自己领了我的情，唯一的法子便是答应明天晚上来赴约。我打算办一个小小的音乐雅集。”

===Original===
Quick as light flashed the thought, “Christine will be there.” He said, promptly: “I will come, and thank you for the invitation. If I am awkward, you must remember that I have never mingled in Chicago society, and for a long time not in any.”

She smiled merrily at him, and said, “Don’t do anything dreadful, Mr. Fleet.”

He caught her mood, and asked what had brought her down from her theological peak to such a valley of humiliation as a mission school.

“You and Miss Ludolph,” she answered, seriously. “Between you, you gave me such a lesson that afternoon at Miss Brown’s that I have led a different life ever since. Christine made all as dark as despair, and against that darkness you placed the fiery Cross. I have tried to cling to the true cross ever since. Now He could not say to me, ‘Inasmuch as ye did it not.’ And oh!” said she, turning to Dennis with a smile full of the light of Heaven, “His service is so very sweet! I heard last week that teachers were wanted at this mission school, so I came, and am glad to find you a neighbor.”

Dennis’s face also kindled at her enthusiasm, but after a moment grew sad again.

===Chinese===
电光火石间，一个念头掠过他的脑海：“克里斯蒂娜也会去。”他立时答道：“我一定去，多谢您的盛情相邀。倘若我举止局促笨拙，还望您念在我在芝加哥从没走动过社交场，而且许久不曾交际的份上，多多包涵。”

她朝他快活地一笑，说道：“可别做出什么吓人的事来呀，弗利特先生。”

他也被她的兴致感染，便问她怎么竟从神学的云端高峰，屈尊降贵来到布道学校这片“谦卑的山谷”了。

“还不是因为您和卢多尔夫小姐，”她郑重其事地答道，“那天下午在布朗小姐家里，你们俩合力给我上了那样深刻的一课，打那以后，我便彻底过上了另一番生活。克里斯蒂娜把一切都描摹得如绝望般漆黑，而您在那一团黑暗之中立起了熊熊燃烧的十字架。从那时起，我便竭力紧紧抓住那座真正的十字架。如今，他总不至于对我说：‘这些事你们既没有作’了。哎呀！”她转向丹尼斯，绽开一个洋溢着天国光辉的微笑，“侍奉他真是无比甘甜！上星期我听说这所布道学校缺教员，便过来了，真高兴能与您作伴比邻。”

丹尼斯的脸庞也因她的热忱而焕发出光采，可片刻之后，神色却又黯淡下来。

===Original===
“I do not always give so lifeless a lesson as today,” he said, in a low voice.

“Mr. Fleet, you are not well. I can see that you look worn and greatly wearied. Are you not in some way overtaxing yourself?”

Again that sensitive flush, but he only said: “I assure you I am well. Perhaps I have worked a little hard. That is all.”

“Well, then, come to our house and play a little tomorrow evening,” she answered from the platform of a street car, and was borne away.

Dennis went to his lonely room, full of self-reproach.

===Chinese===
“我往常讲课，并不总是像今天这样死气沉沉的。”他低声说道。

“弗利特先生，您身子真的不好。我看得出来，您神情倦怠，累得不轻。您是不是在什么事上太耗费心神了？”

那阵敏感的红晕又涌上了他的脸颊，但他只答道：“我向您保证，我好好的。兴许只是近来干活儿略紧了些，仅此而已。”

“那好，明天晚上一定要来我家，弹奏一曲吧。”她站在一辆有轨马车的踏板上朝他应道，随即被车带走了。

丹尼斯回到自己孤寂的斗室，满心自责。

===Original===
“Does she find Christ’s service so sweet, and do I find it so dull and hard? Does human love alone constrain me, and not the love of Christ? Truly I am growing weak. Everyone says I look ill. I think I am, in body and soul, and am ceasing to be a man; but with God’s help I will be one﻿—and what is more, a Christian. I thank you, Miss Winthrop; you have helped me more than I have helped you. I will accept your invitation to go out into the world. I will no longer mope, brood, and perish in the damp and shade of my own sick fancies. If I cannot win her, I can at least be a man without her;” and he felt better and stronger than he had done for a long time. The day was breaking again.

In accordance with a custom that was growing with him ever since the memorable evening when Bill Cronk befriended him, he laid the whole matter before his Heavenly Father, as a child tells an earthly parent all his heart. Then he added one simple prayer, “Guide me in all things.”

The next day was brighter and better than its forerunners. “For some reason I feel more like myself,” he thought. After the excitement and activity of a busy day, he said, “I can conquer this, if I must.”

===Chinese===
“她侍奉基督竟觉得如此甘甜，我却觉得这般枯燥艰难么？难道驱使我的仅仅是世俗男女之爱，而不是基督之爱吗？我的确变得软弱了。人人都说我瞧着像病了。我看我是真的病了——连身带心都病了，快要不像个男子汉了；但靠着上帝的助佑，我要重新做回一个堂堂正正的人——更何况，还要做一个基督徒。谢谢您，温思罗普小姐，您帮我的，远比我帮您的还要多。我要接受您的邀请，走出去看看这世面。我再不要独自垂头丧气、钻牛角尖，在自己病态幻想的阴湿角落里枯萎下去了。即便赢不得她，没有她我至少也得像个男子汉一样活下去。”这一念既定，他顿时觉得身心比许久以来都要爽朗强健得多。天色又一次透出曙光。

自从比尔·克朗克伸出援手、慷慨相助那个难忘的夜晚起，他便渐渐养成了一个习惯：像孩童向人世间的父母倾诉心腹一般，把整桩心事原原本本呈明在天父面前。随后，他又加上了一句简简单单的祷告：“求您在万事上指引我。”

次日果然比前几天明朗舒畅得多。“不知怎的，我觉得自己又恢复了几分本色。”他想。经历了一整天忙碌的奔波与劳作带来的振奋之后，他说：“真到了非克服不可的地步，我也熬得过去。”

===Original===
But when he had made his simple toilet, and was on his way to Miss Winthrop’s residence, his heart began to flutter strangely, and he knew the reason. Miss Winthrop welcomed him most cordially, and put him at his ease in a moment, as only a true lady can. Then she turned to receive other guests. He looked around. Christine was not there; and his heart sank like lead. “She will not be here,” he sighed. But the guests had not ceased coming, and every new arrival caused a flutter of hopes and fears. He both longed and dreaded to meet her. At last, when he had almost given up seeing her, suddenly she appeared, advancing up the parlor on her father’s arm. Never had she seemed so dazzlingly beautiful. He was just then talking to Mr. Winthrop, and for a few moments that gentleman was perplexed at his incoherent answers and the changes in his face. Having paid their respects to the daughter, Mr. and Miss Ludolph came toward Mr. Winthrop, and of course Dennis had to meet them. Having greeted them warmly, Mr. Winthrop said, “Of course you do not need an introduction to Mr. Fleet.”

Dennis had shrunk a little into the background, and at first they had not noticed him. Mr. Ludolph said, good-naturedly, “Glad to see you, Mr. Fleet, and will be still more glad to hear your fine voice.”

But Christine merely bowed as to one with whom her acquaintance was slight, and turned away. At first Dennis had blushed, and his heart had fluttered like a young girl’s; but, as she turned so coolly away, his native pride and obstinacy were aroused.

“She shall speak to me and do me justice,” he muttered. “She must understand that I spoke unconsciously on that miserable morning, and am not to be blamed. As I am a man, I will speak boldly and secure recognition.” But as the little company mingled and conversed before the music commenced, no opportunity offered. He determined to show her, however, that he was no country boor, and with skill and taste made himself agreeable.

===Chinese===
然而，当他简简单单拾掇妥当，动身前往温思罗普小姐府上时，他的心却莫名其妙地剧烈怦动起来，而他也深知其中的缘故。温思罗普小姐极其热忱地迎候了他，片刻间便令他如沐春风、自在安然——这种本事，唯独真正的大家闺秀才具备。随后她转身去迎别的宾客。丹尼斯环顾四周，不见克里斯蒂娜的踪影，一颗心顿时像铅块般沉了下去。“她不会来了。”他暗暗叹息。然而宾客仍在陆续到来，每进来一位新客，便在他心头激起一阵希望与惶惑交织的悸动。他既盼着见她，又畏惧见她。终于，就在他几乎要死心、以为再见不着她时，她竟蓦地现身了，挽着父亲的手臂，仪态万方地顺着客厅款款走来。她从未显得像今夜这般光彩夺目、美艳逼人。此刻丹尼斯恰巧正与温思罗普先生（Mr. Winthrop）攀谈，一时间那位绅士被他语无伦次的应答和脸上的风云变幻弄得莫名其妙。卢多尔夫父女向主人家千金致意过后，便朝温思罗普先生这边走来，丹尼斯自然免不了要与他们照面。温思罗普先生热情地迎上去寒暄了一番，随即说道：“当然了，弗利特先生就不必我替你们引荐了。”

丹尼斯原本略微退到了人后，起初他们倒也没留意到他。卢多尔夫先生和气地说道：“很高兴见到您，弗利特先生，待会儿能再听听您那副好嗓子，我就更高兴了。”

可克里斯蒂娜却只是朝他微微颔首，那神态宛如对待一个仅有几面之缘的泛泛之交，随即便转过身去。起初丹尼斯双颊飞红，心跳得像个小姑娘一般；可一见她如此冷漠地转身走开，他骨子里的自尊与拗劲顿时被激了起来。

“她非得跟我说话，还我一个公道不可，”他暗暗咬牙，“她必须明白，那个倒霉的早晨我说的话纯属无心，怪不得我。只要我还算个男子汉，就定要大大方方地开口，讨回该有的敬重。”然而在奏乐尚未开场前，众宾客三三两两凑在一处寒暄叙话，却始终没有搭话的空隙。不过，他打定主意要让她瞧瞧自己绝非乡野粗鄙之辈，于是谈吐得体、举止优雅，赢得众人满心欢喜。

===Original===
Christine furtively watched him. She was surprised to see him, as the idea of meeting him in society as an equal had scarcely been suggested before. But when she saw that he greeted one after another with grace and ease, and that all seemed to enjoy his conversation, so that a little knot of Miss Winthrop’s most intelligent guests were about him at last, she felt that it would be no great condescension on her part to be a little more affable. In her heart, though, she had not forgiven the unconscious words that had smitten to the ground her ambitious hopes.

Then again, his appearance deeply interested her. A suppressed excitement and power, seen in the glow and fire of his dark eyes, and felt in his tones, stirred her languid pulses.

“He is no vapid society-man,” she said to herself; and her artist eye was gratified by the changes in his noble face.

“Look at Fleet,” whispered her father; “could you believe he was sweeping the store the other day? Well, if we don’t find out his worth and get what we can from him, the world will. We ought to have had him up to sing before this, but I have been so busy since your illness that it slipped my mind.”

===Chinese===
克里斯蒂娜暗中留神观察着他。能在社交场上以平等身份与他相遇，她着实感到有些意外，因为此前这种念头在她心里几乎从未起过。但见他应对众人从容有度、风度翩翩，人人都极爱听他高谈阔论，到后来竟有一小圈温思罗普小姐席上最有见识的宾客围拢在他身旁，她便觉得自己若对他稍加和颜悦色，倒也不算太折身份。只是在她心底里，她依然没原谅那些无心之言——正是那几句话，把她满怀野心的期望击得粉碎。

更何况，丹尼斯这副神采着实深深吸引了她。一股压抑着的激动与力量，流露在他深邃黑眸闪烁的光芒与火焰之中，也渗透在他的言辞声调里，拨动了她向来懒散迟缓的脉搏。

“他可不是那些庸俗无聊的社交场浪子，”她暗自赞叹；而她那双艺术家的眼睛，也为他这张俊朗英挺的脸上不断掠过的丰富神情所折服。

“瞧瞧弗利特，”她父亲低声耳语道，“你敢信前些日子他还在店里扫地么？哼，如果我们不赶紧发掘他的才干、替自己好好用上几分，旁人可就要抢先了。早先本该请他上家里来唱歌的，只是打你病后我一直忙得不可开交，倒把这茬儿给忘了。”

===Original===
Miss Winthrop now led Christine to the piano, and she played a classical piece of music in faultless taste. Then followed duets, solos, quartets, choruses, and instrumental pieces, for nearly all present were musical amateurs. Under the inspiration of this soul-stirring art, coldness and formality melted away, and with jest and brilliant repartee, alternating with song, there gathered around Miss Winthrop’s piano such a group as could never grace the parlors of Miss Brown. Sometimes they would carry a new and difficult piece triumphantly through; again they would break down, with much laughter and good-natured rallying.

Dennis, as a stranger, held back at first; but those who remembered his singing at the tableau party were clamorous to hear him again, and they tested and tried his voice during the evening in many and varied ways. But he held his own, and won greener laurels than ever. He did his very best, for he was before one whom he would rather please than all the world; moreover, her presence seemed to inspire him to do better than when alone. Christine, like the others, could not help listening with delight to his rich, clear tenor, and Mr. Ludolph was undisguised in his admiration.

“I declare, Mr. Fleet, I have been depriving myself of a good deal of pleasure. I meant to have you up to sing with us before, but we have been under such a press of business of late! But the first evening I am disengaged you must surely come.”

Christine had noticed how quietly and almost indifferently Dennis had taken the many compliments showered on him before, but now, when her father spoke, his face flushed, and a sudden light came into his eyes. Dennis had thought, “I can then see and speak to her.” Every now and then she caught his eager, questioning, and almost appealing glance, but he made no advances. “He thinks I am angry because of his keen criticism of my picture. For the sake of my own pride, I must not let him think that I care so much about his opinion;” and Christine resolved to let some of the ice thaw that had formed between them. Moreover, in spite of herself, when she was thrown into his society, he greatly interested her. He seemed to have just what she had not. He could meet her on her own ground in matters of taste, and then, in contrast with her cold, negative life, he was so earnest and positive. “Perhaps papa spoke for us both,” she thought, “and I have been depriving myself of a pleasure also, for he certainly interests while most men only weary me.”

===Chinese===
此时，温思罗普小姐将克里斯蒂娜引至钢琴前，克里斯蒂娜以无懈可击的品味演奏了一首古典乐曲。紧接着便是二重唱、独唱、四重唱、大合唱以及器乐合奏，盖因在座诸位几乎都是热爱音乐的行家里手。在这门直击灵魂的艺术感召下，生分与拘谨渐渐融化，戏谑与机敏的妙语间杂着阵阵歌声，温思罗普小姐钢琴四周聚起了一群绝非布朗小姐客厅所能增色生辉的雅客。有时他们一鼓作气把一首难度颇高的新曲完美奏完；有时却半途卡壳，于是满屋哄笑，彼此打趣逗乐，好不融洽。

丹尼斯作为初来乍到的生客，起初还有些拘束退让；但那些还记得他在活人画游艺会（tableau party）上动人歌喉的人纷纷嚷着要他再献一曲，整个晚上变着法子试探、品鉴他的嗓音。可他稳稳当当应对自如，赢回了比往日更耀眼的喝彩。他使出了浑身解数，只因眼前站着一个他宁可取悦她一人、胜过博得全世界欢心的人；况且，她的在场似乎也激发了他，使他唱得比独处时更为出色。克里斯蒂娜同众人一样，不由自主地沉醉在他那醇厚清亮的男高音里，卢多尔夫先生更是毫不掩饰自己的赞赏之情。

“我真要说句实在话，弗利特先生，我先前真是平白错过了好大的耳福！我早先就打算请您上我家去同我们一块儿唱唱的，偏巧近来店里事务繁杂，脱不开身！不过，只要一有空闲的晚上，您可千万得赏光过来。”

克里斯蒂娜一直留意到，先前面对应接不暇的称赞，丹尼斯始终神色平淡，几乎漫不经心；可此刻她父亲话音刚落，他脸上便骤然泛起红光，眸子里也迸发出一道亮色。丹尼斯心里想的是：“那样我就能见到她、跟她说话了。”她时不时便撞见他投来的那道热切、探询、近乎恳求的目光，但他始终不曾贸然上前。“他准是以为我还在为他尖锐批评我那幅画而生气呢。为了顾全我自己的颜面，我可不能叫他觉得我有多在乎他的看法。”于是克里斯蒂娜暗下决心，让两人之间结起的那层坚冰融化几分。何况，身处他这般氛围之中，她自己也不由自主地对他大感兴味。他身上仿佛正有着她所匮乏的东西。在品味鉴赏上，他能与她并驾齐驱、旗鼓相当；更难得的是，与她那冷漠消极的人生相比，他是那样炽热真挚、积极昂扬。“兴许爸爸那句话正说中了我们俩的心思，”她心想，“我也一直平白错失了一桩乐事，因为旁人多半叫我厌倦，唯独他，确实令我兴味盎然。”

===Original===
Between ten and eleven supper was announced; not the prodigal abundance under which the brewer’s table had groaned, but a dainty, elegant little affair, which inspired and promoted social feeling, though the “spirit of wine” was absent. The eye was feasted as truly as the palate. Christine had stood near Dennis as the last piece was sung, and he turned and said in a low, eager tone, “May I have the pleasure of waiting on you at supper?”

She hesitated, but his look was so wistful that she could not well refuse, so with a slight smile she bowed assent, and placed the tips of her little gloved hand on his arm, which so trembled that she looked inquiringly and curiously into his face. It was very pale, as was ever the case when he felt deeply. He waited on her politely but silently at first. She sat in an angle, somewhat apart from the others. As he stood by her side, thinking how to refer to the morning in the showroom, she said: “Mr. Fleet, you are not eating anything, and you look as if you had been living on air of late﻿—very unlike your appearance when you so efficiently aided me in the rearrangement of the store. I am delighted that you keep up the better order of things.” Dennis’s answer was quite irrelevant.

“Miss Ludolph,” he said, abruptly, “I saw that I gave you pain that morning in the showroom. If you only knew how the thought has pained me!”

Christine flushed almost angrily, but said, coldly, “Mr. Fleet, that is a matter you can never understand, therefore we had better dismiss the subject.”

But Dennis had determined to break the ice between them at any risk, so he said, firmly but respectfully: “Miss Ludolph, I did understand all, the moment I saw your face that day. I do understand how you have felt since, better than you imagine.”

===Chinese===
十点至十一点之间，仆人通传夜宵备妥；这并非那位啤酒商府上压弯了桌腿的奢靡盛宴，而是一席精致清雅的小宴，虽则席间并无“酒神”助兴，却最能催生并助长宾客间的雅兴欢谈。满席珍馐美器，赏心悦目一如悦人口腹。唱罢最后一曲时，克里斯蒂娜恰巧站在丹尼斯近旁，于是他转过身来，压低嗓音急切地问道：“不知我是否有幸在夜宵时为您效劳？”

她迟疑了一下，可他那目光实在太过殷切恳挚，叫她不好回绝，便微微一笑，点头应允，随即把戴着手套的纤细手指轻轻搭上他的臂弯——他的手臂竟颤抖得厉害，令她不禁惊疑又好奇地抬眼打量他的脸庞。那张脸苍白如纸，每逢他动了深情时，向来如此。起初他殷勤侍奉茶点，却始终一言不发。她在屋角一处稍稍避开旁人的地方落座。当他立在她身旁，正盘算着该如何提起展厅那个早晨的事时，她却开口了：“弗利特先生，您自己怎么半点东西也不吃？瞧您近来的模样，倒像是只靠喝风过日子似的——跟当初您那样利落地帮我重新布置店堂时，简直判若两人。如今店里依然保持着那样井然的新气象，我心里真是高兴极了。”丹尼斯的回答却显得颇为牛头不对马嘴。

“卢多尔夫小姐，”他唐突地说道，“展厅那个早晨，我看得出自己伤了您的心。但愿您能明白，一想到这件事，我心里有多痛楚！”

克里斯蒂娜顿时涨红了脸，几乎动了怒，冷冷说道：“弗利特先生，那件事您是永远不会明白的，因此我们还是别再提它为好。”

可丹尼斯早已立定主意，无论冒多大风险也要打破两人之间的僵局，于是他语气坚定而不失恭敬地说道：“卢多尔夫小姐，那天我一看见您的神情，便全都明白了。打那以后您心里的滋味，我也比您想象的更明白。”

===Original===
His manner and words were so assured that she raised a startled face to his, but asked coldly and in an indifferent manner, “What can you know of my feelings?”

“I know,” said Dennis, in a low tone, looking searchingly into her face, from which cool composure was fast fading﻿—“I know your dearest hope was to be among the first in art. You staked that hope on your success in a painting that required a power which you do not possess.” Christine became very pale, but from her eyes shone a light before which most men would have quailed. But Dennis’s love was so true and strong that he could wound her for the sake of the healing and life he hoped to bring, and he continued﻿—“On that morning this cherished hope for the future failed you, not because of my words, but because your artist eye saw that my words were true. You have since been unhappy﻿—”

“What right have *you*﻿—you who were but a few days since﻿—who are a stranger﻿—what right have you to speak thus to me?”

“I know what you would say, Miss Ludolph,” he answered, a slight flush coming into his pale face. “Friends may be humble and yet true. But am I not right?”

“I have no claim on your friendship,” said Christine, coldly. “But, for the sake of argument, grant that you are right, what follows?” and she looked at him more eagerly than she knew. She felt that he had read her very soul and was deeply moved, and again the superstitious feeling crept over her, “That young man is in some way connected with my destiny.”

===Chinese===
他的态度与言辞竟如此笃定，令她惊诧地抬起脸来望向他，嘴上却仍冷淡而漫不经心地问道：“您能知道我什么心思？”

“我知道，”丹尼斯低沉地说道，目光如炬地直视着她的脸，看着那上面原本冷峻镇定的神色飞快消退，“我知道您平生最大的指望，便是在艺术界跻身顶尖之列。您把这份指望全都押在了一幅画的成败上，而要画好那幅画，偏偏需要一种您并不具备的力量。”克里斯蒂娜霎时脸色惨白，双眸中却射出一道令大多数男人都要胆寒的寒光。可丹尼斯的爱实在太过真挚深沉，为了能给她带去他所企盼的医治与生机，他竟敢刺痛她，于是继续说道：“那个早晨，您对未来怀抱的这桩珍贵希望落了空，这并不是因为我的话，而是因为您那双艺术家的眼睛看出我的话句句属实。打那以后，您便一直闷闷不乐——”

“*你*有什么权利——你几天前还不过是个……不过是个素昧平生的外人——你有什么权利这样对我说话？”

“我知道您想说什么，卢多尔夫小姐，”他答道，苍白的脸上泛起一抹微红，“地位卑微的人，也可以是真正的朋友。难道我说得不对吗？”

“我可没攀过您的交情，”克里斯蒂娜冷冷地道，“不过姑且顺着您的话说，就算您说对了，那又怎样？”她望着他的目光，比她自己意识到的还要迫切几分。她觉得他竟一眼看穿了自己的灵魂深处，心头大为震动；与此同时，那个带几分迷信色彩的念头又一次悄然爬上她的心头：“这个年轻人，不知何故，竟与我的命运牵连在了一起。”

===Original===
Dennis saw his power and proceeded rapidly, for he knew they might be interrupted at any moment; and so they would have been had anything less interesting than eating occupied the attention of others.

“I saw in the picture what in your eyes and mine would be a fatal defect﻿—the lack of life and true feeling﻿—the lack of power to live. I did not know who painted it, but felt that anyone who could paint as well as that, and yet leave out the soul, as it were, had not the power to put it in. No artist of such ability could willingly or ignorantly have permitted such a defect.”

Christine’s eyes sank, their fire faded out, and her face had the pallor of one listening to her doom. This deeper feeling mastered the momentary resentment against the hand that was wounding her, and she forgot him, and all, in her pain and despair.

In a low, earnest tone Dennis continued: “But since I have come to know who the artist is, since I have studied the picture more fully, and have taken the liberty of some observation”﻿—Christine hung on his lips breathlessly, and Dennis spoke slowly, marking the effect of every word﻿—“I have come to the decided belief that the lady who painted that picture can reach the sphere of true and highest art.”

The light that stole into Christine’s face under his slow, emphatic words was like a rosy dawn in June; and the thought flashed through Dennis’s mind, “If an earthly hope can so light up her face, what will be the effect of a heavenly one?”

===Chinese===
丹尼斯察觉了自己言语的分量，便趁势飞快说了下去，因为他知道他们随时可能被人打断——事实上若不是眼下正值用膳，旁人的心思都拴在吃喝上，他们早就被人打扰了。

“我在那幅画里，看到了在您眼里和在我眼里都堪称致命的缺陷——缺乏生机与真情——缺乏活起来的力量。那时我并不知道画作者是谁，只觉得谁若能画到这般高妙的境界，却仿佛独独漏掉了灵魂，那他本身大约便没有将灵魂注入画中的能力。但凡有这等造诣的画师，绝不会有意或懵懂无知到容许这等缺陷存在。”

克里斯蒂娜垂下双眸，眼里的火焰骤然熄灭，脸色惨白得宛如正在聆听末日宣判的囚徒。这股更深沉的痛楚压倒了对那只刺伤她之手的一时怨怒，在悲痛与绝望之中，她忘却了他，也忘却了一切。

丹尼斯压低嗓音，诚挚地继续说道：“然而自从我知道了那位画师究竟是谁，自从我更仔细地端详过那幅画，又冒昧地留心观察过一番之后——”克里斯蒂娜屏住呼吸，痴痴地盯着他的双唇，丹尼斯则一字一句缓缓道来，细细留意着每个字在她脸上的回响，“我愈发坚定地相信，绘出那幅画的小姐，完全能够臻至真正最高境界的艺术殿堂。”

听着他那缓慢而掷地有声的话语，一抹光采悄然染上克里斯蒂娜的脸庞，宛如六月清晨粉红的朝霞；一个念头在丹尼斯心头一闪而过：“若连尘世的盼望都能叫她的脸庞焕发出这等光辉，天国的盼望又该在她脸上绽出何等光华呢？”

===Original===
For a moment she sat as one entranced, looking at a picture far off in the future. His words had been so earnest and assured that they seemed reality. Suddenly she turned on him a look as grateful and happy as the former one had been full of pain and anger, and said: “Ah, do not deceive me, do not flatter. You cannot know the sweetness and power of the hope you are inspiring. To be disappointed again would be death. If you are trifling with me I will never forgive you,” she added, in sudden harshness, her brow darkening.

“Nor should I deserve to be forgiven if I deceived you in a matter that to you is so sacred.”

“But how﻿—how am I to gain this magic power to make faces feel and live on canvas?”

“You must believe. You yourself must feel.”

She looked at him with darkening face, and then in a sudden burst of passion said: “I don’t believe; I can’t feel. All this is mockery, after all.”

===Chinese===
有一瞬，她坐着宛如入了迷一般，凝望着遥远未来中的一幅图景。他的话语那样诚挚笃定，竟仿佛已然成了现实。骤然间，她转向他，眼中流露出与方才的痛楚和愤恨同样浓烈的感激与欢喜，说道：“啊，可别骗我，别奉承我。您想象不到您燃起的这份希望是何等甜美、何等有力。若再落空一次，我简直会死。倘若您是在拿我寻开心，我一辈子都不会原谅您！”她忽地话锋一转，语气变得严厉，眉峰紧锁。

“倘若我在对您如此神圣的事上欺瞒于您，我也万万不配得到原谅。”

“可我究竟要怎样——怎样才能获得这种点石成金的魔力，让画布上的面孔活起来、动起情来呢？”

“您必须信。您自己必须动情。”

她脸色一沉地望着他，随即情绪猛地爆发出来，说道：“我不信；我也动不了情。说到底，这一切全都是空话戏弄。”

===Original===
“No!” said Dennis, in the deep, assured tone that ever calms and secures attention. “This is not mockery. I speak the words of truth and soberness. You do not believe, but that is not the same as cannot. And permit me to contradict you when I say you *do* feel. On this subject so near your heart you feel most deeply﻿—feel as I never knew anyone feel before. This proves you capable of feeling on other and higher subjects, and what you feel your trained and skilful hand can portray. You felt on the evening of that miserable day, and sang as I never heard you sing before. Your tones then would move any heart, and my tears fell with the rain in sympathy: I could not help it.”

Her bosom rose and fell tumultuously, and her breath came hard and quick.

“Oh, if I could believe you were right!”

“I know I am right,” he said, so decidedly that again hope grew rosy and beautiful in her face.

“Then again,” he continued, eagerly, “see what an advantage you have over the most of us. Your power of imitation is wonderful. *You can copy anything you see.*”

===Chinese===
“不！”丹尼斯用他那总能安抚人心、引人倾听的深沉而笃定的语调说道，“这绝非空话戏弄。我所言句句皆是真实清醒之辞。您如今是不信，可‘不信’并不等于‘不能’。请允许我驳斥您一句——您说自己动不了情，其实您*确实*能够动情。在这桩最牵动您心肠的事上，您动情之深——实是我生平从未见过的。这就证明您原是有能力对其他更崇高的事物动情的，而凡是您心头所感，您那双训练有素、技艺精湛的手便都能描绘出来。在那倒霉一天的傍晚，您动了真情，唱出了我从未听您唱过的绝妙歌声。那时您的声调足可打动世上任何一颗心，我感同身受，泪水伴着雨水一同落下：我实在情不自禁。”

她的胸口剧烈起伏，呼吸急促而沉重。

“啊，但愿我能相信您说的是真的！”

“我知道我说的千真万确。”他斩钉截铁地说道，于是希望的红晕又一次娇艳地爬上了她的脸颊。

“况且，”他热切地续道，“您还占着旁人大多望尘莫及的天分呢。您的摹写本领简直出神入化。*但凡您亲眼见过的东西，您都能临摹下来。*”

===Original===
“Good evening, Miss Ludolph. Where have you been hiding? I have twice made the tour of the supper-room in my search,” broke in the voluble Mr. Mellen. Then he gave Dennis a cool stare, who acted as if unconscious of his presence. An expression of disgust flitted across Christine’s face at the interruption, or the person﻿—perhaps both﻿—and she was about to shake him off that Dennis might speak further, when Miss Winthrop and others came up, and there was a general movement back to the parlors.

“Why, Christine, what is the matter?” asked her friend. “You look as if you had a fever. What has Mr. Fleet been saying?”

“Oh, we have had an argument on my hobby, art, and of course don’t agree, and so got excited in debate.”

Miss Winthrop glanced keenly at them and said, “I would like to have heard it, for it was Greek meeting Greek.”

“To what art or *trade* did Mr. Fleet refer?” asked Mr. Mellen, with an insinuation that all understood.

===Chinese===
“晚上好，卢多尔夫小姐。您躲到哪儿去了？我为了找您，已经把夜宵厅兜了两圈啦。”口若悬河的梅伦先生（Mr. Mellen）冷不防插了进来。说着，他冷冷瞥了丹尼斯一眼，而丹尼斯则只当他不存在一般。克里斯蒂娜脸上掠过一丝厌恶的神情，不知是恼他打断谈话，还是讨厌他这个人——兴许两者兼而有之——她正想把梅伦打发走，好叫丹尼斯继续说下去，偏偏温思罗普小姐一行人这时走了过来，众人便一道往客厅那边回转。

“哎呀，克里斯蒂娜，这是怎么了？”她的女伴问道，“瞧你脸上像发了烧似的。弗利特先生方才跟你说什么呢？”

“哦，我们正就我的心头好——艺术——争辩了一番，意见自然合不到一块儿去，争着争着倒动起气来了。”

温思罗普小姐敏锐地扫了他们俩一眼，笑道：“真可惜我没听见，想来定是棋逢对手、精彩得很。”

“不知弗利特先生指的，究竟是哪门子手艺还是*营生*呢？”梅伦先生阴阳怪气地问道，那弦外之音在场众人一听便知。

===Original===
“One that you do not understand,” said Christine, keenly.

The petted and spoiled millionaire flushed angrily a moment, and then said with a bow: “You are right, Miss Ludolph. Mr. Fleet is acquainted with one or two arts that I have never had the pleasure of learning.”

“He has at least learned the art of being a gentleman,” was the sharp retort.

The young man’s face grew darker, and he said, “From the *sweeping* nature of your remarks, I perceive that Mr. Fleet is high in your favor.”

“A poor pun made in poorer taste,” was all the comfort he got from Christine.

===Chinese===
“一门您压根儿不懂的艺术。”克里斯蒂娜尖刻地回敬道。

这位受尽娇惯宠坏的百万富翁顿时羞恼地涨红了脸，随即却又鞠了一躬，说道：“您说得对，卢多尔夫小姐。弗利特先生通晓的一两门行当，我可从来无福消受、没学过手。”

“起码他学会了做一名绅士的修养。”克里斯蒂娜毫不留情地反唇相讥。

那年轻人的脸色更加阴沉，开口道：“听您这番‘横扫一片’（*sweeping*，暗讽丹尼斯扫地出身）的高论，我倒看出弗利特先生在您心里分量不轻啊。”

“一个既拙劣又低俗的双关玩笑。”克里斯蒂娜冷冷甩下一句，半点颜面也没给他留。

===Original===
Dennis was naturally of a very jealous disposition where his affections were concerned. His own love took such entire possession of him that he could not brook the interference of others, or sensibly consider that they had the same privilege to woo, and win if possible, that he had. Especially distasteful to him was this rich and favored youth, whose presence awakened all his combativeness, which was by no means small.

Mr. Mellen’s most inopportune interruption and covert taunts provoked him beyond endurance. His face was fairly white with rage, and for a moment he felt that he could stamp his rival out of existence. In the low, concentrated voice of passion he said, “If Mr. Mellen should lose his property, as many do, I gather from his remarks that he would still keep up his idea of a gentleman on charity.”

Mr. Mellen flushed to the roots of his hair, his hands clenched. In the flashing eyes and threatening faces of the young men those witnessing the scene foresaw trouble. A light hand fell on Dennis’s arm, and Miss Winthrop said, “Mr. Fleet, I wish to show you a picture, and ask your judgment in regard to it.”

Dennis understood the act, and in a moment more his face was crimson with shame.

“Miss Winthrop, you ought to send me home at once. I told you I was unfit for society. Somehow I am not myself. I humbly ask your pardon.”

===Chinese===
一旦牵涉到男女情爱，丹尼斯天生便是个嫉妒心极强的人。他这份爱情如此彻底地占据了他整副身心，以至于他容不得旁人半分插足，也绝不肯冷静地体谅旁人原也与他享有同等的权利去追求心上人、倘有可能便将其赢取。偏偏这位富贵得宠的少爷尤其令他生厌，只要对方一露面，便勾起他满腔的好斗心——而丹尼斯的好斗脾气本也着实不小。

梅伦先生这番极不合时宜的打断外加暗箭伤人，彻底激怒了丹尼斯，令他忍无可忍。他气得脸色煞白，有一瞬甚至恨不得把情敌踩在脚下碾个粉碎。他压低嗓门，声音里裹挟着高度凝聚的怒火说道：“依我看，若梅伦先生有朝一日也像世上许多人那样散尽家财，照他这番言谈行事，怕是只能靠旁人施舍救济，才能维持住他那套‘绅士’体面了。”

梅伦先生登时涨红了脸，一直红到耳根，双拳紧握。两个年轻人双目喷火、面露凶相，旁观这幕场景的几个人眼看便要闹出事端。忽然，一只纤手轻轻落在了丹尼斯手臂上，温思罗普小姐说道：“弗利特先生，我有幅画想请您赏鉴，顺便请教一下您的高见。”

丹尼斯立刻领会了她的用意，转瞬之间，羞愧的红潮便涌上了他的面庞。

“温思罗普小姐，您真该立刻打发我回家去。我早说过自己配不上这社交场合。不知怎的，我竟失了分寸。我诚惶诚恐地恳请您原谅。”

===Original===
“So sincere a penitent shall receive absolution at once. You were greatly provoked. I trust you for the future.”

“You may,” was the emphatic answer. After that pledge Mr. Mellen might have struck him and received no more response than from a marble statue.

Mr. Mellen also took a sober second thought, remembering that he was in a lady’s parlor. He walked away with his ears tingling, for the flattered youth had never had such an experience before. The few who witnessed the scene smiled significantly, as did Christine half contemptuously; but Miss Winthrop soon restored serenity, and the remaining hours passed away in music and dancing. Christine did not speak to Dennis again﻿—that is, by word of mouth﻿—but she thought of him constantly, and their eyes often met;﻿—on his part that same eager, questioning look. She ever turned hers at once away. But his words kept repeating themselves continually, especially his last sentence, when the unlucky Mr. Mellen had broken in upon them﻿—“You can copy anything you see.”

“How noble and expressive of varied feeling his face is!” she thought, watching it change under the playful badinage of Miss Winthrop.

“How I would like to copy it! Well, you can﻿—‘You can copy anything you see.’ ” Then like a flash came a suggestion﻿—“You can make him love you, and copy feeling, passion, life﻿—from the *living* face. Whether I can believe or feel, myself, is very doubtful. This I can do: he himself said so. I cannot love, myself﻿—I must not; I do not wish to now, but perhaps I can inspire love in him, and then make his face a study. As to my believing, he can never know how utterly impossible his faith is to me.”

===Chinese===
“如此诚心悔过的人，自当立刻获赦。方才是他太无礼挑衅了。往后我信得过您。”

“您尽管放心。”丹尼斯斩钉截铁地答道。立下这句誓言之后，纵使梅伦先生走过来挥拳打他，他怕也只会像一尊大理石雕像般纹丝不动、毫无反应。

梅伦先生冷静下来转念一想，也记起自己毕竟身处一位淑女的客厅之中。他双耳发烫地走开了——这位平素被捧惯了的少爷，生平还从未有过这等狼狈的经历。寥寥几个目睹方才一幕的人意味深长地笑了笑，克里斯蒂娜唇边也挂着一抹半带轻蔑的笑意；好在温思罗普小姐很快便抚平了风波，余下的时光又在音乐与欢舞之中流淌而过。此后克里斯蒂娜虽未再同丹尼斯交谈——至少未曾动口说话——但她心里却时刻记挂着他，两人的视线也频频相遇；他眼中依旧是那副热切而探询的神情。她每次都立刻移开目光。然而他的话语却不断在耳畔萦绕回响，尤其是那个倒霉的梅伦先生闯进来打断他们前他说的最后那句——“但凡您亲眼见过的东西，您都能临摹下来。”

“他那张脸可真是生得高贵英挺，喜怒哀乐跃然其上！”她暗自赞叹，一边瞧着他的神情在温思罗普小姐俏皮的打趣下变幻无穷。

“我真想把那副神情摹写下来！这有何难，你办得到——‘但凡你亲眼见过的东西，你都能临摹下来。’”霎时间，一个念头电光石火般窜入脑海——“你可以让他爱上你，然后对着一张*活生生*的脸，去临摹其中的情感、激情与生命力。至于我自己能不能信、能不能动情，那实在大成疑问。可眼下这法子我却行得通：他亲口说的。我自己不能爱——绝不能；眼下我也不想爱，但我兴许能点燃他的爱火，再把他的脸拿来做写生临摹的范本。至于信不信他的信仰，他永远也不会明白那套信念于我而言是如何的绝无可能。”

===Original===
Then conscience entered a mild protest against the cruelty of the project. “Nonsense!” she said to herself; “most girls flirt for sport, and it is a pity if I cannot with such a purpose in view. He will soon get over a little puncture in his heart after I have sailed away to my bright future beyond the sea, and perhaps Susie will comfort him;” and she smiled at the thought. Dennis saw the smile and was entranced by its loveliness. How little he guessed the cause!

Having resolved, Christine acted promptly. When their eyes again met, she gave him a slight smile. He caught it instantly and looked bewildered, as if he could not believe his eyes. Again, when a little later, at the urgent request of many, he sang alone for the first time, and again moved his hearers deeply by the real feeling in his tones, he turned from the applause of all, with that same questioning look, to her. She smiled an encouragement that she had never given him before. The warm blood flooded his face instantly. All thought that it was the general chorus of praise. Christine knew that she had caused it, and surprise and almost exultation came into her face. “I half believe he loves me now,” she said. She threw him a few more kindly smiles from time to time, as one might throw some glittering things to an eager child, and every moment assured her of her power.

“I will try one more test,” she said, and by a little effort she lured to her side the offended Mr. Mellen, and appeared much pleased by his attention. Then unmistakably the pain of jealousy was stamped on Dennis’s face, and she was satisfied. Shaking off the perplexed Mr. Mellen again, she went to the recess of a window to hide her look of exultation.

“The poor victim loves me already,” she said. “The mischief is done. I have only to avail myself of what exists from no fault of mine, and surely I ought to; otherwise the passion of the infatuated youth will be utterly wasted, and do no one any good.”

Thus in a somewhat novel way Christine obtained a new master in painting, and poor Dennis and his love were put to use somewhat as a human subject might be if dissected alive.

===Chinese===
此时，良心对这项盘算的残忍之处提出了几声微弱的抗议。“废话！”她暗自驳斥道，“绝大多数姑娘调起情来不过是为了寻开心，我既抱着这样崇高的目的，难道反倒做不得了？等我扬帆远渡重洋、奔赴光辉前程之后，他心口那点小伤很快就会平复的，说不定苏茜还会好好抚慰他一番呢。”想到这里，她不禁微微一笑。丹尼斯恰巧看见了这抹笑意，顿时被她的娇美迷得神魂颠倒。他又哪里猜得出她笑的是什么！

主意既定，克里斯蒂娜立刻付诸行动。当两人的目光再度相接时，她便报以淡淡一笑。丹尼斯登时捕捉到了这一笑，露出茫然惊愕的神色，仿佛简直不敢相信自己的眼睛。过了一会儿，应众人再三恳请，他头一次独唱起来，歌声里的真情实感再次深深打动了在场听众；在一片掌声之中，他移开目光，带着方才那种探询的神情望向她。她便报以一抹从未给过他的鼓励微笑。滚烫的热血瞬间涌遍了他的脸庞。众人都以为那是众人齐声喝彩所致，唯有克里斯蒂娜心里雪亮，那是自己惹出来的，脸上不禁流露出几分惊异与近乎得意扬扬的神采。“我看他眼下八成已经爱上我了。”她暗道。此后她隔三差五便朝他抛去几缕温存的笑意，宛如逗弄一个眼巴巴盼着礼物的孩童，时不时扔出几件亮闪闪的小玩意儿一般；每多一分试探，便越发印证了她对他的掌控之力。

“我且再试最后一次，”她心道，略施小计便把方才恼羞成怒的梅伦先生重新招揽到身旁，还装出一副对他殷勤颇为受用的模样。果不其然，嫉妒的痛楚清清楚楚地刻在了丹尼斯的脸上，她这才心满意足。随即便又把一头雾水的梅伦先生甩开，独自退到一处窗龛里，掩饰起脸上的得意神色。

“这个可怜的猎物已经爱上我了，”她心想，“大局已定。眼下既然生米已成熟饭，绝非我的过错，我只不过顺水推舟善加利用罢了，况且我也理当如此；不然这个痴迷小伙子的一腔深情岂不白白浪费，对谁都没有半点益处？”

就这样，克里斯蒂娜以一种颇为新奇的方式，延请到了一位绘画的新导师；而可怜的丹尼斯连同他的一腔痴爱，便被派上了实际用场——其境遇，倒颇有几分像是被人活生生送上解剖台的活体标本。

## XLVIII Doctor Arten Struck by Lightning / 第四十八章 阿滕医生遭雷击

===Original===
Hastening down into the body of the church, Dennis and Christine found Mrs. Leonard lying on some cushions in a pew. She was scantily clad, her sweet face scorched and blackened, and her beautiful hair almost crisped away.

Her husband was bending over her in an agony of mingled grief and joy. She had just been brought in from wandering aimlessly and alone quite out upon the prairie, singing in a low, plaintive way to herself words suggested by the sudden disaster that had temporarily robbed her of husband, of reason, and almost of life.

Dennis afterward learned from Professor Leonard that when first aroused they had escaped from the hotel, but, not realizing the danger, he had stepped back a moment at her request to get something she valued very much, and they had become separated.

“And thus at last I find the poor child,” he cried, with a look of agony.

Mrs. Leonard did not know any of them, but continued her low, plaintive singing.

===Chinese===
丹尼斯和克里斯蒂娜急步走进教堂正厅，发现伦纳德太太正躺在一排长椅的垫子上。她衣衫单薄，柔美的面庞被烟火灼得焦黑，一头秀发也几乎烤焦卷曲。

她的丈夫俯身守在她身旁，悲喜交加，痛彻心扉。原来她方才独自一人在荒野草地上漫无目的地游荡，被人寻了回来；她一直低声哀婉地自顾哼唱着，词句正是那场突如其来的灾难所激起的呓语——那灾难一时夺走了她的丈夫、理智，乃至险些夺走她的性命。

丹尼斯后来从伦纳德教授口中得知，起初惊醒时他们本已逃出了旅馆，但他当时尚未意识到火势的凶险，只因妻子请求去取一件她极为珍视的东西，便转身回去了一瞬，二人就此失散。

“到头来，我竟是这样才找到这可怜的孩子，”他满面痛苦地呼喊道。

伦纳德太太一个也不认得，仍只是低声哀婉地唱着。

===Original===
Dr. Arten, who had found his way to the church as one of the centres, was soon in attendance, his benevolent face becoming the very embodiment of pity. The crowd were pushed back, and with other kind ladies Christine took charge of her poor unconscious friend, and all was done that skill and tender love could suggest. At last, under the doctor’s opiates, her low, weird singing ceased, and she slept, her husband holding her hand. The thronging fugitives were kept a little away, and Dr. Arten slept near, to be within call.

A lady asked Christine to go home with her, but she thanked her and said, “No, I would rather remain in the church near my friends.”

Dennis saw that she was greatly wearied. Taking her hand, he said: “Miss Ludolph, it is my turn to take care of you again. See, our friends are preparing a place there for the ladies to sleep. Please go to rest at once, for you do indeed need it.”

“I am very tired, but I know I could not sleep. How strange this life is! All day, the world, in spite of what has happened, seemed growing brighter. Now with the night has come the deeper darkness of sorrow. On every side pain and suffering seem to predominate, and to me there will ever be so much mystery in events like my father’s death and my friend Susie’s experience, that I know it will be hard to maintain a childlike faith.”

===Chinese===
阿滕医生把这座教堂当作救治中心之一，此时已寻到这里，很快便上前照料，他那张慈祥的面孔简直成了怜悯的化身。众人被劝退到一旁，克里斯蒂娜同几位热心的女士一道照看她这位可怜而人事不省的朋友，竭尽医术与温柔的爱心所能想到的一切办法。终于，在医生施用的安神药剂作用下，她那低沉凄婉的吟唱停了下来，沉沉睡去，丈夫则一直握着她的手。拥挤的避难人群被稍微隔开一些，阿滕医生就在近旁和衣而卧，以便随时应召。

一位女士请克里斯蒂娜随她回家去住，但她谢绝了，说道：“不了，我宁愿留在教堂里，陪伴在我的朋友们身边。”

丹尼斯看出她已疲惫不堪。他拉起她的手，说道：“卢多尔夫小姐，又该轮到我来照料你了。你看，朋友们正在那边为女眷们收拾休息的地方。请你立刻去歇息吧，你实在太需要休息了。”

“我是很累了，但我知道自己睡不着。这人生真是奇特！整整一天，尽管发生了这么多事，世界却似乎在渐渐变得明亮起来。可如今夜幕降临，悲伤的浓重黑暗也随之而来。四面八方仿佛都被痛苦与煎熬所笼罩；像我父亲的去世和我朋友苏茜的遭遇，在我看来永远隐藏着太多难以参透的奥秘，我知道，要始终怀着孩童般单纯的信心，实在太难了。”

===Original===
“God will help you to trust; you will not be left to struggle alone. Then remember you are His child, and earthly parents do much that little children cannot understand.”

With a faint smile she answered: “I fear I shall be one of those troublesome children that are ever asking why. All day it has seemed so easy to be a Christian, but already I learn that there will be times when I shall have to cling to my Saviour, instead of being carried forward in His arms. Indeed, I almost fear that I shall lose Him in the darkness.”

“But He will not lose you,” replied Dennis. “Since you are not sleepy, let me tell you a short Bible story.”

“Oh, do, please do, just as if I were a little child.”

===Chinese===
“上帝会帮助你去信靠祂的；祂不会任由你独自挣扎。再者，你要记住你是祂的孩子，而地上的父母所做的许多事，小孩子也同样无法明白。”

她淡淡一笑，答道：“只怕我会成为那种老爱问‘为什么’的顽皮孩子。今天一整天，做一名基督徒似乎都那样容易，可我已经明白，总有些时候我必须紧紧攀住我的救主，而不是被祂抱在怀里安然前行。说真的，我几乎害怕自己会在黑暗中失落了祂。”

“但祂绝不会失落你，”丹尼斯答道，“既然你还不困，让我给你讲一个简短的圣经故事吧。”

“哦，好啊，请讲吧，就像把我当成一个小孩子那样讲。”

===Original===
“It is in the New Testament. Jesus had sent His disciples in a boat across the sea of Galilee, while He should go up alone on a mountain to pray. The night came, and with it a storm swept down against the disciples. The smooth sea was lashed into great foam-crested waves which broke over their little ship. They tugged hour after hour at the oars, but in vain. The night grew darker, the wind more contrary, the waves higher and more threatening, their arms wearied, and they may have feared that they would perish alone and without remedy in the black midnight. But we read that ‘He saw them toiling in rowing,’ though they knew it not. From the distant mountain side ‘He saw them’﻿—marked every weary stroke of the oar, and every throb of fear. But at last, when they were most ready to welcome Him, when none could say, ‘We should have rowed through the storm alone,’ He came to them walking safely on the dark waves that threatened them with death, and said, ‘Be of good cheer, it is I; be not afraid.’ Then they gladly received Him into the ship, and immediately the rough waves were hushed, and the keel of the boat grated on the beach toward which they had vainly rowed. Then they that were in the ship came and worshipped Him, saying, ‘Of a truth thou art the Son of God.’

“Now it was on the evening of that very night that these same disciples had engaged in a scene of festivity. They had stood in the sunset on the mountain slope, and seen their Lord feed many thousand. Then all was peace, safety, and good cheer. Life changed as quickly for them as for you, but did not their Divine Master see them as truly in the stormy night as in the sunlight? Did He leave them to perish?

“He is watching you, Miss Ludolph, for He is ever the same; and before this stormy night of your sorrow passes away you will hear His voice, saying, ‘Be of good cheer, it is I; be not afraid.’ ”

“Already I hear it,” she said, in a low, glad voice, smiling through her tears. “I can, I do trust Him, and the conflicting winds of doubt and fear are becoming still. Among all these homeless people there must be many sad, discouraged hearts. You have helped me so much; can you not say a word or sing something that will help them?”

===Chinese===
“这故事记在《新约》里。耶稣曾打发门徒乘船渡过加利利海（Sea of Galilee），祂自己则独自上山祷告。夜幕降临，一阵狂风猛地朝门徒们席卷而来。原本平静的海面被掀成滚滚白沫的巨浪，拍打着他们的小船。他们一小时又一小时地奋力摇橹，却徒劳无功。夜色越来越暗，风势越来越逆，浪头越涌越高、越发凶险，他们的双臂酸痛乏力，或许早已绝望，唯恐自己会在这漆黑的午夜孤立无援地丧命。但经上记着说，‘祂看见他们摇橹甚苦’，尽管他们自己并不知道。从遥远的山坡上，‘祂看见他们’——看清了他们每一次疲惫的划桨，也看清了他们心中每一次恐惧的颤栗。终于，当他们最渴盼迎接祂的时候，当谁也再说不出‘我们靠自己也能划过这场风暴’的时候，祂从容踏着那威胁要吞噬他们性命的漆黑海浪向他们走来，说道：‘你们放心，是我，不要怕。’于是他们欢欢喜喜地接祂上船，霎时间狂风巨浪归于平静，船底的龙骨也擦上了他们此前苦苦划向却始终无法抵达的岸滩。船上的人都来拜祂，说：‘你真是上帝的儿子了。’

“要知道，就在那天傍晚，这同一群门徒还刚刚经历过一场欢欣的盛景。他们曾站在夕阳映照的山坡上，亲眼看着他们的主喂饱了几千人。那时一切都是平安、稳妥与欢喜。他们的生活像你一样转瞬剧变，但他们神圣的主在狂风暴雨的夜里看顾他们，岂不和在阳光下一样真切吗？祂何曾任由他们灭亡呢？

“祂正注视着你呢，卢多尔夫小姐，因为祂永不改变；在这场属于你悲伤的风暴黑夜过去之前，你必会听见祂的声音说：‘你们放心，是我，不要怕。’”

“我已经听见了，”她含泪微笑着，低声而欣喜地说，“我能够信靠祂，我确实信靠祂；怀疑与恐惧那相互激荡的狂风，正在渐渐平息。在这些无家可归的人中间，一定还有许多悲伤、灰心的心灵。你给了我这么大的安慰；你能不能说几句话，或者唱一首歌，也去安慰安慰他们呢？”

===Original===
Dennis thought a moment, and then, in a sweet, clear voice that penetrated every part of the large building, sang:

> “Father in Heaven, the night is around us,
 

 Terror and danger our portion have been;
 

 We cry unto Thee, oh, save and defend us,
 

 Comfort the trembling, and pardon our sin.
> “Hearts that are heavy, look onward and upward;
 

 Though wild was the storm that wrecked your loved homes,
 

 Faith lifts your sad glances hopefully heavenward,
 

 To mansions prepared with glory-crowned domes.
> “Hearts that are breaking, whose lov’d ones have vanished,
 

 Swept down in the seething ocean of fire,
 

 E’en now they may rest where pain is all banished,
 

 And join their glad songs with the heavenly choir.
> “Hearts that are groaning with life’s weary burden,
 

 Who fear to go forward, to sorrow a prey;
 

 Jesus invites you﻿—‘Oh, come, heavy laden’;
 

 Leave sin at His feet, bear mercy away.”

===Chinese===
丹尼斯思忖片刻，随后放开那甜美清亮、足以传遍整座宏大教堂每一个角落的嗓音，唱了起来：

> “天父在上，黑夜已将我们笼罩，  
> 惊恐与危难曾是我们的遭遇；  
> 我们向祢呼求，求祢拯救护卫，  
> 安慰战栗的心灵，赦免我们的罪愆。
>
> “沉重的心啊，请向前向上仰望；  
> 纵使狂暴的烈焰摧毁了你们心爱的家园，  
> 信心却将你们哀伤的目光满怀盼望地举向天上，  
> 望向那荣光加冕的穹顶下早已预备的华宇。
>
> “破碎的心啊，你们的挚爱已然消逝，  
> 被卷入那翻腾咆哮的火海之中；  
> 此刻他们或已安息在一切痛苦尽除之处，  
> 与天上的唱诗班一同欢唱。
>
> “在人生疲惫重担下呻吟的心啊，  
> 因害怕前行而沦为悲伤的猎物；  
> 耶稣呼唤你们——‘哦，劳苦担重担的人啊，到我这里来’；  
> 把罪卸在祂脚前，将怜悯带走。”

===Original===
After the first line there was a breathless hush; but, when he closed, low sobbings might be heard from many of the women, and in the dim light not a few tears shone in the eyes of manhood. Dennis’s voice was sympathetic in its character, and he had the power of throwing into it much feeling.

Christine was weeping quietly, but her tears now were like the warm spring rain as it falls on the precious seed. At last she said, “You have done these people much good.”

“To you belongs all the credit, for it was at your suggestion I sang.”

She shook her head, and then said, “Good night, my friend, I shall never forget this day with its mingled experience; but I think, I hope, I shall never doubt God again;” and she went to her rest.

===Chinese===
第一句唱出之后，四下里顿时屏息静默；而当他唱完时，许多女眷中传出低低的啜泣声，昏暗的灯光下，不少男子汉的眼中也闪烁着泪光。丹尼斯的嗓音天生极富共情之力，他又能把满腔深情倾注其中。

克里斯蒂娜也在悄悄流泪，但此刻她的泪水却宛如落在珍贵种子上的温暖春雨。终于，她说道：“你为这些人带来了莫大的慰藉。”

“功劳全在于你，因为正是听从了你的提议，我才唱的。”

她摇了摇头，随后说道：“晚安，我的朋友，我永远不会忘记这百感交集的一天；不过我想，我也盼望，从此我再也不会怀疑上帝了。”说完，她便去歇息了。

===Original===
The light of the next day brought to view many hard realities, and chief among these was the bread question. Dennis was up with the dawn, and by eager inquiries sought to comprehend the situation. Some were gloomy and discouraged, some apathetic, and some determined, courageous, and hopeful; and to this last class he belonged.

Most thankful that he had come out of the fiery ordeal unscathed, he resolved to contribute his quota toward a new and better Chicago. Young, and sanguine in temperament, he already saw the city rise from its ashes in statelier proportions and richer prosperity. With a thrill of exultation he heard the report that some Napoleonic business men had already telegraphed for building material, and were even now excavating the hot ruins.

Christine had hardly joined him as he stood at the door when a gentleman entered and asked, “Who here are willing and able to work for fair wages?”

“I am at your service,” said Dennis, stepping forward promptly.

===Chinese===
次日的晨光照出了许多严酷的现实，其中首当其冲的便是糊口问题。丹尼斯天一亮便起身了，四处急切打听，试图摸清眼下的局势。人群中有的阴郁沮丧，有的麻木消沉，也有的坚定、勇敢而满怀希望；他正是属于最后这一类人。

他满心感恩自己能从那场烈焰劫难中安然无恙地走出来，决心为建设一座更新、更好的芝加哥尽自己的一份力。他正值青春年华，天性乐观，眼前仿佛已看见这座城市正以更加雄伟的气象和更加丰饶的繁荣从灰烬中崛起。听说已有几位拿破仑般果决的商界人士发电报订购建筑材料，甚至此刻就已经在滚烫的废墟上动工清理，他心中不由涌起一阵振奋的喜悦。

他正站在门口，克里斯蒂娜刚来到他身旁，便有一位先生走了进来，问道：“这里有谁愿意并且能够干活挣一份公道的工钱？”

“我听候差遣，”丹尼斯说着，立刻迈步上前。

===Original===
“You are a gentleman, sir,” said the speaker, impressed with the fact by Dennis’s bearing, though his hat and coat were gone; “I need laborers who can handle the pick and shovel.”

“I will work for less, then, till I can handle these tools as well as a laborer. There is no reason why I should eat the bread of charity a day longer, especially when so many need it more than I.”

“I said you were a gentleman; I now say you are a man, and that to me means a great deal more,” said the energetic stranger. “You shall have two dollars a day with the rest.”

He turned to Christine and said, almost proudly, “The supper you have tonight shall be yours also.”

“That is,” she replied, with a smile, “I shall live on your charity instead of that of someone else.”

===Chinese===
“先生，您是位体面绅士啊，”说话的人虽见丹尼斯连帽子和外衣都没了，仍被他身上流露出的气度所打动，“可我需要的是能抡镐使锹的粗工。”

“那等我能把这些工具使得像老练的苦力一样顺手之前，我少拿些工钱便是。实在没道理让我在救济粮上多吃一天白食，何况有那么多人比我更需要救济。”

“我方才说你是个绅士；现在我要说，你是个真正的男子汉，在我看来，这可贵重得多，”这位精力充沛的陌生人说道，“你跟大伙儿一样，每天两美元。”

他转向克里斯蒂娜，几乎带着几分自豪地说道：“今晚你吃的那顿晚饭，也有你的一份。”

“这么说来，”她微笑着答道，“我不过是不吃别人的施舍，改吃你的施舍罢了。”

===Original===
His face grew sad at once, but he answered, as he went away, “I could not give you charity, Miss Ludolph.”

Christine saw that she had pained him, and was much vexed with herself. But his remark added to the hope and almost belief that she still held her old place in his heart, and she resolved to make amends in the evening for her unlucky speech.

With a smile she said to herself: “If he only knew that I would prefer the coarsest, scantiest fare provided by him to the most costly banquet, he would not have gone away with that long face. How rich life would be if I could commence it with him, and we struggle up together! Oh, Heaven, grant,” she sighed, looking earnestly upward, “that through these wonderful, terrible changes, I may climb the mountain at his side, as he so graphically portrayed it in his picture!”

===Chinese===
他的脸色立刻黯然下来，一边转身离去，一边答道：“卢多尔夫小姐，我断不会对你施舍什么。”

克里斯蒂娜看出自己伤了他的心，不禁十分懊恼。但他的那句话，却又让她添了几分盼望，几乎确信自己在他的心底依然占着从前的位置，于是打定主意今晚一定要为自己这句失言向他赔个不是。

她微笑着暗自忖道：“他要是知道，比起最奢华的盛宴，我宁愿吃他挣来的最粗陋、最菲薄的饭食，他就不会拉长着脸走开了。如果我能同他一道重新开始生活，两个人一起奋力向上挣扎，那人生该有多么丰盈啊！啊，上苍啊，求您垂允，”她虔诚地仰起脸叹息道，“借着这些奇异而又可怖的剧变，让我能伴在他的身旁攀登那座高山，就像他在画作中那样生动描绘过的一样！”

===Original===
Mrs. Leonard still slept, and her husband in an agony of anxiety watched at her side. At last, a little before midday, she opened her eyes and said, in her natural tone: “Why, John, I must have greatly overslept. Where am I?” and then, as her husband fairly sobbed for joy, she started up and said, hurriedly: “What is the matter? What has happened?”

“Oh, be calm!” whispered Christine to the professor. “Everything depends on keeping her quiet.” Then she bent over her friend, and said: “Do not be alarmed, Susie; you are now safe and well, and so is your husband. But you have been ill, and for his sake and your own you must keep quiet.”

She turned inquiringly to her husband, who said, more calmly, “It is all true, and if you can only be careful we can go back to Boston as well as ever.”

“I will do anything you say, John; but why am I in a church?”

“You were taken sick in the street, and this was the nearest place to bring you.”

“Oh, dear! I have had such strange, dreadful dreams. I am so glad they were only dreams, and you are here with me;” and she lay quietly holding her husband’s hands and looking contentedly in his face. It was evident she was herself again, and much better.

===Chinese===
伦纳德太太仍在沉睡，她的丈夫则在焦灼万分的煎熬中守在她身旁。终于，快到正午时分，她睁开眼睛，用平常的口吻说道：“哎呀，约翰（John），我一定睡过头太久了。我这是在哪儿呀？”接着，眼看丈夫竟喜极而泣，她连忙惊起身来，急切问道：“出什么事了？到底发生了什么？”

“啊，千万镇定些！”克里斯蒂娜低声对教授耳语道，“眼下全靠让她保持安静了。”随即她俯下身，对朋友说道：“别害怕，苏茜；你现在安全无恙，你丈夫也平平安安的。只是你生了场病，为了他，也为了你自己，你必须静心养着。”

她探询地望向丈夫，丈夫镇定下来，说道：“都是真的，只要你肯小心将养，我们就能像从前一样安然回到波士顿（Boston）去。”

“约翰，你说什么我都听；可我为什么会在一座教堂里呢？”

“你在街上突然病倒了，这儿是最近的地方，就把你抬进来了。”

“哦，天哪！我做了好些离奇又可怕的梦。幸亏那只是梦，而且有你陪在我身边。”她安静地躺着，握着丈夫的双手，心满意足地望着他的脸。显而易见，她已经恢复了神智，大有好转了。

===Original===
Dr. Arten soon after came and said, cheerily, “All right! all right! will have you out in a day or two as good as new, and then, Miss Ludolph, you will see how much more grateful she is to the old doctor than you were.”

“You must present your bill,” replied Christine, with a smile.

“May I?” retorted the doctor, wiping his lips.

“Oh, I don’t know about that,” cried Christine; adding, quickly, “when I welcome you to my own home you may.”

“An old maid’s hall, I suppose.”

“It will be an orphan’s home, at least,” said Christine, softly and sadly.

===Chinese===
不久，阿滕医生走了过来，兴高采烈地说道：“太好了！太好了！不出两三天就能让你健健康康地走出去，跟从前一样精神；到时候，卢多尔夫小姐，你就会瞧见她对老医生比你懂得感恩多啦。”

“您得开出您的账单才行呀，”克里斯蒂娜微笑着答道。

“我真可以吗？”医生反问道，同时抹了抹嘴角。

“哦，那可说不好，”克里斯蒂娜叫道，随即又飞快地补上一句，“等我迎您到我自己的家里做客时，您就可以开账单了。”

“大概是位老姑娘的宅邸吧。”

“至少，那会是一个孤女的家，”克里斯蒂娜轻声而凄然地说道。

===Original===
Tears filled the old man’s eyes, and putting his arm around her he drew her to him, saying, as he stroked her drooping head: “Poor child! poor child! I did not know. But you shall never want a protector while the old doctor is above ground. As far as possible I will be a father to you;” and Christine knew she had found a friend as true and strong as steel, and she buried her face on his shoulder and cried as trustingly as his own child might have done.

“Oh, Christine!” cried Mrs. Leonard, “I am so sorry for you!”

At the voice of her old friend she at once rallied, and, trying to smile through her tears, said, “God has been so much better to me than I deserved that I have only gratitude when I think of myself; but my poor father﻿—” and again she covered her face and wept.

“Christine, come here,” said Mrs. Leonard, softly, and she put her arms around the weeping girl. “You spoke of God’s being good to you. Have you in truth found and learned to trust Him?”

===Chinese===
老人的眼中顿时噙满泪水，他伸出臂膀揽住她，将她拉到自己怀里，一边轻抚着她低垂的头，一边说道：“可怜的孩子！可怜的孩子！我原不知道啊。不过只要老医生还活在世上一天，你就决不会缺少一位护佑你的人。只要力所能及，我愿意做你的父亲。”克里斯蒂娜知道，自己找到了一位如钢铁般真诚坚毅的挚友，于是把脸埋在他肩头，像他亲生女儿般无比信赖地哭了起来。

“啊，克里斯蒂娜！”伦纳德太太喊道，“我真是为你难过！”

听见老友的声音，她立刻振作起来，强忍泪水露出笑容，说道：“上帝待我远比我所配得的仁厚得多，一想到自己，我心中便只有感恩；只是我可怜的父亲——”说到这儿，她又一次掩面泣不成声。

“克里斯蒂娜，到这儿来，”伦纳德太太柔声说道，伸手搂住了这个哭泣的姑娘，“你方才说起上帝待你仁厚。你果真已经寻见祂，并且学会信靠祂了吗？”

===Original===
“Yes,” she replied, eagerly, joy and peace coming out in her face like the sun shining through clouds and rain. Then with bowed head she whispered low: “The one I wronged on earth led me to the One I wronged in heaven, and both have forgiven me. Oh, I am so glad, so happy!”

“Then you have seen Mr. Fleet.”

“Yes, he saved my life again and again, but in teaching me how to find my Saviour, he has done far more for me.”

“And you will not wrong him any more, will you, Christine? He has loved you so long and faithfully.”

===Chinese===
“是的，”她热切地答道，喜乐与平安瞬间浮现在她脸上，恰似阳光穿透云雨照耀出来。接着，她低下头，轻声细语道：“我在世上亏负的那个人，引领我归向了我在天上亏负的那一位，而他们两位都宽恕了我。啊，我真是太欢喜、太幸福了！”

“这么说，你已经见过弗利特先生了。”

“是的，他一次又一次救了我的性命，可他教我如何寻见我的救主，对我而言更是天大的恩情。”

“那你今后不会再亏负他了，对吗，克里斯蒂娜？他爱你已经那样长久，那样忠贞了。”

===Original===
In reply she lifted an eager face to her friend and said, “Do you think he can love me still after my treatment of him?”

“Give him a chance to tell you,” said Mrs. Leonard, with a half-mischievous smile. “Has he not shown his feelings?”

“He has treated me more as a brother might have done, and yet he is so very respectful and deferential﻿—I hope﻿—but I am not perfectly sure﻿—and then he seems under some restraint.”

Mrs. Leonard said, musingly: “He knows that you are Baroness Ludolph. I told him last week, for I thought he ought to know, and the fact of your approaching departure for Europe has been no secret of late. He thinks you are pledged to a future in which he cannot share; and in your grateful, dependent condition he would not cause you the pain of refusing him. I think that is just where he stands,” she concluded, with a woman’s mastery of the science of love, and taking almost as much interest in her friend’s affair as she had felt in her own. To most ladies this subject has a peculiar fascination, and, having settled their own matters, they enter with scarcely less zest on the task of helping others arrange theirs. Mrs. Leonard rallied faster under the excitement of this new interest than from the doctor’s remedies.

After a few moments’ thought Christine said, decidedly: “All that nonsense about the Baroness Ludolph is past forever﻿—burned up in the fire with many things of more value. I have been fed too long on the husks of human greatness and ambition to want any more of them. They never did satisfy me, and in the light and heat of the terrific ordeal through which I have just passed they shrivelled into utter nothingness. I want something that I cannot lose in a whiff of smoke and flame, and I think I have found it. Henceforth I claim no other character than that of a simple Christian girl.” Then bowing her head on her friend’s shoulder she added, in a whisper, “If I could climb to true greatness by Mr. Fleet’s side, as he portrayed it in his picture, it seems to me heaven would begin at once.”

===Chinese===
她抬起一张热切的脸庞望向朋友，答道：“经过我从前那样待他，你觉得他还会爱我吗？”

“你得给他一个机会，让他亲口告诉你呀，”伦纳德太太带着几分狡黠的笑意说道，“难道他还没有表露心迹吗？”

“他待我倒更像是一位兄长，可又那样恭敬、那样谦逊有礼——我希望——但我又拿不准——而且他似乎还带着几分拘束。”

伦纳德太太沉吟着说道：“他知道你是卢多尔夫女男爵。这是我上星期告诉他的，因为我觉得他理应知道；再说，你即将动身前往欧洲的事近来也早已不是秘密。他以为你已许身于一个他无法参与的未来；眼下你正怀着感激之情、又处于寄人篱下的境地，他自然不愿让你陷入拒绝他的难堪。我想他的心思正是如此。”她带着女人对爱情学问的那份谙熟总结道，谈起朋友的婚事来，兴致几乎不亚于当年操心自己的终身大事。对大多数女子而言，这类话题总有着一种奇特的魔力；等把自己的事情安顿妥当，她们便会兴味盎然、毫不逊色地投身于替别人牵线搭桥的差事之中。伦纳德太太在这一新趣事的鼓舞下，竟比服了医生的药还要恢复得快。

思索了片刻，克里斯蒂娜果断地说道：“什么卢多尔夫女男爵之类的荒唐话，都永远成为过去了——连同许多更宝贵的东西一道，全在大火里烧个精光了。我靠人世显赫与野心的糟粕度日已经太久，再也不想要那些东西了。它们从来不曾令我满足过，在我刚刚熬过的那场骇人劫难的光与热之中，它们早已萎缩成彻底的虚无。我渴望得到的，是哪怕在烟火之中也不会失去的东西，我想我已经找到了。从今往后，我只愿做一名简简单单的基督徒姑娘。”说完，她把头伏在朋友肩上，轻声补充道：“如果我真能像他在画里描绘的那样，伴在弗利特先生身旁攀向真正的崇高，在我看来，天堂此刻便已开始了。”

===Original===
The doctor, who had taken the professor aside, now joined them, and said: “Mrs. Leonard, you have only to take reasonable care of yourself, and you will soon recover from this shock and exposure. I wish all my patients were doing as well.”

She replied with a smile, taking her husband’s hand: “Since I have found my old Greek here, with his learned spectacles, I am quite myself, and I feel as if I were only playing invalid.”

“You may have slept in a church before,” said the doctor, with a twinkle in his eye, “and you must do so again. But no one will thunder at you from the pulpit this time, so I leave you in peace and security, and tonight will be within call.”

===Chinese===
医生方才把教授拉到一旁说了会儿话，此时走了过来，说道：“伦纳德太太，您只需要好好调养几分，很快就会从这场惊吓和风寒中康复过来。真盼望我所有的病人都像您这样见好。”

她微笑着握住丈夫的手答道：“既然找回了我这位戴着博学眼镜的老希腊学者在身边，我整个人都精神过来了，倒觉得自己像是在装病玩儿呢。”

“你从前兴许也在教堂里打过盹儿，”医生眼里闪着促狭的光说，“这回你还得再睡一回。不过这次可没人会从讲坛上对你大声训斥啦，所以你只管安心踏实地歇着，今晚我就在近旁随叫随到。”

===Original===
Christine followed him to the lobby of the church, when the irrepressible joker could not forbear saying: “Now let me give you a little paternal advice. Don’t be too grateful to that young Fleet. He only did his duty, and of course doesn’t deserve any special﻿—”

Christine, with flushing cheeks, interrupted him as if she had not heard: “Doctor, how good and kind you are! Here you are off without any rest to look after the sick and suffering, and you seem to bring health and hope wherever you go.”

“Yes, yes; but I send my bill in too﻿—mind that.” (Some of his poorer patients never received any, and he, when twitted of the fact, would mutter, roughly, “Business oversight﻿—can’t attend to everything.”)

Christine looked for a moment at the face so inspiring in its hearty benevolence, and with an impulse, so unlike the cold, haughty girl of old, sprang forward, threw her arms around his neck, and gave him a kiss which he declared afterward was like a mild stroke of lightning, and said, “And there is the first instalment of what I owe you.”

The old gentleman looked as if he decidedly liked the currency, and with moistened eyes that he vainly tried to render humorous, he raised his finger impressively in parting, and said, “Don’t you ever get out of debt to me.”

===Chinese===
克里斯蒂娜送他走到教堂门厅，这个改不了爱打趣性子的老人忍不住开口道：“现在让我给你几句长辈的忠告。别对那个年轻的弗利特太感激涕零啦。他不过是尽了本分，当然算不得有什么特别的——”

克里斯蒂娜双颊绯红，仿佛没听见似的打断了他：“医生，您真是太良善、太慈爱了！您连一点儿工夫都不歇着，就赶着去照看那些生病受苦的人，您走到哪里，似乎就把健康和希望带到哪里。”

“是啊，是啊；可我也是要寄账单去的——别忘了这一点。”（他的一些贫苦病人从未收到过任何账单，而当别人拿这事打趣他时，他总是粗声粗气地嘟囔一句：“账房疏漏——事儿太多，顾不过来。”）

克里斯蒂娜凝望着那张因由衷仁爱而显得格外动人的面庞片刻，忽地涌起一股冲动——这与她昔日那副冷漠高傲的模样截然不同——她猛地扑上前去，双臂搂住他的脖子，在他脸上吻了一下；医生事后宣称那简直像挨了一记温和的雷击。她说道：“这就是我欠您的第一笔分期偿还的诊费。”

老先生的神情显然对这种“货币”甚为受用，他湿润了眼眶，却又徒劳地想做出一副诙谐的神态，临别时意味深长地竖起一根手指，说道：“你这笔债啊，可千万别还清。”

## XXII Equal to an Emergency / 第二十二章 临危应变

===Original===
The fiery cross that so awed Christine and her little group of auditors was to be the closing scene of the evening entertainment. It was of metal, and by a skilful adjustment of jets was made to appear as if all aflame. While the others were intent on Christine’s words, and she in the interest of her theme had quite forgotten him, Dennis made all his arrangements, and at the critical point narrated in the preceding chapter he turned on the gas with the most startling effect. It seemed a living, vivid refutation of Christine’s words, and even she turned pale. After a moment, for the emblem to make its full impression, Dennis stepped out before them all, his face lighted up by the luminous cross. They admitted that no crusader could look more earnest and brave than he.

“Miss Ludolph,” he said, in a firm, yet respectful tone, “I should evermore be unworthy of your respect and confidence﻿—what is more, I should be false to myself, false to my faith﻿—should I remain silent in view of what I have been compelled to hear. That sacred emblem has not spent its meaning, or its power. Millions today would die for the sake of Him who suffered on it. Many even of those weak, inconsistent ones that you have so justly condemned would part with life rather than with the faint hope that centres there,” pointing to the radiant symbol.

“You are rude, sir,” said Christine, her face pale, but her eyes flashing in turn.

“No, he is right! he is right!” exclaimed Miss Winthrop, springing up with tears in her eyes. “Undeserving as I am of the name of Christian, I would die, I know I would die, before I would give up my poor little hope﻿—though I confess you make me fear that it is a false one. But it’s the best I have, and I mean it shall be better. I think a good touch of persecution, that would bring people out, would do the church more good than anything else.”

“Pardon me, Miss Ludolph,” continued Dennis; “but I appeal to your sense of justice. Could I be a true man and be silent, believing what I do? Could I hear the name of my Best Friend thus spoken of, and say not one word in His behalf?”

===Chinese===
那座令克里斯蒂娜及其小小听众群深感震慑的燃烧十字架，本是为当晚游艺会压轴一幕所设。十字架由金属铸成，经由煤气喷嘴的巧妙调节，宛如通体燃烧。正当众人全神贯注于克里斯蒂娜的言辞，而她本人亦因谈兴正浓而将他忘诸脑后时，丹尼斯已做好全部准备；就在前一章所述的紧要关头，他拧开煤气阀门，霎时间呈现出惊心动魄的效果。这仿佛是对克里斯蒂娜一番话最鲜活、最生动的驳斥，连她也不禁脸色煞白。停顿片刻，待这圣徽充分震撼人心后，丹尼斯跨步走到众人面前，光芒四射的十字架映照着他的面庞。在场众人也不得不承认，即便是十字军战士，也未见得比他更加虔诚而无畏。

“卢多尔夫小姐，”他用坚定而又不失敬意的语调说道，“听完方才不得不入耳的一番话，我若仍保持缄默，便永远不配得到您的敬重与信赖——不仅如此，我更是背叛了自己，背叛了我的信仰。那神圣的徽记并未耗尽它的意义，也未丧失它的力量。时至今日，仍有千百万人甘愿为那位在其上受难的主献出生命。就连您方才严厉谴责的那些软弱而前后矛盾之人当中，也有许多宁可舍弃性命，也不愿放弃寄托在那里的微弱希望。”说着，他指向那熠熠生辉的圣徽。

“你太无礼了，先生。”克里斯蒂娜说道，她脸色苍白，眼中却转而迸出怒火。

“不，他说得对！他说得对！”温思罗普小姐眼含热泪，猛地站起身喊道，“我虽不配基督徒之名，却宁死——我知道自己宁死也绝不放弃我这卑微渺小的盼望——尽管我承认，你的话让我生怕这只是一场虚妄。但这已是我所拥有最珍贵的东西，我立志要让它变得更真切。依我看，来上一场真格的迫害，好把人心里的真伪逼出来，对教会才最有裨益呢。”

“请原谅我，卢多尔夫小姐，”丹尼斯继续说道，“但我恳请您凭良心评判：怀着我这样的信仰，我若保持沉默，还能算是一个真诚的人吗？听闻我这位挚友的圣名被人如此议论，我怎能不为祂说上一句话呢？”

===Original===
“But I spoke most highly of the Christ of the Bible.”

“You spoke of Him as a great, good, but mistaken *man*, an enthusiast. To me He is the mighty God, my Divine Saviour, to whom I owe infinitely more than life. You know that I mean no disrespect to you,” he added, with gentle but manly courtesy. “I regret more deeply than words can express that you honestly think as you do. But if I as honestly believe the Bible, am I not acting as you said a true follower ought? For I assure you it is a heavier cross than you can ever know to speak thus unbidden where I am regarded only as a serving-man. But should I not be false and cowardly if I held my peace? And if you afterward should know that I claimed the name of Christian, would you not despise me as you remembered this scene?”

Christine bit her lip and hesitated, but her sense of justice prevailed, and she said, “I not only pardon you, but commend your course in view of your evident sincerity.”

Dennis replied by a low bow.

At this moment there was a loud ring at the door.

===Chinese===
“可我对《圣经》里的基督，分明是推崇备至的。”

“您只是把祂当作一位伟大、善良却认知有误的*凡人*，一个满腔热忱的空想家。而在我眼中，祂是全能的上帝，是我神圣的救主，我所蒙受的恩典远远重于生命本身。您知道我绝无冒犯您的意思，”他以温和而不失男子气概的礼貌补充道，“您真心实意持此想法，令我深感痛惜，非言语所能道尽。然而，若我也同样真诚地信奉《圣经》，我如今的所作所为，岂不正是您口中真正的追随者应当做的吗？因为我向您保证，在只把我当作仆役的地方，如此不请自来地开口，对我而言实是一副比您所能想象更为沉重的十字架。可我若缄口不言，岂不成了虚伪的懦夫？日后您若得知我也自称基督徒，回想起今日这一幕，岂不会鄙视我么？”

克里斯蒂娜咬了咬嘴唇，略一迟疑，终究是心中的公正占了上风，说道：“鉴于你显然出于一片赤诚，我不仅原谅你，还赞赏你的所为。”

丹尼斯深深鞠躬致意。

就在此时，大门外响起了一阵响亮的门铃声。

===Original===
“There come the gentlemen,” exclaimed Miss Brown. “I am so glad! Oh, dear! what a long, uncomfortable preachment we have had! Now for some fun!”

The colorless young ladies had stared first at Christine, and then at the cross, in blank amazement.

At the word “gentlemen” they were all on the alert and ready for *real* life; but Miss Winthrop left the room for a short time.

A handsome, lively youth entered, scattering bows and compliments on every side with the offhand ease of an accomplished society man. He paid no heed to Dennis, evidently regarding him as the showman.

“Well, ladies, you have done your part,” he said; “your arrangements seem complete.”

“Yes, Mr. Mellen; but where is our tenor?” asked Christine. “We have only three-quarters of an hour for music rehearsal, before we must retire to dress for our parts.”

===Chinese===
“先生们来啦！”布朗小姐欢呼道，“太好了！哎呀天哪，刚才可真是听了好长一通令人坐立难安的说教啊！现在总算能找点乐子了！”

那几位平庸乏味的年轻小姐先是盯着克里斯蒂娜看，又转头盯着那十字架，个个惊愕得呆若木鸡。

一听见“先生们”三个字，她们登时精神一振，准备投入“真正”的社交生活了；温思罗普小姐却暂且离开了房间。

一位相貌英俊、神采飞扬的青年走了进来，一路挥洒着鞠躬与奉承，举手投足尽显老练社交名流的从容潇洒。他根本没正眼瞧丹尼斯，显然只把他当作摆弄机关布景的杂役。

“好啊，诸位小姐，你们的任务都完成了，”他说道，“一切看起来都安排妥当啦。”

“是的，梅伦先生；可是我们的男高音呢？”克里斯蒂娜问道，“我们只剩三刻钟排练音乐了，之后就得退场去换装准备各自的角色。”

===Original===
“Bad news for you, Miss Ludolph,” said Mr. Mellen, coming to her side; “Archer is sick and can’t come.”

“Can’t come?” they all exclaimed in dismayed chorus.
