===Original===
One morning in the latter part of April she seemed more gracious than usual. Their labors were drawing to a close, and, as he had proved so tasteful and efficient in the store, she concluded that he might be equally useful in other ways and places. She could command him at the store, but not in respect to a task that she had in view; so she adopted a little feminine artifice as old as the time when Eve handed Adam the apple, and she looked at him in such a way that he could not refuse.

Blind, honest Dennis, it is needless to say, saw nothing of this little strategy of which he was destined to be the happy, willing victim, and his love expanded and bloomed under the genial light of her presence and kindness, like the flowers of the convolvulus in a bright dawn of June. She brought her general graciousness to a definite and blissful climax by saying, when about to go home, “Well, Mr. Fleet, you have done better than usual today, and I certainly must give you credit for possessing more taste than any young man of my acquaintance.”

Dennis’s heart gave as great a bound as if the laurel crown of all the Olympic games had been placed upon his brow.

“I am now going to ask a favor,” she continued.

“You may command me, Miss Ludolph,” interrupted Dennis.

===Chinese===
四月下旬的一天早晨，她的态度显得比往常更为和蔼可亲。他们在店里的布置工作已近尾声，既然他在此处已证明自己既有品味又颇能干，她便断定，在其他地方、别的事务上，他想必也同样派得上用场。在店里她可以对他发号施令，可眼下她心里盘算的那件事却使唤不得；于是她便施展起一桩女儿家的小小巧思——这手腕古老得一如夏娃将苹果递给亚当的那一刻——只那么抬眼望了他一下，便教他再也说不出半个“不”字。

不用说，憨厚又蒙在鼓里的丹尼斯压根儿没瞧出这桩小计谋——他注定要做这计谋下甘之如饴的快活俘虏；在他心头，爱意沐浴着她陪伴与垂青的融融暖意舒展绽放，恰似六月晴朗破晓时分吐蕊的牵牛花。临动身回家前，她将这番和颜悦色推向了一个明确而又令他狂喜的顶点：“唔，弗利特先生，你今天做得比往常还要好呢，我真得夸你一句，在我认识的年轻人里，数你的品味最高。”

丹尼斯的心头猛地一跃，仿佛奥林匹克竞技会全部的月桂冠都一齐戴在了他额上。

“眼下我还要请你帮个忙。”她接着说道。

“卢多尔夫小姐，您只管吩咐便是。”丹尼斯连忙接话道。

===Original===
“No, not in this case,” she replied. “Whatever you do will be regarded as a personal favor to me. At the same time it will afford you scope for such display of your taste as will secure many compliments.”

“If I am able to satisfy *you* I shall be more than compensated,” said Dennis with a bow.

She smiled and thought to herself, “That isn’t bad for a porter and man-of-all-work,” and explained as follows:

“Some young ladies and gentlemen have decided upon giving an entertainment, consisting of music, tableaux, and statuary. Now, in regard to the two latter parts, we need above all things some person of taste like yourself, whose critical eye and dexterous hand will insure everything to be just right. You will be a sort of general stage manager and superintendent, you know. I feel sure you will be all the more willing to enter upon this work when you know that the proceeds are to go toward the Church of the Holy Virgin. This is going to be a very select affair, and the tickets are five dollars each.”

“Is it a Protestant church?” asked Dennis, in some trepidation.

===Chinese===
“不，这回可不一样，”她答道，“不管你替我做些什么，我都算作是我个人承你的人情。再者，这事儿也能让你大展品味之长，保准赢得众口一词的夸赞。”

“若能教*您*称心，我便求之不得了。”丹尼斯欠身答道。

她嫣然一笑，心里暗忖：“作为一个搬运工兼杂役，这话倒说得不赖。”随即解释起来：

“有几位年轻淑女和绅士商量着要办一场游艺会，节目有音乐、活人画和人体造型。眼下呢，后头这两项正最缺一位像你这样有品位的人，好凭着你挑剔的眼光和灵巧的手艺，把一切都打点得妥妥帖帖。也就是说，你要担起舞台总管兼督导的差事。我想，你若得知这场演出的善款将捐给圣母教堂，定会更加乐意接下这桩活儿的。这回的聚会十分雅致讲究，票价每张五美元呢。”

“那是一座新教教堂吗？”丹尼斯问道，语气中带着几分忐忑。

===Original===
“Oh, certainly,” she answered, with a peculiar smile, “an Episcopal church.”

“It seems a strange name for a Protestant church,” said Dennis. “It is enough for me that you wish it; at the same time it certainly is a pleasure to contribute what little I can to aid any Christian organization.”

“Come, Mr. Fleet, you are narrow,” she said, with a controversial twinkle in her eye. “Why not toward a Catholic church?”

“I fear that all people with decided religious opinions are sometimes regarded as narrow,” he answered, with a smile.

“That is an inadequate answer to my question,” she said; “but I will not find fault since you have so good-naturedly acceded to my request. Come to No. — Wabash Avenue at three this afternoon. Papa gives you leave of absence.”

===Chinese===
“哦，那当然，”她答道，嘴角浮起一抹奇特的笑意，“是圣公会教堂。”

“新教教堂取这么个名儿，倒叫人觉得有些稀奇，”丹尼斯说，“不过只要是您的意思，对我来说便足够了；况且，能尽自己的一点微薄之力去襄助任何基督教团体，本就是一件快事。”

“得了吧，弗利特先生，你未免太狭隘了，”她说着，眼底闪过一丝存心挑衅的神采，“怎么就不能捐给天主教堂了？”

“只怕凡是宗教立场坚定的人，有时都会被旁人看作心胸狭隘吧。”他微笑着答道。

“你这话可算不上答复了我的问题，”她说，“不过既然你这么爽快地应承了我的请求，我也就不再挑剔啦。今天下午三点，你到沃巴什大道（Wabash Avenue）某号来。爸爸已经准你半天假了。”

===Original===
She vanished, and figuratively the sun went down to Dennis, and he was in twilight till he should see her again. He looked forward to the afternoon with almost feverish eagerness, for several reasons. It would be his first introduction to “good society,” for as such the unsophisticated youth regarded the prospect. He had the natural longing of a young, healthful nature for the companionship of those of his own age and culture, and his life in the great city had often been very lonely. He expected, as a matter of course, to be treated as an equal at the artistic entertainment in which he was to participate. In his business relations at the store he had taken a subordinate position and made up his mind to the logical consequences. But now that he was invited to a private house, and would appear there possessing all the qualities of a gentleman, he surely would be treated as one. “Is not this Chicago, whose citizens were nearly all poor a few years ago?” he thought; “and surely, if what Miss Ludolph says is true, I have advantages in my taste over most poor young men.” Moreover, it was his ideal of an entertainment, where art and music should take the place of the coarser pleasures of eating, drinking, and dancing. Chief of all, Christine would be there, and even he in his blindness became a little uneasy and self-conscious as he realized how this thought towered above the others.

She had given him a list of the things he was to bring with him in the afternoon, and he occupied every spare moment in getting them ready. At a quarter past two he summoned the carman of the store, and they loaded up the miscellaneous cargo needed for the coming mysteries, and by three all were before the large elegant mansion to which he had been directed. Dennis rang the bell and was shown by a servant into the front parlor, where he found Miss Ludolph, Miss Brown, a tall, haughty brunette, and the young lady of the house, Miss Winthrop, a bright, sunny-faced blonde, and two or three other young ladies of no special coloring or character, being indebted mainly to their toilets for their attractions. Dennis bowed to Miss Ludolph, and then turned toward the other ladies, expecting as a matter of course to be introduced. No introduction came, but his expectant manner was so obvious that Miss Ludolph colored and looked annoyed, and the other young ladies tittered outright.

Advancing a step or two she said, coldly, “Mr. Fleet, you may help Mapes carry the things into the back parlor, and then we will direct you as to the arrangement.”

Dennis crimsoned painfully. At first he was too confused to think, and merely obeyed mechanically. Then came the impulse to say boldly that this kind of thing might answer at the store, but not here, and he nearly carried it out; but soon followed the sober second thought, that such action would bring a blight over all his prospects, and involve the loss of his position at the store. Such giving way to passion would injure only himself. They would laugh, and merely suffer a momentary annoyance; to him and his the result would be most disastrous. Why should he let those who cared not a jot for him cause such sad injury?

By the time he had carried his first armful into the back parlor, he had resolved for his mother and sisters’ sakes that he would go through the following scenes as well as he could, and then turn his back on society till he could enter it a recognized gentleman; and with compressed lips and flashing eye he mentally vowed that that day should soon come.

===Chinese===
她一转身离去，对丹尼斯来说，便如同太阳沉落了一般，直到再次见到她为止，他都将置身于暮色之中。出于好几重缘故，他几乎怀着发烧似的急切盼着下午的到来。这将是他头一回步入“上流社会”——涉世未深的青年正是如此看待这番机缘的。一颗年轻而健康的灵魂，天生便渴望能与年龄相仿、教养相当的人为伴，而他在大都会里的日子向来过得十分孤寂。他理所当然地以为，在这场自己即将参与其中的艺术游艺会上，大家定会以平等之礼待他。在店里做买卖时，他身处下属之位，对由此带来的一切也早已坦然接受。可如今他受邀登门做客，进的是一户私宅，况且自己周身举止也全然具备一位绅士的风度，旁人岂有不以绅士相待之理？“这儿不就是芝加哥吗？城里的居民几年前几乎还都是穷光蛋呢，”他暗自寻思，“再说，倘若卢多尔夫小姐的话属实，我在品味上比绝大多数寒门子弟都要强出许多。”不仅如此，这正合乎他心目中理想的聚会模样——以艺术和音乐取代吃喝跳舞那些较为粗俗的消遣。而最要紧的是，克里斯蒂娜也会在场；就连蒙在鼓里的他，在意识到这个念头竟远远压倒了其余一切想法时，也不禁微微感到有些局促与不自在。

她先前交给他一张单子，列着下午需要带上同往的物件，于是他抓紧每一个空闲工夫备齐妥当。两点一刻，他叫来店里的车夫，两人把筹备那场即将登台的奇幻演出所需的杂七杂八器物装上车，到三点整，一行人便已停在了他受托前往的那座阔绰气派的大宅门前。丹尼斯按响门铃，由一名仆役引着进了前客厅。只见屋里坐着卢多尔夫小姐、身材高挑且神情傲慢的黑发女子布朗小姐、这户宅邸的小姐——容貌明媚、笑容灿若阳光的金发女郎温思罗普小姐，此外还有两三位姿色与性情皆平平无奇的年轻小姐，她们身上的几分风致主要全靠一身妆扮撑着。丹尼斯先向卢多尔夫小姐鞠了一躬，随即便转向其余几位小姐，理所当然地等着主人替他引见。然而引见并未到来，可他那副翘首以待的神态实在太过明显，惹得卢多尔夫小姐脸色微红、满面愠色，其余几位小姐更是忍不住当场掩口窃笑起来。

卢多尔夫小姐往前迈了一两步，冷冷地开口道：“弗利特先生，你先帮梅普斯把东西搬到后客厅去，待会儿我们再指示你怎么布置。”

丹尼斯的脸刷地涨得通红，羞辱难当。起初他脑中一片混乱，无暇细想，只是木然顺从。紧接着，一股冲动涌上心头，几乎要脱口而出：这套做派在店里兴许还使得，在这儿却万万不行——他险些就这么发作出来；可冷静的理智很快又占了上风：一旦这样顶撞，自己眼下的全部前程都会毁于一旦，连店里的差事也必定保不住。若一时意气用事，吃亏的终究只有他自己。她们不过嘲笑两声，顶多只觉得片刻扫兴；可落在他与家人头上的，却将是灭顶之灾。又何苦让一群压根儿不拿自己当回事的人，给自己招来这般惨重的祸患呢？

待他抱着头一捆物件走进后客厅时，他已打定主意：为了母亲与妹妹们，眼前这场戏，他定要竭力周旋到底；而此后他便彻底背过身去，不再踏足所谓的上流社会，直到有一天，他能以一位名正言顺的绅士身份昂首步入其中——他紧抿着嘴唇，双目灼灼生光，在心底暗暗立誓：那一天必将早早到来。

===Original===
As he was unpacking his materials he could not help hearing the conversation in the front parlor.

“Did you ever see such presumption?” exclaimed Miss Brown. “He evidently expected to be introduced, and that we should rise and courtesy all around.”

“He must have seen better days, for he certainly appeared like a gentleman,” said Miss Winthrop.

“I should hardly give that title to a man who swept a store out every morning,” replied Miss Brown.

“No, indeed!” chorused the three colorless young ladies.

“I know nothing about this young man,” said Miss Winthrop, ruffling her plumage somewhat for an argument, of which she was fond; “but, as a case in hand, suppose a highly educated and refined man for some reason swept a store out every morning, what would you call him?” and she looked around as if she had given a poser.

===Chinese===
他正拆解着带去的材料，前客厅里的谈话声不由自主地飘进了耳中。

“你们可曾见过这么不知天高地厚的人？”布朗小姐大声嚷道，“他分明指望着有人替他引见，好叫咱们全体起身，一个个向他行屈膝礼呢。”

“他从前家境想必体面过，因为他的举止神态确实很像一位绅士。”温思罗普小姐说道。

“每天早上要替铺子扫地的人，我可实在没法把那样的头衔送给他。”布朗小姐回敬道。

“可不是嘛！”那三位寡淡无味的小姐异口同声地附和道。

“我对这位年轻人一无所知，”温思罗普小姐说着，略微竖起羽毛摆出要辩论的架势——这向来是她的嗜好，“不过，就事论事来说，假使有一位受过良好教育、举止文雅的男子，因故每天早晨都去给铺子扫地，你们又该称他作什么呢？”说罢她环顾四周，仿佛抛出了一个教人答不上来的难题。

===Original===
The colorless young ladies looked blank﻿—their natural expression.

“Nonsense!” said the positive Miss Brown; “such men don’t sweep stores. He may have passed current in some country village, but that is not our set.”

“But the case is certainly supposable,” retorted Miss Winthrop, more intent upon her argument than upon Dennis. “Come, what does the Countess say?” she asked, turning to Christine; for that was the familiar name by which she went among her young companions.

“The case is not supposable, but actual,” she answered, so distinctly that it seemed that she meant Dennis to hear. “As far as I have any means of judging, he is a refined, educated man, and I have learned from papa that his motive in sweeping the store is the support of his mother and sisters﻿—certainly a very worthy one. To your question, Susie, I answer unhesitatingly that in accordance with your American principles and professions he is a gentleman, and you ought to treat him as such. But you Americans are sometimes wonderfully inconsistent, and there is often a marvellously wide margin between your boasted equality and the reality. Now in Europe these questions have been settled for ages, and birth and rank define a person’s position accurately.”

“I do not believe in equality,” said Miss Brown, with a toss of her head. (Her father was a mighty brewer, but he and hers were in character and antecedents something like the froth on their own beer.)

===Chinese===
那几位寡淡的小姐面面相觑，一脸茫然——这原本就是她们的常态。

“一派胡言！”斩钉截铁的布朗小姐说道，“那样的人物才不会去扫铺子呢。他或许在哪个乡下村镇里还算得上体面人物，可那并不是咱们这个圈子。”

“可这种情形分明是可以假设的呀，”温思罗普小姐反驳道，她更在乎的是这场争辩本身，而非丹尼斯其人，“来，听听‘女伯爵’（Countess）怎么说？”她转过脸去问克里斯蒂娜——原来这便是她在年轻女伴们中间惯用的昵称。

“这可不是假设，而是实打实摆在眼前的事，”她开口答道，吐字清晰极了，仿佛有意让丹尼斯听见似的，“就我所能判断的而言，他确实是个温文尔雅、饱读诗书的人；我还听爸爸说过，他之所以屈尊扫铺子，是为了奉养母亲和妹妹们——这动机实在难能可贵。至于你的问题，苏茜，我可以毫不犹豫地回答你：按照你们美国人一贯标榜的原则和信条，他就是一位绅士，你们也理应以绅士之礼待他。可惜你们美国人有时候言行实在自相矛盾得出奇，你们引以为傲的平等信条与现实之间，往往隔着一道大得惊人的鸿沟。换在欧洲，这类问题早在千百年前便已定论，出身与门第清清楚楚地界定了一个人的地位。”

“我才不信什么平等呢，”布朗小姐把头一甩，说道。（她父亲是个财大气粗的大啤酒商，只不过他们父女连带全家人的品性与来历，都活脱脱像是自家桶里浮着的那层啤酒沫子。）

===Original===
Miss Winthrop was a little embarrassed at finding her supposed case a real one, for it might involve some practical action on her part. Many an ardent advocate of the people in theory gives them practically the cold shoulder, and is content to stay on the summit of Mt. Olympus. She was a girl of good impulses and strong convictions of abstract right, but rarely had either the courage or the opportunity to carry them out. She was of the old Boston family of Winthrops, and therefore could meet Miss Ludolph on her own ground in the way of pedigree.

But, however Dennis fared, she felt that she must look after her argument, and, having conquered theoretically as far as America was concerned, determined to carry war into Europe, so she said: “Are you not mistaken in saying that birth and rank only settle position abroad? Some of the most honored names there are or were untitled.”

“Oh, certainly, but they were persons of great genius, and *genius* is the highest patent of nobility. But I leave you republicans to settle this question to suit yourselves. I am going to look after the preparations for this evening, as I have set my heart on a success that shall ring through the city.”

But they all flocked after her into the back parlor, now doubly interesting as it contained an object of curiosity in Dennis Fleet﻿—a veritable gentleman who swept a store.

===Chinese===
听闻自己随口设想的事例竟是真人真事，温思罗普小姐反倒有些尴尬起来，因为这兴许意味着她自己也得采取什么实际行动才行。世上许多在口头上热烈拥护平民的人，真到了节骨眼上却往往摆出一副冷眼相待的架势，安安稳稳地坐在奥林匹斯山巅不肯下来。她本是个心地善良、对抽象公理怀有坚定信念的姑娘，却鲜少有勇气或机会将其付诸实践。她出身波士顿名门温思罗普家族，论起家世门第，足可与卢多尔夫小姐分庭抗礼。

不过，无论丹尼斯处境如何，她都觉得眼下总得先顾全自己的论点；既然就美国而论她已经在理论上占了上风，她便决意把战火烧到欧洲去，于是开口道：“你说在海外单凭出身和门第就能决定地位，这话未免有失偏颇吧？那边最受敬重的一些人物，如今或昔日可并没有什么贵族头衔呢。”

“哦，那是自然，可那些人都是大天才，而*天才*本身便是至高无上的封爵诏书。行了，这个问题还是留给你们这些共和派自己慢慢去争个明白吧。我得去盯着今晚的筹备工作了，我可铁了心要办成一场轰动全城的盛会呢。”

然而她们却一窝蜂地跟在她身后涌进了后客厅——眼下那间屋子变得加倍有趣了，因为里面正呆着一件稀罕玩意儿：丹尼斯·弗利特，一个如假包换、却替人扫铺子的绅士。

## XVI Just in Time / 第十六章 恰逢其时

===Original===
At the close of the day on which Dennis received his promotion, and his horizon was widened so unexpectedly, Mr. Ludolph, in passing out, noticed him engaged as usual on one of Pat Murphy’s old tasks. He stopped and spoke kindly, “Well, Fleet, where am I going to find a man to fill your place made vacant today?”

“Would you be willing to listen to a suggestion from me?”

“Certainly.”

“If a young boy was employed to black boots, run errands, and attend to minor matters, I think that by industry I might for a while fill both positions. In a short time the furnace will require no further attention. I am a very early riser, and think that by a little good management I can keep the store in order and still be on hand to attend to my counter when customers are about.”

Mr. Ludolph was much pleased with the proposition, and said, promptly, “You may try it, Fleet, and I will pay you accordingly. Do you know of a boy who will answer?”

===Chinese===
丹尼斯获得提拔、眼界竟出人意料地豁然开朗的那天傍晚，卢多尔夫先生正要出门，看见他仍照常做着帕特·墨菲从前干的那些活计。他停下脚步，和颜悦色地问道：“我说，弗利特，你今天腾出来的那个缺，我上哪儿去找个人来顶上呢？”

“您愿意听我提个建议吗？”

“当然。”

“要是能雇个小男孩来擦靴子、跑跑腿、料理些琐碎杂务，我想只要自己勤快些，眼下这两个差事我一人都能一并兼顾。再过一阵子，暖炉也不用再费神看管了。我向来起得很早，只要稍微安排得当，我既能把店堂收拾得井井有条，等顾客上门时也能照常守在柜台前招呼。”

卢多尔夫先生对这个提议大为满意，当即说道：“你可以试试，弗利特，工钱我也照着相应加给你。你认得合用的孩子吗？”

===Original===
“I think I do, sir. There is a German lad in my mission class who has interested me very much. His father is really a superior artist, but is throwing himself away with drink, and his mother is engaged in an almost hopeless effort to support the family. They have seen much better days, and their life seems very hard in contrast with the past.”

“Can we trust such a boy? Their very necessities may lead to theft.”

“They are not of the thieving sort, sir. I am satisfied that they would all starve rather than touch a penny that did not belong to them.”

“Very well, then, let him come and see me; but I will hold you responsible for him.”

===Chinese===
“我想我认得一个，先生。我那个布道班里有个德国少年，一直很让我挂心。他父亲其实是个极高明的画师，却整日酗酒自毁前程，母亲则咬着牙苦苦支撑全家，眼看快撑不住了。他们从前过过颇为宽裕体面的日子，如今与昔日一比，光景实在艰难得很。”

“这样的孩子信得过吗？穷极了难免会手脚不干净、动起偷摸的念头。”

“他们不是那种偷鸡摸狗的人家，先生。我敢断定，他们宁可一家子挨饿，也绝不会动不属于自己的一文钱。”

“那好吧，叫他来见我；不过他出了什么事，我唯你是问。”

===Original===
Mr. Ludolph, being in a good humor, was disposed to banter Dennis, so he added: “Do you find time to be a missionary, also? Are you not in danger of becoming a jack-at-all-trades?”

“I am not entitled to the first character, and hope to shun the latter. I merely teach a dozen boys in a mission school on Sundays.”

“When you ought to be taking a good long nap, or a row on the lake for fresh air and recreation.”

“I should be dishonest if I spent my Sabbaths in that way.”

“How so?”

“I should give the lie to my profession and belief. I must drop the name of Christian when I live for myself.”

===Chinese===
卢多尔夫先生此刻心情颇佳，有心拿丹尼斯打趣几句，便又添了一句：“你居然还抽得出工夫兼着当传教士？难道就不怕落得个样样沾边、样样不精的万金油吗？”

“头一个名号我担当不起，后一种境地我也唯恐避之不及。我不过是每个礼拜天去一所布道学校，教十来个男孩子念书罢了。”

“那工夫你本该舒舒服服睡上一大觉，或者到湖上划划船，透透新鲜空气、消遣一番才是。”

“我要是那样虚度安息日，便算是不忠不诚了。”

“此话怎讲？”

“那岂不是亲手推翻了我平日所宣称的信条与信仰？我若只为自己而活，便再不配自称基督徒了。”

===Original===
“And if you should drop it, do you think you would be much the loser?”

“Yes, sir,” said Dennis, with quiet emphasis.

“You are expecting great reward, in some sort of Paradise, for your mission work, etc.?”

“Nothing done for God is forgotten or unrewarded.”

“Believing that, it seems to me that you are looking after self-interest as much as the rest of us,” said his employer, with a shrewd smile.

===Chinese===
“即便你摘掉这个名号，你以为自己又会吃多大亏呢？”

“会的，先生。”丹尼斯语气平静却斩钉截铁地答道。

“莫非你还指望着凭那点布道善举之类，来日好在某个天堂里捞到一笔厚赏不成？”

“凡为上帝所做之事，祂一概不会忘怀，也绝不会不予赏赐。”

“照你这么信法，依我看，你还不跟我们大伙儿一样，归根结底都是在算计自己的利益么。”东家露出一丝精明的笑意说道。

===Original===
Looking straight into Mr. Ludolph’s eyes, Dennis said, earnestly: “Without boasting, I think that I can say that I try to serve you faithfully. If you could see my heart, I am sure you would find that gratitude for your kindness is a part of my motive, as well as my wages. In the same manner, while I do not lose sight of the rich rewards God promises and daily gives for the little I can do for Him, I am certain that I can do much out of simple gratitude and love, and ask no reward.”

“Ignorance is certainly bliss in your case, young man. Stick to your harmless superstition as long as you can.”

And he walked away, muttering: “Delusion, delusion! I have not said a word or done a thing for him in which I had not in view my interests only, and yet the poor young fool sees in the main disinterested kindness. Little trouble have the wily priests in imposing on such victims, and so they get their hard-earned wages and set them propagating the delusion in mission schools, when mind and body need change and rest. Suppose there is a Supreme Being in the universe, what a monstrous absurdity to imagine that He would trouble Himself to reward this Yankee youth for teaching a dozen ragamuffins in a tenement-house mission school!”

Thus Mr. Ludolph’s soliloquy proved that his own pride and selfishness had destroyed the faculty by which he could see God. The blind are not more oblivious to color than he was to those divine qualities which are designed to win and enchain the heart. A man may sadly mutilate his own soul.

===Chinese===
丹尼斯直视着卢多尔夫先生的眼睛，诚恳地说道：“并非自夸，我想我可以问心无愧地说，我一向尽心竭力为您效劳。您若能看透我的肺腑，定会发觉促使我这么做的缘由里，除了薪水之外，还有一份感念您厚待之恩的感激之情。同理，尽管我并未忘记自己尽微薄之力侍奉上帝时，祂所应许、并且日日赐予的丰厚恩典，可我也深信，自己全然出于单纯的感恩与爱慕便能为祂做许多事，而不求任何回报。”

“年轻人，无知对你来说倒真是一桩福分。只要守得住，你就只管守着你那套无害的迷信吧。”

说罢他便踱步走开，嘴里兀自嘟囔道：“痴人说梦，真是痴人说梦！我对这小子所说的一字一句、所做的一举一动，哪一样不是纯粹出于我自己的算计？可这可怜的小傻瓜，偏偏只看出一片大公无私的好意来。那些狡猾的教士要哄骗这种冤大头，可真是省心省力——一面骗走他们辛辛苦苦挣来的工钱，一面打发他们在身心最该调剂歇息的时候，跑去布道学校散播这套鬼话。就算这宇宙间真有至高主宰，试想祂竟会屈尊劳神，去赏赐这么一个扬基青年（Yankee），只因他在贫民出租屋的布道学校里教了十来个小叫花子——世上还有比这更荒唐可笑的念头吗！”

卢多尔夫先生这番自言自语恰恰证明，他自身的傲慢与自私，早已摧毁了他用以感知上帝的那种灵性官觉。盲人对色彩如何茫然无知，他对那些本为赢取并萦系人心的神圣品性，也同样视而不见。人竟能如此可悲地残毁自己的灵魂。

===Original===
At a dainty dinner-table Mr. Ludolph and his daughter discussed the events of the day.

“I am glad,” said the latter, “that he is willing to fill Pat’s place, for he keeps everything so clean. A dusty, slovenly store is my abomination. Then it shows that he has no silly, uppish notions so common to these Americans.” (Though born here, Miss Ludolph never thought herself other than a German lady of rank.) “But I do not wish to see him blacking boots again. Yet he is an odd genius. How comical he looked bowing to me with one of Mr. Schwartz’s big boots describing a graceful curve on a level with his head. Let old Schwartz black his own boots. He ought to as a punishment for carrying around so much leather. This Fleet must have seen better days. He is like all Yankees, however, sharp after the dollar, though he seems more willing to work for it than most of them.”

“I’ll wager you a pair of gloves,” said her father, “that they get a good percentage of it down at the mission school. He is just the subject for a cunning priest, because he sincerely believes in their foolery. He belongs to a tribe now nearly extinct, I imagine﻿—the martyrs, who in old-fashioned times died for all sorts of delusions.”

“How time mellows and changes everything! There is something heroic and worthy of art in the ancient martyrdoms, while nothing is more repulsive than modern fanaticism. It is a shame, though, that this young man, with mother and sisters to support, should be robbed of his hard earnings as was Pat Murphy by his priest, and I will try to open his eyes some day.”

“I predict for you no success.”

===Chinese===
在一张精巧雅致的餐桌旁，卢多尔夫先生与女儿聊起了这一日来的种种见闻。

“我倒很高兴他肯顶下帕特的缺，”女儿说道，“因为他把店里里外外收拾得干干净净。一家积灰邋遢的店铺最教我深恶痛绝。再说，这也看得出他没有这些美国人常有的那种可笑又眼高于顶的架子。”（卢多尔夫小姐虽生于此地，心中却从未把自己当作德意志名门贵女之外的任何人。）“不过我可不愿再瞧见他擦靴子了。话虽如此，他倒真是个古怪的奇才。您没见他向我鞠躬时那副滑稽相——手里拎着施瓦茨先生的一只大皮靴，齐着头顶划出一道优美的弧线。让老施瓦茨自己擦靴子去吧。脚上拖着这么大一块牛皮满处晃悠，罚他自己擦才活该。这个弗利特想必也曾有过体面阔绰的日子。不过，他终究和所有扬基佬一样，见了美元就两眼精明得很，只是比他们大多数人更肯卖力气去挣罢了。”

“我拿一副手套跟你打赌，”她父亲接话道，“他挣的钱，准有好大一成被布道学校那帮人抽走了。他简直是狡诈教士最称心的猎物，因为他打心眼儿里相信他们那一套鬼把戏。我看他属于如今几乎绝迹的那一类人——殉道者，就像老早那些年代里，为了形形色色的妄念而白白送命的人一样。”

“岁月真是能把万物都酿得醇厚、改换了面目啊！古代的殉道总带着几分英雄气概，足堪入画入诗，可当代的宗教狂热却再没有比它更令人生厌的了。不过，这年轻人上有老母、下有妹妹要养活，血汗钱竟像帕特·墨菲被他的神父盘剥那样让人白白诈去，倒真是可惜，哪天我非设法点醒他不可。”

“我预言你不会得逞的。”

===Original===
“Why so?﻿—he seems intelligent.”

“I have not studied character all my life in vain. He would regard you, my fair daughter, as the devil in the form of an angel of light tempting him.”

“He had better not be so plainspoken as yourself.”

“Oh, no need of Fleet’s speaking; his face is like the page of an open book.”

“Indeed! a face like a signboard is a most unfortunate one, I should think.”

“Most fortunate for us. I wish I could read everyone as I can Fleet.”

===Chinese===
“何以见得？——他瞧着倒是个聪明人。”

“我活了这半辈子，察人观色可不是白练的。我美丽的女儿，他只会把你当成化作光明天使模样的魔鬼，在存心诱惑他呢。”

“他最好别像您说话这么直白露骨。”

“哦，根本用不着弗利特开口；他那张脸就像翻开的书页一样，什么都写在上面。”

“当真吗？照我看，长着一张招牌似的脸，那可太倒霉了。”

“对我们来说却再幸运不过。但愿我能像看透弗利特那样看透每一个人。”

===Original===
“You trust no one, I believe, father.”

“I believe what I see and know.”

“I wish I had your power of seeing and knowing. But how did he get his artistic knowledge and taste?”

“That I have not inquired into fully, as yet. I think he has an unusual native aptness for these things, and gains hints and instruction where others would see nothing. And, as you say, in the better days past he may have had some advantages.”

===Chinese===
“我看您是谁也不信任，父亲。”

“我只信我亲眼所见、亲身确知的东西。”

“真希望我也有您那双看透世事的慧眼与见识。不过，他那一身艺术学识和鉴赏品味究竟是从哪儿学来的？”

“这我眼下还未细究。我觉得他对这类事物生来就有一种异于常人的领悟力，别人眼底空无一物之处，他却能从中汲取门道与指点。再者，诚如你所说，他从前家境尚好时，或许也曾受过些熏陶。”

===Original===
“Well,” said she, caressing the greyhound beside her, “if Wolf here should go to the piano and execute an opera, I should not be more astonished than I was this morning.”

And then their conversation glided off on other topics.

After dessert, Mr. Ludolph lighted a cigar and sat down to the evening paper, while his daughter evoked from the piano true after-dinner music﻿—light, brilliant, mirth-inspiring. Then both adjourned to their private billiard-room.

===Chinese===
“唉，”她一边抚弄着身旁的灵缇犬一边说道，“就算这只沃尔夫（Wolf）眼下走到钢琴前弹起一出歌剧来，我也不会比今早那会儿更吃惊了。”

随后，父女俩的话题便滑到了别的事情上去。

吃罢甜点，卢多尔夫先生点起一支雪茄，坐下来翻看晚报；他的女儿则在钢琴上奏出地道的饭后小曲——轻快、明丽、教人怡然自得。随后，父女俩一同移步去了私人台球室。

---

===Original===
The scene of our story now changes from Mr. Ludolph’s luxurious apartments in one of the most fashionable hotels in the city to a forlorn attic in De Koven Street. It is the scene of a struggle as desperate, as heroic, against as tremendous odds, as was ever carried on in the days of the Crusades. But as the foremost figure in this long, weary conflict was not an armed and panoplied knight, but merely a poor German woman, only God and the angels took much interest in it. Still upon this evening she was almost vanquished. She seemed to have but one vantage-point left on earth. For a wonder, her husband was comparatively sober, and sat brooding with his head in his hands over the stove where a fire was slowly dying out. The last coal they had was fast turning to ashes. From a cradle came a low, wailing cry. It was that of hunger. On an old chest in a dusky corner sat a boy about thirteen. Though all else was in shadow, his large eyes shone with unnatural brightness, and followed his mother’s feeble efforts at the washtub with that expression of premature sadness so pathetic in childhood. Under a rickety deal table three other and smaller children were devouring some crusts of bread in a ravenous way, like half-famished young animals. In a few moments they came out and clamored for more, addressing﻿—not their father; no intuitive turning to him for support﻿—but the poor, over-tasked mother. The boy came out of his corner and tried to draw them off and interest them in something else, but they were like a pack of hungry little wolves. The boy’s face was almost as sharp and famine-pinched as his mother’s, but he seemed to have lost all thought of himself in his sorrowful regard for her. As the younger children clamored and dragged upon her, the point of endurance was passed, and the poor woman gave way. With a despairing cry she sank upon a chair and covered her face with her apron.

“Oh, mine Gott, Oh, mine Gott,” she cried, “I can do not von more stroke if ve all die.”

In a moment her son had his arms around her neck, and said: “Oh, moder, don’t cry, don’t cry. Mr. Fleet said God would surely help us in time of trouble if we would only ask Him.”

“I’ve ask Him, and ask Him, but der help don’t come. I can do no more;” and a tempest of despairing sobs shook her gaunt frame.

The boy seemed to have got past tears, and just fixed his large eyes, full of reproach and sorrow, on his father.

===Chinese===
咱们故事的舞台，此刻从全城最摩登考究的酒店里卢多尔夫先生那套奢华寓所，骤然转到了德科文街上一间凄凉破败的阁楼。这里正上演着一场生死搏斗——其拼死苦战之惨烈、其抗衡强敌之英勇，丝毫不逊于十字军东征年代的任何一场厮杀。只因这场漫长苦斗里冲在最前头的主角，并非披坚执锐的骑士，而不过是一名贫苦的德国妇人，世上也就唯有上帝与天使才会多加垂注。然而到了今夜，她几乎已油尽灯枯、彻底败下阵来。放眼人世，她似乎只剩下最后一处微弱的仰仗。说来稀奇，她丈夫今晚倒是颇为清醒，正双手抱头、默然枯坐在炉边苦思，炉里的火正一点点熄灭下去，他们仅剩的最后几块煤正迅速化为灰烬。摇篮里传来低微绵长的啼哭，那是饥饿的哀鸣。在昏暗角落的一只旧木箱上，坐着个十三岁左右的男孩。周遭一切都沉没在阴影里，唯有他那双大眼睛闪烁着异样的光亮，顺着母亲在洗衣盆前有气无力的动作一路望去，眼神里满是孩童身上最教人心酸的早熟忧伤。一张摇摇晃晃的松木桌底下，另外三个年纪更小的孩子正狼吞虎咽地啃着几块硬面包皮，活像一群饿疯了的小兽。没过片刻，他们便钻出来嚷着还要吃，喊的对象并非父亲——孩子们的本能压根儿不指望他来遮风挡雨——而是那位精疲力竭、不堪重负的母亲。角落里的男孩走出来，试着把弟妹引开，拿别的事逗他们分心，可这几个小家伙简直像一群饥肠辘辘的小狼崽。那男孩的脸蛋几乎和母亲一样削瘦得见了骨棱、满是饥色，但他在满怀痛惜地挂念着母亲时，仿佛全然忘却了自己的饥苦。小家伙们又吵又闹地死死拽住妇人的衣襟，她终于忍到了极点，一下子垮了下来。可怜的妇人发出一声绝望的悲呼，瘫坐在一张椅子上，抓起围裙掩住了面庞。

“哦，我的上帝啊，我的上帝啊，”她哭喊道，“就算全家一块儿死，我也再干不动一丁点活计了！”

刹那间，儿子扑过去搂住她的脖子，柔声宽慰道：“哦，妈妈，别哭了，别哭了。弗利特先生说过，只要咱们肯向祂祈求，患难之中上帝定会搭救咱们的。”

“我求了祂一遍又一遍，可救星就是不来。我真是再也撑不住了！”一阵绝望的暴风骤雨般的呜咽，剧烈地摇撼着她瘦骨嶙峋的身躯。

男孩仿佛早已哭干了眼泪，只是将一双盛满怨艾与悲戚的大眼睛，直勾勾地盯在父亲身上。

===Original===
The man rose and turned his bloodshot eyes slowly around the room. The whole scene, with its meaning, seemed to dawn upon him. His mind was not so clouded by the fumes of liquor but that he could comprehend the supreme misery of the situation. He heard his children crying﻿—fairly howling for bread. He saw the wife he had sworn to love and honor, where she had fallen in her unequal conflict, brave, but overpowered. He remembered the wealthy burgher’s blooming, courted daughter, whom he had lured away to marry him, a poor artist. He remembered how, in spite of her father’s commands and her mother’s tears, she had left home and luxury to follow him throughout the world because of her faith in him and love for him﻿—how under her inspiration he had risen to great promise as an artist, till fame and fortune became almost a certainty, and then, under the debasing influence of his terrible appetite, he had dragged her down and down, till now he saw her﻿—prematurely old, broken in health, broken in heart﻿—fall helplessly before the hard drudgery that she no longer had strength to perform. With a sickening horror he remembered that he had taken even the pittance she had wrung from that washtub, to feed, not his children, but his accursed appetite for drink. Even his purple, bloated face grew livid as all the past rushed upon him, and despair laid an icy hand upon his heart.

A desperate purpose formed itself within his mind.

Turning to the wall where hung a noble picture, a lovely landscape, whose rich coloring, warm sunlight, and rural peace formed a sharp, strange contrast with the meagre, famine-stricken apartment, he was about to take it down from its fastening when his hand was arrested by a word﻿—“Father!”

He turned, and saw his son looking at him with his great eyes full of horror and alarm, as if he were committing a murder.

“I tell you I must, and I vill,” said he, savagely.

===Chinese===
那男人站起身，一双布满血丝的眼睛缓缓扫过整间屋子。眼前这一幕幕景象及其背后的凄惨意味，似乎猛然间豁然贯通地刺入他的心头。他的神智尚未被酒气熏得彻底糊涂，还足以领会眼下这副绝境深处的无边苦痛。他听见儿女们哭叫——简直是在为一口面包嘶声号哭。他看见自己曾发誓相爱相敬的妻子，在这场悬殊的搏斗里虽已竭尽英勇，终究寡不敌众、轰然倒下。他想起了从前那个富裕市民家里如花似玉、人人竞相追求的娇女，正是他将她哄骗离开家门，下嫁给自己这么个一贫如洗的画匠。他记起她当年如何不顾父亲的严令与母亲的泪水，只凭着对他的信赖与深情，抛下锦衣玉食随他浪迹天涯——在她的鼓舞之下，他作为画家曾如何大放异彩、前途无量，名望与财富几乎已是囊中之物；而随后，在那可怕酒瘾的堕落魔爪之下，他又如何把她一步步拖入深渊，直至今日亲眼见她——未老先衰、百病缠身、心碎肠断——在自己再也无力承担的繁重苦役面前无助倒下。一阵令人作呕的惊骇涌上心头，他猛然记起，甚至连她守着那只洗衣盆辛辛苦苦绞出的一点微薄工钱，都被自己夺了去，喂饱的不是嗷嗷待哺的儿女，而是他那该死的嗜酒恶癖。往昔一幕幕排山倒海般朝他压来，连他那张紫涨浮肿的脸也霎时间变得死灰铁青，绝望伸出一双冰冷的手，死死攥住了他的心脏。

一个孤注一掷的念头在他心头成形。

他转过身望向墙面——那儿挂着一幅气韵高华的画作，画中是一片秀丽明媚的田园风光，丰润绚丽的色彩、和煦温暖的阳光与安宁恬静的乡野景致，同这间饥寒交迫的陋室构成了尖锐而奇异的反差。他正伸手要去把画从挂钩上摘下来，忽然一声呼唤止住了他的手——“爸爸！”

他回过头，只见儿子正用那双大眼睛惊恐万状、满怀骇惧地望着自己，活像他正在行凶杀人一般。

“我告诉你，我非卖不可，非去不可！”他恶狠狠地吼道。

===Original===
His wife looked up, sprang to his side, and with her hands upon his arm, said, “No, Berthold, you must not, you shall not sell dot picture.”

He silently pointed to his children crying for bread.

“Take der dress off my back to sell, but not dot picture. Ve may as vell die before him goes, for we certainly vill after. Dot is de only ding left of der happy past. Dot, in Gott’s hands, is my only hope for der future. Dot picture dells you vat you vas, vat you might be still if you vould only let drink alone. Many’s der veary day, many’s der long night, I’ve prayed dot dot picture vould vin you back to your former self, ven tears and sufferings vere in vain. Leave him, and some day he vill tell you so plain vat you are, and vot you can be, dot you break der horrid spell dot chains you, and your artist-soul come again. Leave him, our only hope, and sole bar against despair and death. I vill go and beg a dousand times before dot picture’s sold; for if he goes, your artist-soul no more come back, and you’re lost, and ve all are lost.”

===Chinese===
妻子猛地抬起头，箭步扑到他身旁，双手死死扳住他的胳膊叫道：“不行，贝特霍尔德，你不能卖，决不许卖那幅画！”

他一言不发，只抬手指了指正哭闹着要面包吃的孩子们。

“扒下我身上的衣裳去卖也好，就是不能动那幅画！与其等它被卖掉，咱们还不如眼下就死光了干净，因为画一走，咱们横竖是活不成的。那是往昔幸福岁月留下的唯一念想了！握在上帝手里，它就是我对将来仅存的指望啊！那幅画在提醒你，你曾经是个什么样的人，只要你肯戒掉酒，往后依然能成什么样的人。多少个精疲力竭的白日，多少个漫漫长夜，在眼泪与受苦都无济于事的时候，我都曾祷告着，求这幅画能把你挽回到从前的模样！留下它吧，总有一天它会清清楚楚地照见你如今的模样与本该有的前程，叫你挣脱那套拴住你的可怖魔咒，让你那颗画家的灵魂重新苏醒过来！留下它吧，它是咱们唯一的盼头，是拦在绝望与死路前头最后一道屏障！要卖那幅画，我宁愿出门讨一千回饭去；因为只要它一走，你那颗画家的灵魂就再也回不来了，你完了，咱们一家子也就全完了！”

===Original===
The man hesitated. His good angel was pleading with him, but in vain.

Stamping his foot with rage and despair, he shouted, hoarsely, “It is too late I am lost now.”

And he tore the picture from its fastening. His wife sank back against the wall with a groan as if her very soul were departing.

But before his rash steps could leave the desolation he had made, he was confronted by the tall form of Dennis Fleet.

===Chinese===
那男人迟疑了。他心中的良善天使正在苦苦哀求着他，却终究徒劳无功。

他恼羞成怒又绝望万分地狠狠一跺脚，嘶哑着嗓子咆哮道：“太迟了！我已经彻底完蛋了！”

说着，他一把将画从墙上的挂钩扯了下来。妻子发出一声凄厉的呻吟，瘫软着靠墙滑倒下去，仿佛连魂魄都要随之一并飞散了。

然而，他鲁莽的脚步尚未迈出自己亲手酿就的这片满目疮痍，面前便蓦然挡住了一个高大的身影——丹尼斯·弗利特。

===Original===
The man stared at him for a moment as if he had been an apparition, and then said, in a hard tone, “Let me pass!”

Dennis had knocked for some time, but such was the excitement within no one had regarded the sound. He had, therefore, heard the wife’s appeal and its answer, and from what he knew of the family from his mission scholar, the boy Ernst, comprehended the situation in the main. When, therefore, matters reached the crisis, he opened the door and met the infatuated man as he was about to throw away the last relic of his former self and happier life. With great tact he appeared as if he knew nothing, and quietly taking a chair he sat down with his back against the door, thus barring egress. In a pleasant, affable tone, he said: “Mr. Bruder, I came to see you on a little business tonight. As I was in something of a hurry, and no one appeared to hear my knock, I took the liberty of coming in.”

The hungry little ones looked at him with their round eyes of childish curiosity, and for a time ceased their clamors. The wife sank into a chair and bowed her head in her hands with the indifference of despair. Hope had gone. A gleam of joy lighted up Ernst’s pale face at the sight of his beloved teacher, and he stepped over to his mother and commenced whispering in her ear, but she heeded him not. The man’s face wore a sullen, dangerous, yet irresolute expression. It was evident that he half believed that Dennis was knowingly trying to thwart him, and such was his mad frenzy that he was ready for any desperate deed.

===Chinese===
那男人定定地瞪着他看了一瞬，仿佛见了幽灵一般，随即声音生硬地喝道：“让开！”

其实丹尼斯刚才已经敲了好一会儿门，只是屋里群情激愤，竟没有一个人听见敲门声。他因而把妻子那番苦苦哀求与丈夫的吼声听了个真切，再加上平日从布道班学生、小男孩恩斯特口中得知的家中底细，眼下的情形他大致已摸透了七八分。于是，眼看事态已迫在眉睫，他便推门而入，迎面拦住了这个正欲亲手断送昔日自我与幸福生涯最后遗物的迷惘汉子。他极其机敏得体地装作浑然不觉的模样，不慌不忙拉过一把椅子，背抵着门板坐了下来，就这样挡住了去路。随即，他用轻松和煦的语调开口道：“布鲁德先生，我今晚来找您，是有点小事想商量。因为手头赶时间，又瞧着似乎没人听见我敲门，我就冒昧自己进来了。”

几个挨饿的小家伙圆睁着充满孩童好奇心的大眼睛望着他，一时倒也止住了哭闹。做妻子的瘫坐进椅子里，双手掩面低垂着头，脸上已是死灰般的麻木与绝望——希望已然破灭。恩斯特一看见敬爱的老师，苍白的小脸上顿时闪过一抹喜色，连忙凑到母亲身旁在她耳边低低说起悄悄话来，可她却恍若未闻。那男人脸上则浮现出一副阴郁、凶险却又犹疑不定的神色。很明显，他半信半疑地猜到丹尼斯是故意要来阻拦自己，而他此刻狂躁癫狂的心境，简直什么亡命之举都干得出来。

## IX Land at Last / 第九章 终于靠岸

===Original===
During the latter part of a busy afternoon, Dennis came to a spacious, elegant store before which the snow lay untouched save as trodden by passersby. Over the high arched doorway was the legend in gilt letters, “Art Building”; and as far as a mere warehouse for beautiful things could deserve the title, this place did, for it was crowded with engravings, paintings, bronzes, statuary, and every variety of ornament. With delighted eyes and lingering steps he had passed slowly through this store a few days previous in his search, but had received the usual cool negative. He had gone reluctantly out into the cold street again as Adam went out of Paradise.

A large florid-looking man with a light curling mustache now stood in the doorway. His appearance was unmistakably that of a German of the highest and most cultivated type. And yet, when he spoke, his English was so good that you detected only a foreign accent. Strong vexation was stamped upon his face as he looked at the snowy, untidy sidewalk.

“Mr. Schwartz,” he asked of one of his clerks, “was Pat here this morning?”

“Yes, sir.”

===Chinese===
繁忙的午后将近尾声，丹尼斯来到一家宽敞雅致的商店门前。店门前的积雪尚未清扫，只被过往行人踩出些许足迹。高高的拱形门楣上方嵌着一行烫金大字：“艺术大厦”；倘若一间单纯陈列美物的库房也配得上这个名号，这里倒真是名副其实——里面琳琅满目地摆满了版画、油画、青铜器、雕像以及各式各样的工艺摆件。几天前他四处谋职时，也曾怀着欣喜的目光、迈着流连的步子从这家店里缓缓穿过，却同样只领受了一句冷淡的回绝。那时他恋恋不舍地重返寒风凛冽的街头，心境正如同亚当被逐出伊甸园一般。

此刻，门口站着一位身材魁梧、面色红润的男子，嘴唇上方蓄着两撇微卷的浅色小胡子。从相貌上看，他无疑属于那种最具教养、最高雅的德国人。不过，他开口说英语时流利得很，只听得出几分外国口音。眼下他望着积雪凌乱的人行道，脸上写满了恼怒。

“施瓦茨先生，”他问其中一个店员，“帕特今天上午来过吗？”

“来过，先生。”

===Original===
“Was he perfectly straight?”

“I cannot say that he was, sir.”

“He is off on a spree again. Send him to me the moment he returns.”

“Shall I clear your sidewalk?” said Dennis, stepping up and touching his hat respectfully.

“Yes,” said the gentleman, scarcely looking at him; “and when you have finished come to the office for your money;” and then he walked back into the store with a frowning brow.

===Chinese===
“他当时人完全清醒吗？”

“我不敢说他清醒，先生。”

“他又跑出去狂饮作乐了。他一回来，立刻叫他来见我。”

“我帮您把人行道清扫干净好吗？”丹尼斯走上前去，恭敬地抬手摸了摸帽檐说道。

“好吧，”那位绅士几乎正眼也没瞧他一下，“扫完了到办公室来领工钱。”说完，他便皱着眉头踱回店里去了。

===Original===
Though Dennis was now pretty thoroughly fatigued with the hard day’s work, he entered on this task with a good will as the closing labor of the day, hoping, from the wide space to be cleared, to receive proportionate recompense. And yet his despatch was not so great as usual, for in spite of himself his eyes were continually wandering to the large show-windows, from which smiled down upon him summer landscapes, and lovely faces that seemed all the more beautiful in contrast with the bleak and darkening street.

He was rudely startled from one of his stolen glances at a sweet, girlish face that seemed peering archly at him from a corner. His ears were assailed by the loud tones and strong brogue of “Pat,” returning thus late to his neglected duties.

“Bad luck to yez! what yez doin’ here?”

“Clearing the sidewalk,” said Dennis, laconically.

“Give me that shovel, or I’ll knock bloody blazes out of yez.”

Dennis at once stood on the defensive, and raised his tool threateningly. At the same time seeing a policeman, he called out, “Will you please cause this drunken fellow to move on?”

===Chinese===
虽然劳累了一整天，丹尼斯此刻早已筋疲力尽，但一想到这是今天的最后一桩活计，而且要清扫的地方这么宽敞，想必能换来一笔相应的酬劳，他便欣然动起手来。只是这一回他的手脚不如往常麻利，因为他的目光总是不由自主地飘向那几扇宽大的橱窗——窗内一幅幅夏日风景画与一张张秀美脸庞正朝他微笑俯瞰，与外面凄清昏暗的街道两相对照，更显得动人无比。

橱窗一角有一张娇俏甜美的少女面庞，似乎正顽皮地探头望着他。丹尼斯正偷偷凝视着那幅画时，却被一阵突如其来的粗嗓门吓了一跳——“帕特”终于回到他玩忽多时的岗位上了，那大嗓门里满是浓重的爱尔兰土音，直往人耳朵里钻。

“见鬼去吧你！你小子在这儿干啥呢？”

“扫人行道。”丹尼斯简短地答道。

“把那把铁锹交出来，不然老子把你揍得稀巴烂！”

丹尼斯立刻摆出防备的架势，举起手里的铁锹以示警告。与此同时，他瞥见一名警察，便高声喊道：“劳驾您让这个醉汉走开好吗？”

===Original===
The officer was about to comply, when the Irishman, with a snort like that of a mad bull, rushed to the door of the art building, wrenched it open, and, leaving it so, tore down the long store, crying, “Misther Ludolph! Misther Ludolph! here’s a bloody spalpane a-doin’ my work.”

He had scarcely got halfway to the office before there was a crash followed by a general commotion.

Pat, in his blind rage, and with steps uncertain from the effects of whiskey, had struck a valuable marble, and it lay broken on the floor. This catastrophe sobered him, and he stood looking in dismay at the destruction he had wrought. His employer, the gentleman whom Dennis had seen at the door, now appeared upon the scene in a towering passion, and scrupled not to heap maledictions upon the head of the unfortunate Hibernian.

“What do you mean by rushing through the store in this mad style?” he demanded.

“There’s an impudent fellow outside a-doin’ my work,” said Pat.

===Chinese===
警察正要上前处置，那爱尔兰人却像一头疯牛似的喷着粗气，猛冲到艺术大厦门口，一把拽开大门，门也顾不上关，便一路狂奔着穿过长长的店堂，大喊大叫：“卢多尔夫先生！卢多尔夫先生！外头有个天杀的混小子在抢我的活儿干！”

他还没跑到通往办公室的一半路程，店里就传来一声脆响，紧接着一片骚动。

原来帕特在盲目的暴怒中，加之威士忌酒劲上头、脚步踉跄，一头撞翻了一尊贵重的大理石雕像，如今那雕像已碎落在地。这场大祸顿时让他醒了酒，他呆立在原地，惊惶失措地望着自己闯下的祸端。他的雇主——正是丹尼斯方才在门口见到的那位绅士——此刻暴跳如雷地赶到现场，毫不留情地对着这个倒霉的爱尔兰人劈头盖脸一顿痛骂。

“你疯了不成，在店里这么横冲直撞算怎么回事？”他厉声质问道。

“外头有个不知死活的家伙在抢我的活儿，”帕特说道。

===Original===
“Why didn’t you do it yourself, instead of going off to the gin-mills this morning? Didn’t I warn you? Didn’t I tell you your last spree should be the last in my employ? Now begone, you drunken idiot! and if you ever show your face on these premises again I’ll have you arrested and compel payment for this marble, and it will take every cent you have in the world, and more too.”

“Ah! Misther Ludolph, if ye’ll only give me one more﻿—”

“I tell you be off! or I will call the policeman at once.”

“But Bridget and the childer will starve.”

“What are Bridget and the children to me? If you won’t take care of them, you can’t expect other people to. Begone!” said his employer, advancing threateningly and stamping his foot.

Pat looked around in vain for help: the clerks were but fainter echoes of their master.

===Chinese===
“那你今天上午怎么不自己干，反倒跑去酒馆买醉？我没警告过你吗？我没跟你说过，你上次胡天胡地喝酒就是你在我手下干活的最后一次吗？现在给我滚蛋，你这个醉醺醺的蠢货！你要是再敢在这片地方露面，我就叫人把你抓起来，逼你赔偿这尊大理石雕像——哪怕倾家荡产把你身上最后一分钱榨干都不够赔！”

“哎呀！卢多尔夫先生，您就再宽容我这一——”

“我叫你滚出去！不然我马上喊警察了。”

“可布里奇特（Bridget）和孩子们会饿死的呀。”

“布里奇特和孩子们关我什么事？连你自己都不肯照管他们，还指望别人替你养活吗？滚！”他的雇主说着，气势汹汹地逼上前一步，重重地跺了跺脚。

帕特徒劳地环顾四周，想找人替自己求情，可店员们不过是东家的应声虫，一个个冷眼旁观。

===Original===
Seeing his case to be hopeless, he turned about then hurried away, his big red face distorted by many contending emotions. Nor did he stop until he reached one of the fatal gin-mills, where he soon drowned memory and trouble in huge potations of the fiery element that was destroying him and bringing wretchedness to “Bridget and the childer.”

Again Dennis had a lesson on drinking for the effects.

He rapidly completed his work and entered the store. A clerk handed him fifty cents.

“May I see Mr. Ludolph a moment?” he asked.

“Yes,” replied the clerk, “he is in the inner office there; but I guess you won’t find him very smooth this evening,” looking at the same time suggestively toward the broken marble.

===Chinese===
见大势已去，他只好转过身匆匆离去，那张通红的大脸因种种交战的情绪而扭曲变形。他一路走个不停，直到钻进一家害人不浅的廉价酒馆方才停步，随即便大口灌起烈酒，把记忆与烦忧全都淹没在那正在毁掉他自己、也把苦难带给“布里奇特和孩子们”的烈焰琼浆里。

丹尼斯又一次亲眼目睹了酗酒招致的恶果，上了一课。

他麻利地扫完积雪，走进店里。一名店员递给他五十美分。

“请问我能见一下卢多尔夫先生吗？只需一会儿工夫。”他问道。

“行啊，”店员答道，同时意味深长地朝那尊碎裂的大理石瞥了一眼，“他就在里面的办公室里；不过我猜，他今晚的脾气恐怕不会太和气。”

===Original===
But Mr. Ludolph was not in as bad a humor as was imagined. This thrifty Teuton had not lost much by the mishap of the afternoon, for a month or two of wages was due Pat, and this kept back would pay in the main for the injury he had done. His whole soul being bent on the acquirement of money, for reasons that will be explained further on, his momentary passion soon passed away when he found he had sustained no material injury. To Dennis’s knock he responded in his usual tone, “Come in!” and Dennis stood in a warm, lighted, cozy office, where the object of his quest sat writing rapidly with his back to the door. Dennis waited respectfully till the facile pen glided through the sentence, and then Mr. Ludolph looked up. Dennis’s bearing and appearance were so unmistakably those of a gentleman that Mr. Ludolph, not recognizing him as the person who had cleared his sidewalk, rose courteously and said, “Did you wish to see me?”

“Yes, sir,” replied Dennis; “I understand that you dismissed a person in your employ this afternoon. I would respectfully apply for his place, if it is not promised.”

The gentleman smiled and said: “You are mistaken, I think. I discharged a drunken Irishman, who had been porter and man-of-all-work about the store, this afternoon; but I have no place vacant, young sir, that you would care to fill.”

“If you think me competent to fill the position of porter and your man-of-all-work, I would be very glad to obtain it; that is, if it will support me and those dependent on me.”

===Chinese===
其实，卢多尔夫先生的心情远没有旁人想象的那么糟。这位精打细算的日耳曼人并未因下午的这场意外蒙受多大损失——他本就还欠着帕特一两个月的工钱，把这笔钱扣下来，大致便足够抵偿损坏雕像的损失了。他全副心神都扑在聚敛钱财上（其中缘由下文自会交代），一旦发觉自己并未遭受实质性的钱财亏损，方才那一阵暴怒很快便烟消云散。听到丹尼斯敲门，他照常应了一声：“请进！”丹尼斯于是走进一间温暖明亮、舒适惬意的办公室。他要找的那个人正背对着门坐在桌前疾书。丹尼斯恭敬地站着等候，直到那支运笔如飞的钢笔滑顺地写完那句话，卢多尔夫先生才抬起头来。丹尼斯的气度与仪表实在太有绅士风范，卢多尔夫先生一时竟没认出他就是刚才清扫门前人行道的人，于是彬彬有礼地起身问道：“您找我有事吗？”

“是的，先生，”丹尼斯答道，“我听说您今天下午辞退了一名雇员。如果那个空缺还没有许给别人，我想恭敬地向您申请这份差事。”

那位绅士笑了笑，说道：“我想你是弄错了。今天下午我确实开除了一个爱尔兰醉鬼，他在店里当杂役兼打杂；可眼下并没有什么您看得上的空缺职位，年轻的先生。”

“如果您认为我能胜任杂役兼为您打杂的差事，我很乐意接下这份工作；当然，前提是这份工钱足以养活我和需要我赡养的家人。”

===Original===
The merchant muttered to himself, “I thought he was a gentleman.”

Then, as this was a business matter of some importance, he caused Dennis to stand full in the light, while he withdrew somewhat in the shadow, and gave it his attention with characteristic shrewdness and caution.

“You seem rather above the situation you ask for,” he said.

“I am not above it in circumstances,” said Dennis, “and it certainly is better than shovelling snow all day.”

“Are you the man that just cleaned my sidewalk?”

===Chinese===
商人低声自言自语道：“我还以为他是个体面绅士呢。”

接着，既然这是一桩颇为要紧的生意事务，他便让丹尼斯站在明亮的灯光下，自己则略微退入阴影里，以他一贯的精明与谨慎仔细审视起这件事来。

“看你的样子，似乎比你求的这份差事体面得多。”他说道。

“以我目前的处境而言，这绝非委屈，”丹尼斯说，“而且这总比整天铲雪强得多。”

“刚才清扫我门前人行道的人就是你？”

===Original===
“I am, sir.”

“You must be aware that your general appearance is very different from that of the man discharged today, and from those seeking the menial place in question. Can you explain this fact satisfactorily?”

“I can readily explain it, and I hope satisfactorily. At any rate I shall be perfectly open;” and Dennis told him briefly, but plainly, just how he was situated.

As the keen man of the world watched with the closest scrutiny the honest young face, he believed every word. Accustomed to deal with all classes of men from childhood, he had learned to read them as the open page of a book.

He asked coolly, however, “Have you no recommendations?”

===Chinese===
“正是我，先生。”

“你应当明白，你的整体仪态与今天被辞退的那个人截然不同，也和寻常来找这种粗活干的人大不一样。你能对此做出令人满意的解释吗？”

“我完全可以解释清楚，也希望您能满意。无论如何，我都会坦诚相告。”随后，丹尼斯简明而直白地把自己的处境向他叙说了一遍。

这位老练的世故商人一边全神贯注地审视着眼前这张诚恳的年轻面孔，一边便信了他的每一句话。他打小就习惯与三教九流打交道，早已练就了一双识人的慧眼，看人就像翻开一页摊平的书一样清楚明白。

不过，他仍冷静地问道：“你没有推荐信吗？”

===Original===
Dennis produced the ministerial letter, which Mr. Ludolph glanced at with good-natured contempt.

“This is all right,” he said; “superstition is an excellent thing for some minds. I managed Pat a year through his priest, and then he got beyond the priest and me too.”

This undisguised contempt of all that he held sacred, and the classing of true faith with gross superstition, pained Dennis; and his face showed it, though he said nothing.

“There,” said the gentleman, “I did not mean to hurt your feelings, but to the educated in our land these things seem very childish.”

“I should serve you none the worse,” said Dennis, with quiet dignity, “if I believed that the duty I owed to you I owed also to God.”

===Chinese===
丹尼斯掏出那封牧师写的推荐信，卢多尔夫先生扫了一眼，神情里带着几分和气的轻蔑。

“这倒不错，”他说道，“对某些人来说，迷信确实是个好东西。我靠帕特的神父管束了他整整一年，后来连神父和我都治不住他了。”

对方如此毫不掩饰地轻蔑自己视为神圣的一切，竟把虔诚的信仰与愚昧的迷信相提并论，这让丹尼斯心中刺痛；他虽一言未发，神色却流露了出来。

“好啦，”那位绅士说道，“我并非有意伤你的感情，只是在我们家乡那些受过教育的人看来，这类东西未免太过幼稚。”

“若我相信自己对您所尽的本分，同时也是对上帝所尽的本分，”丹尼斯沉静而不失尊严地说道，“这只会让我更加尽心为您效劳，绝不会坏事。”

===Original===
Mr. Ludolph looked as if a new idea had struck him, smiled, and said: “Most people’s religion, as far as my experience has gone, is not of this practical kind. But I believe that I can trust you, and your face and story are worth much more to me than this letter. A scamp might possess that as well as an honest youth like you. Now, as to terms: I will give you forty dollars a month for the first two months, and then, if you develop and take well to the work, I will give you sixty.”

Dennis thought that this, with close economy, would enable him to live and support his mother and sisters, and he accepted the terms.

“Moreover, to show the advantage of telling a straightforward story, you may sleep in the store: the building will be safer for having someone in it. I will pay you at the end of every week as long as you suit, so that you can commence sending something to your mother immediately. You see that I take an interest in you,” said the shrewd man, “and expect you to take an interest in my business, and work for me as for yourself.”

Simple, honest Dennis could not see that Mr. Ludolph cared infinitely more for himself than for all the world combined, and made it his life-study to get the most out of it with the least cost to himself. Under the words that seemed so kind and considerate, the young man’s heart swelled with the strong and grateful purpose to spare himself in no way in the service of such an employer. The wily man saw this, and smiled to himself over the credulity of mankind.

===Chinese===
卢多尔夫先生闻言，仿佛突然领悟了什么新鲜念头似的笑了笑，说道：“据我的阅历来看，大多数人的宗教信仰可算不上这么讲求实际。不过我相信你靠得住，你的长相和遭遇对我来说比这封信值钱多了。一封信嘛，无赖也能弄到手，正派的年轻人也能有。现在谈谈工钱：头两个月我每月给你四十美元；之后若是你长进快、干得顺手，我给你涨到六十美元。”

丹尼斯心算了一下，觉得只要精打细算、省吃俭用，这笔钱足够维持自己的生活并贴补母亲和妹妹们，便欣然应允了这个条件。

“再者，为了让你知道实话实说的好处，你可以睡在店里——屋里夜间有人看着，大楼也安全些。只要你合我心意，我每周周末都给你结一次工钱，好让你立刻就能往家里给母亲寄钱。你看，我是很器重你的，”这位精明的商人说道，“我也指望你把我的生意放在心上，替我干活就像替你自己干一样。”

纯朴敦厚的丹尼斯哪里看得出来，卢多尔夫先生爱惜自己远胜过世间万物总和，生平最大的学问便是如何以最小的代价榨取最大的利益。听着这番看似仁厚体贴的话语，年轻人的胸膛顿时充满了感激与干劲，暗暗立誓定要全力以赴、毫不惜力地报答这样一位好雇主。那老谋深算的人将这一切看在眼里，不禁为世人的轻信暗暗发笑。

===Original===
“Have you enough to last till next Saturday night?” he asked.

“I will make it last,” said Dennis, sturdily.

“That is right,” said Mr. Ludolph. “Stand on your own feet if you can. I never give any more help than will barely enable a man to help himself”﻿—a maxim which had the advantage not only of being sound, but of according exactly with his disposition.

After a moment’s thought, Mr. Ludolph spoke in a tone so sharp, and a manner so stern, that Dennis was startled.

“Mark me, young man, I wish a plain understanding in one respect: you take Pat’s place, and I expect you to do Pat’s work. I wish no trouble to arise from your being above your business.”

===Chinese===
“你手头的钱够撑到下周六晚上吗？”他问道。

“我会省着花，一定撑到那时候，”丹尼斯坚毅地回答。

“这就对了，”卢多尔夫先生说，“只要撑得住，就靠自己的双腿站起来。我向来只肯帮人一把，绝不多给一分，刚好够他自助罢了”——这句格言不仅听着极有道理，更妙的是与他本人的吝啬性情丝丝入扣。

沉吟片刻之后，卢多尔夫先生忽而开口，语气之尖锐、神态之严厉，让丹尼斯吃了一惊。

“听好了，年轻人，有一点我得跟你把话说在明处：你顶的是帕特的缺，我就指望你干帕特的活儿。我不希望日后闹出什么麻烦，嫌这差事有失你的身份。”

===Original===
“You will have none,” said Dennis, quietly and firmly.

“All right, then. Mr. Schwartz will show you about closing up the store. Be here early Monday morning, and remember that all depends upon yourself.”

In the depths of his grateful heart Dennis felt how much the success of that day and every day of life depended on God.

Mr. Ludolph put on his coat and gloves and went out with Dennis into the store.

“Gentlemen,” said he to his clerks, “this young man, Dennis Fleet by name, will take the place of Pat Murphy, discharged today. Mr. Schwartz, will you show him what it is necessary to do tonight? He will be here on Monday morning at the usual time for opening the store, and after that will sleep in the building.”

The clerks looked at him for a moment, as they might at a new piece of furniture, or a laborsaving machine, and then coolly finished their duties, and followed their employer. Mr. Schwartz showed him about closing the store, taking care of the furnace, etc., and Dennis saw that his place was no sinecure. Still it was not work, but its lack, that he dreaded, and his movements were so eager and earnest that a faint expression of surprise and curiosity tinged the broad, stolid face of Mr. Schwartz; but he only buttoned his coat to the chin and muttered, “New broom,” and went his way homeward, leaving Dennis to go his.

===Chinese===
“绝不会有这种事，”丹尼斯沉稳而坚定地答道。

“那好。施瓦茨先生会教你晚上怎么关店门。周一一大早到这儿来，记住，一切全靠你自己。”

然而在丹尼斯那颗满怀感恩的心灵深处，他深知今日的转机乃至人生每一天的成败，全赖上帝的眷顾。

卢多尔夫先生穿上大衣、戴上手套，领着丹尼斯走出办公室，来到店堂里。

“诸位，”他对店员们宣布道，“这位年轻人名叫丹尼斯·弗利特，将顶替今天被辞退的帕特·墨菲的位子。施瓦茨先生，麻烦你今晚带他熟悉一下关店前必须做的杂务。他周一早上会在平时开门的钟点准时赶到，从那以后便留宿在大厦里。”

店员们只朝他打量了一眼，那神情就像在看一件新添置的家具或一台省力的机器，随后便冷淡地忙完手头活计，跟着东家走了。施瓦茨先生教他如何锁闭店门、照看火炉等等杂事，丹尼斯这才看出自己这份差事绝非清闲美差。然而，他怕的从来不是劳苦，而是无工可做。他干起活来手脚勤快、神情专注，连施瓦茨先生那张宽大木讷的脸上都不禁掠过一丝淡淡的惊讶与好奇；不过他只是把大衣扣子一路扣到下巴，嘟囔了一句“新笤帚嘛”，便自顾自回家去了，留下丹尼斯也踏上归途。

## III Launched / 第三章 扬帆启程

===Original===
Scarcely was the last word spoken when a sudden glory filled the room. So brilliant was the light that mother and son were startled. Then they saw what had been unnoted before, that day had broken, and that the sun, emerging from a single dark cloud, was shining, full-orbed, into the apartment with a light that, reflected from myriads of snowy crystals, was doubly luminous. Nevertheless it seemed to them a good omen, an earnest, an emblem of the purer, whiter light into which the cleansed and pardoned spirit had entered. The snow-wrapped prairie was indeed pure and bright, but it was *cold*. The Father’s embrace, receiving home the long-absent, erring, but forgiven child, would be warm indeed.

Though the bereaved wife believed that a brighter dawn than that which made the world resplendent around her had come to her husband, still a sense of desolation came over her which only those can understand who have known a loss like hers. For years he had filled the greater part of time, thought, and heart. As she saw her first and only love, the companion of a life which, though hard, still had the light and solace of mutual affection﻿—as she saw him so still, and realized that she would hear him speak no more﻿—*complain* no more (for even the weaknesses of those we love are sadly missed after death)﻿—a flood of that natural sorrow which Christianity consoles, but was never designed to prevent, overwhelmed her, and she gave way utterly.

Her son took her in his arms and held her silently, believing that unspoken sympathy was worth more at such a time than any words.

After the convulsive sobbing had somewhat ceased, he struck the right chord by saying: “Mother, father is not lost to us. He himself said goodbye only for a little while. Then you have us to love and think of; and remember, what could we do without you?”

The unselfish woman would have tried to rise from a bed of death to do anything needed by her loved ones, and this reminder of those still dependent on her care proved the most potent of restoratives. She at once arose and said: “Dennis, you are right. It is indeed wrong for me to give way thus, when I have so much to be thankful for﻿—so much to live for. But, O Dennis! you cannot understand this separation of husband and wife, for God said, ‘They twain shall be one flesh’; and it seems as if half my very life had gone﻿—as if half my heart had been wrenched away, and only a bleeding fragment left.”

===Chinese===
话音刚落，屋子里骤然涌满一片耀眼的荣光。那光芒明亮得令母子二人都吃了一惊。定睛一看，他们才发觉此前未曾留意的晨光早已破晓——一轮圆日正从孤零零的一片乌云后探出身来，将光芒直直照进房内，经屋外万千冰晶雪粒一折射，更显得倍加璀璨。即便如此，在他们眼里，这仍是个吉兆，是一份凭据，更是一道象征——象征着那已蒙洁净、已得赦免的灵魂，此刻已步入更纯净、更皎洁的光明之中。白雪覆盖的草原诚然圣洁明亮，却毕竟冰冷刺骨；而天父张开双臂，迎回那久别迷途、却终获宽宥的浪子时，祂的怀抱该是何等温暖。

尽管丧夫的妻子深信，比眼前这照彻尘世的旭日更灿烂的黎明已经降临到丈夫身上，可一阵孤苦凄凉之感依然漫上心头——这种滋味，唯有亲历过同等失落的人方能体会。多年来，他占据了她大半的光阴、思绪与心田。她望着自己最初也是唯一的爱人，望着这位相濡以沫的伴侣——尽管生活艰辛，两人之间却始终有彼此深情的光亮与慰藉——望着他如此静静地躺着，意识到自己再也听不到他开口说话，甚至再也听不到他抱怨一句（因为人在亡故之后，就连生前那些让人无奈的弱点也会令亲者倍感怀念），一股人情之常的悲恸骤然淹没了她；基督教固然能抚慰这样的哀伤，却从来无意禁绝它的涌流。她再也支撑不住，整个人彻底垮了下来。

儿子走上前，默默将母亲揽入怀中；他深信，在这样的时刻，无声的体恤胜过千言万语。

待母亲剧烈的抽泣稍稍平息，他便恰到好处地拨动了她心头最妥帖的那根弦，轻声说道：“妈妈，爸爸并没有离开我们而消逝。他自己也说了，这不过是暂别片刻罢了。再说，您还有我们这些儿女去疼爱、去牵挂；您想想，要是没有了您，我们又该怎么办呢？”

这位毫无私心的妇人，只要是为了亲人所需，便是躺在临终的病榻上也会挣扎着起身；一想到还有人指望着她的照料，这句提醒立刻化作了最灵验的振奋剂。她随即坐起身来，说道：“丹尼斯（Dennis），你说得对。我有这么多值得感恩的事，有这么多活下去的指望，实在不该如此沉沦。可唉，丹尼斯！你到底还体会不到夫妻死别的滋味，因为上帝说过：‘二人成为一体’；此刻我只觉得自己半条性命都跟着去了——仿佛半颗心被人硬生生撕扯下来，只留下一片鲜血淋漓的残缺。”

===Original===
The patter of feet was heard on the kitchen floor, the door opened, and two little figures in white trailing nightgowns entered. At first they looked in shy wonder and perplexity at their tall brother, whom they had not seen for months, but at his familiar voice, recalling many a romp and merry time together, they rushed to his arms as of old.

Then they drew near the bed to give their father his accustomed morning kiss; but, as they approached, he seemed so still that awe began to creep over their little faces. A dim recollection of the farewell kiss given a few hours before, when they were scarcely awake, recurred to them.

“Father,” said the elder (about five), “we want to give you good morning kiss.”

Seldom had their father been so sick or irritable but that he reached out his arms to his little ones and gave them a warm embrace, that did him more good than he realized. The influence of trusting children is sometimes the most subtle oil that can be thrown on the troubled waters of life.

But as the little ones saw that their father made no response to their approach and appeal, they timidly drew a step nearer, and looked into his wasted, yet peaceful face, with its closed eyes and motionless repose, and then, turning to their mother, said in a loud whisper, with faces full of perplexity and trouble, “Is papa asleep?”

The little figures in their white drapery, standing beside their dead father, waiting to perform the usual, well-remembered household rite, proved a scene too touching for the poor mother’s self-control, and again she gave way to a burst of sorrow. But her son, true to his resolution to be the stay and strength of the family, hastened to the children, and, taking them by the hand, said gently: “Yes, little ones, papa is asleep. It may be a long time before he wakes, but he surely will by and by, and then he will never be sick any more. Come, we will go into the other room and sing a pretty hymn about papa’s sleep.”

===Chinese===
厨房地板上传来一阵细碎的脚步声，房门推开，两个拖着长长白色睡袍的小身影走了进来。起初，她们望着数月未见的高大哥哥，眼里满是怯生生的惊奇与迷惘；可一听到他那熟悉的声音，想起从前一起嬉闹玩耍的无数欢乐时光，两个小家伙便像往常一样，一头扑进了他的怀里。

随后，她们走到床边，想像平日那样给父亲献上一个早安吻；然而走近一看，父亲躺得那样一动不动，两张稚嫩的小脸上渐渐浮起一层敬畏之色。几个小时前她们还睡眼惺忪时献上的那个告别之吻，此刻又模糊地浮现在脑海里。

“爸爸，”年纪稍长些的那个小女孩（大约五岁）轻声说道，“我们要给你一个早安吻。”

往常父亲无论病得多沉重、性子多烦躁，也极少不向他的小宝贝们伸出双臂，给她们一个温暖的拥抱——那拥抱带给他的慰藉，连他自己都未曾完全察觉。幼童毫无保留的信赖，有时正像滴落在人生翻涌波涛上最微妙的一缕香油，能悄然抚平风浪。

然而，两个小姑娘见父亲对她们的靠近和呼唤全无回应，便怯生生地又凑近了一步，凝望着父亲那张虽已消瘦却安详平和的脸庞——双眼紧闭，静谧安息。接着她们转过头去，小脸上写满困惑与不安，压低嗓门却又清晰地问母亲：“爸爸是睡着了吗？”

两个身着白袍的小小身影站在亡父床畔，等待着行那平日里熟记于心的家常礼节——这一幕实在太过凄楚动人，可怜的母亲再也克制不住，又一次放声悲恸起来。但儿子恪守着自己要作全家支柱与依靠的决心，连忙走过去牵起两个孩子的小手，柔声说道：“是的，小宝贝们，爸爸睡着了。他兴许要过好久才会醒来，不过总有一天他一定会醒的，到那时他就再也不会生病啦。来，咱们到隔壁屋里去，唱一首关于爸爸安睡的好听圣诗吧。”

===Original===
The thought of hearing their brother sing lured them away at once, for he had a mellow tenor voice that seemed to the little girls sweeter than a bird’s. A moment later the widow’s heart was comforted by hearing those words that have been balm for so many wounds:

> “Asleep in Jesus! blessed sleep!
 

 From which none ever wakes to weep.”

Then, putting on his sisters’ flannel wrappers, he set them down by the fire, telling stories in the meantime to divert their thoughts from the scene they had just witnessed.

Thus no horror of death was suffered to enter their young minds. They were not brought face to face with a dreadful mystery which they could not understand, but which would have a sinister effect for life. Gradually they would learn the truth, but still the first impression would remain, and their father’s death would ever be to them a sleep from which he would wake by and by, “never to be sick any more.”

===Chinese===
一听说能听哥哥唱歌，两个小家伙立刻就被哄走了——哥哥生就一副温润醇厚的男高音嗓子，在两个小姑娘耳中比小鸟的啼鸣还要悦耳动听。片刻之后，隔壁传来那曾抚平无数创伤的诗句，听得寡居的母亲心头一暖：

> “安息在耶稣里！有福的安眠！
> 从此再无人醒来垂泪哭泣。”

接着，他替两个妹妹披上法兰绒晨袍，抱她们在炉火旁坐下，一边给她们讲故事，好引开她们的心思，免得还惦记着方才目睹的那一幕。

就这样，死亡的阴森恐怖不曾获准闯入她们幼小的心田。她们没有被迫直面一个自己尚且无从理解、却足以对一生造成阴暗影响的骇人奥秘。假以时日，她们终究会渐渐明白真相，但最初印在心底的印象仍会留存下来——在她们眼中，父亲的辞世将永远是一场安眠，总有一天他会从中醒来，“再也不会生病”。

===Original===
Dennis set about preparations for their simple morning meal so deftly and easily as to show that it was no unaccustomed task. A sister older than himself had died while yet an infant, leaving a heartache till he came﻿—God’s best remedy. Then two sisters had died after his day, and he had been compelled to be to his mother daughter as well as son, to make himself useful in every household task. His father had been wrapped up in useless inventions, vain enterprises, and was much away. So mother and son were constantly together. He had early become a great comfort and help to her, God blessing her in this vital respect, though her lot seemed hard in other ways. Thus, while he had the heart and courage of a man, he also had the quick, supple hand and gentle bearing of a woman, when occasion required. As proof of his skill, a tempting meal from the simplest materials was placed smoking on the table, and the little girls were soon chatting contentedly over their breakfast. In the meantime the wife within had drawn near her dead husband and taken his cold hand. For a while she dwelt on the past in strong and tearful agony, then, in accordance with long-established habit, her thoughts went forward into the future. In imagination she was present at her husband’s reception in heaven. The narrow, meagre room melted away, and her feet seemed to stand on the “golden pavement.” The jubilant clash of heavenly cymbals thrilled her heart. She seemed taking part in a triumphal march led by celestial minstrelsy toward the throne. She saw her husband mount its white, glistening steps, so changed, and yet so like his former self when full of love, youth, and hope. He appeared overwhelmed with a sense of unworthiness, but his reception was all the more kind and reassuring. Then as he departed from the royal presence, crowned with God’s love and favor forever, though he had all heaven before him, he seemed looking for her as that he longed for most, and her strong effort to reach his side aroused her from her revery as from a dream. But her vision had strengthened her, as was ever the case, and the bitterness of grief was passed. Imprinting a long kiss on her husband’s cold forehead, she joined her family in the outer room with calm and quiet mien. Her son saw and understood the change in his mother’s manner, and from long experience knew its cause.

We need not dwell on what followed﻿—preparations for burial, the funeral, the return to a home from which one who had filled so large a place had gone﻿—a home on which rested the shadow of death. These are old, familiar scenes, acted over and over every day, and yet in the little households where they occur there is a terrible sense of novelty as if they then happened for the first time. The family feel as if they were passing through a chaotic period﻿—the old world breaking up and vanishing, and a new formation and combination of all the elements that make up life taking place.

Many changes followed. Their farm was sold. Part of a small house in the village of Bankville was rented as their future residence. A very small annuity from some property in the East, left by Mrs. Fleet’s father, was, with Dennis’s labor, all the family had to depend on now﻿—a meagre prospect.

===Chinese===
丹尼斯动手准备起简朴的早饭来，手脚那样麻利自如，一看便知这绝非他生疏的活计。在他出生前，家里曾有一个姐姐在襁褓中夭折，给母亲留下一道隐痛，直到他降生才得以抚平——那是上帝赐下的最好良药。他之后又有两个妹妹相继早逝，于是他不得不既当儿子又做女儿，帮着母亲分担家里大大小小的劳务。父亲一门心思扑在那些毫无用处的发明与徒劳无功的营生上，又常年奔波在外。因此，母子二人总是相依为命。他年纪轻轻便成了母亲莫大的安慰与帮手——尽管母亲在别处命运多舛，上帝却在这最要紧的一桩上厚厚恩待了她。于是，他既有男子汉的胸怀与胆魄，一到需要的时候，又兼有女子般灵巧敏捷的双手和温婉体贴的举止。眼下便是最好的明证：不过是最寻常不过的食材，经他一双巧手烹制，竟化作一顿热气腾腾、诱人胃口的早膳端上了桌，两个小姑娘很快便一边吃着早饭，一边心满意足地叽叽喳喳聊起天来。与此同时，里屋的妻子已走到亡夫身旁，握住他冰凉的手。她先是在痛彻心扉的泪光中缅怀了片刻往昔，随后便顺着积年养成的习惯，将思绪投向了未来。在她的想象之中，自己正亲临天国，见证丈夫在天堂蒙受迎迓。眼前狭小简陋的屋舍悄然消融，她的双脚仿佛踏上了“黄金铺就的街道”。天界铙钹欢欣鼓舞的铿锵鸣响激荡着她的心扉。她仿佛正置身于一支凯旋的行列，在天上乐师的奏乐引领下，向着神圣的宝座行进。她看见丈夫拾级登上那雪白晶莹的台阶——模样已然焕然一新，却又像极了当年那个满怀爱意、风华正茂、意气风发的自己。他似乎因深感自身不配而惶恐难当，可天廷对他的接纳却愈发慈爱而宽慰人心。随后，当他领受了上帝永恒的慈爱与恩宠为冠冕、从君王荣光前退下时，尽管整座天堂都铺展在他面前，他却仿佛仍在四下寻觅着她，把她视作自己最深切的渴盼；她极力想要奔到他身旁，这一用力，反倒把自己从这场恍如梦境的出神遐想中惊醒过来。然而一如往常，这番异象赋予了她无穷力量，悲痛的苦涩已然消散。她在丈夫冰凉的额头上深深印下一吻，随即神色沉静安详地走回外屋，与家人团聚。儿子一眼便看出了母亲神态的变化，也凭着长年相处的默契，心领神会其中的缘由。

随后的种种情形，我们无需赘述——筹备丧仪、举行葬礼，以及散礼后重返那座家宅：屋里少了一个曾占据如此重要位置的人，死荫正沉沉笼罩其上。这些都是世间日复一日反复上演的寻常旧幕，然而在每一个亲历其境的小家庭看来，却偏偏带着一种骇人的陌生感，仿佛自古以来头一遭发生一般。一家人只觉正穿行在一段混沌失序的岁月里——旧有的世界正在土崩瓦解、归于消逝，构成生活的一切要素也正在重新熔铸、另行排布。

接踵而来的是一连串的变故。家里的农场变卖了，他们在班克维尔（Bankville）村租下了一幢小屋的半边，作为日后的栖身之所。弗利特太太（Mrs. Fleet）的父亲在东部留下的一点产业所生出的微薄年金，再加上丹尼斯做工挣来的进项，便是这家人眼下全部的指望——前路实在清苦。

===Original===
But Dennis was very sanguine; for in this respect he had his father’s temperament. The world was all before him, and Chicago, the young and giant city of the West, seemed an Eldorado, where fortune, and perhaps fame, might soon be won. He would not only place the family beyond want, but surround them with every luxury.

Dennis, wise and apt as far as his knowledge went, was in some respects as simple and ignorant as a child. There were many phases and conditions of society of which he had never dreamed. Of the ways of the rich and fashionable, of the character of artificial life, he had not the remotest experience. He could not see or understand the distinctions and barriers that to the world are more impassable than those of ignorance, stupidity, and even gross immorality. He would learn, to his infinite surprise, that even in a Western democratic city men would be welcomed in society whose hand no pure woman or honorable man ought to touch, while he, a gentleman by birth, education, and especially character, would not be recognized at all. He would discover that wealth and the endorsement of a few fashionable people, though all else were lacking, would be a better passport than the noblest qualities and fine abilities. As we follow him from the seclusion of his simple country home into the complicated life of the world, all this will become apparent.

Long and earnest was the conversation between mother and son before they separated. Pure and noble were the maxims that she sought to instil into his mind. They may not have been worldly wise, but they were heavenly wise. Though some of her advice in the letter might avail little, since she knew less of the world than did her son, still in its spirit it contained the best of all wisdom, profitable for this life and the life to come. But she sent him forth to seek his fortune and theirs with less solicitude than most mothers have just cause to feel, for she knew that he had Christian principle, and had passed through discipline that had sobered and matured him far beyond his years. She saw, however, in every word and act his father’s sanguine temperament. He was expecting much, hoping far more, and she feared that he also was destined to many a bitter disappointment. Still she believed that he possessed a good strong substratum of commonsense, and this combined with the lessons of faith and patience taught of God would prove the ballast his father had lacked.

She sought to modify his towering hopes and rose-colored visions, but to little purpose. Young, buoyant, in splendid health, with a surplus of warm blood tingling in every vein, how could he take a prudent, distrustful view of the world? It seemed to beckon him smilingly into any path of success he might choose. Had not many won the victory? and who ever felt braver and more determined than he, with the needs of the dear ones at home added to his own incentives and ambitions? So, with many embraces, lingering kisses, and farewell words, that lost not their meaning though said over and over again, they parted. The stage carried him to the nearest railway station, and the express train bore him rapidly toward the great city where he expected to find all that a man’s heart most craves on earth.

Sanguine as his father, constant as his mother, with a nature that would go right or wrong with tremendous energy, as direction might be given it, he was destined to live no tame, colorless life, but would either enjoy much, or else suffer much. To his young heart, swelling with hopes, burning with zeal to distinguish himself and provide for those he was leaving, even the bleak, snow-clad prairie seemed an arena in which he might accomplish a vague something.

===Chinese===
但丹尼斯却满怀乐观与热忱；在这方面，他继承了父亲的心性。广阔的世界正铺展在他面前，而芝加哥（Chicago）——那座西部年轻而庞大的都会——在他眼里恰似一座黄金国（Eldorado），财富乃至名望仿佛都能在那里一朝功成。他不仅要让家人从此衣食无忧，还要让她们过上应有尽有的优渥生活。

丹尼斯在自己涉猎的领域内固然聪慧敏悟，在另一些方面却天真蒙昧得犹如孩童。世态人情中有许多面相与世道法则，是他做梦也未曾想到的。至于豪富显贵与时髦名流的行事做派，以及矫揉造作的上流生活究竟是何光景，他更是半点阅历也无。世俗社会中横亘着种种界限与屏障，在世人眼中比无知、愚蠢乃至赤裸裸的败德还要难以逾越，而他对此却视而不见、无从理解。日后他将万分愕然地领教到：即便是在一座标榜民主的西部城市里，有些连贞洁女子或正派君子都不屑与之握手的人，竟能在社交场上大受追捧；而像他这样无论论出身、教养，尤其是论人品都堪称真正绅士的人，反倒会被人视若无睹。他还将发现，只要有钱财和几位时髦人物的背书，哪怕其余一概匮乏，也是一张比最高贵的品格与出众的才干更管用的通行证。随着我们跟随他从淳朴幽静的乡间故园步入纷繁复杂的世俗生活，这一切都将纤毫毕现。

离别前夕，母子二人进行了一场绵长而恳切的长谈。母亲竭力向他心头灌输的，尽是纯洁高尚的处世箴言。这些道理或许不算谙熟世故，却饱含属天的智慧。母亲对世事的了解比儿子还要浅些，她那些忠告若拘泥于字面，有些或许派不上太大用场，但就其精神实质而言，却蕴含着世间最上乘的智慧，无论于今生抑或来世皆大有裨益。不过，当她打发儿子出门去为自己也为全家闯荡前程时，心中的忧虑却比绝大多数理应挂心的母亲要少些——因为她深知儿子恪守基督徒的操守，又经历过一番磨砺，使他变得比同龄人沉稳老成得多。然而，在他的一言一行之中，她还是看到了他父亲那股乐观过头的性情。他期待甚高，奢望尤甚，这令她不禁暗自忧心，唯恐他也注定要历经一次次痛彻心扉的失望。好在她仍相信儿子骨子里具备一份厚实稳健的常理心，这份务实再加上上帝教导的信心与忍耐之功课，定能成为他父亲生前所欠缺的压舱石。

母亲设法给他的凌云壮志和玫瑰色幻想降温，却收效甚微。他风华正茂、意气勃发、体魄健旺，浑身每一条血管里都奔涌着炽热澎湃的鲜血，又怎会用审慎多疑的眼光去看待这个世界？在他眼里，世界正含笑向他招手，任凭他挑选哪一条通往成功的大道。难道不是已有许多人摘得了胜利的桂冠吗？况且，除了自身的雄心抱负之外，他肩上还扛着家中亲人的生计所需，这世上又有谁曾比他更觉勇毅决绝呢？于是，在无数次相拥、依依难舍的亲吻，以及虽反复叮咛却丝毫不减深意的道别声中，母子二人就此分别。驿车载着他前往最近的火车站，随后特快列车载着他风驰电掣般驶向那座大都会——他满心指望在那里寻得尘世间男子汉内心最渴望的一切。

他既有父亲般的乐观热忱，又有母亲般的坚贞恒久；他生性如此——一旦认准了方向，无论向善还是向恶，都会迸发出排山倒海般的精力——这样的天性注定他绝不会度过平淡无奇、寡淡无色的一生，他要么会享尽欢欣，要么便要受尽煎熬。在他这颗年轻的心里，希望正在澎湃翻涌，要出人头地、要让留在家中的亲人过上好日子的热忱正在熊熊燃烧；此刻，就连窗外那片荒寒肃杀、白雪皑皑的大草原，在他眼中也仿佛成了一座可供他一展身手、成就一番尚未明晰之伟业的广阔疆场。

## XXVIII Life Without Love / 第二十八章 没有爱的人生

===Original===
As Dennis realized the truth, and remembered what he had said, his face was scarcely less full of pain than Christine’s. He saw that her whole soul was bent on an imitation that none could detect, and that he had foiled her purpose. But Christine’s wound was deeper than that. She had been told again, clearly and correctly, that the sphere of high, true art was beyond her reach. She felt that the verdict was true, and her own judgment confirmed every word Dennis uttered. But she had done her best; therefore her suffering was truly agony﻿—the pain and despair at failure in the most cherished hope of life. There seemed a barrier which, from the very limitations of her being, she could not pass. She did not fail from the lack of taste, culture, or skill, but in that which was like a sixth sense﻿—something she did not possess. Lacking the power to touch and move the heart, she knew she could never be a great artist.

Abruptly and without a word she left the room and store, accompanied by the Winthrops. Dennis felt as if he could bite his tongue out, and Christine’s face haunted him like a dreadful apparition. Wherever he turned he saw it so distorted by pain, and almost hate, that it scarcely seemed the same that had smiled on him as he entered at her invitation.

“Truly God is against all this,” groaned he, to himself; “and what I in my weakness could not do He has accomplished by this unlooked-for scene. She will now ever regard me with aversion.”

Dennis, like many another, thought he saw God’s plan clearly from a mere glimpse of a part of it. He at once reached this miserable conclusion, and suffered as greatly as if it had been God’s will, instead of his own imagination. To wait and trust is often the latest lesson we learn in life.

===Chinese===
丹尼斯猛然醒悟过来，再回想起自己方才说过的话，脸上的痛苦之色竟几乎不亚于克里斯蒂娜。他看出她原是一门心思要摹出一幅谁也识不破的赝品，却被自己一语戳破、坏了她的打算。然而克里斯蒂娜所受的创伤远不止于此。她再一次被人清晰而准确地宣告：真正崇高的艺术殿堂，是她永远无法企及的境界。她心里明白这一评判所言非虚，她自己的眼光也印证了丹尼斯说过的每一个字。可她已经竭尽所能；正因如此，她此刻的痛苦才真可谓锥心刺骨——那是平生最珍视的希望破灭时所带来的剧痛与绝望。在她面前仿佛横亘着一道无形的屏障，受制于自身天性的局限，她无论如何也跨越不过去。她之所以败北，并非因为缺乏品味、修养或技艺，而是缺少了某种宛如第六感般的东西——某种她生来就不曾拥有的东西。缺少了打动人心、拨动心弦的力量，她深知自己永远无法成为一名伟大的艺术家。

她一言不发，在温思罗普父女的陪同下骤然转身，离开了房间与画店。丹尼斯懊悔得恨不得咬断自己的舌头，克里斯蒂娜那张脸庞如同可怖的幽灵一般在他眼前挥之不去。无论他望向何处，看见的都是那张因痛苦——乃至近乎怨恨——而扭曲的面容，几乎教人不敢相信，方才他应她之邀走进屋来时，正是同一张脸曾朝他露出笑意。

“真是天意不容这一切啊，”他暗自呻吟道，“我软弱无力、办不到的事，祂却借着这一场意料之外的变故促成了。从此以后，她定要永远厌憎我了。”

丹尼斯和世上许多旁人一样，仅仅窥见了天意的一鳞半爪，便自以为看清了上帝的全盘安排。他立时得出了这个凄凉的结论，为此饱受煎熬，仿佛这真是上帝的旨意，而不是他自己的臆测。学会耐心等候与信靠，往往是人们一生中最晚才悟透的功课。

===Original===
Mr. Ludolph’s guests, absorbed in the pictures, at first scarcely noticed the departure of the others.

Christine, with consummate skill and care, kept her relationship to the picture unknown to all save the Winthrops, meaning not to acknowledge it unless she succeeded. But in Dennis’s startled and pained face she saw that he had read her secret, and this fact also annoyed her much.

“I should like to know the artist who copied this painting,” said Mr. Cornell.

“The artist is an amateur, and not willing to come before the public at present,” said Mr. Ludolph, so decidedly that no further questions were asked.

===Chinese===
卢多尔夫先生的客人们正全神贯注地端详画作，起初几乎没有察觉到那几位已经离去。

克里斯蒂娜行事向来滴水不漏，除了温思罗普父女之外，这幅画与自己的关联没让任何人知晓，本意就是除非大功告成，否则绝不承认。然而从丹尼斯方才那惊愕而又痛苦的神色里，她分明看出他已经识破了自己的秘密，这同样令她大为光火。

“我真想认识一下临摹这幅画的画师，”康奈尔先生说道。

“作画的是位业余好手，眼下还不愿公开露面，”卢多尔夫先生答得斩钉截铁，旁人也就不好再追问下去了。

===Original===
“I am much interested in that young clerk of yours,” said Mr. French. “He seems to understand himself. It is so hard to find a good discriminating judge of pictures. Do you expect to keep him?”

“Yes, I do,” said Mr. Ludolph, with such emphasis that his rival in trade pressed that point also no further.

“Well, really, Mr. Ludolph,” said one of the gentlemen, “you deal in wonders, mysteries, and all sorts of astonishing things yere. We have an unknown artist in Chicago deserving an ovation; you have in your employ a prince of critics, and if I mistake not he is the same who sang at Brown’s some little time ago. Miss Brown told me that he was your porter.”

“Yes, I took him as a stranger out of work and knew nothing of him. But he proved to be an educated and accomplished man, who will doubtless be of great use to me in time. Of course I promoted him when I found him out.” These last remarks were made for Mr. French’s benefit rather than for anyone’s else. He intended that his rival should knowingly violate all courtesy if he sought to lure Dennis away. After admiring the paintings and other things recently received, the gentlemen bowed themselves out.

===Chinese===
“我对您店里那位年轻店员颇感兴趣，”弗伦奇先生开口道，“他似乎颇有见地。如今想找个眼光独到、懂得鉴赏画作的人可真不容易。您打算长留他吗？”

“那是自然，”卢多尔夫先生答得斩钉截铁，语气之重，教他这位商界对手在这一点上也不好再试探下去了。

“说真的，卢多尔夫先生，”其中一位绅士说道，“您这儿简直是个藏龙卧虎、奇事连连的所在呀。我们芝加哥出了位理当受人喝彩的无名画家；您店里又聘了位评论界的翘楚，若我没记错，他正是前些日子在布朗家献唱的那位。布朗小姐还告诉过我，他原是您的搬运工呢。”

“不错，当初他流落街头、失业无着，我收留他时对他一无所知。谁料他竟是个受过良好教育、颇有才学之人，假以时日，定能为我帮上大忙。我一发现他的才干，自然立刻提拔了他。”这番末了的话，与其说是说给众人听，不如说是专门说给弗伦奇先生听的。他存心要让这位同行对手心里明白：若还敢设法把丹尼斯挖走，那便是明知故犯、有违商界礼数了。众位绅士又赏玩了一番新近运抵的画作与其他珍品，随后便鞠躬告辞了。

===Original===
On leaving the store Mr. Winthrop﻿—feeling awkward in the presence of the disappointed girl﻿—had pleaded business, and bidden her adieu with a warm grasp of the hand and many assurances that she had succeeded beyond his belief.

“I know you mean kindly in what you say,” said Christine, while not the slightest gleam lighted up her pale, sad face. “Goodbye.”

She, too, was relieved, and wished to be alone. Miss Winthrop sought to comfort her friend as they walked homeward.

“Christine, you look really ill. I don’t see why you take this matter so to heart. You have achieved a success that would turn any head but yours. I could not believe it possible had I not seen it. Your ambition and ideal are so lofty that you will always make yourself miserable by aiming at the impossible. As Mr. Fleet said, I do not believe there is another in the city who could have done so well, and if you can do that now, what may you not accomplish by a few years more of work?”

“That’s the terrible part of it,” said Christine, with a long sigh. “Susie, I have attained my growth. I can never be a real artist and no one living can ever know the bitterness of my disappointment. I do not believe in the immortality that you do, and this was my only chance to live beyond the brief hour of my life. If I could only have won for myself a place among the great names that the world will ever honor, I might with more content let the candle of my existence flicker out when it must. But I have learned today what I have often feared﻿—that Christine Ludolph must soon end in a forgotten handful of dust.”

===Chinese===
走出画店后，温思罗普先生面对这位失意落魄的姑娘，一时颇觉局促不安，便推说另有公务在身，紧紧握了握她的手向她道别，连声安慰她说她这一回的成就已远远超乎他的想象。

“我知道您说这些话是一番好意，”克里斯蒂娜说道，苍白哀伤的脸上却连一丝微光也未曾浮现，“再会了。”

她自己倒也松了一口气，巴不得能独自待着。一路走回家去，温思罗普小姐设法宽慰自己的好友。

“克里斯蒂娜，你脸色难看极了，简直像病了一样。我真不明白你何必把这事看得这样重。换作旁人，取得你这样的成就早就乐得忘乎所以了。要不是亲眼所见，我简直不敢相信世上真能做到这一步。你的抱负与理想实在太高远了，总去追求力所不能及的东西，只会让自己平添痛苦。就像弗利特先生说的，满城之中恐怕再也找不出第二个能画得这样好的人；你如今就能有这般水准，再勤勉钻研几年，还怕成不了大器么？”

“可怕的恰恰就在这里，”克里斯蒂娜长叹一声说道，“苏茜，我已经走到头了。我这辈子永远也成不了真正的艺术家，这世上活着的没有一个人能体会我心中的失望有多么苦涩。我不像你那样相信灵魂永生，而画画原是我唯一能让自己在短暂此生之外继续活下去的机会。倘若我真能在世人世代敬仰的伟人名录里挣得一席之地，待到生命之烛不得不熄灭时，我也好更加心安理得地随它摇曳而尽。可今天我终于认清了自己向来惧怕的事实——克里斯蒂娜·卢多尔夫终究很快就会化作一抔被人遗忘的尘土。”

===Original===
“Oh, Christine, if you could only believe!”

“I cannot. I tried in my last sickness, but vainly. I am more convinced than ever of the correctness of my father’s views.”

Miss Winthrop sighed deeply. “Why are you so despondent?” she at last asked.

As if half speaking to herself, Christine repeated the words, “ ‘Painted by one having never felt, or unable to feel, the emotions presented, and therefore one who cannot portray them.’ That is just the trouble. I tried to speak in a language I do not know. Susie, I believe I am about half ice. Sometimes I think I am like Undine, and have no soul. I know I have no heart, in the sense that you have.

“I live a very cold sort of life,” she continued, with a slight shudder. “I seem surrounded by invisible barriers that I cannot pass. I can see, beyond, what I want, but cannot reach it. Oh, Susie, if you knew what I suffered when so ill! Everything seemed slipping from me. And yet why I should so wish to live I hardly know, when my life is so narrowed down.”

“You see the disease, but not the remedy,” sighed Susie.

===Chinese===
“哦，克里斯蒂娜，但愿你能生出信仰才好！”

“我办不到。上次病重时我试过了，却徒劳无功。如今我比从前更加确信，我父亲的看法是对的。”

温思罗普小姐深深地叹了口气。“你何至于如此消沉呢？”她终于问道。

克里斯蒂娜仿佛半是自言自语般，轻声复述着那句话：“‘作画之人从未感受过、或根本无力感受画中所呈现的情感，因而也就无从将它描绘出来。’毛病正出在这里。我试图用一种自己根本不懂的语言去说话。苏茜，我觉得自己多半是冰雕玉琢而成的。有时我甚至觉得自己就像温蒂妮（Undine），没有灵魂。我知道自己没有像你那样的心肠。

“我过着一种冷冰冰的日子，”她说着微微打了个寒噤，“我仿佛被一道道看不见的屏障团团围住，怎么也跨不出去。我能看见屏障外头我想要的东西，却怎么也够不着。哦，苏茜，你是不知道我病得那样重的时候有多苦！一切似乎都要从我指缝里溜走了。可连我自己都几乎不明白，日子过得这般狭窄局促，我又何苦那样执意想活下去呢。”

“你只看见了病症，却没看见药方，”苏茜叹息道。

===Original===
“What is the remedy?”

“*Love.* Love to God, and I may add love for some good man.”

Christine stopped a moment and almost stamped her foot impatiently.

“You discourage me more than anyone else,” she cried. “As to loving God, how can I love merely a name? and, even if He existed, how could I love a Being who left His world so full of vile evils? As to human love, faugh! I have had enough of romantic attachments.”

“Do you never intend to marry?”

“Susie, you are the friend of my soul, and I trust you and you only with our secret. Yes, I expect to marry, but not in this land. You know that in Germany my father will eventually be a noble, the representative of one of the most ancient and honorable families. We shall soon have sufficient wealth to resume our true position there. A husband will then be found for me. I only stipulate that he shall be able to give me position among the first, and gratify my bent for art to the utmost.”

===Chinese===
“什么药方？”

“*爱。*对上帝的爱，或许还可以加上对某个好男人的爱。”

克里斯蒂娜停下脚步，不耐烦得几乎要跺起脚来。

“你比谁都教我灰心！”她叫道，“至于爱上帝，叫我如何去爱一个徒具虚名的字眼？再者，纵然祂果真存在，祂任由自己的世界充斥着这般卑劣的罪恶，叫我又怎能爱得起来？至于人世间的爱，呸！那些风花雪月的恋慕，我已经受够了。”

“难道你打定主意一辈子不成婚吗？”

“苏茜，你是我灵魂的知己，家里的秘密，我只信得过你一个人。不错，我日后是打算嫁人的，但绝不是在这片土地上。你知道，在德国，我父亲终有一天会承袭贵族爵位，成为最古老、最显赫的名门望族之一的家主。用不了多久，我们就会攒足家产，回乡重振门楣、恢复我们应有的地位。到那时，自会有人替我物色一门亲事。我唯一开出的条件，就是他必须能让我跻身头等名流之列，并且尽最大可能成全我对艺术的志趣。”

===Original===
“Well, Christine, you are a strange girl, and your dream of the future is stranger still.”

“Sometimes I think that all is a dream, and may end like one. Nothing seems certain or real, or turns out as one expects. Think of it. A nobody who swept my father’s store the other day has this morning made such havoc in my dream that I am sick at heart.”

“But you cannot blame Mr. Fleet. He did it unconsciously; he was goaded on to do it. No *man* could have done otherwise. You surely do not feel hardly toward him?”

“We do not naturally love the lips and bless the voice that tell us of an incurable disease. Oh, no,” she added, “why should I think of him at all? He merely happened to point out what I half suspected myself. And yet the peculiar way this stranger crosses my path from time to time almost makes me superstitious.”

“And you seem to have peculiar power over him. He would have assuredly left us in the lurch at our tableau party had it not been for you, and I should not have blamed him. And today he seemed troubled and pained beyond expression when he read from your face, as I imagine, that you were the author of the picture.”

“Yes, I saw that he discovered the fact, and this provokes me also. If he should speak his thoughts﻿—”

===Chinese===
“哎呀，克里斯蒂娜，你真是个奇特的姑娘，你对未来的憧憬就更古怪了。”

“有时我觉得这一切都不过是一场梦，兴许也会像梦一样散尽。世上仿佛没有一件事是稳妥真实的，也没有一件事会如人所愿。你想想看吧：前几天还在我父亲店里扫地的一个无名小卒，今早竟把我的美梦搅得支离破碎，教我心如死灰。”
