After they had been at the hotel about a week, Mr. Ludolph received letters that made his speedy return necessary. On the same day the family of his old New York partner arrived at the house on their return from the Catskills. Mrs. Von Brakhiem gladly received Christine under her care, feeling that the addition of such a bright star would make her little constellation one of the most brilliant in the fashionable world.

The ladies of the house were now immersed in the excitement of an amateur concert. Mrs. Von Brakhiem, bent upon shining among the foremost, though with a borrowed lustre, assigned Christine a most prominent part. She half shrank from it, for it recalled unpleasant memories; but she could not decline without explanations, and so entered into the affair with a sort of recklessness.

The large parlors were filled with chairs, which were soon occupied, and it was evident that in point of attraction elegant toilets would vie with the music. Christine came down on her father’s arm, dressed like a princess, and, though her diamonds were few, such were their size and brilliancy that they seemed on fire. Every eye followed Mrs. Von Brakhiem’s party, and that good lady took half the admiration to herself.

A superior tenor, with an unpronounceable foreign name, had come up from New York to grace the occasion. But personally he lacked every grace himself, his fine voice being the one thing that redeemed him from utter insignificance in mind and appearance. Nevertheless he was vain beyond measure, and made the most of himself on all occasions.

===Chinese===
在旅馆住了大约一周后，卢多尔夫先生收到几封信，迫使他必须火速赶回。同一天，他在纽约的老合伙人一家从卡茨基尔山（Catskills）避暑归来，也下榻于这家旅馆。冯·布拉克海姆太太（Mrs. Von Brakhiem）欣然将克里斯蒂娜揽入自己的照拂之下，暗忖有了这样一颗璀璨的新星加入，自己这方小小的星群定会成为时尚社交界最耀眼夺目的一簇。

此刻，旅馆里的女宾们正一头扎进一场业余音乐会的筹备热潮中。冯·布拉克海姆太太一心要在众人之中出尽风头——哪怕靠的是借来的光彩——于是把最出挑的角色分派给了克里斯蒂娜。克里斯蒂娜本有几分退缩，因为这勾起了她不愉快的回忆；但她若推辞，势必要费一番口舌解释，因此索性带着一种破罐破摔的劲头应承了下来。

宽敞的客厅里摆满了椅子，转眼便座无虚席；显然，论起吸引眼球的本事，女士们的华美盛装与动人乐声可谓旗鼓相当。克里斯蒂娜挽着父亲的手臂步下楼梯，一身装束宛如公主，佩戴的钻石虽不多，颗颗却硕大璀璨，仿佛在燃烧发光。一道道目光紧随着冯·布拉克海姆太太一行人移动，而这位好太太则心安理得地把旁人一半的钦羡都算在了自己头上。

一位技艺不俗的男高音歌唱家，顶着个拗口难念的外国姓氏，专程从纽约赶来为这场盛会增光添彩。可惜他本人却半点风雅气度也无，若非还有一副好嗓子，无论才智还是相貌都实在平庸得不值一提。即便如此，他却自负得没边，无论什么场合都要极力卖弄一番。

===Original===
The music was fine, for the amateurs, feeling that they had a critical audience, did their best. Christine chose three brilliant, difficult, but heartless pieces as her contribution to the entertainment (she would not trust herself with anything else); and with something approaching reckless gayety she sought to hide the bitterness at her heart. Her splendid voice and exquisite touch doubled the admiration her beauty and diamonds had excited, and Mrs. Von Brakhiem basked in still stronger reflected light. She took every opportunity to make it known that she was Miss Ludolph’s chaperon.

After her first effort, the “distinguished” tenor from New York opened his eyes widely at her; at her second, he put up his eyeglass in something like astonishment; and the close of her last song found him nervously rummaging a music portfolio in the corner.

But for Christine the law of association had become too strong, and the prolonged applause recalled the evening at Miss Brown’s when the same sounds had deafened her, but when turning from it all she had seen Dennis Fleet standing in rapt attention, his lips parted, his eyes glowing with such an honest admiration that even then it was worth more to her than all the clamor. Then, by the same law of association, she again saw that eager, earnest face, changed pale, dead﻿—dead!﻿—and she the cause. Regardless of the compliments lavished upon her, she buried her face in her hands and trembled from head to foot.

===Chinese===
当晚的乐曲颇为精彩，因为这群业余演奏者深知台下听众眼光挑剔，无不使出浑身解数。克里斯蒂娜挑了三首华丽炫技、难度极高却毫无真情实感的曲子，作为她献给这场演出的节目（她不敢贸然去碰别的曲目）；她带着几近狂放的欢快神色，竭力掩饰心头的苦涩。她那美妙绝伦的歌喉与炉火纯青的琴技，令众人对她美貌与钻饰的赞叹更添一倍，冯·布拉克海姆太太也愈发沐浴在反射而来的耀眼光芒之中。她逢人便找机会炫耀，声称自己正是卢多尔夫小姐的陪护女伴。

第一曲毕，那位来自纽约的“杰出”男高音朝她睁大了眼睛；第二曲终，他架起单片眼镜，面露几分惊愕；待她最后一首歌落幕，他已局促不安地躲在角落里翻找起乐谱夹来。

可对克里斯蒂娜而言，联想的魔力已变得太过强大。这经久不息的掌声，瞬间将她拉回布朗小姐家的那个夜晚——彼时也是这般震耳欲聋的喝彩，可当她转过身去，却看见丹尼斯·弗利特正站在那儿全神贯注地凝神倾听，双唇微启，双眸闪烁着那样诚挚热切的钦佩，即便在当时，那目光对她而言也胜过满堂喧嚣。紧接着，循着同一条联想的锁链，她又看见那张热忱、恳切的面庞陡然变得惨白、毫无生气——死了！——而祸首正是她自己。她顾不得众人如潮水般涌来的溢美之词，猛地用双手捂住脸，浑身上下瑟瑟发抖。

===Original===
But the irrepressible tenor had found what he wanted, and now came forward asking that Miss Ludolph would sing a duet with him.

She lifted a wan and startled face. Must the torturing similarity and still more torturing contrast of the two occasions be continued? But she saw her father regarding her sternly﻿—saw that she was becoming the subject of curious glances and whispered surmises. Her pride was aroused at once, and, goaded on by it, she said, “Oh, certainly; I am not feeling well, but it does not signify.”

“And den,” put in the tenor, “dis is von grand occazeon to *you*, for it is so unfrequent dat I find any von vorthy to sing dis style of music vith *me*.”

“What is the music?” asked Christine, coldly.

To her horror she found it the same selection from Mendelssohn that she had sung with Dennis.

===Chinese===
然而那位按捺不住的男高音已经翻到了心仪的曲谱，此刻正大步走上前，恳请卢多尔夫小姐与他合唱一首二重唱。

她抬起一张苍白惊惶的脸。难道两次场合之间这般折磨人的相似之处，以及更加折磨人的天壤之别，还要一再重演下去吗？可她看见父亲正冷峻地注视着自己——又觉察到四周好奇的目光与窃窃私语的揣测正聚拢到她身上。她的自尊心立时被激了起来，在这股傲气的驱使下，她开口道：“哦，当然可以；我只是觉得身子有些不适，不过不打紧。”

“而且嘛，”男高音插嘴道，“这对*您*来说可算得上一场莫大的盛事，因为我很少能遇上配得起与*我*合唱这类格调乐曲的搭档。”

“是什么曲子？”克里斯蒂娜冷冷地问道。

令她毛骨悚然的是，那竟恰恰是她曾与丹尼斯合唱过的那一首门德尔松（Mendelssohn）选曲。

===Original===
“No,” she said, sharply, “I cannot sing that.”

“Pardon me, my daughter, you can sing it admirably if you choose,” interposed her father.

She turned to him imploringly, but his face was inflexible, and his eyes had an incensed look. For a moment she, too, was angry. Had he no mercy? She was about to decline coldly, but her friends were very urgent and clamorous﻿—“Please do,” “Don’t disappoint us,” echoing on every side. The tenor was so surprised and puzzled at her insensibility to the honor he had conferred, that, to prevent a scene she could not explain, she went to the piano as if led to the stake.

But the strain was too great upon her in her suffering state. The familiar notes recalled so vividly the one who once before had sung them at her side that she turned almost expecting to see him﻿—but saw only the vain little animated music-machine, who with many contortions was producing the harmony. “Just this mockery my life will ever be,” she thought; “all that I am, the best I can do, will always be connected with something insignificant and commonplace. The rich, impassioned voice of the *man* who sang these words, and who might have taught me to sing the song of a new and happier life, I have silenced forever.”

The thought overpowered her. Just then her part recurred, but her voice died away in a miserable quaver, and again she buried her face in her hands. Suddenly she sprang from the piano, darted through the low-cut open window near, and a moment later ordered her startled maid from the room, turned the key, and was alone.

===Chinese===
“不行，”她语气尖利地说，“我不能唱这首。”

“恕我直言，我的女儿，只要你愿意，你完全能唱得精彩绝伦。”她父亲插口道。

她恳求地望向父亲，可他面沉如铁，目光里透着愠怒。一时间，她也动了气。难道他竟没有半点怜悯之心吗？她正待冷漠回绝，身旁的友伴们却七嘴八舌地恳求起哄起来——“求你了，唱吧”“别教我们扫兴啊”，声浪从四面八方涌来。那位男高音见她对自己赐予的荣幸竟如此无动于衷，也露出一副既惊愕又困惑的神色。为了避免闹出一场她根本无从解释的难堪风波，她只得走向钢琴，步履沉重得如同被押赴火刑柱一般。

然而在她这般煎熬的心境下，这重压实在太过沉重了。熟悉的音符如此鲜活地唤起了昔日曾在她身旁同唱此曲的那个人，令她几乎下意识地转过头去，仿佛真能望见他——然而映入眼帘的，却只有那台虚荣矮小、仿佛上了发条的音乐机器，正挤眉弄眼、扭捏作态地挤出一段和声。“我这一生，永远只会是这样一场荒唐的嘲弄罢了，”她心想，“我这个人的一切，我所能做到的一切极致，今后永远只能与卑微庸俗之物纠缠在一起。而曾吟唱这些词句、本可教会我唱响崭新幸福人生之歌的那位*男子汉*，他那醇厚而充满激情的嗓音，已被我永远地掐灭了。”

这念头彻底击垮了她。恰在此时又轮到她接唱，可她的嗓音却化作一阵凄惨的颤音戛然而止，她再次将脸埋进掌心。突然间，她从钢琴前猛地弹起身来，闪身穿过旁边那扇低矮敞开的落地窗，片刻之后便将受惊的贴身女仆撵出房间，反手拧转钥匙，将自己孤零零地关在了屋里。

===Original===
Her father explained coldly to the astonished audience and the half-paralyzed tenor (who still stood with his mouth open) that his daughter was not at all well that evening, and ought not to have appeared at all. This Mrs. Von Brakhiem took up and repeated with endless variations. But the evidences of sheer mental distress on the part of Christine had been too clear, and countless were the whispered surmises of the fashionable gossips in explanation.

Mrs. Von Brakhiem herself, burning with curiosity, soon retired, that she might receive from her lovely charge some gushing confidences, which she expected, as a matter of course, would be poured into what she chose to regard as her sympathizing ear. But she knocked in vain at Christine’s door.

Later Mr. Ludolph knocked. There was no answer.

“Christine!” he called.

After some delay a broken voice answered, “You cannot enter﻿—I am not well﻿—I have retired.”

He turned on his heel and strode away, and that night drank more brandy and water than was good for him.

===Chinese===
面对满座愕然的宾客和那位惊呆当场、至今还张着嘴的男高音，她父亲冷淡地解释说，小女今晚身体极为不适，本就不该出来露面的。冯·布拉克海姆太太立即接过话茬，添油加醋、反反复复地解释了一遍又一遍。然而克里斯蒂娜显露出的纯粹精神痛苦实在太过明显，一时间，这群爱嚼舌根的名流雅士暗地里交头接耳，揣测之辞数不胜数。

冯·布拉克海姆太太自己也按捺不住好奇心，没过多久便告退离席，盘算着从她照管的这位迷人姑娘口中听取一番滔滔不绝的私房倾诉——她理所当然地以为，这番心事必定会倾泻进她自诩富于同情心的耳朵里。可她在克里斯蒂娜的房门外叩了半天，却只是白费工夫。

过了一会儿，卢多尔夫先生前来敲门。屋里毫无应答。

“克里斯蒂娜！”他唤道。

过了好一会儿，里面才传来一个破碎的声音：“您不能进来——我身子不舒服——我已经歇下了。”

他霍然转身，大步流星地走了，那天夜里兑水喝下的白兰地，比他平常所宜的量多出不少。

===Original===
As for Christine, warped and chilled though her nature had been, she was still a woman, she was still young, and, though she knew it not, she had heard the voice which had spoken her heart into life. Through a chain of circumstances for which she was partly to blame, she had been made to suffer as she had not believed was possible. The terrible words of Mr. Bruder’s letter rang continually in her ears﻿—“Mrs. Fleet is not dying a natural death; he has been slain.”

For many long, weary days the conviction had been growing upon her that she had indeed slain him and mortally wounded herself. Until tonight she had kept herself outwardly under restraint, but now the long pent-up feeling gave way, and she sobbed as if her heart would break﻿—sobbed till the power to weep was gone. If now some kind, judicious friend had shown her that she was not so guilty as she deemed herself; that, however, frightful the consequences of such acts, she was really not to blame for what she did not intend and could not foresee; more than all, if she could only have known that her worst fears about Dennis were not to be realized, and that he was now recovering, she might at once have entered on a new and happier life. But there was no such friend, no such knowledge, and her wounded spirit was thrown back upon itself.

At last, robed as she had been for the evening, she fell asleep from sheer exhaustion and grief﻿—for grief induces sleep.

The gems that shone in her dishevelled hair; that rose and fell as at long intervals her bosom heaved with convulsive sobs, like the fitful gusts of a storm that is dying away; the costly fabrics she wore﻿—made sad mockery in their contrast with the pale, tear-stained, suffering face. The hardest heart might have pitied her﻿—yes, even the wholly ambitious heart of her father, incensed as he was that a plebeian stranger of this land should have caused such distress.

===Chinese===
至于克里斯蒂娜，尽管她的天性曾饱受扭曲与冰封，她毕竟还是个女人，依然年轻；而且尽管她自己浑然不觉，她其实已经听见了那个唤醒她沉睡心扉的声音。在一连串她自身也难辞其咎的变故牵引下，她如今尝到了自己从前绝不相信世上会有的苦痛。布鲁德先生信中那几句可怕的字眼，一直在她耳畔轰鸣回荡——“弗利特先生〔原著误作“弗利特太太”（Mrs. Fleet）〕并非死于自然；他是被人杀害的。”

漫长而疲惫的日日夜夜里，一个念头在她心中愈发根深蒂固：她当真杀死了他，同时也给了自己致命一击。直到今晚，她表面上还一直强自克制，可此刻积压已久的情感终于决堤而出，她哭得肝肠寸断——一直哭到连流泪的力气都干涸为止。倘若此刻能有哪位善良而明智的朋友开解她，让她明白自己并不像自认的那样罪孽深重，明白无论那番举动酿成了多么骇人的后果，对于她既非本意、亦未能预见之事，她其实不必担此重责；更要紧的是，倘若她能早一点知道，自己对丹尼斯最坏的担忧并未成真，他如今正在日渐康复，她或许立刻就能踏上一条崭新而更幸福的人生之路。然而世上既无这样的朋友，也无这样的消息，她那颗伤痕累累的灵魂只得再度缩回自己的躯壳之中。

终于，她连晚礼服也未曾脱下，便因极度的精疲力竭与悲恸而昏昏睡去——悲伤原是会催人入眠的。

她凌乱的发髻间闪烁着宝石，她胸前佩饰随偶尔一次痉挛般的抽泣微微起伏，宛如一场行将平息的风暴遗下的阵阵余风，她身上裹着的昂贵衣料——这一切与她那张苍白、挂满泪痕、写满痛苦的脸庞映衬在一起，构成了何等凄凉的讽刺。哪怕世上最铁石心肠的人见了也会心生怜悯——是的，哪怕是她父亲那颗满腔功利野心的心，纵然正因这片土地上的一个寒门异乡人竟惹出这般风波而恼火万分，见此情景恐怕也不免动容。

===Original===
When Christine awoke, her pride awoke also. With bitterness of spirit she recalled the events of the past evening. But a new phase of feeling now began to manifest itself.

After her passionate outburst she was much calmer. In this respect the unimpeded flow of feeling had done her good, and, as intimated, if kindness and sympathy could now have added their gentle ministrations, she might have been the better for it all her life. But, left to herself, she again yielded to the sway of her old and worst traits. Chief among these was pride; and under the influence of this passion and the acute suffering of her unsoothed, unguided spirit, she began to rebel in impotent anger. She grew hard, cynical, and reckless. Her father’s lack of sympathy and consideration alienated her heart even from him. Left literally alone in the world, her naturally reserved nature shut itself up more closely than ever. Even her only friend, Susie Winthrop, drifted away. One other, who might have been﻿—But she could think of him only with a shudder now. All the rest seemed indifferent, or censorious, or, worse still, to be using her, like Mrs. Von Brakhiem and even her own father, as a stepping-stone to their personal ambition. Christine could not see that she was to blame for this isolation. She did not understand that cold, selfish natures, like her own and her father’s, could not surround themselves with warm, generous friends. She saw only the fact. But with flashing eyes she resolved that her heart’s secrets should not be pried into a hair-breadth further; that she would be used only so far as she chose. She would, in short, “face out” the events of the past evening simply and solely on the ground that she had not been well, and permit no questions to be asked.

Cold and self-possessed, she came down to a late breakfast. Mrs. Von Brakhiem, and others who had been introduced, joined her, but nothing could penetrate through the nice polished armor of her courteous reserve. Her father looked at her keenly, but she coolly returned his gaze.

===Chinese===
克里斯蒂娜一觉醒来，她的骄傲也随之苏醒。她满心苦涩地回想起昨晚的种种变故。然而此时，一种新的心绪开始在她心头滋长显露。

痛哭宣泄之后，她平静了许多。从这方面说，情绪毫无阻拦地倾泻而出反倒对她大有裨益；正如前文所暗示的，倘若此刻能有温情与体恤施以柔和的抚慰，她或许终生都会因此受益。然而孤立无援的她，再次屈服于自己旧日最恶劣的性情支配。其中首当其冲的便是傲慢；在这种情绪与她那颗无人安抚、无人指引的灵魂所受剧痛的裹挟下，她开始陷入无力而愤懑的反抗之中。她变得冷硬、愤世嫉俗、肆无忌惮。父亲的毫无同情与体谅，甚至令她的心连对他都疏远了。在这世上真真切切地孤立无援，她生性本就缄默内敛，此刻更是将自己封闭得滴水不漏。就连她唯一的朋友苏茜·温思罗普，也渐渐疏远了。还有另一个人，本有可能成为……可如今只要一想起他，她便不由得浑身战栗。其余的人看起来不是冷漠旁观，就是苛刻指责，更有甚者，就像冯·布拉克海姆太太乃至她自己的父亲那样，不过是把她当作实现个人野心的垫脚石。克里斯蒂娜看不出落得这般孤立正是她自己咎由自取。她不明白，像她自己和父亲这样冷酷自私的性情，原本就招不来热情慷慨的挚友相伴左右。她眼里只看见眼前的事实。然而，她双眸闪动着寒光，暗自打定主意：心底的秘密绝不许外人再窥探半分一毫；别人能利用她的，也只能限于她自己情愿的那一点。简而言之，她决定只管凭着“身体不适”这唯一一条理由，把昨晚那场风波“硬扛过去”，绝不容许任何人盘问半句。

她神色冷峻、镇定自若地踩着点下楼来吃迟到的早饭。冯·布拉克海姆太太以及几位曾引见过的宾客都凑过来陪坐，却无一人能刺穿她那副以礼貌矜持打磨得光洁无瑕的盔甲。她父亲锐利地审视着她，她却淡然冷漠地迎上他的目光。

===Original===
When alone with her soon afterward, he turned and said, sharply, “What does all this mean?”

She looked around as if someone else were near.

“Were you addressing me?” she asked, coldly.

“Yes, of course I am,” said her father, impatiently.

“From your tone and manner, I supposed you must be speaking to someone else.”

===Chinese===
没过多久，趁着与她独处，他转过身，厉声问道：“这究竟是怎么回事？”

她环顾四周，仿佛旁边还有旁人在场似的。

“您是在跟我说话吗？”她冷冰冰地问道。

“是啊，当然是在跟你说话，”她父亲不耐烦地说。

“听您那腔调和态度，我还当您是在训斥别的什么人呢。”

===Original===
“Nonsense! I was speaking to you. What does all this mean?”

She turned on him an indescribable look, and after a moment said in a slow, meaning tone, “Have you not heard my explanation, sir?”

Such was her manner, he felt he could as easily strike her as say another word.

Muttering an oath, he turned on his heel and left her to herself.

===Chinese===
“胡扯！我就是跟你在说话。这究竟是怎么回事？”

她朝他投去一道难以形容的目光，停顿片刻，才用缓慢而意味深长的语调说道：“难道您没听见我的解释吗，先生？”

她这副神态，令他觉得自己再多说一个字简直跟动手打她一样难。

他低声咒骂了一句，霍然转身，撇下她独自一人。

===Original===
The next morning her father bade her “Goodbye.” In parting he said, meaningly, “Christine, beware!”

Again she turned upon him that peculiar look, and replied in a low, firm tone: “That recommendation applies to you, also. Let us both beware, lest we repent at leisure.”

The wily man, skilled in character, was now thoroughly convinced that in his daughter he was dealing with a nature very different from his wife’s﻿—that he was now confronted by a spirit as proud and imperious as his own. He clearly saw that force, threatening, sternness would not answer in this case, and that if he carried his points it must be through skill and cunning. By some means he must ever gain her consent and cooperation.

His manner changed. Instinctively she divined the cause; and hers did not. Therefore father and daughter parted as father and daughter ought never to part.

===Chinese===
次日清晨，父亲向她道别。临行前，他意味深长地说道：“克里斯蒂娜，好自为之！”

她再度向他投去那道奇特的目光，压低嗓音坚定地答道：“这句忠告对您也同样适用。咱们俩都各自留神些吧，免得日后追悔莫及。”

这位工于心计、精于识人的男子，此刻已彻底信服：眼下在女儿身上，他所要打交道的是与他妻子截然不同的天性——站他对面的，是一个与他自己同样骄傲而专横的灵魂。他看得很清楚，强迫、威吓、严厉在此时全都行不通；若想达成自己的目的，唯有用上权谋与狡黠。无论用什么手段，他今后总得先赢得她的首肯与配合才行。

他的态度立刻变了。她本能地洞悉了缘由，因此自己的神色丝毫未变。就这样，父女二人以一种世间父女绝不该有的方式各奔东西。

===Original===
After his departure she was to remain at West Point till the season closed, and then accompany Mrs. Von Brakhiem to New York, where she was to make as long a visit as she chose;﻿—and she chose to make a long one. In the scenery, and the society of the officers at West Point, and the excitements of the metropolis, she found more to occupy her thoughts than she could have done at Chicago. She went deliberately to work to kill time and snatch from it such fleeting pleasures as she might.

They stayed in the country till the pomp and glory of October began to illumine the mountains, and then (to Christine’s regret) went to the city. There she entered into every amusement and dissipation that her tastes permitted, and found much pleasure in frequent visits to the Central Park, although it seemed tame and artificial after the wild grandeur of the mountains. It was well that her nature was so high-toned that she found enjoyment in only what was refined or intellectual. Had it been otherwise she might soon have taken, in her morbid, reckless state, a path to swift and remediless ruin, as many a poor creature all at war with happiness and truth has done. And thus in a giddy whirl of excitement (Mrs. Von Brakhiem’s normal condition) the days and weeks passed, till at last, thoroughly satiated and jaded, she concluded to return home, for the sake of change and quiet, if nothing else. Mrs. Von Brakhiem parted with her regretfully. Where would she find such another ally in her determined struggle to be talked about and envied a little more than some other pushing, jostling votaries of fashion?

In languor or sleep Christine made the journey, and in the dusk of a winter’s day her father drove her to their beautiful home, which from association was now almost hateful to her. Still she was too weary to think or suffer much. They met each other very politely, and their intercourse assumed at once its wonted character of high-bred courtesy, though perhaps it was a little more void of manifested sympathy and affection than before.

Several days elapsed in languid apathy, the natural reaction of past excitement; then an event occurred which most thoroughly aroused her.

===Chinese===
父亲动身之后，她便留在西点直到避暑季结束，随后陪同冯·布拉克海姆太太前往纽约，想住多久便住多久——而她决定住上一阵长长的时日。在西点的山水风光、军官们的社交往来，以及大都会的喧嚣刺激之中，她寻到了比留在芝加哥更能占据心神的消遣。她蓄意打发着光阴，趁势从流逝的岁月里攫取一星半点浮光掠影般的欢愉。

她们在乡间一直逗留到十月绚烂辉煌的秋色开始照亮群山，这才（令克里斯蒂娜颇为惋惜地）启程进城。到了纽约，但凡品味尚且容许的寻欢作乐与纸醉金迷，她一概投身其中；她还频频游逛中央公园（Central Park），并在那里寻得不少乐趣——尽管见识过群山那狂野壮阔的气象之后，这公园显得平淡而做作。幸而她天性高雅，唯独能从精致或富于智识的事物中寻得愉悦。倘若不是如此，以她当时病态而孤注一掷的心境，怕是很快便会走上一条迅速坠入万劫不复的歧途，正如同许多与幸福和真理为敌的可怜人所走过的那样。日子和星期就在这阵令人目眩神迷的狂欢漩涡里（这原是冯·布拉克海姆太太的常态）飞逝而去，直到最后，克里斯蒂娜彻底感到腻味与疲惫，决定回家——哪怕只为换换环境、图个清静。冯·布拉克海姆太太依依不舍地与她作别。她正铆足了劲儿要在社交场上比那些争名夺利、你推我挤的时尚信徒更引人议论、更教人艳羡几分，上哪儿再找这样一位得力的盟友呢？

克里斯蒂娜在倦怠与昏睡中度过了漫漫归途；在一个冬日的暮色里，父亲驾车将她接回了那座华美的宅邸——只因种种往事牵连，这座家宅如今几乎已令她深恶痛绝。不过她实在太累了，连多想或痛苦的力气都没有。父女俩彼此客客气气地相见，相处之间立刻恢复了往常那种彬彬有礼的高门做派，只是比从前似乎更少了些流露于表的温情与关切。

在过往狂热之后必然涌上的倦怠麻木中，又悄然滑过了几天；紧接着，一件事骤然发生，彻底将她惊醒。

## XVII Rescued / 第十七章 获救

===Original===
In a tone of suppressed excitement, which he tried in vain to render steady, Mr. Bruder said: “You haf der advantage of me, sir. I know not your name. Vat is more, I am not fit for bissiness dis night. Indeed, I haf important bissiness elsewhere. You must excuse me,” he added, sternly, advancing toward the door with the picture.

“Pardon me, Mr. Bruder,” said Dennis, politely. “I throw myself entirely on your courtesy, and must ask as a very great favor that you will not take away that picture till I see it, for that, in part, is what I came for. I am in the picture trade myself, and think I am a tolerably fair judge of paintings. I heard accidentally you had a fine one, and from the glimpse I catch of it, I think I have not been misinformed. If it is for sale, perhaps I can do as well by you as anyone else. I am employed in Mr. Ludolph’s great store, the Art Building. You probably know all about the place.”

“Yes, I know him,” said the man, calming down somewhat.

“And now, sir,” said Dennis, with a gentle, winning courtesy impossible to resist, “will you do me the favor of showing me your picture?”

He treated poor Bruder as a gentleman, and he, having really been one, was naturally inclined to return like courtesy. Therefore he said, “Oh, certainly, since you vish to see him. I suppose I might as vell sell him to you as any von else.”

===Chinese===
布鲁德先生竭力想把嗓音稳住，却终归徒劳，只得压抑着激动的语气说道：“先生，您占了我的上风，我还不知道您的大名呢。再说，今晚我不适合谈买卖。实在说，我别处还有紧要的勾当要办。您得包涵了。”他神色冷峻地补充了一句，抱着画径直朝门口走去。

“请原谅，布鲁德先生，”丹尼斯彬彬有礼地说道，“我全凭您高抬贵手，务必恳请您赏个大脸，在我看一看那幅画之前先别把它拿走，因为我这趟登门，多半就是冲着这幅画来的。我自己也是做画作这一行的，自问对油画还算颇有几分眼力。我偶然听说您手里藏着一幅佳作，方才瞥见一眼，想来传言果然不虚。要是这画打算出手，或许我能给您出的价钱并不输给旁人。我在卢多尔夫先生那家大画店‘艺术大厦’里供职。您大概对那地方早有耳闻。”

“不错，我晓得那地方。”那汉子语气缓和了几分说道。

“那么，先生，”丹尼斯以一种温和谦恭、教人实在难以推辞的礼貌问道，“您肯行个方便，让我赏鉴一下您的画作吗？”

他拿穷困潦倒的布鲁德当一位绅士相待；而布鲁德昔日原本就是体面人，天性使然，自然也乐意以礼相还。于是他说道：“哦，那当然，既然您想瞧瞧它。我想，卖给您总跟卖给旁人没什么两样。”

===Original===
Mr. Bruder was a man of violent impulses, and his mad excitement was fast leaving him under Dennis’s cool, businesslike manner. To gain time was now the great desideratum.

The picture having been replaced upon the wall, Mr. Bruder held the lamp so as to throw upon it as good a light as possible.

Dennis folded his arms calmly and commenced its study. He had meant to act a part﻿—to pretend deep interest and desire for long critical study﻿—that he might secure more time, but in a few moments he became honestly absorbed in the beautiful and exquisitely finished landscape.

The poor man watched him keenly. Old associations and feelings, seemingly long dead, awoke. As he saw Dennis manifest every mark of true and growing appreciation, he perceived that his picture was being studied by a discriminating person. Then his artist-nature began to quicken into life again. His eyes glowed, and glanced rapidly from Dennis to the painting, back and forth, following up the judgment on each and every part which he saw written in the young man’s face. As he watched, something like hope and exultation began to light up his sullen, heavy features; thought and feeling began to spiritualize and ennoble what but a little before had been so coarse and repulsive.

Ernst was looking at Dennis in rapt awe, as at a messenger from heaven.

===Chinese===
布鲁德先生向来是个性情暴烈、容易冲动的人；此刻在丹尼斯沉着干练、公事公办的举止面前，他那股狂乱的亢奋正迅速退去。眼下最紧要的，便是争取时间。

画作重新挂回墙上，布鲁德先生举起油灯，好让灯光尽可能明亮地打在画布上。

丹尼斯沉静地抱起双臂，端详起这幅画来。他原本只打算演一出戏——假装兴味盎然、意欲细细品评鉴赏一番——好借此多拖延些时间；然而不过片刻工夫，他便由衷地被这幅秀美绝伦、笔触精微的风景画深深吸引住了。

那可怜人目光如炬地盯着他。那些仿佛早已死去的往昔记忆与情怀，霎时间苏醒了。眼见丹尼斯流露出越来越真切、越来越浓厚的赏识之情，他意识到自己的作品正被一位颇具慧眼的行家细加品味。顿时，他身上那股画家的天性重新蠢蠢欲动、焕发生机。他的双眼熠熠生辉，目光在丹尼斯与画作之间飞快地来回梭巡，顺着年轻人脸上流露出的神情，追踪着他对画面每一处细节的评判。他看着看着，一丝近乎希望与欣喜的光彩渐渐点亮了他那张阴沉呆滞的面庞；方才还显得那么粗鄙令人厌憎的五官，此刻竟在思绪与情感的浸润下透出了灵性与高雅。

恩斯特正屏息凝神、满怀敬畏地望着丹尼斯，宛若仰望一位自天而降的使者。

===Original===
The poor wife, who had listened in a dull apathy to the conversation, raised her head in sudden and intelligent interest when the picture was replaced upon the wall. It seemed that her every hope was bound up in that. As she saw Dennis and her husband standing before it﻿—as she saw the face of the latter begin to assume something of its former look﻿—her whole soul came into her great blue eyes, and she watched as if more than life were at stake.

If that meagre apartment, with its inmates, their contrasts of character, their expressive faces, could have then been portrayed, it would have made a picture with power to move the coldest heart.

At last Dennis drew a long breath, turned and gave his hand to the man, saying with hearty emphasis, “Mr. Bruder, you are an artist.”

The poor man lifted his face to heaven with the same expression of joy and gratitude that had rested on it long, long years ago, when his first real work of merit had received similar praise.

His wife saw and remembered it, and, with an ecstatic cry that thrilled Dennis’s soul, exclaimed, “Ah! mine Gott be praised! mine Gott be praised! his artist-soul come back!” and she threw herself on her husband’s neck, and clung to him with hysteric energy. The man melted completely, and bowed his head upon his wife’s shoulder, while his whole frame shook with sobs.

===Chinese===
起初一直麻木茫然地听着两人交谈的可怜妻子，当那幅画重新挂上墙头时，蓦地抬起头来，眼神里陡然闪现出敏锐而热切的关切。仿佛她这一生的全部指望，都系在这幅画上了。她看见丹尼斯与丈夫并肩站在画前——看见丈夫的脸庞渐渐恢复了几分昔日的神采——她整颗灵魂仿佛都涌进了那双大大的蓝眼睛里，屏息凝视着，仿佛眼前攸关的比性命还要紧要。

倘若当时有人能将那间寒酸的斗室连同屋里的几个人物、他们迥异的性格反差、以及各自脸上生动传神的神情一并摹入画中，那必将成就一幅足以撼动世间最冷酷心肠的杰作。

终于，丹尼斯长长舒了一口气，转过身，向那汉子伸出手去，由衷而郑重地说道：“布鲁德先生，您是一位真正的艺术家。”

这可怜人仰起脸望向苍天，脸上浮现出与许多许多年前如出一辙的欢欣与感激——那是在他平生第一幅真正称得上佳作的作品赢得类似赞誉时，曾流露过的神情。

他的妻子一眼认出了那神情，想起了当年光景，随即发出一声令丹尼斯心弦震颤的狂喜喊声：“啊！赞美我的上帝！赞美我的上帝！他那颗画家的灵魂回来了！”说着，她猛地扑到丈夫怀里，一把抱住他的脖子，近乎歇斯底里地死死依偎着他。那汉子彻底融化了，把头深深埋在妻子肩上，整个身躯因剧烈的抽泣而颤抖不已。

===Original===
“I will be back in half an hour,” said Dennis, hastily, brushing tears from his own eyes. “Come with me, Ernst.”

At the foot of the stairs Dennis said: “Take this money, Ernst, and buy bread, butter, tea, milk, and coal, also a nice large steak, for I am going to take supper with you tonight. I will stay here and watch, for your father must not be permitted to go out.”

“Oh, Gott bless you! Gott bless you!” said the boy, and he hurried away to do his errand.

Dennis walked up and down before the door on guard. Ernst soon returned, and carried the welcome food upstairs. After a little time he stole down again and said: “Father’s quiet and queer like. Mother has given the children a good supper and put them to bed. Better come now.”

“In a few moments more; you go back and sit down quietly and say nothing.”

===Chinese===
“我半个钟头后回来，”丹尼斯连忙抬手拭去自己眼角的泪水，说道，“恩斯特，跟我来。”

走到楼梯脚下，丹尼斯说道：“拿着这些钱，恩斯特，去买些面包、黄油、茶叶、牛奶和煤，再买一块上好的大牛排，因为我今晚要留下来和你们一块儿吃晚饭。我就守在这儿看着，可千万不能让你爸爸出门。”

“哦，上帝保佑您！上帝保佑您！”男孩说着，急匆匆地跑去采买了。

丹尼斯在门前踱来踱去地把守着。没过多久，恩斯特便回来了，把那些教人喜出望外的吃食拎上楼去。过了不多会儿，他又悄悄下楼来，说道：“爸爸安静下来了，只是神情有些古怪。妈妈已经喂弟妹们吃了一顿饱饭，哄他们睡下了。您现在上去吧。”

“再等一小会儿；你先上去静静坐着，什么也别说。”

===Original===
After a little Dennis went up and knocked at the door. Mrs. Bruder opened it, and held out her hand. Her quivering lips refused to speak, but her eyes filled with grateful tears. The children were tucked away in bed. Ernst crouched by the fire, eating some bread and butter, for he was cold and half-famished. Mr. Bruder sat in the dusky corner with his head in his hands, the picture of dejection. But, as Dennis entered, he rose and came forward. He tried to speak, but for a moment could not. At last he said, hoarsely: “Mr. Vleet, you haf done me and mine a great kindness. No matter vat the result is, I dank you as I never danked any living being. I believe Gott sent you, but I fear too late. You see before you a miserable wreck. For months and years I haf been a brute, a devil. Dot picture dere show you vat I vas, vat I might haf been. You see vat I am,” he added, with an expression of intense loathing. “I see him all tonight as if written in letters of fire, and if dere is a vorse hell dan der von I feel vithin my soul, Gott only knows how I am to endure him.”

“Mr. Bruder, you say I have done you a favor.”

“Gott knows you haf.”

“I want you to do me one in return. I want you to let me be your friend,” said Dennis, holding out his hand.

The man trembled, hesitated; at last he said, brokenly, “I am not fit﻿—to touch﻿—your hand.”

===Chinese===
过了一小会儿，丹尼斯走上楼去敲了敲门。布鲁德太太打开门，朝他伸出手来。她颤抖的嘴唇哽咽得说不出话，眼眶里却盈满了感激的泪水。孩子们都已盖好被子睡熟了。恩斯特蜷缩在炉火旁，正啃着几片抹了黄油的面包——他又冷又饿，早就快撑不住了。布鲁德先生独自坐在昏暗的角落里，双手抱头，活脱脱一幅颓丧绝望的模样。不过，丹尼斯一进屋，他便站起身走上前来。他张了张嘴想说话，一时却发不出声。终于，他声音沙哑地说道：“弗利特先生，您对我和我的家人施了天大的恩情。无论日后结果如何，我对您的感激之情，平生从未对任何一个活人有过。我相信是上帝派您来的，只怕终究还是太迟了。您眼前站着的，不过是个惨不忍睹的废人。长年累月以来，我一直活得像个畜生，像个魔鬼。墙上那幅画告诉您我从前是什么样的人，原本又能成为什么样的人。可您瞧瞧我如今这副德行，”他脸上露出极度厌恶的神色，接着说道，“今晚我把这一切全都看清了，仿佛是用火字刻在眼前一般；如果世上还有比我此刻灵魂里所受煎熬更可怕的地狱，天晓得我该如何挨得过去。”

“布鲁德先生，您方才说我帮了您的忙。”

“上帝作证，您确实帮了大忙。”

“那我也想请您帮我一个忙作为回报。我想请您允许我做您的朋友。”丹尼斯说着，朝他伸出了手。

那汉子浑身颤抖，犹豫不决；最后他断断续续地低声道：“我不配——去碰——您的手。”

===Original===
“Mr. Bruder,” said Dennis, gently, “I hope that I am a Christian.”

“Still more, den, I am unfit efer to be in your presence.”

“What! am I greater than my Master? Did not Christ take the hand of every poor, struggling man on earth that would let Him? Come, Mr. Bruder, if you have any real gratitude for the little I have done to show my interest in you and yours, grant me my request.”

“Do you really mean him?” he gasped. “Do you really vant to be drunken old Berthold Bruder’s friend?”

“God is my witness, I do,” said Dennis, still holding out his hand.

“既然如此，我就更永远不配站在您面前了。”

“什么话！难道我比我的主还要高贵不成？凡这世上肯向基督伸出手的穷苦挣扎之人，祂哪一个不曾拉住他们的手？来吧，布鲁德先生，倘若您对我为您和您一家略尽的一点绵薄心意当真怀有谢意，就请答应我的请求。”

“您当真这么想吗？”他喘息着问道，“您当真愿意跟贝特霍尔德·布鲁德这个老酒鬼做朋友？”

“上帝可鉴，我真心愿意。”丹尼斯说着，依旧伸着手等待。

===Original===
The poor fellow drew a few short, heavy breaths, and then grasped Dennis’s hand, and clung to it with the force of a drowning man. “Oh!” said he, after a few moments of deep emotion, “I feel dot I haf a plank under me now.”

“God grant that yon may soon feel that you are on the Rock Christ Jesus,” said Dennis, solemnly.

Fearing the reaction of too great and prolonged emotion, Dennis now did everything in his power to calm and quiet his newfound friends. He told them that he boarded at a restaurant, and he asked if he might take supper with them.

“Him is yours already,” said Mr. Bruder.

“No, it isn’t,” said Dennis﻿—“not after I have given it to you. But I want to talk to you about several matters, for I think you can be of great service to me;” and he told them of his experience during the day; that he had been promoted, and that he wanted Ernst to come and aid him in his duties. Then he touched on the matter nearest his heart﻿—his own wish to be an artist, his need of instruction﻿—and told how by his increase of pay he had now the means of taking lessons, while still able to support his mother and sisters.

===Chinese===
那可怜人急促而沉重地喘了几口气，随即一把抓住丹尼斯的手，宛如溺水之人般使出全身力气死死攥住不放。“哦！”激动良久之后，他开口说道，“我觉得脚底下总算踩着一块救命的木板了。”

“愿上帝赐福，叫您很快就能感到自己正稳稳立在基督耶稣这块磐石之上。”丹尼斯庄重地说道。

丹尼斯唯恐情绪过度激荡、持续太久反倒生出波折，此刻便竭尽所能安抚这几位新结交的朋友，好让他们平复下来。他告诉他们自己平时都在一家餐馆搭伙，问今晚能不能留下来同他们一道用晚餐。

“这顿饭本就是您的呀。”布鲁德先生说道。

“那可不算，”丹尼斯说道，“既是我送给你们的，便是你们的了。不过，我有几件事想跟您商量，因为我觉得您能帮上我的大忙；”于是他把白天的经历告诉了他们：自己得到了提拔，正想让恩斯特去店里帮他打理差事。接着，他又谈起自己最牵肠挂肚的心愿——他渴望成为一名画家，亟需名师指点——并说起如今涨了薪水，他既能照常奉养母亲和妹妹们，手头也终于宽裕出些许余钱，可以拜师学画了。

===Original===
“And now, Mr. Bruder, I feel that I have been very fortunate in making your acquaintance. You have the touch and tone that I should be overjoyed to acquire. Will you give me lessons?”

“Yes, morning, noon, and night, vithout von shent of pay.”

“That will not do. I’ll not take one on those terms.”

“I vill do vatever you want me to,” said the man, simply, “I vish I could be led and vatched over as a little child.”

Dennis saw his pathetic self-distrust, and it touched him deeply.

===Chinese===
“眼下呢，布鲁德先生，我觉得能结识您真是我的造化。您笔下的笔触与色调，正是我梦寐以求想要学到手的。您肯收我为徒、教我作画吗？”

“肯，早中晚什么时候都行，一分钱学费也不要！”

“那可不行。照这个条件，我一节课也不会上。”

“您要我怎样，我就怎样，”那汉子质朴地说道，“我巴不得有人像领着、看管着一个小孩子那样管住我才好。”

丹尼斯看出了他那份令人心酸的自我怀疑，心里深受触动。

===Original===
“As your friend,” he said, with emphasis, “I will not advise you to do anything that I would not do myself.”

So they arranged that Ernst should go to the store in the morning, and that Dennis should come three nights in the week for lessons.

All made a hearty supper save Mr. Bruder. He had reached that desperate stage when his diseased stomach craved drink only. But a strong cup of tea, and some bread that he washed down with it, heartened him a little, and it was evident that he felt better. The light of a faint hope was dawning in his face.

Dennis knew something of the physical as well as moral struggle before the poor man, and knew that after all it was exceedingly problematical whether he could be saved. Before he went away he told Mrs. Bruder to make her husband some very strong coffee in the morning, and to let him drink it through the day. As for Bruder, he had resolved to die rather than touch another drop of liquor.

But how many poor victims of appetite have been haunted to the grave by such resolves﻿—shattered and gone almost as soon as made!

===Chinese===
“作为您的朋友，”他语重心长地说道，“凡是我自己做不到的事，绝不会劝您去做。”

于是他们就此商定：明早恩斯特就去画店报到上工，丹尼斯则每礼拜抽出三个晚上过来学画。

除了布鲁德先生之外，大伙儿都美美地饱餐了一顿。他早已沉溺到那般绝望的境地，病弱的胃口唯独渴求着烈酒。不过，一杯浓茶下肚，再就着茶水咽下几口面包，倒也让他振作了些许，显而易见他觉得舒坦多了。一丝微弱的希望之光，正悄然在他脸上显露出来。

丹尼斯深知摆在这可怜人面前的不仅是道义上的挣扎，更有肉体上的煎熬，也明白他究竟能否真正得救，归根结底仍是个极大的未知数。临走前，他叮嘱布鲁德太太明早给丈夫煮些极浓的咖啡，让他白天整日饮用。至于布鲁德本人，则已打定主意，宁死也绝不再沾半滴酒水。

然而，古往今来又有多少受困于嗜欲的可怜受害者，曾被这般誓言一路纠缠直至坟墓——誓言几乎才刚立下，便已支离破碎、荡然无存！

===Original===
After a long, earnest talk, in which much of the past was revealed on both sides, Dennis drew a small Testament from is pocket and said: “Mr. Bruder, I wish to direct your thoughts to a better Friend than I am or can be. Will you let me read you something about Him?”

“Yes, and dank you. But choose someding strong﻿—suited to me.”

Dennis read something strong﻿—the story of the Demoniac of Gadara, and left him “sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind.”

“Mr. Bruder, permit me as your *friend* to say that I think that is the only safe place for you. Your better self, your true manhood, has been overpowered by the demon of intemperance. I do not undervalue human will and purpose, but I think you need a divine, all-powerful Deliverer.”

“I know you are right,” said Mr. Bruder. “I haf resolved ofer and ofer again, only to do vorse, and sink deeper at der next temptation, till at last I gave up trying. Unless I am sustained by some strength greater dan mine, I haf no hope. I feel dot your human sympathy and kindness vill be a great help to me, and somehow I dake him as an earnest dot Gott vil be kind to me too.”

===Chinese===
经过一番诚挚的长谈，彼此都敞开心扉吐露了许多往事之后，丹尼斯从衣袋里掏出一本袖珍《新约圣经》，说道：“布鲁德先生，我想把您的心思引向一位比我更好、也是我永远无法企及的朋友。您愿意听我给您念一段关于祂的经文吗？”

“愿意，谢谢您。不过请挑一段力道重些的——合我这号人的。”

丹尼斯果真挑了一段力道沉雄的经文来念——正是“加大拉（Gadara）被鬼附的人”的故事，直到念完那人“坐在耶稣脚前，穿着衣服，心里明白过来”。

“布鲁德先生，请允许我以您*朋友*的身份说一句：依我看，那正是您唯一安稳的去处。您身上良善的本性、您真正的男子气概，已经被酗酒无度的恶魔压垮了。我并不轻看人的意志与决心，但我以为，您需要的是一位神圣而全能的拯救者。”

“我知道您说得对，”布鲁德先生说道，“我曾一次又一次地立志戒酒，结果却每况愈下，下一次诱惑一来便陷得更深，到最后我干脆放弃挣扎了。除非有比我自身更强大的力量托住我，否则我绝无半点指望。我觉得您出于人情的同情与善意会给我莫大的助益，而且不知怎的，我把这看作一个凭据，叫我相信上帝也同样会垂怜于我。”

===Original===
“Oh, Mr. Fleet!” he continued, as Dennis rose to go, “how much I owe to you! I vas in hell on earth ven you came. I vould haf been in hell beneath before morning. I proposed, from the proceeds of dot picture, to indulge in von more delirium, and den seek to quench all in der vaters of der lake.”

Dennis shuddered, but said: “And I believe that God purposes that you should have a good life here, and a happy life in heaven. Co-work with Him.”

“If He vill help me, I’ll try,” said the man, humbly. “Good night, and Gott bless you;” and he almost crushed Dennis’s hand.

As the young man turned to Mrs. Bruder, he was much struck by her appearance: she was very pale, and a wonderful light shone from her eyes. She took his hand in both of hers, and looked at him for a moment with an expression he could never forget, and then slowly pointed heavenward without a word.

Dennis hastened away, much overcome by his own feelings. But the silent, deserted streets seemed luminous, such was the joy of his heart.

===Chinese===
“哦，弗利特先生！”丹尼斯起身告辞时，他又接着说道，“我欠您何等深重的情分啊！您来的时候，我正身处人间地狱；若不是您来，天亮之前我早已坠入九幽地狱去了。我原本打定主意，拿卖掉那幅画换来的钱再痛饮一场、最后迷醉一回，随后便投身湖水之中，将这一切彻底了断。”

丹尼斯不禁打了个寒战，随即说道：“而我深信，上帝的旨意是要让您在这尘世过上美善的日子，来日在天国里享永福。请与祂同工吧。”

“只要祂肯扶助我，我一定尽力去试，”那汉子谦卑地说道，“晚安，愿上帝保佑您；”说着，他握着丹尼斯的手用力一捏，几乎都要把那只手攥碎了。

年轻人转向布鲁德太太时，顿时被她的神容深深震住：她的面色惨白如纸，双眸中却闪烁着一种奇异而圣洁的光辉。她用双手捧住丹尼斯的手，定定地凝视了他片刻，那眼神教他终生难忘；接着她一言不发，缓缓抬起手指向天庭。

丹尼斯心潮澎湃，几乎难以自持，匆匆告辞离去。然而在这万籁俱寂、空无一人的街道上，四周仿佛处处流淌着光辉——只因他心中的喜乐原是如此充盈。

## XIV She Speaks to Him / 第十四章 她同他说话了

===Original===
After the plan for the rearrangement of the store had been determined upon, Miss Ludolph began to study its topography. She went regularly through the building, examining closely every part and space, sometimes sketching a few outlines in a little gilt book. Apparently she was seeking by her taste to make the showrooms pictures in themselves, wherein all the parts should blend harmoniously, and create one beautiful effect. Dennis saw what was coming. The carrying-out of the plan he had heard discussed, and he wished with intense longing that he might be her assistant. But she would as soon have thought of sending for Pat Murphy. She intended to select one of the older clerks to aid her. Still Dennis hoped that by some strange and happy turn of fortune part of this work might fall to him.

Every spare moment of early morning and evening he spent in sketching and studying, but he sadly felt the need of instruction, and of money to buy materials. He was merely groping his way as best he might; and he felt that Miss Ludolph could teach him so much, if she would only condescend to the task! He was willing to be a very humble learner at first. If in some way he could only make known his readiness to pick up the crumbs of knowledge that she might be willing out of kindness to scatter in his path, he might expect something from ordinary good nature.

But a week or two passed without his receiving so much as a glance from those cold blue eyes that rested so critically on all before them; and on an unlucky day in March all hope of help from her vanished. Under the influence of spring the streets were again becoming muddy, and his duties as bootblack increased daily. He had arranged to perform this menial task in a remote corner of the store, as much out of sight as possible. The duty had become still more disagreeable since the young lady haunted the place, for he feared she would learn to associate him only with the dust-brush and blacking-brush.

Just behind where he usually stood, a good picture had been hung, under Mr. Schwartz’s system, simply because it accurately fitted the space. It was in a wretched light, and could never be seen or appreciated there. Miss Ludolph in her investigations and plannings discovered this at a time most unfortunate for poor Dennis. While polishing away one morning, he suddenly became conscious that she was approaching. It seemed that she was looking directly at him, and was about to speak. His heart thumped like a trip-hammer, his cheeks burned, and a blur came over his eyes, for he was diffident in ladies’ presence. Therefore he stood before her the picture of confusion, with a big boot poised in one hand, and the polishing-brush in the other. With the instincts of a gentleman, however, he made an awkward bow, feeling, though, that under the circumstances his politeness could only appear ridiculous. And he was right. It was evident from the young lady’s face that her keen perception of the ridiculous was thoroughly aroused. But for the sake of her own dignity (she cared not a jot for him), she bit her lip to control her desire to laugh in his face, and said, rather sharply, “Will you stand out of my way?”

===Chinese===
重新布置店面的方案既经敲定，卢多尔夫小姐便开始细细勘察整座店堂的布局。她定时在楼里巡行，把每一处角落与空间都仔细察看一遍，有时还在那本烫金小本子上勾勒几笔轮廓。看得出，她是想凭借自己的品位，将一间间陈列室本身就经营成一幅幅画作，使各处陈设水乳交融，浑然化作一派优美气象。丹尼斯已看出端倪。他也听人议论过这套方案的具体施行，心中不禁热切盼望自己能有幸给她打下手。可她压根儿不会想到他，就像绝不会想到去叫帕特·墨菲来帮忙一样。她原打算从老伙计里挑一个助她一臂之力。即便如此，丹尼斯仍心存一丝希冀，盼着命运若能走一着出人意料的好棋，或许能把这活计分给他一星半点。

每天清早和傍晚的每一个空闲当口，他都用来素描和研习，只是他深感自己太需要名师指点，也太缺钱置办画材了。他不过是在竭尽所能地摸索前行；他觉得，只要卢多尔夫小姐肯屈尊赐教，能教给他的实在太多了！起初，他甘愿做一个最谦卑的学徒。只要能设法让她明白，她若肯发发善心，在路旁随手撒下些许学问的碎屑，他也甘愿一一拾取，那么哪怕单凭寻常人的好心肠，他或许也能盼来几分指教。

然而一两个星期过去，那双带着挑剔神色审视眼前万物的冷峻蓝眸，却连瞥也没朝他瞥上一眼；到了三月里一个倒霉的日子，指望她相助的最后一丝念想也烟消云散了。开春以后，街道又变得泥泞起来，他擦靴子的差事也一天天繁重了。他特意挑了店堂深处一个僻静角落干这桩卑贱的活计，尽量避开旁人的视线。自从这位年轻小姐常在店里走动以来，这差事就越发叫他难堪，因为他生怕在她的印象里，自己往后就只配跟掸子与黑鞋油刷绑在一处了。

就在他平日站立的身后，按施瓦茨先生那套章法，挂着一幅上佳的画作——原因无他，只因画框尺寸恰好严丝合缝地填满那块墙面。那地方光线糟透了，画挂在那儿根本看不清，也无从赏鉴。卢多尔夫小姐四下查勘筹划时，偏偏赶上对可怜的丹尼斯最不凑巧的当口，发现了这幅画。这天上午，他正埋头起劲地擦着靴子，忽然察觉她朝这边走来。看样子，她目光正直直落到他身上，像是要开口说话。丹尼斯的心顿时像重锤般咚咚狂跳，双颊发烫，眼前一片模糊——他本就不擅应对女子，在闺秀面前总是局促拘谨。于是，他手足无措地立在她面前，活脱脱成了一副窘迫慌乱的模样：一手托着一只大靴子，一手举着擦鞋刷。即便如此，骨子里那份绅士的本能还是驱使他笨拙地鞠了一躬，尽管他心里明白，在这般光景下行礼，只会显得滑稽可笑。事实果真如此。从这位年轻小姐的神情上分明看得出，她心中对滑稽荒唐之事的敏锐触觉已被彻底挑动起来。不过为了顾全自己的体面（至于他，她压根儿不在乎），她咬住嘴唇，强忍住当面笑出声来的冲动，语声颇为冷峭地问道：“你能站开些吗？”

===Original===
*She had spoken to him.*

He was so mortified and confused that in his effort to obey he partially fell over a bronze sheep, designed to ornament some pastoral scene, and the heel of Mr. Schwartz’s heavy boot came down with a thump that made everything ring. There was a titter from some of the clerks. Mr. Ludolph, who was following his daughter, exclaimed, “What’s the matter, Fleet? You seem rather unsteady, this morning, for a church member.”

For a moment he had the general appearance usually ascribed to the sheep, his unlucky stumbling-block. But by a strong effort he recovered himself. Deigning no reply, he set his teeth, compressed his lips, picked up the boot, and polished away as before, trying to look and feel regardless of all the world. In fact there was as much pride in his face as there had ever been in hers. But, not noticing him, she said to her father: “Here is a specimen. Look where this picture is hung. In ‘bootblack corner’ I should term it. It would not sell here in a thousand years, for what little light there is would be obscured much of the time by somebody’s big boots and the artist in charge. It has evidently been placed here in view of one principle alone﻿—dimensions; its length and breadth according with the space in the corner. You will see what a change I will bring about in a month or two, after my plans are matured;” and then she strolled to another part of the store. But, before leaving, Miss Ludolph happened to glance at Dennis’s face, and was much struck by its expression. Surely Pat Murphy never would or could look like that. For the first time the thought entered her mind that Dennis might be of a different clay and character from Pat. But the next moment his expression of pride and offended dignity, in such close juxtaposition to the big boot he was twirling almost savagely around, again appealed to her sense of the ludicrous, and she turned away with a broad smile. Dennis, looking up, saw the smile and guessed the cause; and when, a moment after, Mr. Schwartz appeared, asking in his loud, blunt way, “My boots ready?” he felt like flinging both at his head, and leaving the store forever. Handing them to him without a word, he hastened upstairs, for he felt that he must be alone.

At first his impulse was strong to rebel﻿—to assert that by birth and education he was a gentleman, and must be treated as such, or he would go elsewhere. But, as the tumult in his mind calmed, the case became as clear to him as a sum in addition. He had voluntarily taken Pat Murphy’s place, and why should he complain at Pat’s treatment? He had pledged his word that there should be no trouble from his being above his business, and he resolved to keep his word till Providence gave him better work to do. He bathed his hot face in cool water, breathed a brief prayer for strength and patience, and went back to his tasks strong and calm.

===Chinese===
*她同他说话了。*

他又是羞惭又是慌乱，急着照办，不料一脚绊在一只原是用来点缀某处田园景致的青铜绵羊上，险些跌倒，手里施瓦茨先生那只沉甸甸的大靴子后跟“咣”地砸在地上，震得四周物件叮当作响。几个店员忍不住嗤嗤窃笑起来。跟在女儿身后的卢多尔夫先生高声喝道：“怎么回事，弗利特？对一个教友来说，你今早脚下倒显得颇不稳当啊。”

有一瞬间，他整个人露出的模样，活脱脱就像那只害他绊倒的倒霉绵羊一般蠢笨。但他使足气力勉强镇定下来。他不屑置辩一词，只是咬紧牙关，抿紧双唇，拾起靴子，照旧使劲擦起来，竭力在神情和心境上都摆出视世间万物如无物的架势。事实上，他此刻脸上的傲气，丝毫不亚于她往日流露过的半分。然而她压根儿没留意他，径自对父亲说道：“您瞧瞧这个例子。看看这幅画挂在什么地方。我倒要管这儿叫‘擦鞋匠角落’。挂在这里一千年也卖不出去，本来就少得可怜的那点光亮，多半时候还要被某人的大靴子和那位专司此角的‘艺术家’给遮住。这画分明只按着一条准则挂到这儿的——尺寸；无非是它的长宽恰好合了这角落的空档罢了。等过上一两个月，我的方案琢磨妥当了，您就瞧着我能改出一番什么气象来吧。”说罢，她便信步踱往店堂别处去了。不过临走前，卢多尔夫小姐无意间瞥了丹尼斯的脸一眼，不禁被他脸上的神情震动了一下。帕特·墨菲断然绝不会、也绝不可能露出那样的神色。她平生头一遭生出个念头：这丹尼斯或许跟帕特并不是同一坯泥土塑成的，品性也自不同。可紧接着，他那副傲然却又尊严受辱的神情，竟与他手里几近发狠般转来转去擦拭的大靴子如此紧挨着凑在一块儿，又一次触动了她的谐谑之心，于是她忍俊不禁，脸上绽出掩不住的笑意转身走开了。丹尼斯抬眼望去，正撞见那抹笑意，也猜透了缘由；过了一会儿，施瓦茨先生走过来，用他那大嗓门直愣愣地问道：“我的靴子擦好了没有？”那一刻，丹尼斯恨不得把两只靴子一并朝他脑袋砸过去，就此永远离开这家店铺。他一言不发地把靴子递过去，便匆匆赶上楼去，因为他觉得自己此刻非得一个人静一静不可。

起初，他心中涌起一股强烈的抗拒冲动——他想站出来宣告，论出身和教养，他本是一位绅士，别人必须以绅士之礼待他，否则他便另谋去处。然而，随着心头的激荡渐渐平息，眼下的处境在他心里变得像一道加法算术般一清二楚。当初是他自己心甘情愿顶替了帕特·墨菲的位置，如今遭受到帕特向来所受的待遇，又有什么好怨尤的呢？他曾立下誓言，绝不因自恃高出本职而惹出半点麻烦；于是他下定决心，在天意赐予他更好的差事之前，定要信守诺言。他用冷水掬洗了发烫的脸颊，默念了一段简短的祷词，祈求赐予力量与忍耐，随后便神色笃定、心平气和地回去继续干活了。

## VI “Starve Then!” / 第六章 “那就饿死吧！”

===Original===
Dennis now followed the natural impulse to go to some distant part of the city, entirely away from the region that had become so hateful to him.

Putting the trunk on the front of a streetcar, he rode on till he was in the heart of the south-side district, the great business centre. He took his trunk into a roomy hardware store, and asked if he might leave it there a while. Receiving a good-natured permission, he next started off in search of a quiet, cheap boarding-place. His heart was heavy, and yet he felt thankful to have escaped as he had, for the thought of what might have been his experience if Barney had tried to fulfil his threat sickened him. The rough was as strong as he, and scenes of violence were his delight and daily experience. He rather gloried in a black eye, for he always gave two in exchange, and his own bruised, swollen member paved the way gracefully for the telling of his exploits, as it awakened inquiry from the lesser lights among whom he shone. But what would Dennis have done among the merchants with “a head on him,” as the barkeeper understood the phrase? He would have had to return home, and that he felt would be worse than death. In fact, he had come nearer to a desperate struggle than he knew, for Barney rarely resisted so inviting an opportunity to indulge his pugilistic turn, and had he not seen the policeman going by just at that time, there would have been no idle threats in the case.

Dennis set his teeth with dogged resolution, determined if necessary, to persevere in his search till he dropped in the street. But as he remembered that he had less than five dollars left, and no prospect of earning another, his heart grew like lead.

He spent several weary hours in the vain search for a boardinghouse. He had little to guide him save short answers from policemen. The places were either too expensive, or so coarse and low that he could not bring himself to endure them. In some cases he detected that they were accompanied by worse evils than gambling. Almost in despair, tired, and very hungry (for severe indeed must be the troubles that will affect the appetite of healthful youth on a cold winter day), he stopped at a small German restaurant and hotel. A round-faced, jolly Teuton served him with a large plate of cheap viands, which he devoured so quickly that the man, when asked for more, stared at him for a moment, and then stolidly obeyed.

===Chinese===
丹尼斯此刻顺从了心底最自然的冲动，打算去城里某个偏远的地段，彻底离开这片已令他深恶痛绝的街区。

他把行李箱搁在有轨电车车头，一路坐到南区腹地——那片繁盛的商业中心。他拎着箱子走进一家宽敞的五金店，问能不能把箱子暂存片刻。店家和颜悦色地应允后，他便动身去寻一处清静便宜的寄宿处。他心里沉甸甸的，却又暗自庆幸能这样脱身，因为一想到倘若巴尼真动手兑现威胁，自己会落得何等下场，他便一阵犯恶心。那粗汉身板跟他一样结实，打架斗殴更是家常便饭、生平一大乐事。被人打青一只眼眶，他反倒引以为荣，因为他总要还对方两拳；自己脸上那块青肿，正好顺理成章地引出他大谈战绩的话头，引得那帮在他光环底下讨生活的小角色纷纷凑上来打听。可要是丹尼斯真像酒保说的那样，“顶着一脑袋青紫”去见各家商号老板，他又该怎么办呢？他只怕得灰溜溜打道回府，而在他看来，那比死还难受。事实上，他离一场拼死恶斗比自己以为的还要近得多，因为巴尼向来难得抗拒这般送上门来施展拳脚的好机会；要不是偏巧那时他瞥见一个警察正从外头走过，方才那番话绝不会只是虚张声势的空头威胁。

丹尼斯咬紧牙关，凭着一股顽强的决绝打定主意：哪怕非要寻到街头力竭倒下，也绝不半途而废。可一想起兜里只剩下不到五美元，又半点看不出下一块钱从哪儿挣来，他的心顿时沉得像灌了铅。

他精疲力竭地奔波了好几个钟头，四处寻觅寄宿旅店，却一无所获。除了路上警察冷冰冰甩来的几句简短指点，他几乎两眼一抹黑。找到的去处不是收费太贵，就是粗鄙肮脏得教他实在忍受不了；有几家他甚至敏锐地察觉，里头还藏着比赌博更乌烟瘴气的勾当。他几乎陷入绝望，又累又饿得发慌（毕竟寒冬腊月里，除非遇上天大的愁苦，否则哪能压得住一个健壮小伙子的胃口），最后在一家德国人开的小餐馆兼旅店前停住了脚步。一个圆脸、快活的德国汉子给他端来一大盘廉价饭菜，他三下五除二便风卷残云般扫了个精光；等他开口添菜时，那汉子愣愣地盯了他片刻，随后才木然地点头照办。

===Original===
“What do you ask for a small room and bed for a night?” said Dennis.

“Zwei shillen,” said the waiter, with a grin; “dot ish, if you don’t vant as pig ped as dinner. Ve haf zwei shillen for bed, and zwei shillen for efery meal﻿—von dollar a day﻿—sheap!”

The place was comparatively clean. A geranium or two bloomed in the window, and lager instead of fiery whiskey seemed the principal beverage vended. Dennis went out and made inquiries, and everyone in the neighborhood spoke of it as a quiet, respectable place, though frequented only by laboring people. “That is nothing against it,” thought Dennis. “I will venture to stay there for a night or two, for I must lose no more time in looking for a situation.”

He took his trunk there, and then spent the rest of the day in unavailing search. He found nothing that gave any promise at all. In the evening he went to a large hotel and looked over the files of papers. He found a few advertisements for clerks and experts of various kinds, but more from those seeking places. But he noted down everything hopeful, and resolved that he would examine the morning papers by daylight for anything new in that line, and be the first on hand. His new quarters, though plain and meagre, were at least clean. Too weary to think or even to feel more than a dull ache in his heart, he slept heavily till the dawn of the following day. Poor fellow! it seemed to him that he had lived years in those two days.

===Chinese===
“请问要一间带床的小屋住一宿，怎么个价钱？”丹尼斯问道。

“两先令，”伙计咧嘴一笑，操着浓重的德国口音说道，“那是说，只要你不指望床铺也像这顿饭一样大。我们这儿睡一宿两先令，吃一顿两先令——一天一美元——便宜吧！”

这地方还算干净。窗台上盛开着一两盆天竺葵，店里卖的主要酒水似乎是淡啤酒，而非烈性威士忌。丹尼斯出门向街坊打听了一圈，附近人人都在夸这儿是个安稳体面的去处，只不过常来光顾的都是些卖力气的做工之人。“那算不得什么毛病，”丹尼斯暗想，“我且先在这儿住上一两宿，眼下分秒必争，耽搁不得找差事的工夫。”

他把行李箱搬进店里，随后把余下的大半天全花在四处奔走求职上，可依然无功而返。他没找着半点像样的门路。傍晚，他走进一家大旅馆，翻阅起报架上的报纸合订本。上面虽有几则招聘店员和各色行家的广告，可求职者的启事却比招工的还多。即便如此，他还是把所有沾点希望的信息一一抄了下来，打定主意天一亮就去翻晨报，看看有没有新登出的类似招工启事，好抢在头一个登门应聘。他这间新住处虽说简陋寒酸，好歹还算洁净。他累得连思索的力气都没有了，只觉心口隐隐作痛，倒头便沉沉睡去，一直睡到次日破晓。可怜的小伙子！短短两天工夫，于他却仿佛熬过了漫长的数年光阴。

===Original===
He was up by daylight, and found a few more advertisements that looked as if they might lead to something. As early as it was possible to see the parties, he was on the ground, but others were there as soon as himself. They had the advantage of some knowledge and experience in the duties required, and this decided the question. Some spoke kindly, and suggested that he was better fitted for teaching than for business.

“But where am I to find a position at this season of the year, when every place is filled?” asked Dennis. “It might be weeks before I could get anything to do, and I must have employment at once.”

They were sorry, hoped he would do well, turned away, and went on doing well for themselves; but the majority merely satisfied themselves that he would not answer their purpose, and bade him a brief, businesslike good morning. And yet the fine young face, so troubled and anxious, haunted a good many of those who summarily dismissed him. But “business is business.”

The day passed in fruitless inquiry. Now and then he seemed on the point of succeeding, but only disappointment resulted. There were at that season of the year few situations offering where a salary sufficient for maintenance was paid, and for these skilled laborers were required. Dennis possessed no training for anyone calling save perhaps that of teacher. He had merely the fragment of a good general education, tending toward one of the learned professions. He had fine abilities, and undoubtedly would in time have stood high as a lawyer. But now that he was suddenly called upon to provide bread for himself and those he loved, there was not a single thing of which he could say, “I understand this, sir, and can give you satisfaction.”

He knew that if he could get a chance at almost anything, he could soon learn enough to make himself more useful than the majority employed, for few had his will and motive to work. But the point was to find someone who would pay sufficient for his own and his mother’s support while he learned.

It is under just such circumstances that so many men, and especially women, make shipwreck. Thrown suddenly upon their own resources, they bring to the great labor-market of the world general intelligence, and also general ignorance. With a smattering of almost everything, they do not know practically how to do *one thing well*. Skilled hands, though backed by neither heart nor brains, push them aside. Take the young men or the young women of any well-to-do town or village, and make them suddenly dependent upon their own efforts, and how many could compete in any one thing with those already engaged in supplying the market? And yet just such helpless young creatures are every day compelled to shift for themselves. If to these unfortunates the paths of honest industry seem hedged and thorny, not so those of sin. They are easy enough at first, if any little difficulty with conscience can be overcome; and the devil, and fallen humanity doing his work, stand ready to push the wavering into them.

===Chinese===
天刚蒙蒙亮他就起了床，又从报上找着几则看似有门道的招工启事。刚到登门拜访最早不算失礼的时辰，他便赶到了现场，可旁人也跟他一样早早候在了那里。那些人占着熟悉业务、有过经验的优势，胜负立时便见了分晓。有几个主顾态度和气，劝他说他看起来更适合去教书，不太适合做买卖。

“可眼下正值隆冬，各处教席早已满员，我上哪儿去谋个教书的职位呢？”丹尼斯问道，“等上几个星期也未必能着落，而我急需立刻就找到活计。”

对方嘴上说着遗憾，祝他好运，转过身便继续各自顾好自己的兴旺营生去了；不过大多数人只是打量明白他不合用，便公事公办地简短道一声“早安”，就此打发了他。话虽如此，那张忧心忡忡、焦灼万分的俊秀年轻面庞，倒也让好些干脆利落回绝他的人心头久久挥之不去。然而，“在商言商”嘛。

这一天又在徒劳的奔走问询中熬了过去。偶尔也有那么一两回看似就要成了，结果却仍是空欢喜一场。眼下这种时节，薪水足以糊口的差事本就寥寥无几，而这些位置全都要招熟手。除了或许勉强能当个教书先生，丹尼斯对别的任何行当都未受过专门训练。他不过受过半吊子良好的通识教育，原本是朝着博学专精的体面职业去的。他天资过人，假以时日，毫无疑问定能成为一名出类拔萃的律师。可如今猛然间要靠双手为自己和挚爱亲人挣出温饱来，世上竟找不出哪怕一件事能让他底气十足地开口说道：“先生，这行我懂，包管让您满意。”

他心里清楚，只要能得个机会——哪怕几乎无论什么行当都行——他很快就能摸熟门道，做得比店里多数老伙计还强，因为很少有人像他这样肯下苦功，又有如此迫切的苦衷非干不可。可难就难在，上哪儿去找这么一位肯在他学徒期间就付足工钱、好让他养活自己和母亲的东家呢。

许许多多的男男女女——尤其是女子——正是落入这般境地，才惨遭人生的灭顶之灾。猝然之间被抛出来自谋生路，他们带进这世上偌大劳力市场的，是一份泛泛的聪慧，却也是一份样样不通的茫然。他们看似什么都略知一二，真动起手来，却连*一桩事*也做不地道。那些手脚熟练的老手，哪怕既无热忱又缺头脑，也能把他们挤到一边。试想从随便哪个殷实乡镇里挑出些青年男女，教他们忽然间全凭自己双手讨生活，又有几个人能在哪一行里敌得过早就在市场上讨饭吃的熟手呢？然而，正是这样一群束手无策的年轻生灵，天天都在被生活逼着独自闯荡。在这些走投无路的可怜人眼中，正经勤勉谋生的道路处处荆棘丛生、四下碰壁；可通往罪恶的歧途却不然。起初走上去顺当得很，只要能把良心上那点小小的不安压下去就行；而魔鬼，以及甘当魔鬼爪牙的堕落世人，早已守在路旁，随时准备把心志动摇的人推下深渊。

===Original===
At the close of the next day, spent in weary search, Dennis met a temptation to which many would have yielded. As a last resort he had been going around among the hotels, willing to take even the situation of porter, if nothing better offered. The day was fast closing, when, worn out and dejected, he entered a first-class house, and made his usual inquiry. The proprietor looked at him for a moment, slapped him on the back, and said: “Yes, you are the man I want, I reckon. Do you drink? No! might have known that from your face. Don’t want a man that drinks for this place. Come along with me, then. Will give you two and a half a day if you suit, and pay you every night. I pay my help promptly; they ain’t near so apt to steal from you then.”

And the man hurried away, followed by Dennis with beating heart and flushed, wondering face. Descending a flight of stairs, they entered a brilliantly lighted basement, which was nothing less than a large, elegantly arranged barroom, with card and lunch-tables, and easy-chairs for the guests to smoke and tipple in at their leisure. All along one side of this room, resplendent with cut glass and polished silver, ran the bar. The light fell warm and mellow on the various kinds of liquor, that were so arranged as to be most tempting to the thirsty souls frequenting the place.

Stepping up to the bulky man behind the bar the landlord said: “There, Mr. Swig, is a young man who will fill capitally the place of the chap we dismissed today for getting tight. You may bet your life from his face that he don’t drink. You can break him in in a few days, and you won’t want a better assistant.”

For a moment a desperate wish passed through Dennis’s mind, “Oh, that wrong were right!” Then, indignant with himself, he spoke up, firmly﻿—“I think I have a word to say in this matter.”

“Well, say on, then; what’s the trouble?”

===Chinese===
又在疲惫不堪的奔波中熬到次日傍晚，丹尼斯撞上了一个换作旁人十有八九都会屈服的诱惑。走投无路之下，他一家家旅馆挨个儿问过去，心想实在没有更好的差事，哪怕去做个搬运杂役也认了。天色飞快暗了下来，他筋疲力尽、垂头丧气地走进一家头等大旅馆，照例开口打听。店主上下打量了他片刻，一巴掌拍在他肩上，说道：“对头，我看你就是我要找的人。喝酒不？不喝！打你脸上就能看出来。我这地方正用不得贪杯的人。那好，跟我来吧。要是干得合用，一天给你两块半，每晚现结。我给伙计发工钱向来爽快；这样他们才不至于轻易手脚不干净。”

老板说完便步履匆匆地往前走，丹尼斯一颗心怦怦直跳，满脸通红又惊疑不定地跟在后头。两人走下一段楼梯，踏进一间灯火辉煌的地下室——那竟是一座宽敞气派、陈设考究的大酒吧，里头摆着牌桌、餐桌和安乐椅，供客人们闲适地吞云吐雾、浅斟慢酌。大厅一整面墙边都设着长长的吧台，雕花玻璃器皿与擦得雪亮的银具流光溢彩。柔和温暖的灯光倾泻在各式美酒上，那番精心的陈列，直把常来光顾的贪杯之徒勾得心痒难耐。

店主走到吧台后面那个身材魁梧的胖汉跟前，说道：“瞧这儿，斯威格先生（Mr. Swig），今天那个喝醉酒被咱们撵走的伙计，让这小伙子来顶替再合适不过。瞧他那张脸，你拿性命担保他都滴酒不沾。你调教他几天，保准再找不出比他更得力的帮手了。”

刹那间，一个绝望的念头闪过丹尼斯心头：“唉，但愿错的能变成对的啊！”紧接着他便暗自羞愤起来，昂然开口，声音坚定地说道：“这事儿，我想我也有句话要说。”

“那你就说吧；有什么难处？”

===Original===
“I cannot do this kind of work.”

“You will find plenty harder.”

“None harder for one believing as I do. I will starve before I will do this work.”

The man stared at him for a moment, and then coolly replied, “Starve then!” and turned on his heel and walked away.

Dennis also rushed from the place, followed by the coarse, jeering laugh of those who witnessed the scene. In his morbid, suffering state their voices seemed those of mocking demons.

===Chinese===
“这种差事我干不了。”

“往后比这苦的活儿多着呢。”

“照我这样的信条，再没有比这更难的活计了。我宁可饿死，也决不干这一行。”

那老板盯着他愣了片刻，随即便冷冷回了一句：“那就饿死吧！”说完掉转脚跟扬长而去。

丹尼斯也转身冲出了那地方，身后追来在场看客粗鄙刺耳的嘲笑声。在他此刻病态而痛苦的心境里，那些声音听上去宛如恶魔在肆意讥笑。

===Original===
The night had now fallen. He was too tired and discouraged to look any further. Wearily he plodded up the street, facing the bitter blast filled with snow that had begun to fall.

This then was the verdict of the world﻿—“Starve!” This was the only prospect it offered﻿—that same brave world which had so smilingly beckoned him on to great achievements and unbounded success but a few days since﻿—“Starve!” Every blast that swept around the corners howled in his ears, “Starve!” Every warmly clad person hurrying unheedingly by seemed to say by his indifference, “Starve! who cares? there is no place for you, nothing for you to do.”

The hard, stern resolution of the past few days, not to yield an inch, to persist in hewing his way through every difficulty, began to flag. His very soul seemed crushed within him. Even upon the threshold of his life, in his strong, joyous youth, the world had become to him what it literally was that night, a cold, wintry, stormy place, with a black, lowering sky and hard, frozen earth.

His father’s old temptation recurred to him with sudden and great power. “Perhaps father was right,” he mused. “God was against him, and is also against me, his son. Does He not visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation? Not but that He will save us at last, if we ask Him, but there seems some great wrong that must be severely punished here. Or else if God does not care much about our present life, thinking only of the hereafter, there must be some blind fate or luck that crushes some and lifts up others.”

Thus Dennis, too sad and morbid to take a just view of anything, plodded on till he reached his boarding-place, and stealing in as if he had no business to be there, or anywhere else, sat down in a dusky corner behind the stove, and was soon lost to surrounding life in his own miserable thoughts.

===Chinese===
夜幕此时已然降临。他实在又累又灰心，再也迈不动步子去别处碰运气了。他迎着夹杂起纷飞雪花的刺骨寒风，步履沉重地沿着长街往回挪去。

原来这就是世道给他的判决——“饿死吧！”就在几天前，这般好世界还曾笑吟吟地向他招手，许诺着宏图大业与无限前程，如今它所给出的唯一出路，竟只有一句——“饿死吧！”每一阵掠过街角的狂风都在他耳边呼啸：“饿死吧！”每一个裹得暖暖和和、匆匆掠过而毫不在意的行人，似乎都在用他的冷漠说着：“饿死吧！谁管你呢？这世上没有你的容身之处，也没有你的活儿可干。”

连日来那股寸步不让、誓要在重重险阻中硬生生劈出一条生路的铁石决心，此刻终于开始萎顿下来。他只觉连灵魂都在体内被碾得粉碎。明明才刚踏上人生的门槛，正值年富力强、朝气蓬勃的青春时节，这世界于他却已变成了此刻眼前这般彻头彻尾的景象——一个凛冽、肃杀、风雪交加的地方，头顶是低垂的黑沉天幕，脚下是坚硬冰冷的冻土。

父亲当年心头盘踞过的诱惑，此刻陡然以排山倒海之势重又袭上他的心头。“兴许父亲是对的，”他黯然暗想，“上帝当年与他作对，如今也同样与我这做儿子的作对。他岂不是将父亲的罪孽追讨到儿子身上，直到三四代吗？倒不是说我们若恳求他，他最终不肯拯救我们，只是人世间似乎存在某种重大的罪过，非得在今生严加惩处不可。要不然，便是上帝本就不大过问我们眼下的光景，只管着来世的事，于是世间只好任凭某种盲目的命运或运气摆布，将一些人碾得粉碎，又将另一些人托举起来。”

丹尼斯就这样满腹悲凉、心神郁结，看什么都再难持平之论，一路蹒跚着走回了他的寄宿店。他悄悄溜进门去，仿佛自己原就不配待在这里，也不配待在这世上任何角落似的，随后在火炉后面一个昏暗的角落里坐了下来，很快便沉溺进自己凄苦万分的思绪之中，对周遭的一切浑然不觉。

## XL Suggestive Pictures and a Prize / 第四十章 寓意画与奖项
===Original===

At last the day of the exhibition dawned. Dennis had sent his picture, directed to Mr. Cornell, with his own name in an envelope nailed to its back. No one was to know who the artists were till after the decision was given. Christine had sent hers also, but no name whatever was in the envelope attached to it.
At an early hour, the doors were thrown open for all who chose to come. The committee of critics had ample time given them for their decision, and at one o’clock this was to be announced.
Although Dennis went rather early, he found that Christine was there before him. She stood with Professor and Mrs. Leonard, Mr. Cornell, and her father, before his picture. He could only see her side face, and she was glancing from the printed explanation in the catalogue to the painting. Mrs. Leonard was also at her side, seeing to it that no point was unnoted. Christine’s manner betrayed intense interest and excitement, and with cause, for again Dennis had spoken to her deepest soul in the language she best loved and understood.
As before, she saw two emblematic pictures within one frame merely separated by a plain band of gold.
The first presented a château of almost palatial proportions, heavy, ornate, but stiff and quite devoid of beauty. It appeared to be the abode of wealth and ancestral greatness.
Everything about the place indicated lavish expenditure. The walks and trees were straight and formal, the flowers that bloomed here and there, large and gaudy. A parrot hung in a gilded cage against a column of the piazza. No wild songsters fluttered in the trees, or were on the wing. Hills shut the place in and gave it a narrow, restricted appearance, and the sky overhead was hard and brazen. On the lawn stood a graceful mountain ash, and beneath it were two figures. The first was that of a man, and evidently the master of the place. His appearance and manner chiefly indicated pride, haughtiness, and also sensuality. He had broken a spray from the ash-tree, and with a condescending air was in the act of handing it to a lady, in the portraiture of whom Dennis had truly displayed great skill. She was very beautiful, and yet there was nothing good or noble in her face. Her proud features showed mingled shame and reluctance to receive the gift in the manner it was bestowed, and yet she was receiving it. The significance of the mountain ash is “Grandeur.”

===Chinese===

展览会的日子终于来临。丹尼斯早已将自己的画作送去，收件人写的是康奈尔先生，画框背面钉着一只信封，里面封着他的名字。在评奖结果揭晓之前，谁也不知道哪幅画出自哪位画家之手。克里斯蒂娜也送去了她的画，只是她那幅画附带的信封里空无一物，连半个名字也没有。

一大早，展厅的大门便向所有前来参观的人敞开。评审委员会获得了充裕的评鉴时间，最终结果定于午后一点公布。

丹尼斯去得已经算早了，却发现克里斯蒂娜到得比他还早。她正同伦纳德教授夫妇、康奈尔先生以及她父亲一起，站在他的画作前面。他只能看见她的侧脸，只见她的目光在手里图录上的文字说明与画布之间来回流连。伦纳德太太也立在她身旁，留神确保她不漏过画中任何一处细节。克里斯蒂娜的神情流露出极大的关切与激动，这也难怪，因为丹尼斯再一次用她最钟爱、也最能心领神会的语言，叩响了她灵魂深处的门扉。

同上一回一样，她在一只画框里看见了彼此呼应的两幅寓意画，中间仅以一道素净的金线隔开。

第一幅画展现了一座几乎堪比宫殿的宏伟宅邸，厚重、华丽，却又板滞生硬，丝毫看不出半分美感。那分明是一处财富与门第显赫的象征之所。

宅邸内外无一处不透着挥霍无度的奢华。园中的小径与林木修剪得笔直规整，零星盛开的花朵硕大却俗艳。一只鹦鹉关在镀金鸟笼里，吊在柱廊的一根石柱旁。树丛间既不见野鸟翩跹，天空中也无飞禽掠影。四周群山将这片宅院紧紧合围，平添了几分局促狭隘之感；头顶的天空更是铁板一块，透着刺目的铜光。草坪上立着一株亭亭玉立的花楸树，树下站着两个人。头一个是位男子，显然便是这片产业的主人。他的一举一动、神态容貌，无不透出傲慢、矜持以及几分声色犬马的俗气。他刚从花楸树上折下一枝花梢，正带着施舍般的居高临下之态，递向身旁的一位女士——在这位女士的刻画上，丹尼斯委实倾注了极为高妙的画技。她容貌绝美，眉眼间却寻不出半点良善或高洁之气。她那张骄傲的脸庞上交织着羞惭与抗拒，显然并不情愿以这种方式接过这份馈赠，可她的手却终究还是伸了出去。而花楸树所象征的寓意，正是“显赫与排场”。

===Original===

The whole scene was the portrayal, in the beautiful language of art, of a worldly, ambitious marriage, where the man seeks mere beauty, and the woman wealth and position, love having no existence.
It possessed an eloquence that Christine could not resist, and she fairly loathed the alliance she knew her father would expect her to make after their arrival in Germany, though once she had looked forward to it with eagerness as the stepping-stone to her highest ambition.
The second picture was a beautiful contrast. Instead of the brazen glare of the first, the air was full of glimmering lights and shades, and the sky of a deep transparent blue. Far up a mountain side, on an overhanging cliff, grew the same graceful ash-tree, but its branches were entwined with vines of the passionflower that hung around in slender streamers. On a jutting rock, with precarious footing, stood a young man reaching up to grasp a branch, his glance bold and hopeful, and his whole manner full of daring and power. He had evidently had a hard climb to reach his present position; his hat was gone; his dress was light and simple and adapted to the severest effort.
But the chief figure in this picture also was that of a young girl who stood near, her right hand clasping his left, and steadying and sustaining him in his perilous footing. The wind was in her golden hair, and swept to one side her light, airy costume. Her pure, noble face was lilted up toward *him*, rather than toward the spray he sought to grasp, and an eager, happy light shone from her eyes. She had evidently climbed *with* him to their present vantage-point, and now her little hand secured and strengthened him as he sought to grasp, for her, success and prosperity joined with unselfish love. The graceful windflowers tossed their delicate blossoms around their feet, and above them an eagle wheeled in its majestic flight.
Below and opposite them on a breezy hillside stood a modern villa, as tasteful in its architecture as the former had been stiff and heavy. A fountain played upon the lawn, and behind it a cascade broke into silver spray and mist. High above this beautiful earthly home, in the clear, pure air rose a palace-like structure in shadowy, golden outline, indicating that after the dwelling-place of time came the grander, the perfect mansion above.

===Chinese===

整幅画面以艺术那优美动人的语言，描绘出了一桩世俗而功利的婚姻：男方所图不过美色，女方所慕无非富贵与地位，唯独不见半点爱情的踪影。

这幅画拥有一种令克里斯蒂娜无法抗拒的雄辩力量。一想到他们抵达德国之后，父亲指望她缔结的那门亲事，她便打心底里生出厌恶之情——尽管从前她曾热切盼望着它，视之为登上平生最高野望的阶梯。

第二幅画则构成了鲜明的对照，美不胜收。画中没有了前一幅里刺眼的铜光燥气，空气中浮动着明暗交错的微光，头顶的天穹呈现出一片澄澈通透的湛蓝。在遥远的山腰上，一处悬崖峭壁凌空探出，上面同样生长着那株优美的花楸树，只是枝桠间缠绕着西番莲的藤蔓，纤细的蔓条凌风垂落。在一块突出崖外的岩石上，站着一个立足颇为险峻的年轻人，正伸长手臂去攀折高处的一枝树梢；他的目光大胆而满怀希冀，浑身上下洋溢着勇毅与力量。显而易见，他经历了一番艰苦攀登才来到眼下这处所在：他的帽子早已不知去向，衣衫轻便素净，正是为了应付最严酷的跋涉。

然而，这幅画中真正的主角，却是站在他身旁的一位年轻姑娘——她正用右手紧紧握住他的左手，在险象环生的立足之地稳稳扶住并支撑着他。山风吹拂着她的金发，将她那一身轻盈飘逸的衣裙吹向一侧。她那张纯洁高贵的脸庞仰望着他，而非他伸手欲折的那枝花梢；一双明眸中闪烁着热切而欢欣的光彩。显然，她是与他一同攀登到这处高险之地的；而此刻，她正用那双纤小的手稳固他、鼓舞他，让他为了她去摘取那份与无私之爱融为一体的成功与荣昌。娇柔的银莲花在他们脚边摇曳着纤细的花朵，而在他们头顶的高空，一只雄鹰正展开双翼，威严地盘旋翱翔。

在他们下方对面的半山坡上，风清景明，矗立着一座现代别墅；它在建筑格调上有多么雅致隽永，前一幅中的城堡就有多么呆板沉重。草坪上喷泉飞溅，屋后一道瀑布跌落成银色的水花与薄雾。而在这座优美人间家园的高处，在清澈纯净的碧空之中，一座宛若宫殿的华美建筑隐约浮现，闪烁着金色轮廓——寓意着尘世时光的居所之后，还有那更为宏伟、臻于至善的天上天国大厦。

===Original===

Christine looked till her eyes were blinded with tears, and then dropped her veil. In the features of the lady in each case she had not failed to trace a faint likeness, sufficient to make it clear to herself. She said in a low, plaintive tone, with quivering lips, “Mr. Fleet painted that picture.”
“Yes,” said Mrs. Leonard, looking at her with no little wonder and perplexity.
By a great effort Christine recovered herself and said, “You know how deeply fine paintings always affect me.”
Dennis of course knew nothing of Christine’s feelings. He could only see that his picture had produced a profound effect on her, and that she had eyes for nothing else. But he overheard Mr. Cornell say, “It is indeed a remarkable painting.”
“Do you know its author?” asked Mr. Ludolph, with a heavy frown.
“No, I do not. It is still a mystery.”
“Will it take the prize, do you think?”
“I am not at liberty to give an opinion as yet,” replied Mr. Cornell, with a smile. “There is another picture here, almost if not quite as fine, though much smaller and simpler;” and he took Mr. Ludolph off to show him that.
Dennis was now recognized by Mrs. Leonard and her husband, who came forward and greeted him cordially, and they started on a tour of the gallery together. Though his heart beat fast, he completely ignored Christine’s presence, and responded coldly to Mr. Ludolph’s slight bow.
Christine, on being aware of his presence, furtively devoured him with her eyes. The refining influences of his life were evident in his face and bearing, and she realized her ideal of what a man ought to be. Eagerly she watched till he should discover her painting where it hung opposite his own, and at last she was amply rewarded for all her toil. He stopped suddenly and stood as if spellbound.
The picture was very simple, and few accessories entered into it. Upon a barren rock of an island stood a woman gazing far out at sea, where in the distance a ship was sailing *away*. Though every part had been worked up with exquisite finish, the whole force and power of the painting lay in the expression of the woman’s face, which was an indescribable mingling of longing and despair. Here also Christine had traced a faint resemblance to herself, though the woman was middle-aged and haggard, with famine in her cheeks.
As Dennis looked and wondered, the thought flashed into his mind, “Could *she* have painted that?”

===Chinese===

克里斯蒂娜凝望着画布，直到泪水模糊了双眼，方才放下脸上的面纱。在两幅画中那位女子的眉宇之间，她都不难辨认出几分与自己相似的轮廓，这已足以令她心下雪亮。她唇瓣微微颤抖，用低沉而哀婉的嗓音说道：“这幅画是弗利特先生画的。”

“正是，”伦纳德太太应了一声，目光里带着几分惊诧与困惑地望着她。

克里斯蒂娜竭力镇定下心神，说道：“您知道的，上乘的画作向来总能深深打动我。”

丹尼斯自然无从知晓克里斯蒂娜此刻的心境。他只看见自己的画作在她身上激起了极深的触动，令她眼中再容不下别物。不过他却无意中听见康奈尔先生赞道：“这确实是一幅了不起的杰作。”

“您知道作者是谁吗？”卢多尔夫先生沉着脸，眉头紧锁地问道。

“不，我不知道。至今仍是个谜。”

“依您看，这幅画能夺得大奖吗？”

“眼下我还不便发表意见，”康奈尔先生微笑着答道，“这里还有另一幅画，即便算不上更胜一筹，也几乎同样精妙，尽管尺幅小得多，构图也更简练些。”说着，他便领着卢多尔夫先生走开，去看那另一幅画。

这时，伦纳德太太和她的丈夫认出了丹尼斯，连忙走上前来热情地同他寒暄，随后三人便结伴在画廊里逛了起来。丹尼斯虽然心跳得飞快，却完全无视了克里斯蒂娜的存在，面对卢多尔夫先生略微欠身的致意，也只是冷淡地应付了一礼。

克里斯蒂娜察觉到他的到来，便暗地里用目光贪婪地注视着他。如今他身上那股经过生活砥砺而越发温润雅致的气度，清晰地显露在他的面容与举止之间，恰恰印证了她心目中男子汉应有的理想风范。她热切地守望着，只盼他能早些发现自己那幅就挂在他画作对面的作品；功夫不负有心人，她多日来的心血终于得到了最丰厚的回报——只见他突然停下脚步，宛如着了魔一般呆立在原地。

这幅画作构图极简，几乎没有多余的陪衬景物。在一座孤岛光秃秃的礁石上，伫立着一位女子，极目远眺着茫茫大海；海天尽头，一艘船正扬帆远去。尽管画中每一处细节都描绘得精致绝伦，但整幅作品最震撼人心的力量，却全凝聚在那女子脸上的神情之中——那是一种难以言喻、将无穷眷恋与彻骨绝望揉碎在一起的复杂神色。在这张面孔上，克里斯蒂娜同样添上了几分与自己隐约相像的神韵，只不过画中人已步入中年，形容枯槁，双颊深陷，写满了饥馑与沧桑。

丹尼斯一边凝神端详、满心惊愕，脑海中一边猛然闪过一个念头：“莫非是她画的？”

He turned suddenly toward her and was convinced that she had done so; for she was looking at him with something of the same expression, or at least he fancied so. She blushed deeply and turned hastily away. He was greatly agitated, but in view of the eyes that were upon him controlled himself and remained outwardly calm.
Mr. Ludolph also was convinced that his daughter had painted the picture, and he frowned more heavily than before. He turned a dark look on her, and found her regarding Dennis in a manner that caused him to grind his teeth with rage. But he could only sit down and watch the course of events.
The people were now thronging in. The gentlemen who made up the prize, with their committee of award, of which Mr. Cornell was chairman, were also present. Most critically they examined each picture till at last their choice narrowed down to the two paintings above described. But it soon became evident that their choice would fall upon the larger one, and Dennis saw that he was to be the victor. At one o’clock Mr. Cornell came forward and said: “Ladies and gentlemen, and especially do I address that group of liberal citizens who are so generously seeking to encourage art in our great and prosperous city, it gives me pleasure to inform you that your munificence has brought forth rich fruit, for here are many paintings that would do credit to any gallery. We hesitated a little time between two very superior pictures, but at last we have decided that the larger one is worthy of the prize. The smaller picture is one of great merit; its treatment is unusually fine, though the subject is not new.
“The two emblematic pictures in some parts show crude and hasty work; indeed some minor parts are quite unfinished. The artist evidently has not had sufficient time. That all may know our verdict to be fair, we state on our honor that we do not know by whom a single painting present was executed. Dr.

他猛地转过身望向她，心里登时确信无疑——这画正是出自她手；因为此时此刻，她正以几乎如出一辙的神情凝望着他，至少在他眼里看来确是如此。她双颊顿时飞起一抹深红，慌忙扭过头去。丹尼斯心潮激荡，但碍于四周众人目光的注视，只得强自按捺，表面上仍维持着一派镇定自若。

卢多尔夫先生同样确信这幅画是女儿画的，他的眉头锁得比方才更紧了。他阴沉地瞪了她一眼，却正撞见她注视着丹尼斯的那般神态，气得他暗暗咬紧了牙关。然而在众目睽睽之下，他也只能寻个位子坐下，静观事态发展。

此时展厅里的来宾已是摩肩接踵。出资设立此次奖项的诸位绅士，以及以康奈尔先生为主席的评奖委员会也都悉数在场。他们极其审慎地逐一审视了每一幅参展画作，最终将目光锁定在上述那两幅作品之上。很快便能看出，评审们的倾向正落向尺幅较大的那一幅，丹尼斯也明白自己胜券在握。然而令他感到意外的是，克里斯蒂娜对评选的结果似乎毫不在意。他哪里知道，当她提笔创作这幅画时，心中根本从未有过争奖的念头。她在那画作对他产生的影响里，早已收获了自己想要的全部报偿。

下午一点整，康奈尔先生走上前台致辞道：“诸位女士、诸位先生，尤其是各位慷慨解囊、热心扶植我们这座繁荣大都市艺术事业的开明市民们，我非常荣幸地向大家宣布，你们的盛情资助已经结出了丰硕的果实，因为今天在座展出的许多画作，足以为任何一座美术馆增光添彩。我们在两幅极为卓越的作品之间曾有过片刻难舍难分的斟酌，但最终一致认定，尺幅较大的那一幅当之无愧地配得上这份大奖。那幅尺幅较小的作品同样功力非凡，其笔法与处理尤为精妙，虽说题材并不算新颖。

“那组两联寓意画在某些局部还显出几分仓促与生涩，诚然，有几处次要的细节甚至尚未完全收工。显见得这位画家的时间并不十分充裕。然而整幅作品的主要构思刻画得极为老道，通篇流露出的魄力与独创性深深打动了我们，因此，正如我方才所言，我们将桂冠授予了这幅作品。为了让在场诸位深信我们的评判公允无私，我们在此以名誉担保，在场任何一幅画作究竟出自哪位画家之手，我们皆一无所知。

Amid breathless expectation, Dr. Arten stepped forward, took down the envelope, and read in a loud, trumpet-like voice﻿—

阿滕医生，作为本次奖项最大的赞助人，委员会特推举您来亲自颁授此奖。在画框背面有一只信封，里面封存着这位我们全体都愿致以敬意的画家的姓名。”

在全场屏息凝神的期待中，阿滕医生迈步上前，取下那只信封，随后用洪亮如号角般的声音高声念道——

“**丹尼斯·弗利特。**”

## XXXIX Susie Winthrop Appears Again / 第三十九章 苏茜·温思罗普再度登场
===Original===

Our story passes rapidly over the scenes and events of the summer and fall of ’71. Another heavy blow fell upon Dennis in the loss of his old friend and instructor, Mr. Bruder.
By prayer and effort, his own and others, he was saved morally and spiritually, but he had been greatly shattered by past excess. He was attacked by typhoid fever, and after a few days’ illness died. Recovery from this disease depends largely upon strength and purity of constitution. But every one of the innumerable glasses of liquor that poor Bruder had swallowed had helped to rob him of these, and so there was no power to resist.
Under her husband’s improved finances, Mrs. Bruder had removed to comfortable lodgings in Harrison Street, and these she determined to keep if possible, dreading for the sake of her children the influences of a crowded tenement house. Dennis stood by her, a stanch and helpful friend; Ernst was earning a good little sum weekly, and by her needle and washtub the patient woman continued the hard battle of life with fair prospects of success.
Dennis’s studio was on the south side, at the top of a tall building overlooking the lake. Even before the early summer sun rose above the shining waves he was at his easel, and so accomplished what is a fair day’s work before many of his profession had left their beds. Though he worked hard and long, he still worked judiciously. Bent upon accomplishing what was almost impossible within the limited time remaining, he determined that, with all his labor, Dr. Arten should never charge him with suicidal tendencies again. Therefore he trained himself mentally and morally for his struggle as the athlete trains himself physically.
He believed in the truth, too little recognized among brain-workers, that men can develop themselves into splendid mental conditions, wherein they can accomplish almost double their ordinary amount of labor.
The year allotted to the competitors for the prize to be given in October was all too short for such a work as he had attempted, and through his own, his mother’s, and Mr. Bruder’s illness, he had lost a third of the time, but in the careful and skilful manner indicated he was trying to make it up. He had a long conversation with shrewd old Dr. Arten, who began to take a decided interest in him. He also read several books on hygiene.

===Chinese===

我们的故事就此迅速掠过1871年夏秋两季的种种景况与事端。丹尼斯又遭逢了一次沉重的打击——他失去了自己的老朋友兼良师布鲁德先生。

凭借他自己以及旁人的祈祷与努力，布鲁德先生在道德与灵性上已然得救，然而过往多年的沉湎放纵早已严重摧垮了他的身子骨。他染上了伤寒热，病倒不过数日便撒手人寰。染上这种疫病能否康复，很大程度上取决于体格是否强健、血气是否清正。可怜的布鲁德生前饮下的那无数杯烈酒，早已一滴一滴将他的元气淘空，教他再无半分抵御病魔的气力。

此前趁着丈夫手头宽裕了些，布鲁德太太已搬到哈里森街一处舒适的寓所里；如今为了几个孩子着想，她生怕搬进拥挤杂乱的廉租大杂院会带坏孩子，于是打定主意无论如何也要保住这处住所。丹尼斯始终守在她身旁，做她忠实得力的帮手；恩斯特每周也能挣上一笔颇为可观的小钱；这位耐劳坚韧的妇人靠着一双巧手操持针线活计、洗衣浆裳，就这样在艰难的人生搏斗中顽强撑了下来，前景也还算过得去。

丹尼斯的画室设在南区一栋俯瞰湖面的高楼顶层。初夏的朝阳尚未跃出波光粼粼的湖面，他便已立在画架前动笔了，往往同行们许多人还未起身离床，他便已做完了寻常一整天的活计。虽然他日夜苦干、工时漫长，干起活来却极有章法分寸。他一心要在所剩无几的有限时间里完成那桩近乎不可能的壮举，却也下定决心，无论怎么拼命劳作，也绝不让阿滕医生再有机会指责他是在自寻短见。于是，他像运动员磨炼体魄那样，在精神与品性上严格操练自己，好迎接这场硬仗。

他深信一条在脑力劳动者当中鲜少受人重视的道理：人是可以把自己调理到一种极佳的精神状态的，置身其中，所能完成的工作量几乎可达寻常时候的两倍。

原定十月颁发的奖项只给了参赛者一年期限，对丹尼斯所尝试的这般鸿篇巨制而言本就捉襟见肘；再加上他自己、母亲以及布鲁德先生先后病倒，他又平白耽搁了三分之一的光阴，只能照着上述审慎得法的方式力图抢回进度。他曾同精明通达的老阿滕医生有过一番长谈，这位老医师也开始对他产生了浓厚的关切。他还研读了好几部关于卫生养生的著作。

===Original===

Thus he worked under the guidance of reason, science, Christian principle, instead of mere impulse, as is too often the case with genius.
In the absorption of his task he withdrew utterly from society, and, with the exception of his mission class, Christian worship on the Sabbath, and attendance on a little prayer-meeting in a neglected quarter during the week, he permitted no other demands upon his time and thoughts.
His pictures had sold for sufficient to provide for his sisters and enable him to live, with close economy, till after the prize was given, and then, if he did not gain it (of which he was not at all sure), his painting would sell for enough to meet future needs.
And so we leave him for a time earnestly at work. He was like a ship that had been driven hither and thither, tempest-tossed and in danger. At last, under a clear sky and in smooth water, it finds its true bearings, and steadily pursues its homeward voyage.
The Christine whom he had first learned to love in happy unconsciousness, while they arranged the store together, became a glorified, artistic ideal. The Christine whom he had learned to know as false and heartless was now to him a strange, fascinating, unwomanly creature, beautiful only as the Sirens were beautiful, that he might wreck himself body and soul before her unpitying eyes. He sought to banish all thought of her.
Christine returned about midsummer. She was compelled to note, as she neared her native city, that of all the objects it contained Dennis Fleet was uppermost in her thoughts. She longed to go to the store and see him once more, even though it should be only at a distance, with not even the shadow of recognition between them. She condemned it all as folly, and worse than vain, but that made no difference to her heart, which would have its way.
Almost trembling with excitement she entered the Art Building the next day, and glanced around with a timidity that was in marked contrast to her usual cold and critical regard. But, as the reader knows, Dennis Fleet was not to be seen. From time to time she went again, but neither he nor Ernst appeared. She feared that for some reason he had gone, and determined to learn the truth. Throwing off the strange timidity and restraint that ever embarrassed her where he was concerned, she said to Mr. Schwartz one day: “I don’t like the way that picture is hung. Where is Mr.

===Chinese===

就这样，他凭着理性、科学以及基督徒的准则指引着自己去作画，而不是像许多天才那样一味任凭一时冲动。

为了全神贯注于手头的画作，他彻底断绝了一切社交往来，除了主持布道班、安息日赴教堂参加基督徒崇拜，以及周间抽空去一处偏僻贫困的街区参加一个小小的祈祷会之外，他不允许任何别的事情来占用自己的时间与心思。

此前卖画所得的钱，已足够接济几个妹妹，也够他省吃俭用地撑到十月评奖之后；而到那时，即便没能夺魁（对于能否得奖，他心里也着实毫无把握），他这幅新画也足以卖出个好价钱，应付日后的开销。

且让我们暂且别过这位埋头苦干的青年。他恰似一艘曾在惊涛骇浪中四处飘摇、险象环生的船只，终于驶入了风平浪静的澄澈水域，在朗晴的天宇下找准了真正的航向，正沉稳地朝着故园的港湾破浪前行。

昔日他们在店里一道整理画作时，他在幸福的不知不觉间爱上的那个克里斯蒂娜，如今在他心中升华成了一个光彩照人的艺术理想；而后来他看清了其虚伪与冷酷的那个克里斯蒂娜，此刻在他眼里却成了一个奇异、迷人却全无妇德的女子——她美丽得只如希腊神话中的塞壬海妖一般，好叫他就在她毫无怜悯的目光注视下，连肉体带灵魂一并撞得粉身碎骨。他极力想将关于她的一切念头统统逐出脑海。

克里斯蒂娜约莫在盛夏时分回到了城里。越是临近故乡这座城市，她越是不得不察觉到：在城中林林总总的一切人和事里，占据她心头最要紧位置的竟是丹尼斯·弗利特。她多么渴望去画店里再见他一面——哪怕只是远远地望上一眼，哪怕彼此之间连一丝相认的影子也没有。她痛斥自己这般念头实在愚蠢，甚至比虚妄更为不堪，可这丝毫左右不了她的心——那颗心偏要一意孤行。

次日，她几乎是激动得浑身微颤地踏进了艺术大厦，怯生生地环顾四周，那副神态与她平日里冷若冰霜、挑剔审视的做派形成了鲜明的反差。然而正如读者所知，丹尼斯·弗利特已不在其间。接连好些日子，她又去过几趟，却既不见他的身影，也未曾见到恩斯特。她心里生出一种恐惧，生怕他因故已经离开，于是下定决心非要弄个水落石出。她抛开一碰到他的事就总是令自己窘迫的那种古怪羞怯与矜持，有一天开口问施瓦茨先生道：“我不喜欢那幅画的挂法。弗利特先生呢？”
