With a courtly smile Mr. Ludolph replied, “And I have lived long enough, my daughter, to know that what people *intend*, and what they *do* are two very different things.”
She flushed angrily and said: “It was most unjust to discharge him as you did. Do you not remember that he offered his mother’s services as nurse when I was dreading the smallpox?”
“You are astonishingly grateful in this case,” said her father, with a meaning that Christine understood too well; “but, if you will read the records of the Ludolph race, you will find that its representatives have often been compelled to do things somewhat arbitrarily. Since you have been gone, I have received letters announcing the death of my brother and his wife. I am now Baron Ludolph!”
But Christine was too angry and too deeply wounded to note this information, which at one time would have elated her beyond measure. She coldly said, “It is a pity that noblemen are compelled to aught but noble deeds;” and, with this parting arrow, she left him.
Even her father winced, and then with a heavy frown said, “It is well that this Yankee youth has vanished; still, the utmost vigilance is required.”
Again he saw the treacherous maid and promised increased reward if she would be watchful, and inform him of every movement of Christine.
In the unobtrusive ways that her sensitive pride permitted, Christine tried to find out what had become of Dennis, but vainly. She offered her maid a large reward if she would discover him, but she had been promised a larger sum not to find him, and so did not.

And the maid learned, as did Mr. Ludolph, that she was not dealing with a child.
During Monday, October 2, Dennis was employed all the long day in giving the finishing touches to his picture. It was not worked up as finely as he could have wished; time did not permit this. But he had brought out his thought vividly, and his drawings were full of power. On the following Saturday the prize would be given.
In the evening he walked out for air and exercise. As he was passing one of the large hotels, he heard his name called. Turning, he saw on the steps, radiant with welcome, his old friend, Susie Winthrop. Her hand was on the arm of a tall gentleman, who seemed to have eyes for her only. But in her old impulsive way she ran down the steps, and gave Dennis a grasp of the hand that did his lonely heart good. Then, leading him to the scholarly-looking gentleman, who was gazing through his glasses in mild surprise, she said: “Professor Leonard, my husband, Mr. Fleet. This is the Dennis Fleet I have told you about so often.”
“Oh‑h,” said the professor, in prolonged accents, while a genial light shone through his gold spectacles. “Mr. Fleet, we are old acquaintances, though we have never met before. If I were a jealous man, you are the only one I should fear.”
“And we mean to make you woefully jealous tonight, for I intend to have Mr. Fleet dine with us and spend the evening. No, I will take no excuse, no denial. This infatuated man will do whatever I bid him, and he is a sort of Greek athlete. If you do not come right along I shall command him to lay violent hands on you and drag you ignominiously in.”
Dennis was only too glad to accept, but merely wished to make a better toilet.
“I have just come from my studio,” he said.
“And you wish to go and divest yourself of all artistic flavor and become commonplace. Do you imagine I will permit it? No! so march in as my captive. Who ever heard of disputing the will of a bride? This man” (pointing up to the tall professor) “never dreams of it.”
Dennis learned that she was on her wedding trip, and saw that she was happily married, and proud of her professor, as he of her.

“今夜我们可正打算教您大吃一坛飞醋呢，因为我要留弗利特先生跟我们一块儿吃晚饭，再陪我们聊上一晚上。不成，什么托辞、推辞我一概不听。我身边这位神魂颠倒的丈夫对我向来言听计从，而且他生得宛如古希腊体育健将一般结实。您要是不乖乖跟我进来，我可就下令叫他动手把您强行拖进去，教您颜面扫地啦。”

“我刚从画室出来呢，”他说道。

“怎么，您还想回去洗掉身上所有的艺术气息，换得平庸无奇不成？您以为我会准许吗？绝不！乖乖当我的俘虏跟进来吧。您什么时候听说过有人敢违拗一位新娘子的圣旨？这位仁兄”（她手指着高个子教授）“可是连想都不敢想呢。”

With feminine tact she drew his story from him, and yet it was but a meagre, partial story, like the play of *Hamlet* with Hamlet left out, for he tried to be wholly silent on his love and disappointment. But in no respect did he deceive Mrs. Leonard. Her husband went away for a little time. In his absence she asked, abruptly, “Have you seen Miss Ludolph lately?”
“No!” said Dennis, with a telltale flush. Seeing her look of sympathy, and knowing her to be such a true friend, the impulsive young man gave his confidence almost before he knew it. She was just the one to inspire trust, and he was very lonely, having had no one to whom he could speak his deeper feelings since his mother died.
“Miss Ludolph wronged me in a way that a man finds it hard to forget or forgive,” he said, in a low, bitter tone; “but I should have tried to do both had she not treated my mother most inhumanly;” and he told his story over again with Hamlet in.
Mrs. Leonard listened with breathless interest, and then said: “She is a strange girl, and that plan of making you her unconscious model is just like her, though it was both cruel and wicked. And yet Mr. Fleet, with shame for my sex I admit it, how many would have flirted with you to the same degree from mere vanity and love of excitement! I have seen Miss Ludolph, and I cannot understand her. We are no longer the friends we once were, but I cannot think her utterly heartless. She is bent upon becoming a great artist at any cost, and I sometimes think she would sacrifice herself as readily as anyone else for this purpose. She looks to me as if she had suffered, and she has lost much of her old haughty, cold manner, save when something calls it out. Even in the drawing-room she was abstracted, as if her thoughts were far away. You are a man of honor, and it is due that you should know the following facts. Indeed I do not think that they are a secret any longer, and at any rate they will soon be known. If Mr. Ludolph were in Germany he would be a noble. It is his intention to go there this fall, and take his wealth and Christine with him, and assert his ancestral titles and position. Christine could not marry in this land without incurring her father’s curse, and I think she has no disposition to do that﻿—her ambition is fully in accord with his.”
“Yes,” said Dennis, bitterly, “and where other women have hearts, she has ambition only.”

“没有！”丹尼斯脱口而出，脸上却瞬间飞起一阵藏不住的红晕。看见她眼中流露出的关切与同情，又深知她是位真正靠得住的挚友，这位性情坦率的年轻人几乎在不知不觉间便向她吐露了心曲。她本就是个极易赢得人信赖的女子，而丹尼斯实在太孤单了——自母亲过世以来，他还没有过任何一个可以倾诉肺腑深情的人。

“卢多尔夫小姐伤我太深，那样对待一个男人，实在让人难以忘怀，也难以宽宥，”他压低声音，带着几分苦涩说道，“可她若不是那样灭绝人性地对待我母亲，我原也想试着两样都做到。”于是，他把那段有“哈姆雷特”在其中的完整故事从头到尾又讲了一遍。

伦纳德太太屏息凝神地听完，随后说道：“她真是个古怪透顶的姑娘，想出把你当作不知情的模特儿那种主意，倒真像是她干得出来的事，尽管那既残忍又恶劣。可话又说回来，弗利特先生，我实在替我们女性感到羞愧——单是出于虚荣和寻求刺激，又有多少姑娘会用同样的方式去玩弄你的感情呢！我见过卢多尔夫小姐了，可我也实在捉摸不透她。我们已不再是从前那样的朋友了，但我还是无法把她看成一个彻底铁石心肠的人。她一心一意不惜一切代价要成为一名大画家，有时候我甚至觉得，为了这个目标，她随时会像牺牲别人一样毫不犹豫地牺牲自己。在我看来，她倒像是受过一番煎熬，身上少了许多从前那种盛气凌人、冷若冰霜的架子，除非遇上什么事把她激出来。哪怕在客厅里坐着，她也常常神思恍惚，仿佛魂魄飘到千里之外去了。你是个正派的君子，下面这些实情理应让你知晓。其实我想这早已算不得什么秘密，无论如何很快就会人尽皆知了。卢多尔夫先生如果在德国，原本就是一位贵族。他打算今年秋天就动身回德国去，把他的家产连同克里斯蒂娜一并带走，去继承恢复他祖上的爵位与门第。克里斯蒂娜若敢在这片土地上嫁人，势必会招致她父亲的诅咒，而依我看，她也绝无违逆父命的意思——她的野心与她父亲可谓完全一拍即合。”

“不错，”丹尼斯苦笑着说，“别的女人长着一颗心的地方，她只长了一副野心。”

===Original===

The professor returned and the subject was dropped.
Dennis said, on taking his leave: “I did not expect to show anyone my picture till it was placed on exhibition with the others, but, if you care to see it, you may tomorrow. Perhaps you can make some suggestions that will help me.”
They eagerly accepted the invitation, and came the following morning. Dennis watched them with much solicitude. When once they understood his thought, their delight and admiration knew no bounds. The professor turned and stared at him as if he were an entirely different person from the unpretending youth who had been introduced on the preceding evening.
“If you do not get the prize,” he said, sententiously, “you have a great deal of artistic talent in Chicago.”
“ ‘A Daniel come to judgment!’ ” cried his wife.

这时教授走了回来，话头就此打住。

临别时丹尼斯说道：“在画作送去与其他作品一同公开展出之前，我本没打算先让任何人看，不过二位若是有兴致瞧一瞧，明天不妨过来。兴许你们还能给我出出主意，指点一二。”

夫妻俩欣然应邀，次日一早便登了门。丹尼斯满怀忐忑与殷切地注视着他俩。待二人一旦领悟了他画中的立意，那份喜悦与赞叹简直无以复加。教授转过头来直勾勾地打量着他，仿佛站在面前的根本不是昨晚那个初次引见的谦逊小伙子，而是另一个截然不同的人物。

“倘若你拿不到这个奖，”他言辞笃定地评判道，“那芝加哥可真是卧虎藏龙、艺术天才多得不得了了。”

“‘又一个但以理来断案了！’”他的妻子欢呼道。

## XLVII Susie Winthrop / 第四十七章 苏茜·温思罗普
===Original===

Waiting with multitudes of others, Christine and Dennis at last received an army biscuit (hardtack in the soldier’s vernacular) and a tin-cup of what resembled coffee. To him it was very touching to see how eagerly she received this coarse fare, proving that she was indeed almost famished. Too weak to stand, they sat down near the door on the sidewalk. A kind lady presently came and said, “If you have no place to go you will find it more comfortable in the church.”
They gladly availed themselves of her permission, as the thronged street was anything but pleasant.
“Mr. Fleet,” said Christine, “I am now going to take care of you in return for your care last night,” and she led him up to a secluded part of the church by the organ, arranged some cushions on a seat, and then continued: “As I have obeyed you, so you must now be equally docile. Don’t you dare move from that place till I call you;” and she left him.
He was indeed wearied beyond expression, and most grateful for a chance to rest. This refuge and the way it was secured seemed almost a heavenly experience, and he thought with deepest longing, “If we could always take care of each other, I should be perhaps too well satisfied with this earthly life.”
When after a little time Christine returned he was sleeping as heavily as he had done before upon the beach, but the smile his last thought occasioned still rested on his face.
For some little time she also sat near and rested, and her eyes sought his face as if a story were written there that she never could finish. Then she went to make inquiries after her father. But no one to whom she spoke knew anything about him.
Bread and other provisions were constantly arriving, but not fast enough to meet the needs of famishing thousands. Though not feeling very strong she offered her services, and was soon busily engaged. All present were strangers to her, but, when they learned from the inquiries for her father that she was Miss Ludolph, she was treated with deference and sympathy. But she assumed nothing, and as her strength permitted, during the day, she was ready for any task, even the humblest. She handed food around among the hungry, eager applicants, with such a sweet and pitying face that she heard many a murmured blessing. Her efforts were all the more appreciated as all saw that she too had passed through the fire and had suffered deeply.

===Chinese===

克里斯蒂娜和丹尼斯随着大批难民一道排队等候，终于领到了一块军用硬饼干（士兵口中的“压缩干粮”）和一铁皮杯勉强算是咖啡的饮品。看到她如此急切地接过这般粗糙的食物，丹尼斯心中深受触动——这足以证明她确实已经饿到了极点。两人虚弱得几乎站立不住，便在门旁的人行道上坐了下来。不多时，一位善良的女士走过来说道：“若是你们没有落脚之处，进教堂里去待着会舒坦些。”

大街上人潮汹涌、嘈杂不堪，绝非久留之地，他们便欣然接受了她的好意。

“弗利特先生，”克里斯蒂娜说，“昨晚承蒙您悉心照料，眼下该换我来照顾您了。”说着，她领着他走到教堂风琴旁一处僻静的角落，在长椅上垫好几只软垫，接着又吩咐道，“从前我如何听您的话，如今您也得同样乖乖听话。没有我的传唤，您可千万别擅自离开这地方。”说完她便走了开去。

他确实已疲惫到了无以复加的地步，能有这样一个歇脚之处，着实感激不尽。这处避难所，以及这番照拂的来历，简直如天国般的恩赐；他满怀深切的眷恋暗自想道：“若是我们能永远这样彼此照料下去，只怕我会太过贪恋这尘世的生活了。”

过了一会儿克里斯蒂娜回来时，他已沉沉睡去，熟睡的模样竟与先前在湖滩上时别无二致，只是方才那抹念头牵起的一丝微笑，依旧安详地停留在他脸上。

她也在一旁坐下来歇了片刻，目光久久流连在他的脸庞上，仿佛那上面写着一部她永远也读不完的故事。随后她起身去打听父亲的下落。可她问遍了身边的人，竟没有一个知道卢多尔夫先生的消息。

面包和其他救济口粮正源源不断地运来，却仍远远赶不上成千上万饥民的需求。克里斯蒂娜虽然自觉体力还很虚弱，还是主动上前搭把手，很快便忙碌起来。在场众人与她素不相识，但一听她打听父亲时说起的名字，便知她是卢多尔夫小姐，顿时对她敬重有加、关怀备至。然而她却丝毫没有摆架子，白天只要体力尚可，无论多卑微的杂活她都肯干。她端着食物分发给那些饥肠辘辘、急切盼食的难民，脸上带着那般温柔悲悯的神情，耳畔不时听见人们低声为她献上的祝福。大家见她自己也明显经历过这场劫火、吃尽了苦头，对她的这份善举便愈发感激不尽。

===Original===

At last a kind, motherly lady said: “My dear, you look ready to drop. Here, take this,” and she poured out a glass of wine and gave her a sandwich; “now, go and find some quiet nook and rest. It’s your duty.”
“I have a friend who has suffered almost everything in saving me. He is asleep now, but he has had scarcely anything to eat for nearly three days, and I know he will be very hungry when he wakes.”
“Nothing to eat for three days! Why, you must take him a whole loaf, and this, and this,” cried the good lady, about to provision Dennis for a month.
“Oh, no,” said Christine, with a smile, “so much would not be good for him. If you will give me three or four sandwiches, and let me come for some coffee when he wakes, it will be sufficient;” and she carried what now seemed treasures to where Dennis was sleeping, and sat down with a happy look in her face.
The day had been full of sweet, trustful thoughts. She was conscious of a presence within her heart and all around that she knew was Divine, and in spite of her anxiety about her father and the uncertainty of the future, she had a rest and contentment of mind that she had never experienced before. Then she felt such a genuine sympathy for the sufferers about her, and found them so grateful when she spoke to them gently and kindly, that she wondered she had never before discovered the joy of ministering to others. She was entering a new world, and, though there might be suffering in it, the antidote was ever near, and the pleasures promised to grow richer, fuller, more satisfying, till they developed into the perfect happiness of heaven. But every Christian joy that was like a sweet surprise﻿—every thrilling hope that pointed to endless progress in all that is best and noblest in life, instead of the sudden blank and nothingness that threatened but yesterday﻿—and, above all, the animating consciousness of the Divine love which kept her murmuring, “My Saviour, my good, kind Heavenly Father,” all reminded her of him who had been instrumental in bringing about the wondrous change. Often during the day she would go and look at him, and could Dennis only have opened his eyes at such a moment, and caught her expression, no words would have been needed to assure him of his happiness.

终于，一位慈祥得像母亲般的女士走过来说道：“亲爱的，瞧你累得快撑不住了。来，吃点这个吧。”她倒了一杯葡萄酒，又递给她一只三明治，“快去找个清静角落歇着去，这是你眼下最该尽的本分。”

“我有一位朋友，为了救我差点受尽了折磨。他此刻正睡着呢，可他已经将近三天几乎粒米未进了，我想他醒来一定饿坏了。”

“三天没吃东西！哎呀，那你得给他拿一整条面包去，还有这个，还有这个，”好心的女士惊呼着，简直要把够丹尼斯吃上一个月的口粮都塞给她。

“哦，不用，谢谢您，”克里斯蒂娜微笑着婉拒，“吃太多反而对他肠胃不好。劳驾您给我三四只三明治，等他醒来再容我过来讨些热咖啡，那就足够了。”说罢，她捧着这些此刻堪比珍宝的食物，回到丹尼斯沉睡的地方，满脸幸福地坐了下来。

这一整天，她心中都充盈着甘甜而笃信的思绪。她真切地感受到自己心底以及周遭万物之间，洋溢着一股神圣的同在；尽管依旧牵挂父亲的安危，也面对着未卜的前程，她的心境却获得了一种平生从未体味过的安宁与满足。不仅如此，她对身旁受难的同胞怀着如此真挚的怜悯，每当她温和慈爱地同他们说话时，又看到他们那般感恩戴德，竟令她暗自惊诧，自己从前为何从未发觉过服侍他人的快乐。她正步入一个全新的世界——诚然，这世界里依旧会有苦难，可解药总近在咫尺，而其中的喜乐则应许着将会愈发丰沛、饱满、令人心满意足，直到最终化作天国那至善至美的永福。然而，每当那份如同甜蜜惊喜般的基督徒喜乐涌上心头，每当那振奋人心的盼望在她眼前铺开一条通往生命中至善至美之境的无尽坦途——不再是昨日还悬在头顶的骤然虚空与寂灭——尤其是那股令她不断低声呢喃着“我的救主，我良善慈爱的天父啊”的圣爱感召，无一不令她想起那个促成她脱胎换骨的人。这一天里，她时常走过去静静端详他；倘若丹尼斯能在那样的一刻恰好睁开双眼，捕捉到她脸上的神情，便再无需任何言语来向他印证自己的幸福了。

===Original===

The low afternoon sun shone in gold and crimson on his brow and face through the stained windows before he gave signs of waking, and then she hurried away to get the coffee hot from the urn.
She had hardly gone before he arose greatly refreshed and strengthened, but so famished that a roast ox would have seemed but a comfortable meal. His eye at once caught the sandwiches placed temptingly near.
“That is Miss Ludolph’s work,” he said; “I wonder if she has saved any for herself.” He was about to go and seek her when she met him with the coffee.
“Go back,” she said; “how dare you disobey orders?”
“I was coming to find you.”
“Well, that is the best excuse you could have made, but I am here; so sit down and drink this coffee and devour these sandwiches.”
“Not unless you share them with me.”
“Insubordinate! See here,” and she took out her more dainty provision from behind a seat and sat down opposite, in such a pretty, companionable way that he in his admiration and pleasure forgot his sandwiches.
“What is the matter?” she asked. “You are to eat the sandwiches, not me.”
“A very proper hint, Miss Ludolph; one might well be inclined to make the mistake.”
“Now that is a compliment worthy of the king of the Cannibal Islands.”
“Miss Ludolph,” said Dennis, looking at her earnestly, “you do indeed seem happy.”
A ray of light slanting through a yellow diamond of glass fell with a sudden glory upon her face, and in a tone of almost ecstasy she said: “Oh, I am so glad and grateful, when I realize what might have been, and what is! It seems that I have lost so little in this fire in comparison with what I have gained. And but for you I might have lost everything. How rich this first day of life, real, true life, has been! My Heavenly Father has been so kind to me that I cannot express it. And then to think how I have wronged Him all these years!”
“You have indeed learned the secret of true eternal happiness, Miss Ludolph.”
“I believe it﻿—I feel sure of it. All trouble, all pain will one day pass away forever; and sometimes I feel as if I must sing for joy. I do so long to see my father and tell him. I fear he won’t believe it at first, but I can pray as you did, and it seems as if my Saviour would not deny me anything. And now, Mr.

“我相信——我对此深信不疑。一切烦恼、一切痛苦终有一天都会永远消逝；有时候我觉得自己简直要欢呼歌唱起来。我多么盼望能见着父亲，把这一切告诉他。只怕起初他不会相信，但我可以像您那样祈祷，我觉得我的救主不会拒绝我的任何祈求。现在呢，

===Original===

Fleet, when you have finished your lunch, I am going to ask one more favor, and then will dub you truest knight that ever served defenceless woman. You will find my father for me, for I believe you can do anything.”
Even in the shadow where he sat she caught the pained expression of his face.
She started up and grasped his arm.
“You know something,” she said; then added: “Do not be afraid to find my father now. When he knows what services you have rendered me, all estrangement, if any existed, will pass away.”
But he averted his face, and she saw tears gathering in his eyes.
“Mr. Fleet,” she gasped, “do you know anything I do not?”
He could hide the truth no longer. Indeed it was time she should learn it. Turning and taking her trembling hand, he looked at her so sadly and kindly that she at once knew her father was dead.
“Oh, my father!” she cried, in a tone of anguish that he could never forget, “you will never, never know. All day I have been longing to prove to you the truth of Christianity by my loving, patient tenderness, but you have died, and will never know,” she moaned, shudderingly.
He still held her hand﻿—indeed she clung to his as to something that might help sustain her in the dark, bitter hour.
“Poor, poor father!” she cried; “I never treated him as I ought, and now he will never know the wealth of love I was hoping to lavish on him.” Then, looking at Dennis almost reproachfully, she said: “Could you not save him? You saved so many others.”
“Indeed I could not, Miss Ludolph; I tried, and nearly lost my life in the effort. The great hotel behind the store fell and crushed all in a moment.”
She shuddered, but at last whispered, “Why have you kept this so long from me?”
“How could I tell you when the blow would have been death? Even now you can scarcely bear it.”
“My little beginning of faith is sorely tried. Heavenly Spirit,” she cried, “guide me through this darkness, and let not doubt and unbelief cloud my mind again.”
“Such prayer will be answered,” said Dennis, in a deep, low tone.
They sat in the twilight in silence. He still held her hand, and she was sobbing more gently and quietly. Suddenly she asked, “Is it wrong thus to grieve over the breaking of an earthly tie?”
“No, not if you will say as did your Lord in His agony, ‘Oh, my Father, Thy will be done.’ ”
“I will try,” she said, softly, “but it is hard.”

可他却偏过脸去，她分明看见泪水正盈满他的眼眶。

“弗利特先生，”她倒抽一口冷气，喘着气问道，“您是不是知道了什么我还不知道的事？”

他再也瞒不下去了。事实上，也确是该让她知道真相的时候了。他转过身来，握住她那双微微发颤的手，用极其悲悯而温存的目光望着她——她瞬间便明白了，她的父亲已经不在人世了。

“啊，我的父亲！”她发出一声他毕生难忘的凄厉痛呼，“您再也、再也无从知晓了。整整一天，我都在盼着能用我满腔的爱意与耐心的温柔，向您印证基督信仰的真实，可您却已经走了，再也不会知道了。”她浑身战栗着哀恸呻吟。

他依然紧握着她的手——其实此刻她紧紧攥着他的手，仿佛那是能在这黑暗苦涩的时辰里撑住自己的唯一依托。

“可怜的、可怜的父亲！”她哭喊道，“我从前从未尽过做女儿的本分，如今他再也无从知晓我原指望倾注在他身上的那份深爱了。”接着，她近乎带着几分责备地望向丹尼斯，说道：“难道您就没能救出他来吗？您明明救了那么多旁人。”

“我实在无能为力，卢多尔夫小姐；我尽力了，为此几乎连自己的性命也搭了进去。画店背后那座大旅馆轰然倒塌，转瞬之间便将一切压了个粉碎。”

她浑身一颤，过了好半晌才低声问道：“您为什么瞒了我这么久才说？”

“当时那记打击足以要了您的命，我又怎能对您说出口？哪怕到了此刻，您也几乎承受不住。”

“我这一点点初萌的信心正经受着何等严酷的试炼啊。天上的圣灵啊，”她仰天呼求，“请引领我穿过这片黑暗，切莫让怀疑与不信再度蒙蔽我的心智。”

“这样的祈祷必蒙应允。”丹尼斯低沉而笃定地说道。

暮色之中，两人静默无言地坐着。他依旧握着她的手，她的啜泣渐渐轻缓下来，趋于平静。突然，她问道：“为尘世亲情纽带的断裂而如此悲痛，难道是有罪吗？”

“不，只要您也能像您的主在极度痛苦中所说的那样祈祷：‘我父啊，愿你的旨意成全。’”

“我会尽力去做的，”她轻声说，“可这实在太难了。”

===Original===

“He is a merciful and faithful High Priest. For in that He Himself hath suffered, being tempted, He is able to succor them that are tempted.”
“Do you know that I think my change in feeling makes me grieve all the more deeply? Until today I never loved my father as I ought. It is the curse of unbelief to deaden everything good in the heart. Oh, I do feel such a great, unspeakable pity for him!”
“Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear Him.”
“Is that in the Bible?” she asked.
“Yes.”
“It is very sweet. He indeed must be my refuge now, for I am alone in the world.”
“He has said, ‘I will never leave thee nor forsake thee.’ I have passed through this sorrow so recently myself that I can sympathize with you as a fellow-sufferer.”
“True, true, you have,” she answered. “Is that the reason that Christ suffered with us﻿—that we might know He sympathized with us?”
“Yes.”
“How unspeakably comforting is such sympathy, both human and divine! Tell me about your mother.”
“I fear I cannot without being unmanned. She was one of Heaven’s favorites, and I owe everything to her. I can tell you one thing, though, she prayed for you continually﻿—even with her dying lips, when my faith had broken down.”
This touched Christine very deeply. At last she said, “I shall see her some day.”
“I wish you had seen her,” he continued very sadly, looking as if at a scene far away.
“You cannot wish it more than I. Indeed I would have called on her, had it not been for an unfortunate accident.”
He looked at her with some surprise, as if not understanding her remark, but said, “She greatly wished to see you before she died.”
“Oh, I wish I had known it!”
“Did you not know it?” he asked, in a startled manner.
“No, but I felt grateful to her, for I understood that she offered to take care of me in case I had the smallpox. I wanted to visit her very much, and at last thought I would venture to do so, but just then I sprained my ankle. I sent my maid to inquire, but fear she didn’t do my errand very well,” added Christine, looking down.
“She never came, Miss Ludolph.” Then he continued, eagerly: “I fear I have done you a great wrong. A little time before my mother died, she wrote you a line saying that she was dying and would like to see you. I did not know you could not come﻿—I thought you would not.”

“无论来自人间还是天上，这般的体恤同情该是多么难以言喻的慰藉啊！同我讲讲您的母亲吧。”

“只怕我一讲起来便要失态落泪。她是蒙上天格外宠爱的人，我所有的一切皆归功于她。不过有一件事我可以告诉您：她一直在为您祈祷——哪怕到了弥留之际、连我的信心都已崩溃的时候，她仍用临终的嘴唇为您祷告。”

这番话深深打动了克里斯蒂娜。良久，她轻声说道：“总有一天，我会见到她的。”

“我真盼望您生前能见过她一面，”他神情无比哀伤地接着说道，目光仿佛投向了遥远的过往。

“您的盼望绝不会比我更切。若不是碰上一桩不幸的意外，我原是一定会去登门拜望她的。”

他略带诧异地望着她，似乎不太明白她这话的意思，但仍说道：“她在临终前曾非常想见您一面。”

“哦，我要是早知道就好了！”

“难道您不知道吗？”他神色惊愕地追问。

“不知道，但我心里一直很感激她，因为我听说在我害怕染上天花的时候，她曾提出要来照料我。我当时非常想去探望她，最后终于鼓起勇气打算去了，可偏偏就在那时扭伤了脚踝。我曾打发女仆去打听您的消息，只怕她没替我把差事办妥。”克里斯蒂娜垂下眼帘补充道。

“她从来没有来过，卢多尔夫小姐。”随后他急切地接着说道，“只怕我是大大冤枉您了。我母亲临终前不久，曾给您写过一张字条，说她已病入膏肓，很想见您一面。我不知道您是来不了——我还以为您是不肯来呢。”

Crimson with shame and humiliation, Christine buried her burning cheeks in her hands and murmured, “I never received it.”
“And did you send the exquisite flowers and fruit?” he asked. “Ah, I see that you did. I am so glad﻿—so very glad that I was mistaken! I sincerely ask your pardon for my unjust thoughts.”
“It is I who should ask pardon, and for a long time I have earnestly wished that I might find opportunity to do so. My conduct has been simply monstrous, but of late it has seemed worse than the reality. Everything has been against me. If you only knew﻿—but﻿—” (and her head bowed lower). Then she added, hastily, “My maid has been false, and I must have appeared more heartless than ever.” But, with biter shame and sorrow, she remembered who must have been the inspirer of the treachery, and, though she never spoke of it again, she feared that Dennis suspected it also. It was one of those painful things that must be buried, even as the grave closes over the frail, perishing body.
Let those who are tempted to a wicked, dishonorable deed remember that, even after they are gone, the knowledge of it may come to those who loved them, like an incurable wound.
Dennis’s resolution not to speak till Christine should be no longer dependent on him was fast melting away, as he learned that she had not been so callous and forgetful as she had seemed. But before he could add another word, a wild, sweet, mournful voice was heard singing:

> “O fiery storm, wilt never cease?

Thy burning hail falls on my heart;

Bury me deep, that I in peace

May rest where death no more can part.”

In awed, startled tones they both exclaimed, “**Susie Winthrop!**”

羞惭与屈辱瞬间染红了克里斯蒂娜的脸颊，她把发烫的脸埋进双手里，低声呢喃道：“我从来没有收到过那张字条。”

“那么那些精致的鲜花和水果，也是您派人送来的吗？”他问，“啊，我看得出确实是您送的。我太高兴了——太庆幸自己当时看错了您！我诚挚地请求您宽恕我从前对您怀有的不公想法。”

“该请求宽恕的是我才对，好长一段时间以来，我都热切盼望着能寻到这样一个开口赔罪的机会。我从前的所作所为简直荒唐透顶，可近来我在您眼里竟显得比实际还要不堪。仿佛一切都同我作对似的。倘若您知道——可是——”（她的头垂得更低了）。接着她急急补充道，“我的女仆背叛了我，想来我在您眼里一定更显得铁石心肠了。”然而，怀着一阵痛彻心扉的羞愧与悲哀，她心里明镜似的，清楚这桩背信弃义的勾当背后究竟是谁在指使；尽管她此后绝口不再提起此事，却生怕丹尼斯心里也已猜到了几分。那是世间最令人痛心的隐秘之一，只宜深深掩埋，正如坟墓将那脆弱易朽的躯壳掩盖一般。

凡是受了诱惑、想要做出卑劣不义之举的人都应当引以为戒：即便在他们撒手人寰之后，知晓真相的那一刻仍可能降临到爱他们的人头上，宛如一道永难愈合的创伤。

丹尼斯原本暗下决心，在克里斯蒂娜不再仰仗自己照拂之前绝不吐露心声，可此刻得知她并非表面看来那般冷酷薄情、忘恩负义，他那道防线顿时迅速土崩瓦解了。然而他还没来得及再开口说出一个字，忽然听见一个野性、甜美而又凄婉的声音唱了起来：

> “啊，烈焰的风暴，你何时方肯休止？

你灼热的冰雹正砸落我的心头；

将我深埋吧，好教我在安宁之中，

长眠于死亡再也不能分离的尽头。”

两人又惊又敬，失声齐呼：“**苏茜·温思罗普！**”

## XXXVIII The Gates Open / 第三十八章 天门洞开
===Original===

At Dennis’s request, Dr. Arten called and carefully inquired into Mrs. Fleet’s symptoms. Her son stood anxiously by awaiting the result of the examination. At last the physician said, cheerily: “There is no immediate occasion for alarm here. I am sorry to say that your mother’s lungs are far from strong, but they may carry her through many comfortable years yet. I will prescribe tonics, and you may hope for the best. But mark this well, she must avoid exposure. A severe cold might be most serious in its consequences.”
How easy to say, “Do not take cold!” How many whose lives were at stake have sought to obey the warning, but all in vain! Under Dr. Arten’s tonics, Mrs. Fleet grew stronger, and Dennis rejoiced over the improvement. But, in one of the sudden changes attendant on the breaking up of winter, the dreaded cold was taken, and it soon developed into acute pneumonia.
For a few days she was very ill, and Dennis never left her side. In the intervals of pain and fever she would smile at him and whisper: “The harbor is near. This rough weather cannot last much longer.”
“Mother, do not leave us; we cannot spare you,” ever pleaded her son.
Contrary to her expectations, however, she rallied, but continued in a very feeble state. Dennis was able to resume his duties in the store, and he hoped and tried to believe that the warm spring and summer days soon to come would renew his mother’s strength. But every day she grew feebler, and Dr. Arten shook his head.
The Bruders were very kind, and it was astonishing how much Mrs. Bruder, though burdened with her large family, found time to do. If Mrs. Fleet had been her own mother she could not have bestowed upon her more loving solicitude. Mr. Bruder was devotion itself. He removed his easel to an attic-room in Mrs. Fleet’s house; and every hour of Dennis’s absence heard him say: “Vat I do for you now? I feel no goot unless I do someding.”
Some little time after Mrs. Fleet was taken sick a mystery arose. The most exquisite flowers and fruits were left at the house from time to time, marked in a bold, manly hand, “For Mrs. Fleet.” But all efforts to discover their source failed.
The reader will guess that Christine was the donor, and Dennis hoped it﻿—though, he admitted to himself, with little reason.
Mrs. Fleet had not much pain.

===Chinese===

应丹尼斯的请求，阿滕医生前来登门诊视，仔细询问了弗利特太太的症状。儿子焦灼地站在一旁，等待着检查的结果。终于，老医生神色轻松愉快地开口道：“眼下倒不必立刻惊慌。虽说令堂的肺部确实相当虚弱，教人惋惜，但照样兴许还能撑着她舒舒坦坦再过上好些年头呢。我开几服滋补调理的药方，你们大可往好处盼着。不过千万记牢一点：她切不可受寒着凉。一旦染上重伤风，后果只怕极为严重。”

嘴上说一句“切不可着凉”何其容易！古往今来多少性命攸关的病人竭力谨遵医嘱，到头来却仍是一场空！服了阿滕医生开的补药，弗利特太太的精神果真健旺了些，丹尼斯见了满心欢喜。然而就在冬春交替、气候骤变的一场寒流里，那最令人提心吊胆的伤风还是找上了门来，并且很快转成了急性肺炎。

有好几天，她病势沉重无比，丹尼斯寸步不离地守在榻前。在病痛与高热稍歇的间隙，她会对他微微一笑，气若游丝地低语道：“港湾近在眼前了。这阵风浪不会再刮太久了。”

“母亲，千万别丢下我们；我们离不得您啊。”儿子总是一遍又一遍地苦苦哀求。

然而出乎她自己的意料，她竟勉强缓过了一口气，只是身子依旧虚弱不堪。丹尼斯得以重返画店操持差事，心中满怀希望，也极力说服自己：眼看温暖的春夏季节就要来了，母亲的元气定能渐渐恢复。可事实上，她一天比一天衰弱下去，连阿滕医生也不住地摇头。

布鲁德一家极是厚道热心，尤以布鲁德太太最教人惊叹——她自己拖着一大家子人，忙得不可开交，竟还能挤出那么多工夫来帮忙。纵使是伺候亲生母亲，她对弗利特太太也断然倾注不出更深挚体贴的关怀了。布鲁德先生更是忠心耿耿、无微不至。他索性把画架搬进了弗利特太太家的阁楼小屋；每逢丹尼斯外出，他隔一个钟头便要问上一句：“这会儿我替你干点啥呀？我不干点啥活儿，心里头就浑身不自在。”

弗利特太太病倒后不久，家里添了一桩奇事。每隔一段日子，总有人往屋里送来最精美的鲜花与鲜果，上头用刚劲豪迈的男子笔迹写着：“敬呈弗利特太太”。可不管怎么打听追查，始终查不出究竟是谁送来的。

读者诸君想必能猜到送花人正是克里斯蒂娜，而丹尼斯心底也隐隐盼着是她——尽管他自己心里也承认，这盼头实在没什么凭据。

弗利特太太倒并未受多少剧痛折磨。

===Original===

She seemed gently wafted as by an ebbing tide away from time and earth, Kindly but firmly she sought to prepare Dennis’s mind for the change soon to take place. At first he could not endure its mention, but she said, earnestly: “My son, I am not dying. I am just entering on the true, real, eternal life﻿—a life which is as much beyond this poor feeble existence as the sun is brighter than a glowworm. I shall soon clasp my dear husband to my heart again, and, oh, ecstasy! I shall soon in reality see the Saviour whom I now see almost continually in vision.”
Then again she would turn toward her earthly treasures with unutterable yearning and tenderness.
“Oh, that I could gather you up in my arms and take you all with me!” she would often exclaim. Many times during the day she would call the little girls from their play and kiss their wondering faces.
One evening Dennis came home and found a vase of flowers with a green background of mint at his mother’s bedside. Their delicate fragrance greeted him as soon as he entered. As he sat by her side holding her hand, he said, softly: “Mother, are not these sprays of mint rather unusual in a bouquet? Has the plant any special meaning? I have noticed it before mingled with these mysterious flowers.”
She smiled and answered, “When I was a girl its language was, ‘Let us be friends again.’ ”
“Do you think﻿—can it be possible that *she* sends them?” said he, in a low, hesitating tone.
“Prayer is mighty, my son.”
“And have you been praying for her all this time, mother?”
“Yes, and will continue to do so to the last.”
“Oh, mother! I have lost hope. My heart has been full of bitterness toward her, and I have felt that God was against it all.”
“God is not against her learning to know Him, which is life. Jesus has loved her all the time, and she has wronged Him more than she has you.”
Dennis bowed his head on his mother’s hand, and she felt hot tears fall upon it. At last he murmured: “You are indeed going to heaven soon, dear mother, for your language is not of earth. When will such a spirit dwell within me?”
“Again remember your mother’s words,” she answered, gently; “prayer is mighty.”
“Mother,” said he, with a sudden earnestness, “do you think you can pray for us in heaven?”
“I know of no reason to the contrary.”
“Then I know you will, and the belief will ever be a source of hope and strength.”
Mrs.

===Chinese===

她仿佛正被一股缓缓退去的潮水轻柔托起，从光阴与尘世之间慢慢漂远。她温言软语却又坚定无比地开导丹尼斯，好叫他提前做好心理准备，迎接那即将来临的别离。起初，丹尼斯一听见提及此事便承受不住，她便诚恳地说道：“我的儿，我不是要死了。我不过是正要步入那真实、真切、永恒的生命——比起这具可怜柔弱的肉身存续，那永生要光明宏阔得多，就像太阳比一只萤火虫更耀眼一般。不久我便又能将我亲爱的丈夫紧紧拥入怀中，而且——啊，何等狂喜！——我很快就能亲眼瞻仰救主，如今我在异象之中几乎时时刻刻都能望见他。”

可紧接着，她又会回过头来，带着难以言喻的眷恋与温柔望向她尘世间的宝贝骨肉。

“唉，真恨不得把你们统统搂进怀里，一并带走啊！”她常常这样感叹。白日里，她总要好几次把正在玩耍的小姑娘们唤到床前，亲吻她们那一双双满怀疑惑的小脸蛋。

一天傍晚，丹尼斯回到家，发现母亲床头摆着一只花瓶，簇拥的鲜花底下衬着一片青翠的薄荷叶。他一进门，那缕清幽的芬芳便扑鼻而来。他在床沿坐下，握住母亲的手，轻声说道：“母亲，这束花里插着几枝薄荷，岂不是颇不寻常？这草木可有什么特别的寓意？先前那些来历不明的鲜花里，我也曾留神见过它。”

她微微一笑，答道：“我年轻当姑娘的时候，它的花语是：‘让我们重归于好吧。’”

“您觉得——莫非真是她送来的？”他压低嗓音，迟疑地问道。

“祈祷大有能力，我的儿。”

“母亲，这些日子您一直在为她祈祷吗？”

“是的，而且直到我咽下最后一口气，我也还会一直为她祈祷下去。”

“哦，母亲！我已经绝望了。我心里对她积满了苦毒与怨恨，我甚至觉得连上帝都在阻拦这一切。”

“上帝绝不会阻拦她去认识他，认识他便是生命。耶稣一直都爱着她，而她得罪耶稣，远比她得罪你更深得多。”

Mr. Bruder carried it, but most unfortunately Christine was out, so that her maid, ever on the alert to earn the price of her treachery, received it. It was slightly sealed. She opened it, and saw from its contents that it must be given to Mr. Ludolph. He with a frown committed it to the flames.
“I have written to her,” she whispered to her son in the evening, “and think she will come to see me.”
Dennis was sleepless that night, through his hope and eager expectation. The following day, and the next passed, and she came not.
“I was right,” exclaimed he, bitterly. “She is utterly heartless. It was not she who sent the flowers. Who that is human would have refused such a request! Waste no more thought upon her, for she is unworthy, and it is all in vain.”
“No!” said Mrs. Fleet in sudden energy. “It is not in vain. Have I not prayed again and again? and shall I doubt God?”
“Your faith is stronger than mine,” he answered, in deep despondency.
“God’s time is not always ours,” she answered, gently.
But an angry fire lurked in Dennis’s eyes, and he muttered to himself as he went to his room: “She has snapped the last slender cord that bound me to her. I could endure almost anything myself, but that she should refuse to visit my dying mother proves her a monster, with all her beauty.”
As he was leaving the house in the morning, his mother whispered, gently, “Who was it that said, ‘Father, forgive them, they know not what they do?’ ”
“Ah, but she does know,” said he, bitterly. “I can forgive nearly everything against myself, but not slights to you.”
“The time will come when you will forgive everything, my son.”
“Not till there is acknowledgment and sorrow for the wrong,” answered he, sternly. Then with a sudden burst of tenderness he added: “Goodbye, darling mother. I will try to do anything you wish, even though it is impossible;” but his love, through Janette’s treachery, suffered the deepest wound it had yet received.
Christine of her own accord had almost decided to call upon Mrs. Fleet, but before she could carry out her purpose while hastily coming downstairs one day, she sprained her ankle, and was confined to her room some little time.
She sent Janette with orders for the flowers, who, at once surmising their destination, said to the florist that she was Miss Ludolph’s confidential maid, and would carry them to those for whom they were designed.

五月上旬的一天清晨，弗利特太太已是极度虚弱，丹尼斯怀着沉重的不安离家去了店里。上午他照例打发恩斯特回家去看看母亲的光景，谁知恩斯特很快便脸色惨白、慌张失措地跑回来，大喊道：“快回家去！”

丹尼斯一把撇下惊愕的顾客，飞奔回家，转眼便赶到了母亲榻前。布鲁德夫妇正站在床尾低声抽泣，两个小妹妹分别扑在床两侧哀哀哭求——“哦，妈妈！求求您别走呀！”

“嘘，别哭！”丹尼斯神色肃穆地低喝了一声。众人被他的神情所慑，霎时间都安静了下来。他俯下身去，贴近床榻轻声唤道：“母亲，您要离开我们了。”

Mr. Bruder, unable to control his feelings any longer, hurried from the room. His wife, with streaming eyes, silently dressed the little girls, and took them home with her, crying piteously all the way for mamma.
Pale, tearless, motionless, Dennis sat, hour after hour holding his mother’s hand. He noted that her pulse grew more and more feeble. At last the sun in setting broke through the clouds that had obscured it all day, and filled the room with a sudden glory.
To Dennis’s great surprise, his mother’s eyes opened wide, with the strange, far-off look they ever had when she was picturing to herself the unknown world.
Her lips moved. He bent over her and caught the words: “Hark! hear!﻿—It never was so sweet before. See the angels﻿—thronging toward me﻿—they never came so near before.”
Then a smile of joy and welcome lighted up her wan features, and she whispered, “Oh, Dennis, husband﻿—are we once more united?”
Suddenly there was a look of ecstasy such as her son had never seen on any human face, and she cried almost aloud, “Jesus﻿—my Saviour!” and received, as it were, directly into His arms, she passed from earth.
We touch briefly on the scenes that followed. Dennis took the body of his mother to her old home, and buried it under the wide-spreading elm in the village churchyard, where as a happy child and blooming maiden she had often sat between the services. It was his purpose to remove the remains of his father and place them by her side as soon as he could afford it.
His little sisters accompanied him east, and he found a home for them with a sister of his mother, who was a good, kind, Christian lady. Dennis’s salary was not large, but sufficient to insure that his sisters would be no burden to his aunt, who was in rather straitened circumstances. He also arranged that the small annuity should be paid for their benefit.
It was hard parting from his sisters, whose little hearts seemed breaking at what appeared to them to be a new bereavement.
“How can I leave them!”

Mrs. Von Brakhiem and her party quite took possession of the Ludolph mansion, and often made it echo with gayety.

In truth, she had little to do with the affair; it was quite impromptu, and Mr. Ludolph and Mrs. Von Brakhiem were responsible for it.

“我多希望能有法子去宽慰他、抚平他的伤痛啊！”她幽幽叹息，“可我只怕自己比世上任何人都更无能为力。说真的，如今他看起来简直对我厌恶透顶、恨之入骨了。横亘在我们之间的高墙与屏障，真是一天比一天更坚固、更高耸了。倘若……一切原本该有多么不同啊。可叹这些折磨人的‘倘若’又有何用？抗拒这盲目无情、将幸福赐予一人却把另一人碾得粉碎的命运，又有何用呢？”

她身心俱疲、满怀颓丧地乘车回到那座自己几乎寻不到半点乐趣的华丽宅邸。

谁料刚一进门，竟撞见从纽约前来的冯·布拉克海姆太太——她正带着一群兴高采烈的游伴往西进发，准备前往落基山脉和加利福尼亚畅游一番。他们顺道在芝加哥停脚小住几日，打定主意非要把克里斯蒂娜也捎带上一同同行不可。她父亲大力赞成这一计划。克里斯蒂娜虽一眼便看穿了父亲的用心，却也懒得抗拒。既然很快就要同丹尼斯永别，少见他一面，心里便能少受一分煎熬。何况，她那颗酸楚沉重的心正巴不得有任何新鲜的变故来麻痹忘忧；于是这桩行程便迅速敲定了下来。

冯·布拉克海姆太太和她那帮朋友几乎成了卢多尔夫公馆的主人，整日里将这座宅院闹得欢声笑语回荡不息。

就在丹尼斯安葬母亲的那天傍晚，恩斯特受卢多尔夫先生之托，上门来送一封信。他一跨进门，只见宅邸里正在举行一场时髦奢华的狂欢夜宴。客厅里丝竹管弦齐鸣、舞影翩跹，餐厅那边则传来阵阵碰杯声与肆意的大笑——这番景象足以证明，这绝非克里斯蒂娜从前向父亲描绘过的那种雅致聚会。其实，这场宴会她自己几乎毫无干系；它完全是临时起意办起来的，主谋正是卢多尔夫先生与冯·布拉克海姆太太。

然而恩斯特无从知晓内情，在他眼里，眼前这一幕简直骇人听闻。

===Original===

The simple funeral service taking place on that day in the distant New England village had never been absent from his thoughts a moment. Since early morning he had gone about with his little face composed to funereal gravity.
His simple, warmhearted parents felt that they could only show proper respect for the occasion by the deepest gloom. Their rooms were arranged in stiff and formal manner, with crape here and there. All unnecessary work ceased, and the children, forbidden to play, were dressed in mourning as far as possible, and made to sit in solemn and dreadful state all day. It would not have surprised Ernst if the whole city had gone into mourning. Therefore the revelry at the Ludolph mansion seemed to him heartless and awful beyond measure, and nearly the first things he told Dennis on the latter’s return was that they had had “a great dancing and drinking party, the night of the funeral, at Mr. Ludolph’s.” Then, trying to find some explanation for what seemed to him such a strange and wicked thing, he suggested, “Perhaps they meant it for a wake.”
Poor little Ernst’s ideas of the world, outside of his home, had been gathered from a very low neighborhood.
He also handed Dennis a letter that Mr. Ludolph requested should be given him on his return. It read as follows:

> “I have been compelled to supply your place in your absence: therefore your services will be no longer needed at this store. Enclosed you will find a check for the small balance still due you,
> August Ludolph.”

===Chinese===

那一天远在遥远新英格兰乡村里举行的朴素葬礼，自清晨起便一刻也不曾离开过他的脑海。打大清早开始，他那张稚嫩的小脸便一直绷得庄严肃穆，满是奔丧般的凝重。

他那对心地纯良、淳朴热忱的父母觉得，唯有展现出最深沉的哀戚，才算对得起这桩丧事。家里屋子被收拾得拘谨肃穆，四处都挂起了黑纱。一切非必要的活计全部停摆，孩子们不准玩耍，尽其所能地换上素服孝衣，一整天都被按在椅子上正襟危坐，神色凝重得教人发怵。就算全芝加哥城都跟着披麻戴孝，恩斯特也不会觉得有半分稀奇。因此，卢多尔夫宅邸里这番载歌载舞的狂欢，在他看来简直冷酷残忍、荒唐透顶到了极点。等到丹尼斯一回来，他头一桩禀报的事，便是“葬礼那天晚上，卢多尔夫先生家里办了一场盛大的跳舞喝酒派对”。随后，为了替这件在他眼里如此怪异缺德的举动勉强寻个解释，他又小声揣测道：“兴许他们是把那当成一场守灵宴了吧。”

可怜的小恩斯特，他对家门之外这个大千世界的认知，原都是从极底层贫寒的街区里耳濡目染得来的。

他还转交给丹尼斯一封信，那是卢多尔夫先生特意吩咐等他一回来便交到他手上的。信中写道：

> “阁下离职期间，本店已不得不另聘他人接替您的职位：故尔本店今后不再需要您的效劳。随函附上结清尚欠您微薄余薪的支票一张。
> 奥古斯特·卢多尔夫。”

===Original===

Dennis’s brow grew very dark, and in bitter soliloquy he said, half aloud, as he strode up and down his little room in great agitation: “And so it all ends! The girl at whose side my mother would have watched in the most dangerous and loathsome of diseases; the woman of ice whom I sought to melt and render human by as warm, true love as ever man lavished on one who rewarded his affection﻿—this beautiful monster will not even visit my mother when dying; she holds a revel on the day of the funeral; and now, through her influence no doubt, I am robbed of the chance of winning honest bread. She cannot even endure the sight of the man who once told her the unvarnished truth. Poor as you deem me, Christine Ludolph, with God’s help not many years shall pass before it will be condescension on my part to recognize you.”
He would not even go to the store again. The Bruders, having heard what had occurred, took Ernst away also; but Dennis soon found him a better situation elsewhere.
The day on which Dennis returned, Christine was speeding in a palace-car toward the Rocky Mountains, outwardly gay, determined to enjoy herself and carry out her reckless purpose to get the most possible out of life, cost what it might.
If she had been a shallow girl, thoughtless and vain, with only mind enough to take in the events of the passing moment, she might have bought many fleeting pleasures with her abundant wealth. But this she was not, with all her faults, and wherever she went, in the midst of gayest scenes, and in the presence of the grandest and most inspiring scenery, thought and memory, like two spectres that no spell could lay, haunted her and robbed her of peace and any approach to happiness. Though possessing the means of gratifying every whim, though restrained by no scruples from doing what she chose, she felt that all around were getting more from life than she.
During her absence she experienced a sudden and severe attack of illness. Her friends were much alarmed about her, and she far more about herself. All her old terror returned. In one respect she was like her mother; she had no physical courage, but shrank with inexpressible dread from danger, pain, and death. Again the blackness of darkness gathered round her, and not one in the gay pleasure party could say a word to comfort her.

===Chinese===

丹尼斯看完信，浓眉顿时沉了下来，在自己那间小屋里激愤地来回踱着步子，半是自语、半是出声地苦笑叹道：“一切竟落得如此收场！倘若她染上最凶险恶毒的疫病，我母亲原本连死都不怕也要去守在她榻前；我曾倾注一个男人所能献给心上人的最炽热、最真挚的爱意，指望融化这尊冰雪美人、教她生出几分人情味——可这个美若天仙的怪物，竟连我母亲弥留之际都不肯屈尊探望一眼；偏偏赶在母亲下葬那一天大摆筵席狂欢；如今，毫无疑问又是在她的唆使之下，连我赖以挣口正经饭吃的生计也被剥夺了！她甚至连瞧上一眼那个曾当面戳破真相的男人，都觉得刺眼难耐！克里斯蒂娜·卢多尔夫，不管你在眼里把我瞧得多么寒微贫贱，但蒙上帝助佑，不用几年工夫，轮到我肯抬眼认你的时候，那便是我的俯就了！”

他甚至再也不肯踏进那家画店半步。布鲁德夫妇听说了事情的经过，也立刻把恩斯特领了回来；不过丹尼斯很快就在别处替他寻着了一桩更好的差事。

就在丹尼斯返回芝加哥的同一天，克里斯蒂娜正乘着一节豪华卧铺车厢风驰电掣地奔向落基山脉。她表面上显得兴致盎然，暗地里却打定了横下一条心的念头：无论付出什么代价，也要尽量从人生中榨取享乐，及时行乐。

倘若她果真是个浅薄轻浮、没心没肺、只顾着虚荣享乐、脑子里只装得下眼前一刻喧嚣的姑娘，她大可用手头挥霍不尽的财富买来无数转瞬即逝的欢愉。然而纵然有千般缺点，她偏偏生就了一颗并非如此的心；无论走到哪里，哪怕身处最热闹欢腾的宴乐场中，哪怕置身最雄奇壮丽、最令人心旷神怡的湖光山色之前，思虑与回忆总像两道任何符咒也驱不散的幽灵，如影随形地纠缠着她，夺走了她所有的安宁以及任何贴近幸福的可能。尽管她拥有满足一切任性念头的财力，尽管行事毫无顾忌、不受任何良心准则的约束，她却清晰地感觉到，身边每一个人从生活里收获的欢欣都要比自己多得多。

旅途之中，她突然染上了一场急病，来势汹汹。同伴们着实为她捏了一把汗，而她自己更是惊恐万状。从前那股刻骨的恐惧再次排山倒海般袭来。在有一点上，她像极了她的母亲：她毫无肉体上的勇气，面对危险、病痛与死亡，只会生出一种难以言喻的畏缩与战栗。浓墨般的黑暗再度向她兜头压来，而这群寻欢作乐的旅伴当中，竟无一人能说出一句宽慰她心神的话。

===Original===

She recovered, and soon regained her usual health, but her self-confidence was more thoroughly shaken. She felt like one in a little cockleshell boat out upon a shoreless ocean. While the treacherous sea remained calm, all might be well, but she knew that a storm would soon arise, and that she must go down, beyond remedy. Again she had been taught how suddenly, how unexpectedly, that storm might rise.
Dennis resolved at once to enter on the career of an artist. He sold to Mr. French, at a moderate price, some paintings and sketches he had made. He rented a small room that became his studio, sleeping-apartment﻿—in brief, his home, and then went to work with all the ordinary incentives to success intensified by his purpose to reach a social height that would compel Christine to look upward if their acquaintance were renewed.
Disappointment in love is one of the severest tests of character in man or woman. Some sink into weak sentimentality, and mope and languish; some become listless, apathetic, and float down the current of existence like driftwood. Men are often harsh and cynical, and rail at the sex to which their mothers and sisters belong. Sometimes a man inflicts a well-nigh fatal wound and leaves his victim to cure it as best she may. From that time forth she may be like the wronged Indian, who slays as many white men as he can. Not a few, on finding they cannot enter the beautiful paradise of happy love, plunge into imbruting vice, and drown not only their disappointment but themselves in dissipation. Their course is like that of some who deem that the best way to cure a wound or end a disease is to kill the patient as soon as possible. If women have true metal in them (and they usually have) they become unselfishly devoted to others, and by gentle, self-denying ways seek to impart to those about them the happiness denied to themselves.
But with all manly young men the instinct of Dennis is perhaps the most common. They will rise, shine, and dazzle the eyes that once looked scornfully or indifferently at them.
As he worked patiently at his noble calling this smaller ambition was gradually lost in the nobler, broader one, to be a true artist and a good man.

===Chinese===

后来她侥幸痊愈，不久便恢复了往常的康健，可她心底那股盲目的自信却遭到了更加彻底的动摇。她只觉自己仿佛正乘着一叶扁舟般的贝壳小船，飘荡在一片无边无际的大洋之上。只要这诡谲莫测的大海风平浪静，倒也相安无事；可她心里明镜似的，风暴迟早会骤然掀翻海面，到那时自己便会万劫不复地沉入海底。这场病再一次教会了她，那场风暴可能来得何等迅猛、何等出人意表。

丹尼斯当即立断，决意正式踏上职业画家的道路。他以公道平实的价钱，将自己平日作的一些画作和素描卖给了弗伦奇先生。他租下一间小屋，既是画室，又是卧室——简而言之，便是他的家；随后便全身心投入创作之中，而这股在常人眼中本就强烈的成功动力，又因他立誓要攀上一座足以迫使克里斯蒂娜日后重逢时不得不仰望的社会高度，而变得愈发炽烈无比。

情场失意，乃是考验男女品格最严酷的试金石之一。有的人从此沉溺于软弱伤感的多愁善感之中，终日愁眉不展、萎靡消沉；有的人则变得百无聊赖、麻木不仁，宛如一根浮木随波逐流地混完余生。男人们往往会变得刻薄乖戾、愤世嫉俗，对着他们自己母亲与姐妹所属的整个女性群体大加嘲讽诋毁。有时，一个男人留下一道几乎致命的创伤，便撒手不管，任由受害者自行去舔舐疗伤。自那以后，她兴许就会变得像遭人欺凌的印第安人一样，见一个白人杀一个，以泄心头之恨。更有不少人一见进不去美满爱情那座瑰丽的伊甸园，便一头扎进堕落兽性的泥潭，把失望连同自己一并淹死在纸醉金迷、放浪形骸之中。他们的行径，活像那些认为治好伤口或终结病痛最好的法子就是趁早把病人一刀宰了的庸医一般。至于女子，倘若骨子里有真材实料（而她们大多确实有），便会转而无私地奉献于他人，用温柔克己的善行，把那份自己无缘享有的幸福播撒给周遭的人。

但凡是有血性有志气的青年男子，最常见的本能反应恐怕还是像丹尼斯这般：他们偏要奋发崛起、绽放光芒，好教那双曾经轻蔑或冷漠打量过自己的眼睛，日后被耀眼的光彩刺得睁不开眼。

随着他日复一日耐心地耕耘于这门高尚的艺术事业，起初那点狭隘好胜的野心也渐渐消融在一桩更崇高、更博大的志向里——他立志要成为一名真正的艺术家，一名正直良善的人。

===Original===

During his illness some gentlemen of large wealth and liberality, who wished to stimulate and develop the native artistic talent of their city, offered a prize of two thousand dollars for the finest picture painted during the year, the artist also having the privilege of selling his work.
On his return after his illness Dennis heard of this, and determined to be one of the competitors. He applied to Mr. Cornell, who had the matter in charge, for permission to enter the lists, which that gentleman granted rather doubtfully. He had known Dennis only as a critic, not as an artist. But having gained his point, Dennis went earnestly to work on the emblematic painting he had resolved upon, and with what success the following chapters will show.
His mother’s sickness and death, of course, put a complete shop to his artistic labors for a time, but when entering on his new career, he gave himself wholly to this effort.
The time for exhibition and decision was fixed﻿—Saturday morning October 7, 1871.

===Chinese===

在他先前卧病期间，几位家财万贯、慷慨乐善的绅士有心扶持并培育本城土生土长的艺术人才，于是出资设立了一项高达两千美元的大奖，重赏当年之内创作出的最优秀画作，同时画家还享有自行出售获奖作品的权利。

丹尼斯大病初愈回到城里后听闻此事，当即决意报名角逐。他向主持此事的康奈尔先生递交了参赛申请；康奈尔先生原本只知丹尼斯擅长鉴赏评论，却从未见识过他亲自执笔作画，因此颇带几分怀疑地勉强准了他参赛。既已如愿获准，丹尼斯便聚精会神地投入到他早已构思妥当的那幅寓意画的创作之中——至于最终成色如何，后文自见分晓。

母亲的病重与辞世，自然令他的绘画事业一度彻底停摆；然而一旦重新踏上这条崭新的征程，他便将全部身心都倾注在了这幅心血之作上。

画展揭幕与评奖揭晓的日期业已敲定——1871年10月7日，星期六上午。

## X The New Broom / 第十章 新扫帚
===Original===

The following Sabbath was a bright winter day without, but bright summer in Dennis’s heart. He inquired his way to a neighboring church, and every word of prayer, praise, and truth fell on a glad, grateful spirit. Returning, he wrote a long letter to his mother, telling her all he had passed through, especially dwelling on the truth he had discovered of God’s wish to make this life happy and successful, as well as the life beyond.
In closing, he wrote: “Here I am, Dennis Fleet, who a few days since thought the world scarcely large enough for what I meant to do, standing contentedly and gratefully in Pat Murphy’s shoes. I will not conceal from you, speaking figuratively (the fates forbid that it should be literally true), that I hope to outgrow them, and arrive at something better before many months pass. In the meantime I am indeed thankful for the means of winning honest bread for us all. It is quite a comedown from the classics and law to the position of porter and man of-all-work in a picture and music store, but if God means me to rise He can lead me upward from my lowly standpoint as well as from the most favored that I could have chosen for myself. I have learned that if I will *trust Him* and do present duty thoroughly, He will not forget me.”
On Monday morning, half an hour before the specified time, Dennis stood at the store. Impatiently he walked up and down before what would become the scene of joys and sorrows such as he had never before experienced. But we will not anticipate.
In due time Mr. Schwartz appeared. He gave Dennis a cool nod, and said, “Glad to see you so prompt,” then muttered again to himself, “New broom.”
In Mr. Schwartz’s slow, plodding soul the fire of enthusiasm had never burned. He was eminently conservative, and looked with wary suspicion on anything that appeared like earnestness. In the midst of a driving, bustling Western city, he stuck in the mud of his German phlegm, like a snag in the swift current of the Mississippi. Yet Mr. Ludolph found him a most valuable assistant. He kept things straight. Under his minute supervision everything had to be right on Saturday night as well as on Monday morning, on the 31st of December as well as on the 1st of January. He was one who through life would be satisfied with a subordinate position, conscious of the lack of enterprise needful to push his own way in the world.

===Chinese===

紧接着的那个安息日，窗外冬日晴朗和煦，丹尼斯心头更如盛夏般光明敞亮。他打听着去了附近的一座教堂，每一句祷告、赞美与真理之言，都如同甘霖般落进他欢欣感恩的心田。回到住处，他给母亲写了一封长信，将自己连日来的经历悉数告知，尤其着重倾诉了新近领悟到的真理——上帝不仅愿人在来世蒙福，同样愿人在今生也过得幸福而有所成。

信末他写道：“您瞧我如今的光景——就在几天前，我丹尼斯·弗利特还觉得这世界几乎容不下我的宏图大志，眼下却心满意足、满怀感恩地穿上了帕特·墨菲留下来的鞋子。坦白说，打个比方（老天爷保佑千万别成真话），我倒指望着不用过几个月便能脚长过这双鞋，挣个更好的前程。但眼下能寻着一条靠本事挣来干净饭吃的门路，我已经感激不尽。从古典学和法学一路落到一家画片乐器店里当搬运工兼杂役，这落差着实不小；可上帝若有意要抬举我，从我眼下这卑微的立足点起步，也照样能引领我步步高升，丝毫不亚于我自己所能挑拣的任何得意起点。我已经明白，只要我肯*信靠他*，把眼前分内的差事踏踏实实做好，他是绝不会忘记我的。”

星期一清晨，离约定的时刻还有整整半个钟头，丹尼斯便已站在了画店门前。他怀着按捺不住的急切心情，在这座日后将要见证他生平从未体味过的悲欢离合的店门前踱来踱去。不过，眼下且不忙预言后事。

到点后，施瓦茨先生露面了。他冷淡地冲丹尼斯点了点头，说道：“很高兴见你来得这么准时，”随后又自言自语地嘟囔了一句，“新扫帚嘛。”

在施瓦茨先生那颗迟缓笃实、一步一个脚印的心里，热情的火苗是从来不曾燃起过的。他骨子里保守到家，凡是透出几分急切热忱的劲头，都要投以警惕怀疑的目光。置身于这座节奏飞快、忙忙碌碌的西部大都会里，他却稳稳陷在自己那股德国式的迟钝泥淖里，活像密西西比河急流中一根纹丝不动的沉木。然而卢多尔夫先生却觉得他是个极得力的助手。店里万事经他手都能井井有条。在他事无巨细的监督下，无论星期六晚上还是星期一早晨，无论是 12 月 31 日还是 1 月 1 日，样样事务都必须规规矩矩、分毫不差。他属于那种一辈子甘心居于副手之位的人，自知缺乏闯荡世道、自立门户所需的进取魄力。

===Original===

His painstaking, methodical spirit was just the kind to pervade a large warehouse like that he had in charge, and prevent loss and confusion in the multiplicity of objects it contained. Pat’s careless Irish ways had vexed his soul beyond words, and now Dennis’s eager manner suggested a harebrained Yankee youth who would raise a dust for a week and then be off at something else. He was therefore cool and curt, seeking by frostiness of manner to nip the budding enthusiasm that annoyed him.
Dennis heeded him not, but bent every faculty to the mastery of the duties required of him. He was to mop out the store with damp cloths, so as to raise no dust, to look after the furnace and graduate the heat throughout the building, to receive boxes, to assist in packing and unpacking pianos and other musical instruments that occupied part of the upper floors, and to make himself generally useful. So far from being an easy position, it was one that required great strength and despatch, and these had been Pat’s qualities save when drink got the better of him. For one of his age, Dennis was very strong, and his experience in helping his mother in household duties had made him quick and dexterous, where most young men would have been awkward and slow. After a day or two Mr. Schwartz relaxed his grimness somewhat, for if Dennis worked eagerly he also worked well for a beginner. Still it would require several years of well-doing to satisfy old Schwartz that all was right. But Mr. Ludolph, with his quick insight into character, watched this “new broom” a few days, and then congratulated himself on gaining another decided help toward the object nearest his heart.
The other clerks were of German descent, and under Mr. Schwartz’s rigid system each one filled his appropriate niche, and performed carefully the duties assigned.
Even to Dennis’s uncultivated eye there was an inartistic formality about the whole establishment. His sense of this was at first but a feeling﻿—a vague impression that grew upon him without his quite knowing why. He soon discovered, however, that everything was arranged squarely, according to system, order, and not with a view of placing in the best lights and shadows the beautiful things to be sold. He saw that Mr. Ludolph was annoyed by the same defect.

===Chinese===

他那股一丝不苟、按部就班的精神，恰恰最适合掌管这般规模宏大的货栈，能让店里林林总总的货品免于散失与混乱。帕特那套粗心大意的爱尔兰散漫做派曾令他苦不堪言，而眼下丹尼斯这副急切殷勤的模样，又叫他疑心这是个毛躁轻狂的美国佬小子，兴许也就折腾出一周的热乎劲儿，转眼便要撂挑子另谋他处去了。因此他摆出一副冷若冰霜、言简意赅的架势，指望用这股寒气把丹尼斯身上那股叫人心烦的热乎劲儿早早冻灭。

丹尼斯却浑不在意，使出浑身解数去熟悉、钻研分内的一切杂务。他的差事包括：用湿布擦洗店面地板以免扬起灰尘；照管暖炉、调节整栋大楼的温度；签收货箱；帮着拆装、打包摆放在楼上各层的钢琴与其他乐器；以及随时随地搭把手干些杂活。这绝不是什么轻省差事，反而极需力气与手脚利索——只要没被酒瘾绊倒，帕特从前正具备这些本事。论起他这年纪，丹尼斯体格格外强健，再加上往日帮母亲操持家务练就了一双巧手，寻常小伙子干起来笨手笨脚、磨磨蹭蹭的活计，到他手里却干净利落。过了一两天，施瓦茨先生板着的冷脸便稍微松动了些，因为丹尼斯干起活来虽说风风火火，但作为新手却实在挑不出毛病。话虽如此，要想让老施瓦茨彻底放下心来认定一切稳妥，恐怕还得看他安分守己干上好几年才行。倒是卢多尔夫先生眼光毒辣，一眼便能看透人心；他暗中观察了这把“新扫帚”几天，便暗自得意，觉得自己朝着平生最牵肠挂肚的大计又添了一名实实在在的帮手。

店里其余几名店员都是德国裔，在施瓦茨先生严丝合缝的规矩之下，每个人各安其位，小心翼翼地履行着指派给自己的差事。

然而即便以丹尼斯那双尚未受过专业熏陶的眼睛来看，整间画店的陈设也显得呆板拘谨、毫无艺术气息。起初他只是隐约有这种感觉——一种说不清道不明的模糊印象，日积月累地在他心头滋长。不过很快他便琢磨出了门道：店里所有的货品都是照着规整对称的死板章法一排排码放的，半点也没考虑如何摆放到最佳的光影角度下，去衬托这些待售珍品的美丽。他看出卢多尔夫先生自己也对这桩毛病颇为恼火。

===Original===

One bright day, when everything stood out with glaring distinctness, he seemed provoked beyond measure by this inartistic rigidity, and stormed through the store at a great rate.
“This art building and everybody and everything in it look as if they had swallowed a ramrod,” snarled he. “Mr. Schwartz, can’t you teach the young men to throw a little ease and grace into the arrangement of the articles under their charge?”
Mr. Schwartz looked at him with a blank, impassive face, and his employer felt that he might as well ask an elephant to teach dancing.
Turning suddenly on a stolid youth, he exclaimed, “By the gods! if you have not arranged all the statuettes on your counter in straight lines, and half of them with their backs toward the door at which our customers enter! Here, gather round me while I give you some ideas of arrangement.”
The clerks gathered around him, while with hands of skill and taste he placed everything artistically. The effect of a little transposition was marvellous, and Mr. Schwartz acknowledged that the groups looked doubly pretty and inviting. Dennis stood at a respectful distance, but was a close observer. He was the only one who gained much benefit from the lesson, because the only one capable of receiving it. With quick, appreciative eye he saw the grouping needful to produce the desired effect.
As Mr. Ludolph looked up he caught Dennis’s intelligent gaze.
“That is right, Fleet,” he said; “you learn, too, if you can, and when you are dusting around see if you cannot combine a little order and grace.”
From that day forward the hand and taste of Dennis Fleet gradually, and almost imperceptibly at first, gave a new aspect and created a new atmosphere in the Art Building. But at first he was kept busy enough at his humble routine duties. Everyone felt and expressed a little surprise at his getting into harness so quickly, but Mr. Schwartz’s influence was not conducive to conversation or emotions, however faint. All went forward quietly and orderly, like well-oiled machinery. Customers received every attention, and though many no doubt had the undefined feeling that something was wrong in the arrangement of the store, each found an abundance of beautiful things suited to his taste and purse, and so trade was good, even though the holiday season was over.
As for Dennis, he was to a certain extent in Paradise.

===Chinese===

一个阳光明媚的日子，店里每一件器物都在亮晃晃的日光下纤毫毕现，卢多尔夫先生似乎被这种毫无美感的僵硬摆设彻底惹火了，怒气冲冲地在店里走来走去，好一阵大发雷霆。

“这座艺术大厦，连同里头每一个人、每一件东西，看着都像是吞了根通条似的直挺挺！”他怒吼道，“施瓦茨先生，难道你就不能教教这帮年轻人，摆弄自己照管的物件时稍微带出点舒展与雅致来吗？”

施瓦茨先生一脸木然、毫无波澜地望着他，老板顿时觉得自己简直像是在求一头大象去教人跳交际舞。

卢多尔夫先生猛地转身冲着一个呆头呆脑的小伙子喊道：“老天爷在上！你居然把你那张柜台上的小雕像全都排成一条笔直的队列，而且其中一半还背对着顾客进门的方向！来，都围到我这儿来，我给你们示范示范什么叫布局陈设！”

店员们纷纷聚拢过来，只见卢多尔夫先生用一双灵巧而极富品味的双手，将一件件器物错落有致地摆弄开来。区区一番挪动之后呈现出的效果简直令人惊叹，连施瓦茨先生也不得不承认，那几组陈设显得比方才漂亮诱人了何止一倍。丹尼斯恭恭敬敬地站在稍远一点的地方，却在暗中凝神细观。这堂示范课上，唯独他真正受益匪浅，因为在场众人之中，只有他才具备领悟这番门道的灵性。他用一双敏锐而懂得欣赏的眼睛，一眼便看穿了造就这般赏心悦目效果所必需的构图章法。

卢多尔夫先生抬起头时，正撞见丹尼斯那双闪着悟性的眼睛。

“这样才对，弗利特，”他说道，“你也留心学着点，能学多少算多少；往后你四处掸灰打扫的时候，也试着把规整和雅致揉到一块儿去。”

打那天起，丹尼斯·弗利特那双手和他的审美品味，便一点一滴、起初几乎令人察觉不到地，悄然为艺术大厦换上了一副崭新的面貌，营造出一种全新的氛围。不过头些日子里，他光应付日常那些卑微琐碎的差事便已忙得团团转了。大伙儿见他这么快便驾轻就熟，心里都略感意外、嘴上也啧啧称奇；只不过施瓦茨先生在场时的那股严肃气氛，向来不利于人们闲聊或流露半点情绪，哪怕再微弱也不行。店里的一切都悄无声息、有条不紊地运转着，宛如一架上足了润滑油的机器。每一位顾客都得到了周到的侍奉；虽说不少人心里多半隐隐觉得店堂的陈设似乎哪儿不太对劲，可各自总能挑出合乎自己品味与财力的精美物件，因此即便年节旺季已过，店里的生意依然红火。

至于丹尼斯，他几乎算得上置身于一片乐园之中了。

===Original===

Nature had given him a deep, earnest love of the beautiful, and a keen perception of it.
Though his days were busy indeed, he found time gradually to study every pretty thing in the store. Though much was mystery to him as yet, he felt that he had crossed the threshold of a beautiful world﻿—the world of art. When a boy in New England he had taken drawing-lessons, and had shown remarkable aptness. While at college, also, he had given some attention to drawing and coloring, but circumstances had prevented him from following the bent of his taste. Now the passion awoke with tenfold force, and he had not been in his place a week before he began to make sketches of little things that pleased him. Some of the pictures and bronzes became almost dear because of the pleasure and inspiration that they occasioned, and at their sale his feeling was akin to regret. Early in the morning, when refreshed and brightened by the night’s rest, he would walk through the store as through fairyland, and, forgetting that he was a humble servitor, would feel as if all were his. But in fact was not his possession truer than that of many whose palace walls glow with every rich gem of art, and yet whose eyes are blind and their hearts dull to the beauty they have paid for?
A few days after his arrival, a little incident occurred that was hard and practical enough, and might justly cause him to feel that he occupied a humble place, not only in the world of art, but in the world in general. There had been a day of rain, slush, and mud. One of the younger clerks had been sent out on an errand, and came in well splashed. Drawing off his boots, he threw them to Dennis, saying: “Here you, Fleet! black my boots as quick as you can. I must go out again.”
Dennis reddened, and for a moment drew himself up as if he had been struck. The young man saw it and said, in a loud, coarse tone that could be heard by several customers: “Vat! you above your biz? I thought it vould be so.”
Dennis acted with decision. He meant to have the matter settled at once. Picking up the muddy boots, he marched straight into Mr. Ludolph’s office. That gentleman looked up, impatient at interruption, and saw his man-of-all-work standing before him with the splashed boots dangling in his hands.
“Well, what is it?” asked he, sharply.
“Mr. Berder threw me those boots and told me to black them.

===Chinese===

天性赋予了他一颗深沉真挚、热爱美好事物的心灵，以及一双敏锐的慧眼。

尽管白日里忙得脚不沾地，他还是抽空一点一滴地揣摩起店里的每一件精美器物。虽然许多门道于他而言尚且是个谜，他却真切觉得自己已然跨进了一个瑰丽绝伦的新世界——艺术的世界。幼时在新英格兰老家，他曾上过绘画课，而且显露出颇为不凡的天资；在大学念书期间，他也曾对素描与设色颇下过一番工夫，只可惜因故未能顺从心愿深造下去。如今，那股热爱骤然以十倍的烈度苏醒过来；他进店还不到一个礼拜，便开始抽空勾勒起那些令他心仪的小物件的速写。店里有些油画与青铜雕像因为常带给他愉悦与灵感，甚至成了他心头的挚爱，每当它们被人买走时，他心里竟隐隐泛起一丝怅然若失。清晨时分，经过一夜安眠而神清气爽的他，独自穿行在画店之中，仿佛漫步于仙境一般，甚至会暂时忘却自己不过是个卑微的杂役，只觉得眼前这一切仿佛全都归自己所有。可说到底，比起许多自家豪宅四壁挂满名画珍宝、眼里却盲目麻木、心里对花重金买来的美感浑然不觉的富豪来，他这份精神上的拥有，岂不比他们更真实百倍？

然而在他进店几天之后，发生了一件冷酷而现实的小插曲，足以顺理成章地提醒他：无论在艺术界还是在人世间，他所处的位置终究不过是一个卑微的末流。那一天外面雨雪交加、泥泞满地。一名年轻店员奉命出门跑了趟腿，回来时靴子上溅满了泥点。他脱下靴子，随手朝丹尼斯扔了过来，喝道：“喂，弗利特！赶紧把我的靴子擦亮了！我等会儿还得再出门呢。”

丹尼斯涨红了脸，有一瞬间挺直了脊梁，仿佛平白挨了一记耳光似的。那年轻店员见状，故意放大嗓门、粗声粗气地嚷嚷起来，声音大得连好几位顾客都听得清清楚楚：“咋了！还嫌这活儿委屈了你这大爷不成？我就料到你得摆这臭架子！”

丹尼斯当机立断。他打定主意要立刻把这事当面说清、立下规矩。他弯腰拾起那双沾满泥巴的靴子，径直大步走进了卢多尔夫先生的办公室。卢多尔夫先生正嫌被人打扰，不耐烦地抬起头，却见自己新雇的杂役正站在面前，手里拎着一双滴着泥水的靴子。

“怎么了？什么事？”他厉声问道。

“贝尔德先生把这双靴子扔给我，叫我给他擦亮。

Is this a part of my duty here?” said Dennis, in a firm, quiet tone.
“Curse it all!” said Mr. Ludolph, with much irritation; “I thought there would be trouble with your uppishness.”
“There shall be no trouble whatever,” said Dennis; “but I prefer to take my orders from you, and not from Mr. Berder. If you say this is expected, the disagreeable task shall be done as well as I can do it.”
Mr. Ludolph looked sharply at the young man for a moment and hesitated. In his heart he felt that he was speaking to a gentleman, and that it was not the thing to ask of him such menial work. “Yes, sir,” said Dennis.
“It seems to me, then, that this settles the question,” said Mr. Ludolph, coolly, turning to his writing; but he furtively and carefully watched Dennis’s course.
Determined to show that he was not above his business, that he accepted the bitter with the sweet, Dennis went upstairs to his room, got blacking and brush, and taking his station in a corner where Mr. Ludolph could plainly see him through the glass doors of his office, he polished away as vigorously as if that were his only calling. Mr. Ludolph looked and smiled. His was a nature that could be pleased with a small triumph like this. 请问这也是我在店里分内的差事吗？”丹尼斯用沉稳而平静的语气问道。

丹尼斯下定决心要证明自己绝不嫌弃本职低微，既端得起这碗饭，就咽得下其中苦辣。他上楼回到自己屋里，拿来鞋油和刷子，特意挑了办公室玻璃门外一个角落蹲下——卢多尔夫先生一抬眼就能清清楚楚地瞧见他——随即便卖力地刷擦起来，专注得仿佛擦鞋便是他毕生唯一的正业。卢多尔夫先生望见这幕，嘴角露出了一丝微笑。他正是那种能从这般小小胜利中感到快意的人。然而其他店员瞧见贝尔德先生居然得手，一个个也打定主意要出一份力，好照他们自己的说法，“煞一煞丹尼斯的威风”，于是纷纷把自己的靴子也拎了过来；贝尔德先生下午又把他的靴子拿来让他再擦一遍。丹尼斯依旧当着卢多尔夫先生的面不声不响地刷个不停。直到这时，卢多尔夫先生才懊恼地发觉，要是把自己的杂役变成全店上下的专职擦鞋匠，那店里正经的活计他可就没工夫干了。好在那以后接连几场严寒与大雪让街面冻得干爽洁净，这桩风波也就不了了之。此后很少再有人拿靴子来找他；即便偶有送来的，他也一声不吭地擦得锃亮。与此同时，他在履行日常职责时展现出的能力与忠实，连同他那初露头角的审美品味与判断力，也渐渐开始得到了赏识；

## XXIII The Revelation / 第二十三章 恍然顿悟
===Original===

The toilets of the young ladies were nearly completed, but, without waiting to add another touch, all hastened to the place where they had left Dennis. One of the colorless young ladies appeared upon the scene with a shawl around her bare shoulders, and a great deal of color on one cheek, and none on the other as yet; but this slight discrepancy was unnoted in the dire calamity they feared.
Many were the exclamations and lamentations.
“Why, the people will be here in fifteen minutes,” said Miss Winthrop, in a nervous tremor.
“Did he leave no word?” asked Miss Brown of the servants.
“No word, mum,” was the dismal echo.
“What shall we do?” they said, looking at one another with blank faces; but none could answer.
“I do hate such proud, freakish people. There is no managing or depending on them,” said Miss Brown, spitefully.
Miss Winthrop bit her lips to keep from saying to her hostess what would be more true than polite. There was a flash of anger in Christine’s dark blue eyes, and she said, coldly: “I imagine that you have finished the business this time, Miss Brown. But I confess that I am greatly surprised, for he said I could depend upon him for tonight.”
“So you can,” said Dennis, coming in behind them. “I am sorry you have had this needless alarm. But the fact is, I am a plain, ordinary mortal, and live in a very material way.”
“There was plenty of lunch in the dining-room,” said Miss Brown, tartly. “You need not have gone out and made all this trouble.”
“Pardon me for slighting your hospitality,” said Dennis, with slight emphasis on the word.
Again significant glances were exchanged. Miss Brown darted a black look at Dennis, and left the room.
“I can assure you, ladies,” added he, “that all is ready. I can lay my hand in a moment on whatever is needed. Therefore you need give yourselves no further anxiety.”
There was a general stampede for the dressing-rooms, but Miss Winthrop lingered. When Dennis was alone she went up to him and frankly gave her hand, saying: “Mr. Fleet, I wish to thank you for your course today. Between Miss Ludolph’s unwitting sermon and your brave and unexpected vindication of our faith, I hope to become more deserving of the name of Christian. You are a gentleman, sir, in the truest and best sense of the word, and as such it will ever be a pleasure to welcome you at my father’s house;” and she gave him her card.

温思罗普小姐紧咬住嘴唇，生怕自己忍不住向女主人说出几句虽然大实话却有失礼数的话来。克里斯蒂娜那双深蓝色的眼睛里闪过一丝怒意，冷冷地开口道：“我看这一回多半是你自己把事情搞砸了吧，布朗小姐。不过我倒真觉得有些意外，因为他原说过今晚只管指望他便是。”

“你们确实只管指望我便是，”丹尼斯恰好从她们身后走过来，接过话茬道，“诸位白白受了这场虚惊，实在抱歉。只因说到底，我不过是个食人间烟火的寻常凡人，总得照着很实在的法子讨生活填肚子。”

“餐厅里明明摆着那么丰盛的午宴，”布朗小姐酸溜溜地说，“你原用不着跑出去，平白惹出这么一通乱子。”

“那便请原谅我怠慢了您的盛情款待，”丹尼斯说道，故意在“盛情款待”几个字上略微加重了语气。

众人之间再度飞快地交换了意味深长的眼神。布朗小姐狠狠剜了丹尼斯一眼，转身拂袖而去。

“诸位小姐，我可以向你们保证，”他接着说道，“一切都已妥妥当当。但凡用得着什么物件，我一伸手便能立刻取来。所以诸位大可不必再为此事忧心了。”

A flush of grateful surprise and pleasure mantled Dennis’s face, but before he could speak she was gone.
The audience were soon thronging in. By half-past eight the performers were all in the back parlor, and there was a brilliant army of actors and actresses in varied and fanciful costume, many coming to the house dressed for their parts. There were gods and goddesses, shepherds and shepherdesses, angels, crusaders, who would take leave of languishing ladies, living statuary, and tableaux of all sorts. Dennis was much shocked at the manner in which ladies exposed themselves in the name of art and for the sake of effect. Christine seemed perfectly Greek and pagan in this respect, yet there was that in her manner that forbade a wanton glance. But, as he observed the carriage of the men around him, he was more than satisfied that no plea of art could justify the “style,” and felt assured that every pure-minded woman would take the same view if she realized the truth. Under the name of fashion and art much is done in society that would be simply monstrous on ordinary occasions.
The music, as far as possible, was in character with the scenes. The entertainment went forward with great applause. Everyone was radiant; and the subtle, exhilarating spirit of assured success glowed in every eye, and gave a richer tone and coloring to everything.
Christine appeared in several and varied characters, and Dennis had eyes only for her. The others he glanced over critically as the artist in charge, and then dismissed them from his thoughts; but on Christine his eyes rested in a spellbound admiration that both amused and pleased her. She loved power of every kind, and when she read approval in the trained and critical eye of Dennis Fleet she knew that all the audience were applauding.
But Dennis had little time for musing, so great was the strain upon him to prevent confusion. His voice excited great surprise and applause, many inquiring vainly who he was. When he and Christine sung together the audience were perfectly carried away, and stormed and applauded without stint. Indeed, it seemed that they could not be satisfied. The call was so urgent that several asked Christine to sing again, and she did so alone. For ten minutes she held the audience perfectly entranced, and no one more so than Dennis.

很快，宾客们便络绎不绝地涌了进来。八点半一到，所有演出的青年男女已悉数齐聚在后客厅里；放眼望去，宛如一支衣袂斑斓、奇装异服的华丽军团，其中许多人来赴宴时便已早早穿好了各自角色的戏装。席间有希腊天神与女神、牧童与牧羊女、天使、正要与娇柔闺秀挥泪诀别的十字军骑士、活人雕塑以及各式各样的静态活画。看到姑娘们打着艺术的旗号、为了舞台效果竟那般坦胸露臂地显露身姿，丹尼斯着实吃了一惊。克里斯蒂娜在这方面似乎活脱脱一副古希腊异教神女的派头，然而她举止间自有一股凛然不可侵犯的气度，教人不敢生出半点轻薄邪念。可当丹尼斯转眼打量周围那些男士的神态举止时，他便愈发确信，任何艺术的借口都不足以替这种“时髦风尚”开脱；他深信，任何一位心地纯洁的女子若看清了这背后的真相，也必定会持同样的见解。世俗社交场上打着风尚与艺术的名义所做的许多勾当，放在寻常场合简直荒唐透顶、伤风败俗。

背景音乐也尽可能地与每一幕场景严丝合缝。整场游艺会在经久不息的喝彩声中顺顺当当地推进。人人脸上容光焕发；大获成功的微妙欢欣与亢奋在每一双眼睛里闪耀，也为周遭的一切镀上了一层更加浓郁绚丽的色泽。

克里斯蒂娜轮番扮演了好几个截然不同的角色，而丹尼斯的眼里却自始至终只有她一人。其余人等，他不过是作为总管舞台的画师，挑剔地扫视几眼便抛诸脑后；唯有落在克里斯蒂娜身上的目光，始终带着一种失魂落魄般的倾慕，这既教她觉得好笑，又令她暗自得意。她酷爱各种形式的掌控与征服之力；每当她在丹尼斯·弗利特那双训练有素、眼光挑剔的眼眸里读出赞许之意时，她便笃定全场观众都在为她鼓掌喝彩。

然而丹尼斯并没有多少工夫沉溺于遐思之中，为了确保全场秩序井然不出纰漏，他整晚都紧绷着神经。他亲自领唱时那副嗓音更是引来满堂惊艳与如雷掌声，许多人纷纷四处打听他是何许人也。待到他与克里斯蒂娜联袂合唱时，台下观众彻底如痴如醉，欢呼喝彩声如暴风雨般经久不绝、毫不吝惜。看那架势，大伙儿简直百听不厌。观众呼声如此热烈，好几位来宾甚至请求克里斯蒂娜再独唱一曲，她便应邀独自登台献唱。整整十分钟里，她令全场听众如醉如痴、神魂颠倒，而其中尤以丹尼斯为最。

Usually she was too cold in all that she did, but now in her excitement she far surpassed herself, and he acknowledged that he had never heard such music before.
The very soul of song seemed breathed into her, and every nook and corner of the house appeared to vibrate with melody. Even the servants in distant rooms said that it seemed that an angel was singing. After she ceased, the audience sat spellbound for a moment, and then followed prolonged thunders of applause, the portly brewer, Mr. Brown himself, leading off again and again.
“Now let the tenor sing alone,” he said, for, though a coarse man, he was hearty and good-natured.
The audience emphatically echoed his wish, but Dennis as decidedly shook his head.
Then came a cry, “Miss Ludolph and the tenor again”; and the audience took it up with a clamor that would not be denied.
Christine looked inquiringly at Dennis, and he replied in a low tone, “You command me this evening.”
Again she thanked him with her eyes, and from a music stand near chose a magnificent duet from Mendelssohn, in which he must sing several difficult solos.
“Act your pleasure. I am familiar with it,” he said, smiling at the way she had circumvented him in his refusal to sing alone.
Christine sat down and played her own accompaniment, while Dennis stood at her side. He determined to do his best and prove that though he swept a store he could also do something else. Many of the strains were plaintive, and his deep and unconscious feeling for his fair companion in song gave to his voice a depth, and at times a pathos, that both thrilled and *touched* the heart, and there were not a few wet eyes in the audience. Unconsciously to himself and all around, he was singing his love; and even Christine, though much preoccupied with her part, wondered at the effect upon herself, and recognized the deep impression made upon the audience.
As the last notes died away the sliding-doors were closed.
Dennis had achieved a greater success than Christine, because, singing from the heart, he had touched the heart. His applause could be read in moist eyes and expressive faces rather than in noisy hands. She saw and understood the result. A sad, disappointed look came into her face, and she said in a low, plaintive tone, as if it were wrung from her: “There must be something wrong about me. I fear I shall never reach true art.

平日里她无论做什么事总显得过于冷漠矜持，可今晚在兴奋之情的激荡下，她竟远远超出了往常的水准，连丹尼斯也不得不承认，自己平生从未听过这般动人心魄的歌声。

歌声的灵魂仿佛被一字一句吹进了她的胸膛，整座宅邸的每一个角落似乎都在随之震颤回响。就连远在偏房里的佣人们也私下赞叹，听着简直像有位天使在放声高歌。一曲唱罢，满堂宾客先是痴迷地静默了一瞬，随即便爆发出经久不息、震耳欲聋的雷鸣掌声——连那位体态富态的大啤酒商布朗先生本人，也一马当先地一遍又一遍带头拍手叫好。

“现在该请咱们这位男高音独唱一曲啦！”他洪声喊道——虽说他是个粗人，性子却倒也爽朗热诚、古道热肠。

全场宾客异口同声地附和他的提议，丹尼斯却同样坚定地摇了摇头。

于是台下又响起一片呼声：“请卢多尔夫小姐和男高音再合唱一曲！”满堂宾客群情沸腾，喊声如潮水般势不可挡。

克里斯蒂娜转头探询地望向丹尼斯，他压低声音答道：“今晚全凭您做主吩咐。”

她再次用眼神向他致谢，随即从近旁的乐谱架上挑出了一首门德尔松（Mendelssohn）笔下气势恢宏的二重唱——其中正包含着好几段极富难度的男高音独唱华彩。

“请便吧，这曲子我熟得很。”他微笑着说道，言下显然看穿了她巧施妙计，绕过了自己刚才婉拒独唱的推辞。

克里斯蒂娜款款落座，亲自弹奏钢琴伴奏，丹尼斯便立在她身侧。他暗暗下了决心要拿出十二分的本事，证明自己虽在店里扫过地板，却也绝非只会干粗活的庸人。乐曲中许多旋律凄婉缠绵，而他心底对身旁这位美貌搭档怀有的深沉而尚不自知的情意，赋予了他的歌声一种深邃乃至时而近乎悲怆的感染力，既震颤人心，又柔情*叩心*，台下竟有不少人湿润了眼眶。他自己与旁人皆未察觉，他其实是在用歌声倾诉着自己的爱恋；就连克里斯蒂娜，尽管全副心神大半都扑在自己的琴键与唱段上，也不由惊诧于这歌声在自己心头掀起的波澜，更清楚地感到了全场听众深受震撼的深切反响。

当最后几个音符袅袅散尽，客厅的推拉隔门缓缓合拢。

丹尼斯今晚赢得了比克里斯蒂娜更胜一筹的成功——因为他发自肺腑而歌，故而直击人心。他的掌声不在于喧闹的拍手，而写在无数双湿润的眼眸与动容的脸庞上。克里斯蒂娜一眼便看穿并领会了这个结果。一抹哀伤而失落的神色浮上她的脸颊，她仿佛从心底生生挤出这句话似的，用低沉而幽怨的语气说道：“我身上必定是少了些什么。只怕我这辈子永远也触及不到真正的艺术殿堂。

Dennis was about to speak eagerly, when they were overwhelmed by the rush and confusion attendant on the breaking up of the entertainment. Part of the older guests at once left for their homes, and the rest stayed for supper. The parlors were to be cleared as soon as possible for dancing. Christine was joined by her father, who had sat in the audience, scarcely believing his eyes, much less his ears. Was that the young man who was blacking old Schwartz’s boots the other day?
His daughter was overwhelmed with compliments, but she took them very coolly and quietly, for her heart was full of bitterness. That which her ambitious spirit most desired she could not reach, and to the degree that she loved art was her disappointment keen. She almost envied poor Dennis, but she knew not the secret of his success; nor did he, either, in truth. His old manner returned, and he busied himself in rapidly packing up everything that he had brought. Mr. Ludolph, who had received a brief explanation from Christine, came and said, kindly, “Why, Fleet, you have blossomed out strongly today.”
“Indeed, sir, I think I have never had a more rigorous pruning,” was the reply.
When the story had been told Mr. Ludolph in full, he understood the remark. Christine was waiting for the crowd to disperse somewhat, in order to speak to Dennis also, for her sense of justice and her genuine admiration impelled her to warm and sincere acknowledgment. But at that moment Mr. Mellen came in, exclaiming, “Miss Ludolph, they are all waiting for you to lead the dance, for to you is given this honor by acclamation, and I plead your promise to be my partner;” and he carried her off, she meaning to return as soon as possible, and supposing Dennis would remain.
A moment after, light, airy music was heard in the front parlor, followed by the rhythmical cadence of light feet and the rustle of silks like a breeze through a forest.
For some reason as she went away Dennis’s heart sank within him. Reaction followed the strong excitements of the day, and a strange sense of weariness and despondency crept over him. The gay music in the other room seemed plaintive and far away, and the tripping feet sounded like the patter of rain on autumn leaves. The very lights appeared to burn dimmer, and the color to fade out of his life.

他女儿顿时被如潮的恭维话围了个水泄不通，可她却显得格外冷淡平静，因为她心里正积满了苦涩。她那颗好胜心切、志向高远的心最渴求的境界，她竟偏偏够不着；她有多么热爱艺术，此刻的失望便有多么刺骨。她几乎有些妒忌起可怜的丹尼斯来，却根本不知道他成功背后的秘诀——事实上，连丹尼斯自己也尚未参透。他很快又恢复了往日那副低调勤勉的做派，麻利地收拾打包起自己带过来的全部物件。卢多尔夫先生刚从克里斯蒂娜那里听了个大概解释，这时走上前来，和颜悦色地说道：“唔，弗利特，你今天可真是大放异彩、满树开花了呀。”

“诚然，先生，不过我想自己挨过的修剪恐怕也是平生最严苛的一回。”丹尼斯答道。

待克里斯蒂娜将白日里的风波原原本本告诉父亲之后，卢多尔夫先生方才领会了那句话里的机锋。克里斯蒂娜原想等人潮稍微散开些再去同丹尼斯说几句话，因为她心底的正义感与发自真心的钦佩，都驱使着她非向他致以一番诚挚热切的赞誉不可。然而恰在此时，梅伦先生走了进来，高声呼唤道：“卢多尔夫小姐，大伙儿可都在等您领舞呢，全场一致推举将这份殊荣献给您，我也谨请您履行先前的允诺，做我的舞伴！”说着便将她请了出去；她心里原本打定主意尽快抽身回来，以为丹尼斯必定还会留在原地。

片刻之后，前客厅里响起了轻快飘逸的舞曲声，紧接着便是轻盈舞步踏出的节奏韵律，以及绫罗绸缎摩挲出的沙沙声响，恰似微风拂过林梢。

不知何故，随着她转身离去，丹尼斯的一颗心蓦地沉了下去。白天一场接着一场的强烈激动过后，骤然袭来的反差感令他周身泛起一阵莫名的疲惫与消沉。隔壁客厅里欢快的乐曲听起来竟显得那么哀婉遥远，那轻快的脚步声响在他耳畔仿佛秋雨敲打落叶。连屋里的灯光似乎都黯淡了几分，人生的色彩也仿佛一下子褪了个干净。

Someone pushed back the sliding-door a little and passed into the room. Through the opening he caught a glimpse of the gay scene within. Suddenly Christine appeared floating lightly through the waltz in her gauzy drapery, as if in a white, misty cloud. Through the narrow opening she seemed a radiant, living portrait. But her partner whirled her out of the line of vision. Thus in the mazes of the dance she kept appearing and disappearing, flashing in sight one moment, leaving a blank in the crowded room the next.
“So it will ever be, I suppose,” he said to himself, bitterly; “chance and stolen glimpses my only privilege.”
Again she appeared, smiling archly on the man whose arm clasped her waist.
A frown black as night gathered on Dennis’s brow; then a sudden pallor overspread his face to his very lips. The revelation had come! Then for the first time he knew﻿—knew it as if written in letters of fire before him﻿—that he loved Christine Ludolph.
At first the knowledge stunned and bewildered him, and his mind was a confused blur; then as she appeared again, smiling upon and in the embrace of another man, a sharp sword seemed to pierce his heart.
Dennis was no faint shadow of a man who had frittered away in numberless flirtations what little heart he originally had. He belonged to the male species, with something of the pristine vigor of the first man, who said of the one woman of all the world, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh”; and one whom he had first seen but a few short months since now seemed to belong to him by the highest and divinest right. But could he ever claim his own?
In his morbid, wearied state, there seemed a “great gulf fixed” between them. For a moment he fairly felt faint and sick, as if he had received a wound. He was startled by hearing Miss Winthrop say at his side: “Mr. Fleet, you will not leave yet. I have many friends wishing an introduction to you. What is the matter? You look as if you were ill.”
At her voice he flushed painfully. He was so vividly conscious of his love himself that he felt that everyone else must be able to see it, and darkness and solitude now seemed a refuge.

他机械地将剩下的几件零碎物什收拾打点妥当，留待明早派人来取，随后沉重地靠在一根廊柱上，打算歇上一口气，再独自一人走进茫茫夜色之中。

这时有人推开一点推拉门，侧身走了进来。透过那道门缝，他瞥见了里面那片欢歌笑语的热闹景象。突然间，克里斯蒂娜一身轻纱曳地，乘着华尔兹的旋风轻盈飘过，宛如置身于一团洁白的迷雾流云之中。透过那道狭窄的门隙望去，她恰似一幅流光溢彩、栩栩如生的画中人。然而舞伴一个旋转，又将她卷出了他的视线。就这样，在舞池错综交织的人影迷宫里，她时隐时现，这一瞬耀眼地撞入眼帘，下一瞬又在拥挤的大厅里留下一片空茫。

“我想，往后永远也就是这样了吧，”他苦涩地暗自思忖，“只能靠着偶一为之的机缘与偷偷一瞥，权作我唯一享有的特权。”

她又一次旋身出现，正冲着那位手臂揽在她腰间的男子娇俏地微笑。

一道黑沉如夜的阴云瞬间聚拢在丹尼斯眉宇之间；紧接着，一阵突如其来的惨白从他脸颊一直蔓延到嘴唇。那恍然顿悟的时刻降临了！直到那一刻，他才生平头一回明白——清清楚楚地明白，仿佛那几个字正用熊熊火焰书写在他眼前一般——他爱上了克里斯蒂娜·卢多尔夫。

起初，这个念头震得他晕头转向、神魂俱散，脑子里一片混乱模糊；紧接着，当她再次旋转着进入视野、在另一个男人的怀抱里向对方展颜微笑时，仿佛有一柄利剑狠狠刺穿了他的胸膛。

丹尼斯绝不是那种在无数次逢场作戏的调情里把原本寥寥无几的一点真心挥霍殆尽的轻浮男子。他是顶天立地的真正男儿，血脉里还流淌着人类始祖那股纯朴炽烈的刚劲——当年那最初的男人望着世间独一无二的女子时曾说过：“这是我骨中的骨，肉中的肉”；而这个他不过短短数月前才初见的女子，此刻在他心中却仿佛凭着至高至圣的天命合该归属于他。然而，他这辈子果真能将属于自己的她迎回身边吗？

在他此刻病态而疲惫的心境中，两人之间仿佛横亘着一道“深渊隔绝”的鸿沟。有那么一瞬间，他真切地感到一阵头晕目眩、胃里翻搅，宛如当胸挨了一记重创。直到听见温思罗普小姐在身旁开口，他才猛然惊醒：“弗利特先生，您这就打算走了吗？我还有好几位朋友盼着让我替他们引见您呢。您怎么了？瞧您脸色难看得像是病了。”

听到她的声音，他窘迫得涨红了脸。他自己对这份爱意觉察得太过真切炽烈，竟疑心旁人也都一眼看得透彻，此刻只觉得黑暗与独处才是唯一能遮蔽自己的避风港。

Recovering himself by a great effort he said, “Pardon me, I do﻿—I am not well﻿—nothing is the matter﻿—a little rest and I shall be myself again.”

Pray do not judge Chicago society altogether by what you have seen here. Let me get you some refreshment, and then I will acquaint you with some people who can recognize a gentleman when they meet him.”
“No, Miss Winthrop,” said Dennis, courteously but firmly; “you are not in your own home, and by staying I should not be accepting your hospitality. “I am not surprised that you feel as you do. But give me the pleasure of welcoming you at my own home as soon as possible,” she said, and gave her hand to him in parting.
Dennis took it respectfully and bowed low, saying, “I shall not willingly deny myself so great a pleasure,” and was gone.

“瞧你对这位穿着一身旧铁锈铠甲的无名骑士倒是兴致勃勃得很哪。”（丹尼斯身上的那套礼服确实已经磨得相当破旧了。）
