Are you ready, with your aristocratic notions, to recognize chiefly Miss Brown’s title to position? What could her coat-of-arms be but the dollar symbol and the beer-barrel?”
“Come, remember she is our hostess.”
“You are right; I should not speak so here; but my indignation gets the better of me.”
“Would you invite him to your house?”
“Certainly. I have asked him; and what is more, he has promised to come. Supposing that he is poor, are not many of your noblemen as poor as poverty? My parlors shall be haunted only by men of ability and character.”
“You are not going to shut out this little heathen,” said Christine, putting her arm about her friend.
“Never!” said Miss Winthrop, returning the embrace with double warmth. Then she added, sadly: “You are not an unbeliever from conviction and knowledge, Christine, but from training and association. While I admire and honor your father as a splendid and gifted man, I regret his and your scepticism more deeply than you can ever know.”
“Well, Susie,” said Christine, with a smile, “if they shut out such as you from your Paradise, I do not wish to go there.”
“If, with my clear knowledge of the conditions of entrance, I *shut myself out*, I shall have no right to complain,” said Miss Winthrop, sadly.
But the absence of two such belles could not long remain unnoted; and, having been discovered, they were pounced upon by half a dozen young gentlemen, clamorous for the honor of their hands in the “German.”
In spite of herself, Christine was vexed and annoyed. Dennis had seemed, in his obscurity, a nice little bit of personal property, that she could use and order about as she pleased. He had been so subservient and eager to do her will, that she had never thought of him otherwise than as her “humble servant.” But now her own hand had suddenly given him the role of a fine gentleman. Christine was too logical to think of continuing to order about a man who could sing Mendelssohn’s music as Dennis had done.
She congratulated herself that the arrangement of the store was nearly completed, and that only one showroom was unfinished.
“I suppose he will be very dignified when we meet again,” she thought to herself. “I should not be at all surprised if my impulsive little friend Susie loses her heart to him. Well, I suppose she can to anyone she chooses.

“好吧，苏茜，”克里斯蒂娜微微一笑，说道，“倘若连你这样的人都被他们关在你们那个天国乐园的门外，那我可也压根儿不想去了。”

“倘若我明明清清楚楚地知晓进门的准则，却偏要*把自己关在门外*，那我便无权抱怨半句了。”温思罗普小姐神情忧伤地说道。

然而两位这般耀眼的美人缺席太久，终究瞒不过众人的眼睛；她们很快便被人寻着，立时被五六位年轻绅士一拥而上团团围住，个个争先恐后地抢着恳求有幸邀她们共跳一曲“德国风舞”。

克里斯蒂娜自己也不由得一阵莫名的烦躁与懊恼。先前丹尼斯籍籍无名、默默无闻的时候，他仿佛只是她手边一件合心顺意的小玩意儿，任凭她随心所欲地使唤差遣。他向来那般恭顺听命、急于讨她欢心，教她从来没把他当作别的人物，只当他是自己一名“卑微的听差”。可如今，竟是她自己亲手一把将他推上了风度翩翩的绅士席位。克里斯蒂娜素来头脑清醒、极讲逻辑，断不会糊涂到还指望去继续随意使唤一个能像丹尼斯方才那样唱出门德尔松乐章的男人。

她只好暗自庆幸店里的陈设布置已接近尾声，眼下只剩下一间陈列室尚未完工。

“想来下次再见面时，他一定会摆出一副端方持重的架子了，”她暗自思忖道，“要是我那位容易冲动的好友苏茜果真对他动了芳心，我也丝毫不会觉得稀奇。罢了，反正她爱倾心于谁便倾心于谁去吧。

至于我呢，无论贫富、无论愚智，这片土地上的男人都是一副德行。”她半声轻叹，随即毅然一头扎进了今晚喧嚣的欢宴之中，仿佛想要借此逃离自己的心事。

## XXX The Two Heights / 第三十章 两座高峰
===Original===

Dennis went home in a strange tumult of hopes and fears, but hope predominated, for evidently she cared little for Mr. Mellen. “The ice is broken at last,” he said. It was, but he was like to fall through into a very cold bath, though he knew it not. He was far too excited to sleep, and sat by his open window till the warm June night grew pale with the light of coming day.
Suddenly a bright thought struck him; a moment more and it became an earnest purpose. “I think I can paint something that may express to her what I dare not put in words.”
He immediately went up into the loft and prepared a large frame, so proportioned that two pictures could be painted side by side, one explanatory and an advance upon the other. He stretched his canvas over this, and sketched and outlined rapidly under the inspiration of his happy thought.
Christine came with her father to the store, as had been her former custom, and her face had its old expression. The listless, disappointed look was gone. She passed on, not appearing to see him while with her father, and Dennis’s heart sank again. “She surely knew where to look for me if she cared to look,” he said to himself. Soon after he went to the upper showroom to see to the hanging of a new picture.
“I am so glad your taste, instead of old Schwartz’s mathematics, has charge of this department now,” said a honeyed voice at his side. He was startled greatly.
“What is the matter? Are you nervous, Mr. Fleet? I had no idea that a lady could so frighten you.”
He was blushing like a girl, but said, “I have read that something within, rather than anything without, makes us cowards.”
“Ah, then you confess to a guilty conscience?” she replied, with a twinkle in her eye.
“I do not think I shall confess at all till I have a merciful confessor,” said Dennis, conscious of a deeper meaning than his light words might convey.
“ ‘The quality of mercy is not strained,’ therefore it is unfit for my use. I’ll none of it, but for each offence impose unlimited penance.”
“But suppose one must sin?”
“He must take the consequences then. Even your humane religion teaches that;” and with this parting arrow she vanished, leaving him too excited to hang his picture straight.
It all seemed a bewildering dream. Being so thoroughly taken by surprise and off his guard, he had said far more than he meant. But had she understood him?

===Chinese===

丹尼斯怀着希望与恐惧交织的奇异心潮回到家中，不过占上风的终究还是希望——因为显而易见，克里斯蒂娜对梅伦先生并无多少情意。“冰层总算是破开了！”他自言自语道。诚然，冰面是破开了，可他却不知自己险些一脚踩空、跌进刺骨的冰水里。他兴奋得全无睡意，索性坐在敞开的窗前，一直守到六月温暖的夜色渐渐褪去、泛起黎明将至的微光。

突然间，一个绝妙的念头闪过他的脑海；转瞬之间，这念头便化作了一桩笃定的志向。“我想，我能用画笔向她倾诉那些我不敢用言语说出口的心意。”

他立刻起身走上阁楼，动手做了一只大画框，尺寸比例恰好能容得下两幅画并排绘制——一幅彼此呼应、阐明心迹，另一幅则在境界上更进一层。他在画框上绷紧画布，乘着这股幸福灵感的驱使，迅速勾勒出草图与轮廓。

克里斯蒂娜照旧随父亲来到画店，脸上又恢复了往日那副冷峻神情。那股百无聊赖、黯然失落的模样已然消失无踪。她随父亲从旁走过时，似乎全未看见他，丹尼斯的心顿时又沉了下去。“她若真有心瞧我一眼，自然知道该往哪儿寻我。”他暗自叹道。不久之后，他上楼去陈列室照看一幅新画的悬挂。

“我真高兴眼下掌管这个部门的是你的品味，而不是老施瓦茨那套死板的算术章法。”身旁忽然响起一个甜蜜动听的声音。他猛地吓了一跳。

“怎么了？弗利特先生，你紧张什么？我可不知道一位女士竟能把你吓成这副模样。”

他顿时像个小姑娘似的涨红了脸，却镇定答道：“我曾在书上读过，真正使人变成懦夫的，往往不是身外之物，而是内心的某些东西。”

“啊，这么说来，你是招认自己问心有愧喽？”她眼波流转，眨着眼睛戏谑地回道。

“在寻到一位肯施慈悲的听忏悔神父之前，我可不打算招认半个字。”丹尼斯说道，心里清楚自己这句看似轻松的玩笑话里藏着更深的意味。

“‘慈悲不是出于勉强’，故而于我毫无用处。我可半点也不要什么慈悲，反倒要针对每一桩罪过课以无休无止的苦行赎罪。”

“可倘若有人明知是罪却身不由己呢？”

“那他便只管承担后果便是。连你们那一套讲究仁慈的宗教不也是这么教导的吗？”她丢下这支临别冷箭，转身便没了踪影，只留下他心潮澎湃、手忙脚乱，连手里那幅画都挂不端正了。

这一切恍如一场迷离恍惚的梦境。方才猝不及防、毫无防备之下，他脱口说出的话远比自己本意想说的多得多。可她听懂他的弦外之音了吗？

Yes, better than he had himself, and laughed at his answers with their covert meanings.
She spent the next two days in sketching and outlining his various expressions as far as possible from memory. She would learn to catch those evanescent lines﻿—that something which makes the human face eloquent, though the lips are silent.
Dennis was in a maze, but he repeated to himself jubilantly again, “The ice is broken.” That evening at Mr. Bruder’s he asked for studies in ice.
“Vy, dat is out of season,” said Mr. Bruder, with a laugh.
“No, now is just the time. It is a nice cool subject for this hot weather. Please oblige me; for certain reasons I wish to be able to paint ice perfectly.”
Arctic scenery was Mr. Bruder’s forte, on which he specially prided himself. He was too much of a gentleman to ask questions, and was delighted to find the old zest returning in his pupil. They were soon constructing bergs, caves, and grottoes of cold blue ice. Evening after evening, while sufficient light lasted, they worked at this study. Dennis’s whole soul seemed bent on the formation of ice. After a month of labor Mr. Bruder said, “I hope you vill get over dis by fall, or ve all freeze to death.”
“One of these days I shall explain,” said Dennis, smiling.
The evening of the second day after the little rencounter in the showroom, Mr. Ludolph sat enjoying his cigar, and Christine was at the piano playing a difficult piece of music.
“Come, father,” she said, “here is a fine thing just from Germany. There is a splendid tenor solo in it, and I want you to sing it for me.”
“Pshaw!” said her father, “why did I not think of it before?” and he rang the bell. “Here, Brandt, go down to the store, and if Mr. Fleet is there ask him if he will come up to my rooms for a little while.”
Brandt met Dennis just starting for his painting lesson, but led him a willing captive, to give Christine instruction unconsciously.
She, whose strategy had brought it all about, smiled at her success. It was not her father’s tenor she wanted, but Dennis’s face; and her father should unknowingly work her will. The girl had learned so much from the wily man of the world that she was becoming his master.
Dennis came and entered with a thrill of delight what was to him enchanted ground. Mr. Ludolph was affable, Christine kind, but she looked more than she said.

丹尼斯踏进这间在他眼中恍如仙境般的房间时，心头涌起一阵欣喜的战栗。卢多尔夫先生和蔼可亲，克里斯蒂娜也温婉有礼，只是她眼神所传递的意味，远比嘴上说出来的话多得多。

Dennis sang the solo, after one or two efforts, correctly. Then Mr. Ludolph brought out a piece of music that he wished to try; Christine found others; and before they knew it the evening had passed. Quite a knot of delighted listeners gathered in the street opposite. This Christine pointed out to her father with evident annoyance.
“Well, my dear,” he said, “hotel life in a crowded city renders escape from such things impossible.”
But a purpose was growing in her mind of which she spoke soon after. Throughout the evening she had studied Dennis’s face as much as she could without attracting notice, and the thought grew upon her that at last she had found a path to the success she so craved.
“You seem to have gone to work with your old interest,” said her father, as he came out of his room the next morning and found Christine at her easel.
“I shall try it again,” she said, briefly.
“That is right,” said he. “The idea of being daunted by one partial failure! I predict for you such success as will satisfy even your fastidious taste.”
“We shall see,” she said. “I hope, too.” But she would not have her father know on what grounds. He might regard the experiment as a dangerous one for herself as well as for Dennis, and she decided to keep her plan entirely secret.
She now came to the store daily, and rarely went away without giving Dennis a smile or word of recognition. But he noticed that she ever did this in a casual manner, and in a way that would not attract attention. He also took the hint, and never was obtrusive or demonstrative, but it was harder work for his frank nature. When unobserved, his glances grew more ardent day by day. So far from checking these, she encouraged them, but, when in any way he sought to put his feelings into words, she changed the subject instantly and decidedly. This puzzled him, for he did not understand that looks could be painted, but not words. The latter were of no use to her. But she led him on skilfully, and, from the unbounded power his love gave her, played upon his feelings as adroitly as she touched her grand piano.
Soon after the company at Miss Winthrop’s, she said to him, “You received several invitations the other evening, did you not?”
“Yes.”
“Accept them. Go into society. It will do you good.” Thus he soon found himself involved in a round of sociables, musicales, and now and then a large party.

Christine was usually present, radiant, brilliant, the cynosure of all eyes, but ever coolly self-possessed. At first she would greet him with distant politeness, or pretend not to see him at all, but before the evening was over would manage to give him a half-hour in which she would be kind and even gentle at times, but very observant. Then for the rest of the evening he would find no chance to approach. It appeared that she was deeply interested in him, enjoyed his society, and was even becoming attached to him, but that for some reason she determined that no one should notice this, and that matters should only go so far. Poor Dennis could not know that he was only her unconscious instructor in painting, paid solely in the coin of false smiles and delusive hopes. At times, though, she would torture him dreadfully. Selecting one of her many admirers, she would seem to smile upon his suit, and poor Dennis would writhe in all the agonies of jealousy, for he was very human, and had all the normal feeling of a strong man. She would then watch his face grow pale and his manner restless, as quietly and critically as an entomologist regards the struggles of an insect beneath his microscope. Again, she would come to him all grace and sweetness, and his fine face would light up with hope and pleasure. She would say honeyed nothings, but study him just as coolly in another aspect.
Thus she kept him hot and cold by turns﻿—now lifting him to the pinnacle of hope, again casting him down into the valley of fear and doubt. What she wanted of him was just what she had not﻿—feeling, intense, varied feeling, so that, while she remained ice, she could paint as if she felt; and with a gifted woman’s tact, and with the power of one loved almost to idolatry, she caused every chord of his soul, now in happy harmony, now in painful discord, to vibrate under her skilful touch. But such a life was very wearing, and he was failing under it. Moreover, he was robbing himself of sleep in the early morning, that he might work on his picture in the loft of the store, for which he asked of poor Mr. Bruder nothing but ice.

Christine desired the change for several reasons. There was a room in the house that would just suit her as a studio. She detested the publicity of a hotel. The furnishing of an elegant house was a form of activity most pleasing to her energetic nature, and she felt a very strong wish to try her skill in varied effect before her grand effort in the Ludolph Hall of the future.
But in addition to these motives was another, of which she did not speak to her father. In the privacy of her own home she could pursue that peculiar phase of art study in which she was absorbed. Her life had now become a most exciting one. She ever seemed on the point of obtaining the power to portray the eloquence of passion, feeling, but there was a subtle something that still eluded her. She saw it daily, and yet could not reproduce it. She seemed to get the features right, and yet they were dead, or else the emotion was so exaggerated as to suggest weak sentimentality, and this of all things disgusted her. Every day she studied the expressive face of Dennis Fleet, the mysterious power seemed nearer her grasp. Her effort was now gaining all the excitement of a chase. She saw before her just what she wanted, and it seemed that she had only to grasp her pencil or brush, and place the fleeting expressions where they might always appeal to the sympathy of the beholder. Nearly all her studies now were the human face and form, mainly those of ladies, to disarm suspicion. Of course she took no distinct likeness of Dennis. She sought only to paint what his face expressed.

===Chinese===

卢多尔夫先生沉吟着说道，“你这股异想天开里头，倒比我料想的更有几分章法盘算。容我仔细斟酌斟酌，毕竟这步棋干系甚大，马虎草率不得。”

卢多尔夫先生果然认真琢磨了一番；处理完店里几桩紧要事务后，他便亲自过去看了一趟那处房产。几天之后，他回来吃晚饭，随手把地契扔进了女儿膝头。她草草扫了一眼，双眸顿时闪烁起欣喜与得胜的光芒。

“您且瞧着，为了报答您这份盛情，我要把您的日子打理得多么舒适惬意吧。”她说道。

“哦，别来这套，”她父亲大笑着摆摆手，“那可不是重点。这是一笔生意投机，赌上的可是你的商业眼光与名声。”

“我愿接受考验。”她胸有成竹地点了点头，应声答道。

克里斯蒂娜执意要搬出来自立门户，原是出于好几重缘故。那栋宅子里正好有一间屋子极合她意，最宜改作画室；她向来深恶痛绝旅馆里那种众目睽睽的喧嚣公开；亲手布置一栋雅致豪宅正合她精力充沛的性子，而且在日后大显身手打造未来的卢多尔夫庄园之前，她也很想先试一试自己驾驭各种艺术格调的本领。

然而除却这些摆在明面上的动机之外，她心底还藏着另一桩绝不肯对父亲吐露的私心。在自家宅院深锁的私密天地里，她就能毫无顾忌地钻研自己眼下全神贯注的那门奇特画艺了。如今她的生活简直变得紧张刺激到了极点。她总觉得自己离掌握那种能描绘出炽烈情感与澎湃激情之神韵的笔力只有一步之遥，可总有一丝微妙难言的神髓在指尖悄然溜走。她天天亲眼看见它，却偏偏落不到画布上。五官轮廓明明画得毫厘不差，画面却偏偏死气沉沉；要不就是把情绪渲染得太过夸张，显得像廉价的矫揉造作——而在世上一切事物当中，唯有矫揉造作最令她作呕。她一天天仔仔细细地揣摩着丹尼斯·弗利特那张富于表现力的脸庞，那股神秘莫测的笔力仿佛离她越来越近。如今她这番苦功已然带上了一场围猎追逐般的全部刺激与狂热。她眼睁睁看着自己梦寐以求的猎物近在咫尺，仿佛只需一把抓起铅笔或画笔，便能将那些转瞬即逝的神情稳稳定格在画布上，叫它日后永远扣动观者的心弦。眼下她几乎所有的习作都是人物的面容与体态，且为免生疑窦，画的多半是女性肖像。她当然绝不曾照着丹尼斯的模样去画半点肖像轮廓；她所要捕捉描摹的，仅仅是他脸庞上流露出的那份真情实感。

===Original===

At times she seemed about to succeed, and excitement brought color to her cheek and fire to her eye that made her dazzlingly beautiful to poor Dennis. Then she would smile upon him in such a bewitching, encouraging way that it was little wonder his face lighted up with all the glory of hope.
If once more she could have him about her as when rearranging the store, and, without the restraint of curious eyes, could play upon his heart, then pass at once to her easel with the vivid impression of what she saw, she might catch the coveted power, and become able to portray, as if she felt, that which is the inspiration of all the highest forms of art﻿—feeling.
That evening, Dennis, at Mr. Ludolph’s request, came to the hotel to try some new music. During the evening Mr. Ludolph was called out for a little time. Availing himself of the opportunity, Dennis said, “You seem to be working with all your old zest and hope.”
“Yes,” she said, “with greater hope than ever before.”
“Won’t you show me something that you are doing?”
“No, not yet. I am determined that when you see work of mine again the fatal defect which you pointed out shall be absent.”
His eyes and face became eloquent with the hope she inspired. Was her heart, awakening from its long winter of doubt and indifference, teaching her to paint? Had she recognized the truth of his assurance that she must feel, and then she could portray feeling? and had she read in his face and manner that which had created a kindred impulse in her heart? He was about to speak, the ice of his reserve and prudence fast melting under what seemed good evidence that her smiles and kindness might be interpreted in accordance with his longings. She saw and anticipated.
“With all your cleverness, Mr. Fleet, I may prove you at fault, and become able to portray what I do not feel or believe.”
“You mean to say that you work from your old standpoint merely?” asked Dennis, feeling as if a sunny sky had suddenly darkened.
“I do not say that at all, but that I do not work from yours.”
“And yet you hope to succeed?”
“I think I am succeeding.”
Perplexity and disappointment were plainly written on his face. She, with a merry and half-malicious laugh, turned to the piano, and sung:

> “From Mount Olympus’ snowy height

The gods look down on human life:

Beneath contending armies fight;

All undisturbed they watch the strife.”

===Chinese===

有些时候，她几乎眼看就要大功告成，那股亢奋令她双颊飞红、双眸炯炯放光，落在可怜的丹尼斯眼里简直美得炫目夺魂。每逢此时，她又会对着他绽放出那般妖娆迷人、充满鼓舞意味的浅笑，也难怪他整张脸顿时被希望的光彩照得熠熠生辉。

只要能像从前一起重新布置画店时那样，再度把他留在自己身旁，避开那些窥探好奇的眼睛，随心所欲地拨弄他的心弦，然后趁着脑海中映象鲜活滚烫，立刻转身奔回画架前挥毫落笔，她兴许就能一把抓住那梦寐以求的本领——哪怕自己心里其实麻木无感，却能画得宛如动了真情一般，从而掌控一切最高艺术殿堂共同的灵魂源泉——“真情”。

那天傍晚，丹尼斯应卢多尔夫先生之邀来到旅馆，试唱几首新到的曲谱。其间卢多尔夫先生因事被人叫出去耽搁了片刻。丹尼斯趁着这难得的空当开口道：“近来您似乎又带着往日全副的热忱与希望动笔作画了。”

“是的，”她答道，“比从前任何时候都更有希望。”

“能让我瞧瞧您眼下正在画的作品吗？”

“不行，还不到时候。我已立下誓言，等你下次再看到我的画作时，你从前点破的那个致命缺陷，定然已经荡然无存。”

他双眸炯炯，神采飞扬，浑身上下都在诉说着被她燃起的希望。莫非她那颗长久以来冰封在怀疑与冷漠严冬里的心终于苏醒过来，开始教她如何作画了吗？莫非她终于领悟了他曾笃定告诉她的那句真理——人必须先有真情，方能画出真情？莫非她已从他的神色与举止中读出了那份情意，也在自己心头激起了同样的涟漪？他正要吐露心声，平日里严防死守的那层矜持与审慎的坚冰，眼看就要在这些看似足以印证她浅笑温存绝非虚情假意的证据面前迅速消融。可克里斯蒂娜一眼便看穿了他的心思，抢先截住了话头。

“弗利特先生，任你再聪明绝顶，说不定我偏要证明你看走了眼——即便我自己既不动情也不相信，我照样能画得情真意切、维妙维肖。”

“您这话是说，您至今仍完全站在从前那个立场上作画吗？”丹尼斯问道，只觉头顶原本晴朗灿烂的天空仿佛刹那间乌云密布。

“我可根本没这么说，我只是说，我绝不站在你的立场上作画。”

“可即便如此，您仍指望能够成功？”

“我想我正在走向成功。”

困惑与深深的失望清清楚楚地写在了他脸上。她却发出一串欢快而又带着几分恶作剧意味的轻笑，转身坐回钢琴前，放声唱道：

> “自奥林匹斯冰雪皑皑之巅，

众神冷眼俯瞰尘世悲欢：

山脚下两军拼杀血战正酣，

天庭诸神自顾自悠然旁观。”

===Original===

Dennis looked at her earnestly, and after a moment said, “Will you please play that accompaniment again?”
She complied, and he sang:

> “Your Mount Olympus’ icy peak

Is barren waste, by cold winds swept:

Another height I gladly see,

Where God o’er human sorrow wept.”

She turned a startled and almost wistful face to him, for he had given a very unexpected answer to her cold, selfish philosophy, which was so apt and sudden as to seem almost inspired.
“Do you refer to Christ’s weeping over Jerusalem?” she asked.
“Yes.”
She sat for a little time silent and thoughtful, and Dennis watched her keenly. Suddenly her brow darkened, and she said, bitterly: “Delusion! If He had been a God He would not have idly wept over sorrow. He would have banished it.”
Dennis was about to reply eagerly, when Mr. Ludolph entered, and music was resumed. But it was evident that Dennis’s lines had disturbed the fair sceptic’s equanimity.

===Chinese===

丹尼斯凝重地注视着她，过了片刻，开口说道：“劳驾您，能把刚才那段伴奏再弹一遍吗？”

她依言重弹，他随即放声和唱道：

> “你那奥林匹斯冰雪寒峰，

不过荒原寥廓、朔风凛冽：

我却欣然仰望另一座高峰，

神在彼处曾为人间哀哭洒泪。”

她猛地转过脸来，神情震惊中透着几分怅然渴望地望着他——因为她那套冰冷自私的人生哲学，竟遭到了这般出人意料、偏又贴切迅捷得宛如神启般的回击。

“你指的莫非是基督为耶路撒冷哀哭那件事？”她问道。

“正是。”

她沉默着坐了一会儿，若有所思，丹尼斯则在旁目不转睛地观察着她。突然间，她的眉头阴沉下来，带着几分苦涩冷笑道：“荒诞妄念！倘若他真是位神明，又何必面对世间苦痛白白徒劳掉眼泪？他大可直接将苦痛一扫而空便是。”

丹尼斯正要急切地开口辩驳，恰在此时卢多尔夫先生推门走了进来，弹唱只得重新接续下去。但显而易见，丹尼斯刚才唱出的那几行诗句，已经深深搅乱了这位美丽怀疑论者内心的平静。

## XXXIII The Two Pictures / 第三十三章 两幅画作
===Original===

When Christine saw that Dennis was not in the room, she rushed to a window only in time to see his retreating form passing down the street. For a moment she felt like one left alone to perish on a sinking wreck. His words, so assured in their tones, seemed like those of a prophet. Conscience echoed them, and a chill of fear came over her heart. What if he were right? What if she had let the one golden opportunity of her life pass? Even though she had stolen her inspiration from him through guile and cruelty, had he not enabled her to accomplish more than in all her life before? To what might he not have led her, if she had put her hand frankly and truthfully in his? There are times when to those most bewildered in mazes of error light breaks, clear and unmistakable, defining right and wrong with terrible distinctness. Such an hour was this to Christine. The law of God written on her heart asserted itself, and she trembled at the guilty thing she saw herself to be. But there seemed no remedy save in the one she had driven away, never to return, as she believed. After a brief but painful revery she exclaimed: “But what am I thinking of? What can he or any man of this land be to me?”
Then pride, her dominant trait, awoke as she recalled his words.
“He despises me, does he? I will teach him that I belong to a sphere he cannot touch﻿—the poor infatuated youth! And did he dream that I, Christine Ludolph, could give him my hand? He shall learn some day that none in this land could receive that honor, and none save the proudest in my own may hope for it. The idea of my giving up my ancient and honorable name for the sake of this unknown Yankee youth.”
Bold, proud words that her heart did not echo.
But pride and anger were now her controlling impulses, and with the strong grasp of her resolute will she crushed back her gentler and better feelings, and became more icy and hard than ever.
By such choice and action, men and women commit moral suicide.
With a cold, white face, and a burnished gleam in her eyes, she went to the easel and commenced painting out the ominous black stain.
“I’ll prove him a false prophet also. I will be an artist without passing through all his sentimental and superstitious phases that have so amused me during the past weeks. I have seen his lovelorn face too often not to be able to reproduce it and its various expressions.”

===Chinese===

克里斯蒂娜发觉丹尼斯已不在屋里，连忙奔到窗前，却只来得及看见他沿着长街渐行渐远的背影。有那么一瞬间，她只觉自己宛如被人独自抛弃在一艘正在沉没的破船上，孤立无援地静待灭顶之灾。他临走前那番话语声调笃定，简直宛若先知的预言。良心在心底阵阵回响，一阵寒意刺透了她的心房。倘若他说得对呢？倘若她亲手放走了平生唯一一次千载难逢的良机呢？纵然她是用诡计与残忍手段从他身上窃取了灵感，可难道不是他才令她画出了毕生从未企及的佳作吗？倘若她肯坦荡真诚地将手交到他手里，他本该能引领她登上何等境界啊！有些时候，哪怕对于深陷谬误迷宫而茫然失措的人，一道澄明无误的灵光也会骤然破空而至，以令人战栗的清晰将是非对错界画分明。对于克里斯蒂娜而言，此刻正是这样一个时刻。铭刻在她心版上的上帝律法苏醒了，她看着自己这副有罪的灵魂，不禁浑身战栗。然而，除了那个已被她赶走、且她深信永不会再回头的人之外，世上似乎再无解救之方。短暂而痛苦地沉思了片刻之后，她忽然失声叫道：“可我到底在胡思乱想些什么？他，或者这片土地上的任何男人，与我又有什么相干？”

随后，她回忆起他方才的言辞，骨子里那股最根深蒂固的骄傲瞬间被激醒了。

“他竟敢鄙夷我，是吗？我偏要让他明白，我属于一个他高攀不上的世界——这个可怜的痴心妄想的小子！他莫非还真做起白日梦来，以为我克里斯蒂娜·卢多尔夫会下嫁于他不成？有朝一日他自会明白，在这片土地上绝无一人配得上那份殊荣，纵使在我的故土，也唯有最高门第的俊彦方敢心存冀望。竟幻想我为了这么个不知从哪儿冒出来的美国佬小子，舍弃自己古老而尊贵的姓氏！”

话说得斩钉截铁、傲气十足，心底却偏偏没有半点回响。

然而此刻傲慢与怒火已然彻底主宰了她的心神，她咬紧牙关，凭着那股铁石般坚毅的意志力，硬生生将内心深处柔善温情的一面狠狠压了回去，变得比以往任何时候都更加冷酷、更加坚硬。

世间男女正是凭着这般抉择与行径，亲手扼杀了自己的道德良知。

她脸色惨白如冰，眼底闪着一道冷冽锐利的寒光，走到画架前，动手涂去画布上那块不祥的黑斑。

“我还要证明他是个假先知！用不着经历他过去几周里叫我看得发笑的那些多愁善感与迷信痴狂，我照样能成为一名大画家！他那副魂不守舍的情痴模样，我早已瞧过无数遍，闭着眼睛也能把它以及它的千般神态重现出来。”

===Original===

Her strokes were quick and almost fierce.
“Mrs. Dennis Fleet, ha! ha! ha!” and her laugh was as harsh and discordant as the feeling that prompted it.
Again, a little later: “He despises me! Well, he is the first man that ever dared to say that;” and her face was flushed and dark with anger.

Dennis at first walked rapidly from the scene of his bitter disappointment, but his steps soon grew slow and feeble. The point of endurance was passed. Body and mind acting and reacting on each other had been taxed beyond their powers, and both were giving way. He felt that they were, and struggled to reach the store before the crisis should come. Weak and trembling, he mounted the steps, but fell fainting across the threshold. One of the clerks saw him fall and gave the alarm. Mr. Ludolph, Mr. Schwartz, and others hastened to the spot. Dennis was carried to his room, and a messenger was despatched for Dr. Arten. Ernst, with flying feet, and wild, frightened face, soon reached his home in De Koven Street, and startled his father and mother with the tidings.
The child feared that Dennis was dead, his face was so thin and white. Leaving the children in Ernst’s care, both Mr. and Mrs. Bruder, prompted by their strong gratitude to Dennis, rushed through the streets as if distracted. Their intense anxiety and warm German feeling caused them to heed no more the curious glances cast after them than would a man swimming for life note the ripple he made.
When Dennis regained consciousness, they, and Mr. Ludolph and Dr. Arten, were around him. At first his mind was confused, and he could not understand it all.
“Where am I?” he asked, feebly, “and what has happened?”
“Do not be alarmed; you have only had a faint turn,” said the doctor.
“Oh, Mr. Fleet, you vork too hart, you vork too hart; I knew dis vould come,” sobbed Mrs. Bruder.
“Why, his duties in the store have not been so onerous of late,” said Mr. Ludolph, in some surprise.
“It is not der vork in der store, but he vork nearly all night too. Den he haf had trouble, I know he haf. Do he say no vort about him?”
Dennis gave Mrs. Bruder a sudden warning look, and then, through the strong instinct to guard his secret, roused himself.
“Is it anything serious, doctor?” he asked.

她落笔迅疾，几乎带着几分狠劲。

“丹尼斯·弗利特太太，哈哈哈！”她的笑声刺耳而走调，一如催生出这串笑声的心境。

过了一会儿，她又咬牙切齿地念叨了一句：“他鄙夷我！哼，他倒是平生头一个敢对我说出这种话的男人！”说罢，她气得满脸涨红，神色阴沉。

---

丹尼斯起初大步流星地逃离了那个令他心碎绝望的地方，可没走多远，脚步便渐渐变得沉重而虚浮。他早已熬过了身心所能承受的极限。肉体与精神彼此牵扯、互相煎熬，双双耗损到了油尽灯枯的地步，终于一齐垮了下来。他清楚感觉到大限将近，只拼着最后一口气挣扎着要赶回画店，免得在半路上倒下。他步履蹒跚、浑身发抖地踏上台阶，却一头栽倒在门槛上昏死过去。一名店员瞧见他倒地，连忙高声呼救。卢多尔夫先生、施瓦茨先生等人闻讯急忙赶了过来。众人将丹尼斯抬回他自己的屋子，又立刻打发人去请阿滕医生。恩斯特撒开飞毛腿，一张小脸吓得惨白失色，一路狂奔跑回德科文街的家，把这个消息惊慌失措地告诉了父母。

看丹尼斯瘦削苍白得没有半点血色，这孩子真怕他已经死了。布鲁德夫妇记挂着丹尼斯的救命大恩，顾不得多想，把弟妹全托付给恩斯特照看，双双神色惶急地穿过街头狂奔而来。那份揪心的焦虑与德国人特有的炽热真情，叫他俩对路人投来的诧异目光浑然不觉，宛如一个在生死线上挣扎泳渡的人绝不会去留意身旁溅起了几朵水花。

等丹尼斯苏醒过来时，布鲁德夫妇、卢多尔夫先生和阿滕医生正围在榻前。起初他神思恍惚，怎么也弄不清眼前的情形。

“我这是在哪儿？”他气若游丝地问道，“出了什么事？”

The physician looked grave, and said, “Your pulse and whole appearance indicate great exhaustion and physical depression, and I also fear that fever may set in.”
“I think you are right,” said Dennis. “I feel as if I were going to be ill. My mind has a tendency to wander. Mr. Ludolph, will you permit me to go home? If I am to be sick, I want to be with my mother.”
Mr. Ludolph looked inquiringly at the doctor, who said significantly, in a low tone, “I think it would be as well.”
“Certainly, Fleet,” said his employer; “though I hope it is only a temporary indisposition, and that you will be back in a few days. You must try and get a good night’s rest, and so be prepared for the journey in the morning.”
“With your permission I will go at once. A train leaves now in an hour, and by morning I can be at home.”
“I scarcely think it prudent,” began the doctor.
“Oh, certainly not tonight,” said Mr. Ludolph, also.
“Pardon me, I must go at once,” interrupted Dennis, briefly and so decidedly that the gentlemen looked at each other and said no more.
“Mr. Bruder,” he continued, “I must be indebted to you for a real proof of your friendship. In that drawer you will find my money. The key is in my pocketbook. Will you get a carriage and take me to the depot at once? and can you be so kind as to go on home with me? I cannot trust myself alone. Mrs. Bruder, will you pack up what you think I need?” His faithful friends hastened to do his bidding.
“Mr. Ludolph, you have been very kind to me. I am sorry this has occurred, but cannot help it. I thank you gratefully, and will now trespass on your valuable time no longer.”
Mr. Ludolph, feeling that he could be of no further use, said: “You will be back in a week, Fleet. Courage. Goodbye.”
Dennis turned eagerly to the doctor and said: “Can you not give me something that will reduce the fever and keep me sane a little longer? I know that I am going to be delirious, but would reach the refuge of home first.”
A prescription was given and immediately procured, and the doctor went away shaking his head.
“This is the way people commit suicide. They know no more about, or pay no more heed to, the laws of health than the laws of China. Here is the result: This young fellow has worked in a way that would break down a cast-iron machine, and now may never see Chicago again.”

In the gray dawn Ethel Fleet, summoned from her rest, received her son, weak, unconscious, muttering in delirium, and not recognizing even her familiar face. He was indeed a sad, painful contrast to the ruddy, buoyant youth who had left her a few short months before, abounding in hope and life. But she comforted herself with the thought that neither sin nor shame had brought him home.
We need not dwell on the weary weeks that followed. Dennis had every advantage that could result from good medical skill and the most faithful nursing. But we believe that his life lay rather in his mother’s prayers of faith. In her strong realization of the spiritual world she would go continually into the very presence of Jesus, and say, “Lord, he whom Thou lovest is sick”; or, like parents of old, she would seem by her importunity to bring the Divine Physician to his very bedside.
Mr. Bruder, too, insisted on remaining, and watched with the unwearied faithfulness of one who felt that he owed to Dennis far more than life. It was indeed touching to see this man, once so desperate and depraved, now almost as patient and gentle as the mother herself, sitting by his unconscious friend, often turning his eyes heavenward and muttering in deep guttural German as sincere a prayer as ever passed human lips, that Dennis might be spared.
The hand of God seemed about to take him from them, but their strong, loving faith laid hold of that hand, and put upon it the restraint that only reverent, believing prayer can. Dennis lived. After many days delirium ceased, and the confused mind became clear. But during his delirium Ethel and Mr. Bruder learned from the oft-repeated words, “Cruel, cruel Christine!” the nature of the wound that had nearly destroyed his life.

随后那几个漫长难熬的星期，我们不必细表。丹尼斯得到了高明医术与最尽心照料所能带来的一切益处。但我们深信，真正挽回他性命的，更是他母亲出于信心的迫切祈祷。在她对灵界无比真切的感知中，她仿佛时常径直走到耶稣面前恳求：“主啊，你所爱的人病了”；又仿佛古时候那些苦苦哀求的父母一般，凭着那份执拗不懈的恳切，竟将那位神圣的大医师请到了儿子的病榻之畔。

Fleet was here this afternoon, and gave some finishing touches to my studio. I do not think I shall need him any more.”

“What is the matter?” said her father, hastily; “you are not going to faint also, are you?”
“No,” said Christine, quietly again; “but I am tired and nervous, and you told your news so abruptly! Why, it seemed but a moment ago he was here at work, and now he is dangerously ill. What an uncertain stumbling forward in the dark life is!”
This was a style of moralizing peculiarly distasteful to Mr. Ludolph﻿—all the more repugnant because it seemed true, and brought home in Dennis’s experience. Anything that interfered with his plans and interests, even though it might be God’s providence, always angered him. And now he was irritated at the loss of one of his best clerks, just as he was becoming of great value; so he said, sharply: “I hope you are not leaning toward the silly cant of mysterious providence. Life is uncertain stumbling only to fools who can’t see the chances that fortune throws in their way, or recognize the plain laws of health and success. This young Fleet has been putting two days’ work in one for the past four months, and now perhaps his work is done forever, for the doctor looked very grave over him.”
Again the shadow of night proved most friendly to Christine. Her face had a frightened, guilty look that it was well her father did not see, or he would have wrung from her the whole story. She felt the chill of a terrible dread at heart. If he should die, her conscience would give a fearful verdict against her. She stood trembling, feeling almost powerless to move.
“Come,” said her father, sharply, “I am hungry and tired.”
“I will ring for lights and supper,” said Christine hastily, and then fled to her own room.
When she appeared, her father was sitting at the table impatiently awaiting her. But her face was so white, and there was such an expression in her eyes, that he started and said, “What is the matter?”
His question irritated her, and she replied as sharply as he had spoken.

Again the whole scene passed before her, and she dwelt upon every word, as she was beginning often to do now, in painful revery. When she came to the words, “I too mean to be an artist. I could show you a picture that would tell you far more of what I mean than can my poor words,” she started up, and, hastily arraying herself for the street, was soon on her way to the Art Building.
No one heeded her movements there, and she went directly upstairs to his room. Though simple and plain, it had unmistakably been the abode of a gentleman and a person of taste. It was partially dismantled, and in disorder from his hasty departure, and she found nothing which satisfied her quest there. She hastened away, glad to escape from a place where everything seemed full of mute reproach, and next bent her steps to the top floor of the building. In a part half-filled with antiquated lumber, and seldom entered, she saw near a window facing the east an easel with canvas upon it. She was startled at the throbbing of her heart.
“It is only climbing these long stairs,” she said; but her words were belied by the hesitating manner and eager face with which she approached and removed the covering from the canvas.
She gazed a moment and then put out her hand for something by which to steady herself. His chair was near, and she sank into it, exclaiming: “He has indeed painted more than he﻿—more than anyone﻿—could put into words. He has the genius that I have not. All here is striking and original;” and she sat with her eyes riveted to a painting that had revealed to her﻿—herself.
Here was the secret of Dennis’s toil and early work. Here were the results of his insatiable demand for the incongruous elements of ice and sunlight.
Side by side were two emblematic pictures. In the first there opened before Christine a grotto of ice. The light was thin and cold but very clear. Stalactites hung glittering from the vaulted roof. Stalagmites in strange fantastic forms rose to meet them.

===Chinese===

一连好几天，她咬着牙死撑着画下去，却发觉自己的灵感早已枯竭殆尽。

终于，她绝望地把画笔一扔，失声喊道：“我再也抓不住那种神韵了！那个可恶的家伙，眼里不是对着我笑，就是冲着我皱眉冷视。只怕他真是说对了：我那唯一的一次成功，既是头一回，也是最后一回！”说着，她闷闷不乐、满怀绝望地将头埋进了双掌之中。那一幕幕往事再次浮现在眼前，正如她如今常做的那样，她在痛苦的追忆中细细咀嚼着他说过的每一个字。当回想起那句“我也立志要成为一名画家。我能给您看一幅画，比起我这笨拙的言辞，它更能向您道出我心中百倍千倍的真意”时，她猛然站起身来，胡乱换上一身出门的衣裳，匆匆朝着艺术大厦赶去。

大厦里没人留神她的行踪，她径直走上楼，进了丹尼斯从前的房间。那屋子虽说简朴素净，却处处透着一位教养良好、品味不俗的绅士之居所的风范。因他仓促离去，屋里略显凌乱、东西也搬空了大半，她在此处并未寻见自己要找的东西。她急忙抽身离去，巴不得赶紧逃离这个仿佛每一件器物都在无声谴责她的所在；紧接着，她迈步登上了大楼的顶层。在一间半堆着陈年旧杂物、平日罕有人至的偏僻角落里，她看见东向窗边架着一只画架，上面绷着一块画布。自己的心跳声震得她心头猛地一惊。

“不过是爬了这么几层长楼梯罢了，”她嘴上强自镇定地念叨着，可她走近画架、揭开蒙布时那副迟疑畏怯的举止与迫不及待的神色，却彻底出卖了她。

她凝视了片刻，随即伸手摸索着想要扶住点什么来稳住摇摇晃晃的身子。他的椅子就摆在一旁，她一屁股瘫坐上去，失声惊呼道：“他果真用画笔画出了超越他自己——超越世上任何人——用言语所能道尽的一切！他拥有我所没有的真正天才。这里的一笔一画无不震撼人心、独具匠心！”就这样，她呆呆地坐在椅子上，双眸仿佛被钉在了画布上——因为这幅画向她揭示出来的，正是她自己。

这便是丹尼斯日夜熬心血、披星戴月埋头苦画的秘密所在。这便是他先前没日没夜向布鲁德先生讨教冰块与阳光这两种格格不入之物所结出的硕果。

画框里并排绘着两幅寓意画。第一幅画中，展现在克里斯蒂娜眼前的是一座冰雪洞窟。光线幽微清冷，却又纤毫毕现、剔透玲珑。一根根闪烁微光的冰钟乳从穹顶倒悬而下，奇形怪状的冰笋从地面拔起，遥遥迎向它们。

===Original===

Vivid brightness and beauty were on every side, but of that kind that threw a chill on the beholder. All was of cold blue ice, and so natural was it that the eye seemed to penetrate its clear crystal. To the right was an opening in the grotto, through which was caught a glimpse of a summer landscape, a vivid contrast to the icy cave.
But the main features of the picture were two figures. Sleeping on a couch of ice was the form of a young girl. The flow of the drapery, the contour of the form, was grace itself, and yet all was ice. But the face was the most wonderful achievement. Christine saw her own features, as beautiful as in her vainest moments she had ever dared to hope. So perfect was the portrait that the delicate blue veins branched across the temple in veiled distinctness. It was a face that lacked but two things, life and love; and yet in spite of all its beauty the want of these was painfully felt﻿—all the more painfully, even as a lovely face in death awakens a deeper sadness and regret.
One little icy hand grasped a laurel wreath, also of ice. The other hand hung listless, half open, and from it had dropped a brush that formed a small stalagmite at her side.
Bending over her in most striking contrast was the figure of a young man, all instinct with life, power, and feeling. Though the face was turned away, Dennis had suggested his own form and manner. His left hand was extended toward the sleeping maiden, as if to awaken her, while with the right he pointed toward the opening through which was seen the summer landscape, and his whole attitude indicated an eager wish to rescue her. This was the first picture.
The second one was still more suggestive. At the entrance of the grotto, which looked more cold than ever, in its partial shadow, Christine saw herself again, but how changed! She now had a beauty which she could not believe in﻿—could not understand.
The icy hue and rigidity were all gone. She stood in the warm sunlight, and seemed all warmth and life. Her face glowed with feeling, yet was full of peace.
Instead of the barren ice, flowers were at her feet, and fruitful trees bent over her. Birds were seen flitting through their branches. The bended boughs, her flowing costume, and the tress of golden hair lifted from her temple, all showed that the summer wind was blowing.

===Chinese===

四周处处充盈着夺目的光彩与瑰丽的美感，却是一种教观者浑身发寒的冷艳之美。满目所见皆是森冷湛蓝的坚冰，画得如此逼真自然，目光仿佛能直透进那澄澈晶莹的冰晶深处。画面右侧开着一道洞口，透过洞口望出去，依稀可见一片明媚的夏日风景，与这座冰封洞窟形成了鲜明的对比。

然而整幅画最核心的焦点，却是画中的两个人影。躺在一张寒冰卧榻上沉睡的，是一位年轻姑娘的倩影。衣褶垂落的流丽线条、身姿的窈窕轮廓，无一不是优雅的化身，然而通体上下却全都是冰雕玉琢而成。而最令人叹为观止的传神之笔，莫过于那张脸庞——克里斯蒂娜在画中清晰地认出了自己的容貌，美得恰如她生平最虚荣得意时所敢幻想的极致模样。那肖像画得如此精微入神，甚至连太阳穴上那几条纤细的淡青色血管，都在薄冰般的肌肤下隐约可辨。这是一张唯独欠缺了两样东西的脸庞——生命与爱；然而尽管美貌倾城，这两样东西的匮乏却令人感到刺骨的痛楚——愈是美得动人心魄，便愈发令人感到撕心裂肺，正如一张绝美却已断气的面容总能唤起更深沉的哀恸与惋惜。

她一只冰冷的小手紧握着一顶桂冠——那桂冠同样也是冰做的。另一只手无力地垂落着、半张开着，一根画笔从指间滑落下去，竟在身旁凝结成了一根小小的冰笋。

俯身在她身旁、与她构成最触目惊心对照的，是一位年轻男子的身影——浑身上下充满着生机、力量与炽热的情感。尽管画中人背转着脸，丹尼斯仍不难教人看出那正是他自己的身形与神态。他的左手朝着沉睡的少女伸去，仿佛想要唤醒她；右手则指着洞外那片透过洞口隐约可见的夏日风光，整个人浑身上下无不透出一股急切要将她救出寒窟的迫切愿望。这便是第一幅画。

第二幅画的寓意则更令人深思。在冰窟的洞口处——置身半明半暗的阴影中，那冰窟越发显得阴森凛冽——克里斯蒂娜再次看见了自己，可这一次她却发生了翻天覆地的变化！此刻的她拥有一种她自己简直不敢相信、也无从理解的动人之美。

往日那层冰冷的色调与僵硬的线条已然荡然无存。她亭亭玉立地站在温暖的阳光之下，浑身上下洋溢着暖意与蓬勃生机。她的面庞因真情而光彩焕发，眉眼间却充盈着一片安详宁静。

脚下不再是寸草不生的寒冰，而是繁花簇拥；头顶不再是冰棱，而是硕果累累的果树低垂着枝桠。林间枝头可见欢快的飞鸟穿梭翩跹。被风吹弯的枝条、她身上飘逸舒展的衣裙，以及从她鬓边被轻风撩起的一缕金色发丝，无一不在诉说着盛夏的微风正在轻柔吹拂。

===Original===

Everything, in contrast with the frozen, deathlike cave, indicated life, activity. Near her, a plane-tree, which in nature’s language is the emblem of genius, towered into the sky; around its trunk twined the passionflower, meaning, in Flora’s tongue, “Holy love”; while just above her head, sipping the nectar from an open blossom, was a bright-hued butterfly, the symbol of immortality. By her side stood the same tall, manly form, with face still averted. He was pointing, and her eyes, softened, and yet lustrous and happy, were following where a path wound through a long vista, in alternate light and shadow, to a gate, that in the distance looked like a pearl. Above and beyond it, in airy outline, rose the walls and towers of the Holy City, the New Jerusalem.
For a long time she sat in rapt attention. Moment by moment the paintings in their meaning grew upon her. At last her eyes filled with tears, her bosom rose and fell with an emotion most unwonted, and in low tones she murmured: “Heavenly delusion! and taught with the logic I most dearly love. Oh, that I could believe it! I would give ten thousand years of the life I am leading to know that it is true. Is there, can there be a path that leads through light or shade to a final and heavenly home? If this is true, in spite of all my father’s keen and seemingly convincing arguments, what a terrible mistake our life is!”
Then her thoughts reverted to the artist.
“What have I done in driving him away with contempt in his heart for me? I can no more affect haughty superiority to the man who painted those pictures. Though he could not be my lover, what a friend he might have been! I fear I shall never find his equal. Oh, this world of chaos and confusion! What is right? What is best? *What is truth?* He might have taught me. But the skilful hand that portrayed those wonderful scenes may soon turn to dust, and I shall go to my grave burdened with the thought that I have quenched the brightest genius that will ever shine upon me;” and she clasped her hands in an agony of regret.
Then came the thought of securing the pictures. Dropping a veil over her red eyes, she went down and got some large sheets of paper, and by fastening them together made a secure covering. Then she carried the light frame with the canvas to the second floor, and, summoning Ernst, started homeward with her treasure.

===Chinese===

与那座冰封死寂的洞窟相比，画中万物无不透出勃勃生机与跃动的活力。在她身旁，一株在大自然的物语中象征着“天才”的悬铃木直耸入云；树干上缠绕着西番莲的藤蔓，在花神弗洛拉（Flora）的语言里，它的花语正是“圣洁之爱”；而在她头顶上方，一只色彩斑斓的蝴蝶正伏在一朵盛开的花蕊上吮吸花蜜，象征着“永恒不朽”。在她身侧，依然伫立着那位高大挺拔、男子气概十足的青年身影，面庞依旧背转过去。他正抬手指向远方；她那双变得柔和温润、却又清亮欢欣的眼眸，正顺着他手指的方向望去——只见一条蜿蜒小径穿过一片光影交错、明暗交替的幽深林荫长廊，一直通向远方一座宛如珍珠般莹润闪耀的城门。而在那珍珠门之上、更为高远的云端天际，隐约浮现着圣城“新耶路撒冷”那如梦似幻的城墙与高塔轮廓。

她坐在椅子上出神凝望了许久。一分一秒过去，这两幅画的深意在她心头越来越清晰、越来越沉重。终于，热泪盈满了她的眼眶，胸口随着一股生平罕有的激荡情绪剧烈起伏；她压低嗓音，幽幽呢喃道：“好一个天国般的幻梦！而且偏偏用我平生最爱的严密逻辑铺陈出来。啊，但愿我能信以为真！只要能确知这一切是真的，我情愿拿我眼下过的这种日子一万年去换！莫非这世上当真存在、果真能有那样一条穿过光明与幽暗、最终通往天上永恒归宿的道路吗？倘若这是真的，那我父亲那些看似犀利无懈、无往不利的雄辩推理，岂不把我们的一生全都引向了一场可怕至极的错误！”

随后，她的思绪又转回到了那位画师身上。

“我究竟干了什么蠢事，竟把他逼得怀着满腔鄙夷拂袖而去！面对画出这样画作的男人，我再也摆不出往日那副高高在上的傲慢架子了。纵然他做不成我的恋人，他原本该能成为我何等难得的知己良友啊！只怕我这一生再也寻不到第二个堪与他匹敌的人了。啊，这个混沌纷乱的世界！究竟什么是对？什么才是最好的？*何为真理？*他原本是可以教导我的。可如今，那双描绘出这般奇迹画卷的巧手，兴许很快就要化作一抔黄土；而我将带着自己亲手扑灭了此生所能照耀我的最璀璨天才之火的愧疚，抱憾终生，直至入土！”说着，她在刺骨的追悔与痛苦中紧紧绞住了双手。

紧接着，她念头一转，决定把这两幅画妥善收好。她放下垂在哭红的双眼前的面纱，下楼找来几张大开白纸，拼贴成一只严实的封套。随后她把轻巧的画框连同画布一道搬到二楼，唤来恩斯特，捧着自己这件稀世珍宝动身回家。

===Original===

The boy obeyed with reluctance. Since the time she had surprised him out of his secret in regard to the strawberries, he had never liked her, and now he felt that in some way she was the cause of the sickness of his dearest friend. Christine could not bear the reproach of his large, truthful eyes, and their walk was a silent one. At parting she handed him a banknote, but he shook his head.
“Have you heard from Mr. Fleet?” she asked, with a flush.
The boy’s lip quivered at the mention of that name, and he answered, hastily: “Fader wrote moder Mr. Fleet was no better. I fear he die;” and in an agony of grief he turned and ran sobbing away.
From under her veil Christine’s tears were falling fast also, and she entered her elegant home as if it had been a prison.

===Chinese===

男孩极不情愿地听从了差遣。打从上次她出其不意套出他关于草莓的秘密以后，他就打心底里再也不喜欢她；如今他更觉得，自己最敬爱的好朋友之所以病倒，归根结底多半就是她惹出来的祸。克里斯蒂娜实在受不了他那双又大又真诚的眼睛里透出的无声谴责，两人一路上默默无言。临别时，她递给他一张钞票，他却倔强地摇了摇头。

“你听到弗利特先生的消息了吗？”她脸颊微红，开口问道。

一听见那个名字，男孩的嘴唇顿时微微颤抖起来，急促地答道：“爸爸写信给妈妈说，弗利特先生一点儿也没见好。我生怕他会死掉！”说完，他悲痛欲绝地扭过头，抽抽噎噎地飞奔而去。

在面纱的遮掩下，克里斯蒂娜的泪水也正簌簌滚落；当她踏进自己那座华美精致的豪宅时，脚步沉重得仿佛跨进了一座冷冰冰的牢笼。

## XI Too Much Alike / 第十一章 太过相像
===Original===

One of the duties that Dennis enjoyed most was the opening of new goods. With the curiosity and pleasure of a child he would unpack the treasures of art consigned to his employer, and when a number of boxes were left at the front door he was eager to see their contents. During his first three weeks at the store, there had not been many such arrivals of goods and pictures. But now new things were coming in; and, above all, Mr. Ludolph was daily expecting pictures imported directly from Europe.
One afternoon early in February a large flat box was brought to the store. Mr. Ludolph examined its marks, smiled, and told Dennis to open it with great care, cutting every nail with a chisel. There was little need of cautioning him, for he would have bruised his right hand rather than mar one line of beauty.
The Art Building contained two or three small showrooms, where the more valuable pictures could be exhibited in a good light. Into one of these the large box was carried, and most carefully opened. The two clerks who were helping Dennis laughed at his eager interest, and called him under their breath a “green ’un.” Mr. Schwartz looked upon him as a mild sort of lunatic. But Mr. Ludolph, who stood near, to see if the picture was safe and right, watched him with some curiosity. His manner was certainly very different from Pat Murphy’s at such a time, and his interest both amused and pleased his employer.
When at last the picture was lifted from the box and placed on a large easel, all exclaimed at its beauty save Dennis. On looking at him, they saw that his eyes had filled with tears, and his lips were quivering so that he could not have spoken.
“Is she a relation of yours?” asked Mr. Schwartz, in a matter-of-fact tone.
A loud laugh followed this sally from such an unusual source. Dennis turned on his heel, left the room, and busied himself with duties in a distant part of the store the rest of the day. It seemed to him that they were like savages bartering away gold and pearls, whose value they could not understand; much less could they realize his possession of a nature of exquisite sensibility to beauty.
When all were gone he returned to the room, and sat down before the picture in rapt attention. It was indeed a fine work of art, finished in that painstaking manner characteristic of the Germans.
The painting was a winter scene in Germany.

===Chinese===

丹尼斯最乐意干的差事之一，便是开箱拆封新到的货品。他总是怀着孩童般的好奇与欢喜，拆开寄交东家的件件艺术珍宝；每当大门口卸下一批木箱时，他便迫不及待地想一睹里面究竟装了些什么。他在画店头三个星期里，这类货品与画作到得并不算多。不过眼下新货正陆续运抵；最要紧的是，卢多尔夫先生天天盼望着一批直接从欧洲进口的油画。

二月上旬的一天下午，店里送来一只扁平的大木箱。卢多尔夫先生端详了箱上的唛头，露出微笑，嘱咐丹尼斯务必小心开启，用凿子把每一颗钉子细细撬断。其实压根儿用不着叮嘱他，因为宁可砸伤自己的右手，丹尼斯也绝不肯刮花半寸艺术线条。

艺术大厦里设着两三间小陈列室，专门用来在充沛的光线下展出较为名贵的画作。众人将这只大箱子抬进其中一间，极其仔细地撬开。一旁帮忙的两个店员见他那副兴致勃勃、目不转睛的模样，纷纷窃笑，压低嗓门管他叫“愣头青”。施瓦茨先生则简直把他当成个性情温和的疯子来看待。倒是站在近旁察看画作是否完好无损的卢多尔夫先生，颇带几分兴味地打量着他。这年轻人在这种场合下的神态，确实与从前的帕特·墨菲截然不同，他流露出的那份痴迷既教东家觉得好笑，又令东家暗自欢喜。

终于，那幅油画被抬出木箱，架上了一座大画架；在场众人除了丹尼斯之外，无不齐声赞叹画作绝美。大伙儿转头朝他望去，却见他眼里竟已盈满泪水，嘴唇微微颤抖着，激动得连一句话也说不出口。

“画里这姑娘莫非是你家哪门子亲戚？”施瓦茨先生一本正经地问道。

这句冷幽默居然出自如此不苟言笑之人之口，引得众人哄堂大笑。丹尼斯猛地转身，大步走出陈列室，余下的大半天便独自躲到画店最偏远的角落里埋头干活去了。在他看来，这帮人简直就像拿着黄金和珍珠当白菜倒腾的野蛮人，根本不懂得手头珍宝的价值；更休指望他们能体会到他天性中对美那份细腻入微、敏锐至极的感受力。

等到众人都散去之后，他才悄悄回到陈列室，在那幅画前坐下，如痴如醉地凝神端详起来。这诚然是一幅上乘的艺术杰作，以德国画派特有的那种精雕细琢、一丝不苟的笔法绘成。

画面描绘的是德国的一幅冬日雪景。

===Original===

In the far background rose wooded and snow-clad hills. Nearer in the perspective was a bold bluff, surmounted by a half-ruined castle. At the base of the bluff flowed a river, now a smooth glare of ice, and in the distance figures were wheeling about upon skates. In the immediate foreground were two persons. One was a lovely young girl, dressed in black velvet trimmed with ermine. The basque fitted closely to her person, revealing its graceful outlines, and was evidently adapted to the active sport in which she was engaged. While the rich warm blood mantled her cheeks, the snow was not whiter than her temples and brow. Down her shoulders flowed a profusion of wavy hair, scattered threads of which glistened like gold in the slanting rays of the sun. Her eyes, of a deep violet, were turned, in sympathy with the scorn of the full, smiling mouth, upon the figure of a young man kneeling before her, making awkward attempts to fasten her skate to the trim little foot. It was evident that the favor was too much for him, and that his fluttering heart made his hands trembling and unskilful. But the expression of the maiden’s face clearly indicated that her heart was as cold toward him as the ice on which he kneeled.
The extreme beauty of the picture and its exquisite finish fascinated Dennis, while the girl’s face jarred upon his feelings like a musical discord. After gazing fixedly for a long time, he said, “What possessed the man to paint such a lovely face and make its expression only that of scorn, pride, and heartless merriment?”
All the long night the face haunted and troubled him. He saw it in his dreams. It had for him a strong interest that he could not understand﻿—that strange fascination which a very beautiful thing that has been marred and wronged has for some natures. So powerful was this impression upon his sensitive nature that he caught himself saying, as of a living being, “Oh, that I could give to that face the expression God meant it to have!”
And then he laughed at his own folly. His watchfulness caused him to oversleep the next morning, and he was later than usual in getting through the routine duties of the store. At length, about nine o’clock, dusty and begrimed from mopping, feeding the furnace, etc., he stood with duster and brush in hand before the painting that had so disturbed his rest.

===Chinese===

远景处绵亘着林木葱郁、白雪皑皑的群山。中景稍近处是一座陡峭险峻的悬崖，崖顶矗立着一座半倾圮的古堡。悬崖脚下流淌着一条大河，此刻已冻成一面光滑如镜的坚冰，远处隐约可见几个人影正在冰面上踩着冰刀盘旋滑行。近景前景处则画着两个人。其中一位是位貌美如花的年轻姑娘，身着镶着白鼬毛边的黑天鹅绒冬装。修身的紧身短上衣贴合着她窈窕的身段，勾勒出曼妙的曲线，显见得正是为了眼前这项轻捷活泼的运动而特意裁制的。双颊上泛着一抹鲜活暖融的红晕，而她光洁的鬓角与额头却比白雪还要晶莹白皙。一头浓密微卷的秀发如瀑布般垂落肩头，在斜斜洒下的阳光里，几缕散落的发丝闪烁着金子般的光芒。她那双深紫罗兰色的眼眸，带着与她丰润微笑的双唇如出一辙的轻蔑神气，正俯视着跪在自己面前的一个年轻人——那青年正手忙脚乱、笨手笨脚地试图将一只冰刀鞋系到她那双精巧纤小的小脚上。明眼人一望便知，能蒙伊人垂青效劳实在令他受宠若惊过了头，扑通狂跳的心搅得他双手发颤、手足无措。然而那少女脸上的神情却清清楚楚地表明，她对他的一颗心，竟与他膝下跪着的那片寒冰一般冰冷。

这幅画绝伦的美感与精妙的画工令丹尼斯心醉神迷，可画中少女脸上的神情却像乐章里一声刺耳的杂音，狠狠撞在他心坎上。他目不转睛地凝视了许久，终于低声叹道：“这画家究竟中了什么邪，既画出如此绝代佳人的容貌，偏偏只赋予她一副傲慢、轻蔑、毫无心肝的戏谑神情？”

漫漫长夜里，这张脸庞一直在他脑海里盘旋纠缠、令他心神不宁。他在梦里也见着了她。这幅画对他产生了一种连他自己也说不清道不明的强烈吸引力——那是某种绝美之物遭人玷污或亵渎之后，在敏感心灵上激起的奇异魔力。这股印象在他纤敏的心灵里刻得如此之深，甚至教他仿佛面对一个活生生的人似的，脱口喃喃自语道：“唉，真恨不得能由我来赋予那张脸庞上帝原本打算赐予它的神情啊！”

说完，他又忍不住嗤笑自己的痴傻。这番胡思乱想害得他次日清晨睡过了头，比平日更晚才着手做完店里的日常杂务。好不容易到了约莫九点钟，他刚擦完地板、添完暖炉煤块，浑身上下沾满灰尘煤灰，手里攥着鸡毛掸子和刷子，又站到了那幅搅得他一夜好梦难安的油画前面。

===Original===

He was in his shirtsleeves, and in careful economy had a large coarse apron of ticking girded about his person. His black, dishevelled locks looked like an inverted crow’s nest, and altogether he was unpresentable, appearing more like the presiding divinity of a dust-heap than of an “Art Building.”
After gazing a few moments on the scornful, beautiful face that might have obtained its haughty patrician lineaments from the old barons of the ruined castle just above, he seemed to grow conscious of this himself, and shrunk behind the picture half ashamed, as if the fair girl could see him.
While engaged in cleaning off some stains and marks upon the frame, he did not hear a light footstep in the room. Finishing his task, he stepped out from behind the picture with the purpose of leaving the apartment, when a vision met his gaze which startled him to that degree that he dropped his brush and duster upon the floor, and stood transfixed. There before him, in flesh and blood it seemed, stood the lady of the picture﻿—the same dress, the same beautiful blond face, and, above all, the same expression. He was made conscious of his absurd position by a suppressed titter from the clerks at the door, and a broad laugh from Mr. Ludolph. The beautiful face turned toward him for a moment, and he felt himself looked over from head to foot. At first there was an expression of vexation at the interruption, and then, as if from the ludicrousness of his appearance, the old laughing, scornful look returned. Casting a quick, furtive glance at the picture, which seemed to satisfy him, Dennis, with hot cheeks, gathered up his tools and beat a hasty retreat. As he passed out, Mr. Ludolph asked, good naturedly, “Why, Fleet, what is the matter?”
“Indeed, sir, I hardly know,” answered the bewildered youth, “but it seems to me that I have lost my wits since that picture came. For a moment I thought that the lady on the canvas had stepped out upon the floor.”
“Now that you speak of it,” exclaimed Mr. Ludolph, advancing into the room, “there is a striking resemblance.”
“Nonsense! father,” Dennis heard the young lady say; “you are too old to flatter. As for that harebrained youth of the dust-brush, he looked as if he might have the failing of poor Pat, and not always be able to see straight.”

===Chinese===

他只穿了一件衬衫，为了省俭不弄脏衣裳，腰间还系着一条粗布条纹大围裙。他那一头乌黑蓬乱的头发翘得活像个倒扣过来的乌鸦窝，整个人邋遢寒酸得实在拿不出手，瞧着与其说是“艺术大厦”的管事，倒更像是哪座垃圾堆上的守护神。

他在那张傲慢绝美的脸庞前凝望了片刻——那副目空一切的贵族气派兴许正是承袭自画中崖顶古堡里的历代老男爵——随后仿佛忽然意识到了自己眼下这副尊容，竟半带羞惭地缩身躲到了画架背后，仿佛画里那位美貌少女真能瞧见他似的。

正当他埋头擦拭画框上的几处污渍与印痕时，却浑然未曾听见陈列室里响起了一阵轻盈的脚步声。好不容易擦拭完毕，他刚从画架背后走出来打算离开这间屋子，迎面撞入眼帘的一幕景象却惊得他魂飞魄散，手中的刷子和鸡毛掸子“啪嗒”一声全掉在地上，整个人如同被施了定身法般僵在原地。眼前站着的，仿佛正是画中那位姑娘化作了有血有肉的真人——一模一样的黑天鹅绒镶毛衣裙，一模一样明艳动人的白皙金发容颜，最要命的是，连脸上那副神情也一般无二！直到门口几个店员压抑着的窃笑声，以及卢多尔夫先生爽朗的大笑声响起，他才猛然醒悟自己此刻的模样有多么荒唐可笑。那张绝美的面庞朝他转了过来，停留了一瞬，丹尼斯只觉自己从头到脚被人狠狠打量了一遍。起初那张脸上流露出一丝被打扰的不悦，随即似乎因他这副滑稽狼狈的打扮而忍俊不禁，往日里那副戏谑轻蔑的神情又回到了眉梢眼角。丹尼斯飞快地偷偷瞥了一眼画布，似乎要确认一下，随即满脸发烧，匆忙拾起地上的工具，狼狈不堪地落荒而逃。打他身旁擦肩而过时，卢多尔夫先生和颜悦色地问了一句：“咦，弗利特，这是怎么了？”

“说真的，先生，我自己也糊涂得很，”这个神魂颠倒的青年结结巴巴地答道，“可我觉得打从这幅画进店以来，我就像是丢了魂儿似的。刚才有一瞬间，我真以为画布上的那位小姐活生生走下地来站在面前了。”

“听你这么一说，倒真是！”卢多尔夫先生一边往陈列室里迈步，一边惊叹道，“简直活脱脱一个模子刻出来的！”

“胡说八道！父亲，”丹尼斯听见那位年轻小姐清脆地说道，“您这把年纪了，何必还学人奉承夸口。至于那个挥着鸡毛掸子、毛毛躁躁的小伙子，瞧他那副呆样儿，只怕也染上了可怜的帕特那点坏毛病，两只眼睛总不能老看直喽。”

===Original===

At this Dennis’s cheeks grew hotter still, while a low laugh from one or two of the clerks near showed that they were enjoying his embarrassment.
Dennis hastened away to his room, and it was well that he did not hear the conversation that followed.
“Oh, no!” responded Mr. Ludolph, “that is not Dennis’s failing. He is a member of a church in ‘good and regular standing.’ He will be one of the ‘pillars’ by and by.”
“You are always having a fling at superstition and the superstitious,” said his daughter, laughingly. “Is that the reason you installed him in Pat’s place?”
“Can you doubt it, my dear?” replied her father, in mock solemnity.
“Well,” said she, “I think your new factotum fails decidedly in good manners, if nothing else. He stared most impudently at me when he came out from behind the picture. I should have reprimanded him myself if I had not been so full of laughter at his ridiculous appearance.”
“That’s the joke of it. It was as good as a play to see him. I never saw a man more startled and confused. He evidently thought for a moment, as he said, that the girl in the painting had stepped out upon the floor, and that you were she.”
“How absurd!” exclaimed his daughter.
“Yes; and now that I think of it, he glanced from you to the picture, to satisfy himself that his senses were not deceiving him, before he started to come away.”
“I cannot see any special resemblance,” she replied, at the same time inwardly pleased that she should be thought like the beautiful creature on the canvas.
“But there is a strong resemblance,” persisted her father, “especially in general effect. I will prove it to you. There is old Schwartz; he is not troubled with imagination, but sees things just as they are. He would look at you, my dainty daughter, as if you were a bale of wool, and judge as composedly and accurately.”
“I fear, my father,” replied she, smilingly, “that you have conspired with him to pull the entire bale over my eyes. But let him come.”
By this time Dennis had returned, and commenced dusting some pictures near the entrance, where he could see and hear. He felt impelled by a curiosity that he could not resist. Moreover he had a little natural vanity in wishing to show that he was not such a guy, after all. It was hard for him to remember that he stood in Pat Murphy’s position. What difference did it make to the lady whether such as he was a fright or not?

===Chinese===

听到这话，丹尼斯的脸颊顿时烧得更烫了，近旁一两个店员发出几声压低的窃笑，显见得正乐得看他出洋相。

丹尼斯快步躲回自己屋里去了；幸好他没听见随后客厅里接下去的那番对话。

“哦，那倒没有！”卢多尔夫先生应道，“丹尼斯可没那个毛病。他可是教会里‘品行端正、名声清白’的正式教友呢。过不了多久，没准还得成为教会的‘顶梁柱’哩。”

“您老人家向来总爱拿迷信和信教的人打趣，”他女儿笑着说道，“莫非这就是您找他来顶替帕特位子的缘故？”

“我的乖女儿，这还用怀疑吗？”父亲一本正经地打趣答道。

“依我看哪，”她接话道，“您这位新来的大总管，别的不说，单论礼数教养就大成问题。他刚才从画架背后走出来的时候，直勾勾地盯着我瞧，实在放肆无礼极了。要不是他那副滑稽模样实在叫我笑得直不起腰来，我当场就该好好训斥他一顿。”

“这正是笑话最妙的地方嘛。瞧他刚才那副魂不守舍的模样，简直比看戏还精彩！我活这么大岁数，从未见过哪个男人吓得那么手足无措、晕头转向。显然就像他自己说的，有那么一瞬间，他真以为画里的姑娘走到了地板上，而你就是她。”

“真是荒唐透顶！”女儿嗔道。

“可不是嘛；如今细想起来，他在动身逃走之前，还特意拿眼在你和画布之间来回瞄了一遍，好确认自己那双眼睛没看花呢。”

“我倒看不出有什么特别相像的地方，”她嘴上这么答道，心里却着实暗暗受用，欢喜旁人觉得自己酷似画布上那个绝代佳人。

“可确实像得惊人啊，”她父亲坚持道，“尤其是神韵气派上。我这就证明给你看。外头就有老施瓦茨在；他脑子里可没有半点幻想的细胞，眼珠子只照着事物原本的模样老老实实看。就算站在他面前的是一位娇滴滴的千金小姐，我的乖女儿，他也能像打量一捆羊毛似的，照样沉着冷静、分毫不差地评判一番。”

“我的父亲大人，”她微笑着回道，“只怕您早就同他串通一气，要把整捆羊毛全蒙到我眼睛上糊弄我吧。不过随他进来就是。”

这时候，丹尼斯已经折返回来，正挨着入口处擦拭几幅油画上的灰尘，那位置恰好既看得见里头，又听得清谈话。一股抑制不住的好奇心驱使着他非留下来看看不可。此外，他心底也多少存着一点凡人难免的虚荣心，总想证明自己其实并不像方才那般滑稽寒酸得像个怪物。一时间，他委实很难时刻提醒自己眼下不过顶着帕特·墨菲的卑微差事。像他这样的小人物究竟寒不寒酸，在人家千金小姐眼里又有什么干系呢？

===Original===

Mr. Schwartz entered, and at Mr. Ludolph’s bidding looked at the living and the painted girl. In his slow, sententious tones, one could not help feeling that he was telling just how things appeared to him. The young lady stood beside the painting and unconsciously assumed the expression of her fair shadow. Indeed it seemed an expression but too habitual to her face.
“Yes,” he said, “there is a decided resemblance﻿—close in dress﻿—close in complexion﻿—color of hair much the same﻿—eyes much alike﻿—Miss Ludolph not quite so tall,” etc. Then with an awkward attempt at a compliment, like an elephant trying to execute a quickstep, he continued:
“If I may be permitted to be so bold as to speak﻿—express an opinion﻿—I should beg leave to say that Miss Ludolph favors herself﻿—more favored﻿—is better-looking,” he blurted out at last, backing out of the door at the same time, with his brow bathed in perspiration from the throes of this great and unwonted effort at gallantry.
“Bah!” said Dennis to himself, “the old mole left out the very chief thing in tracing the likeness﻿—the expression! See her now as she listens to his awkward attempt at compliment. She is looking at him with the same scornful, laughing face that the girl in the picture wears toward the bungling admirer at her feet. He is right in one thing though, she is better-looking.”
But the moment Mr. Schwartz’s bulky figure vanished from the doorway, Miss Ludolph caught the critical, intelligent gaze of Dennis Fleet, and the expression of her face changed instantly to a frown. But, to do her justice, it was more in vexation with herself than with him. Her innate delicacy of feeling showed her that it looked like small vanity to be standing there while comparisons like the above were instituted. Her manner at once became cold, observant, and thoroughly self-possessed. She stepped out into the store, and by a few keen, critical glances seemed to take in its whole effect. Again disapprobation clouded her fair brow, and she pronounced audibly but one word﻿—“Stiff.”
Then she passed into her father’s private office.

===Chinese===

施瓦茨先生走了进来，奉卢多尔夫先生之命，轮流端详了一番眼前活生生的少女与画布上的少女。听着他那慢条斯理、一板一眼的腔调，任谁也觉不出半点虚言，分明字字都是照他眼中所见直抒胸臆。那位年轻小姐亭亭立在油画身旁，不知不觉间便摆出了与画中那位美丽倩影一模一样的神情。说到底，那本就是她脸上早已习以为常的神态。

“不错，”他开口道，“确实有十分明显的相像之处——衣着相近——肤色相近——发色大抵一致——眼眸颇为相似——卢多尔夫小姐身量略微娇小一些。”如此这般逐条细数了一遍之后，他竟笨拙地试图献上一句恭维，活像一头大象硬要学人跳轻快舞步似的，结结巴巴地接下去道：

“倘若容我胆敢冒昧直言——发表一点浅见——我斗胆敬呈一言，卢多尔夫小姐更胜其画——更为得天独厚——生得更美貌动人！”最后一个字刚一出口，他便一边躬身倒退着退出了门外，一边拿手帕擦着额角——为了挤出这辈子头一遭如此绞尽脑汁的殷勤奉承话，他急得满脑门都沁出了汗水。

“呸！”丹尼斯在心里暗骂一声，“这只老瞎眼鼹鼠，在对比相像之处时偏偏漏掉了最要紧的一桩——神情！瞧瞧她这会儿听他那番笨拙恭维时的模样吧！她盯着他看的那副轻蔑又好笑的脸庞，跟画里那姑娘俯视脚下那个手忙脚乱的追求者时简直一模一样！不过老家伙倒有一点没说错，她本人确实生得更美。”

然而就在施瓦茨先生那笨重的身影刚从门口消失的刹那，卢多尔夫小姐蓦地撞见了丹尼斯·弗利特那双挑剔而聪慧的眼睛；她脸上的神情顿时一变，紧蹙起了眉头。不过平心而论，她这番恼怒与其说是冲着他，倒不如说是冲着她自己。她天性中那份敏锐的矜持与自尊提醒着她：任由旁人站在这里对着自己品头论足、拿画作比方，显得实在太过浅薄虚荣。她的神态刹那间恢复了冷峻、锐利与彻底的冷静自持。她迈步走出陈列室，走进外头大店堂，几道敏锐挑剔的目光扫过去，似乎便将全店的布局格调尽收眼底。不悦的阴云再次笼罩了她光洁的额头，她清清楚楚地吐出了仅此一个词——“呆板。”

说罢，她便转身步入了父亲的私人办公室。

## XIII Very Cold / 第十三章 冷若冰霜
===Original===

When Dennis entered Mr. Ludolph’s store Christine was absent on a visit to New York. On her return she resumed her old routine. At this time she and her father were occupying a suite of rooms at a fashionable hotel. Her schooldays were over, Mr. Ludolph preferring to complete her education himself in accordance with his peculiar views and tastes. She was just passing into her twentieth year, and looked upon the world from the vantage points of health, beauty, wealth, accomplishments of the highest order, and the best social standing. Assurance of a long and brilliant career possessed her mind, while pride and beauty were like a coronet upon her brow. She was the world’s ideal of a queen.
And yet she was not truly happy. There was ever a vague sense of unrest and dissatisfaction at heart. She saw that her father was proud and ambitious in regard to her, but she instinctively felt that he neither loved nor trusted her to any great extent. She seemed to be living in a palace of ice, and at times felt that she was turning into ice herself; but her very humanity and womanhood, deadened and warped though they were, cried out against the *cold* of a life without God or love. In the depths of her soul she felt that something was wrong, but what, she could not understand. It seemed that she had everything that heart could wish, and that she ought to be satisfied.
She had at last concluded that her restlessness was the prompting of a lofty ambition, and that if she chose she could win worldwide celebrity as an artist. This, with the whole force of her strong nature, she had determined to do, and for over two years had worked with an energy akin to enthusiasm. She had resolved that painting should be the solid structure of her success, and music its ornament.
Nor were her dreams altogether chimerical, for she had remarkable talent in her chosen field of effort, and had been taught to use the brush and pencil from childhood. She could imitate with skill and taste, and express with great accuracy the musical thought of the composer; but she could not create new effects, and this had already begun to trouble her. She worked hard and patiently, determined to succeed. So great had been her application that her father saw the need of rest and change, and therefore her visit to New York.

===Chinese===

丹尼斯初进卢多尔夫先生画店那阵子，克里斯蒂娜恰巧出门去纽约游历未归。如今回来之后，她又恢复了往日那套起居作息。彼时她与父亲在一座时髦奢华的旅馆里包下了一整套房间。她的学校课业早已修毕，而卢多尔夫先生更乐意亲自按照自己独到的见解与品位，亲手替她完成余下的深造教育。她正值即将步入二十岁芳华的妙龄，站在集健康、美貌、财富、顶级才艺与最优越社会地位之巅俯瞰着这个世界。对于漫长而辉煌的前程，她早已胸有成竹、笃信不疑，而骄傲与美貌宛如一顶璀璨的华冠戴在她额前。在她所处的那个世界里，她正是人们心目中理想女王的化身。

然而，她却并不真正快乐。在她心底深处，始终潜藏着一丝隐约的不安与不满。她看得出来，父亲为她感到骄傲，也在她身上寄托着极大的野心，可她凭直觉却敏锐地感觉到，父亲其实并不怎么爱她，也并不怎么信任她。她仿佛置身于一座冰晶筑成的宫殿之中，有时甚至觉得自己也正在一点点变成一块寒冰；然而她天性里与生俱来的人性与女儿本色——即便已被麻木、扭曲得不成样子——却仍在暗中呐喊着，抗拒这种没有上帝、也没有爱的*冰冷*人生。在她灵魂的最深处，她隐约觉得哪儿出了大差错，可究竟错在哪里，她却百思不得其解。按理说，世间凡是人心所能希冀的一切她似乎都已拥有，理应心满意足才是。

思来想去，她终于给自己得出一个结论：心头那股焦躁不安，不过是源于自己胸怀大志、雄心万丈的驱策——她认定，只要她愿意，自己完全能够以大画家的身份扬名立万、享誉世界。凭着她那刚烈倔强的全部天性，她打定了主意非做到不可，并且两年多来一直以近乎狂热的干劲埋头苦学。她立志要把绘画铸成自己功成名就的坚实大厦，而以音乐作为点缀其间的华美装饰。

她的梦想也并非全是镜花水月，因为她在自己选定的这门行当里确实天赋异禀，更何况自幼便受过素描与油画的严格调教。她能够极其灵巧而有品味地临摹前人，也能丝毫不差地精准传达出作曲家的乐思；然而她却无法独创出崭新的艺术意境，而这一局限早已开始令她苦恼不已。她夜以继日、忍耐坚毅地苦练，铁了心非闯出一番名堂不可。她用功之狠、耗神之巨，连她父亲都看出她必须歇一歇、换换环境，这才有了她前一阵子的纽约之行。

===Original===

She had now returned strengthened, and eager for her former studies, and resumed them with tenfold zest.
The plan of rearranging the store on artistic principles daily grew in favor with her. It was just the exercise of taste she delighted in, and she hoped some day to indulge it on palace walls that would be her own. Her father’s pride caused him to hesitate for some time, but she said: “Why, Chicago is not our home; we shall soon be thousands of miles away. You know how little we really care for the opinions of the people here: it is only our own pride and opinion that we need consult. I see nothing lowering or unfeminine in the work. I shall scarcely touch a thing myself, merely direct; for surely among all in your employ there must be one or two pairs of hands not so utterly awkward but that they can follow plain instructions. My taste shall do it all. We are both early risers, and the whole change can be made before the store is opened. Moreover,” she added (with an expression indicating that she would have little difficulty in ruling her future German castle, and its lord also), “this is an affair of our own. Those you employ ought to understand by this time that it is neither wise nor safe to talk of our business outside.”
After a moment’s thought she concluded: “I really think that the proper arrangement of everything in the store as to light, display, and effect, so that people of taste will be pleased when they enter, would add thousands of dollars to your sales; and this rigid system of old Schwartz’s, which annoys us both beyond endurance, will be broken up.”
Won over by arguments that accorded with his inclinations, Mr. Ludolph gave his daughter permission to carry out the plan in her own way.
She usually accompanied her father to the store in the morning. He, after a brief glance around, would go to his private office and attend to correspondence. She would do whatever her mood prompted. Sometimes she would sit down for a half-hour before one picture; again she would examine most critically a statue or a statuette. Whenever new music was received, she looked it over and carried off such pieces as pleased her fancy.
She evidently was a privileged character, and no one save her father exercised the slightest control over her movements.

===Chinese===

如今她养足了精神归来，对往日的功课渴盼不已，立刻以十倍的热忱重新投入了研习。

将整间画店照着艺术原则彻底重新布置的念头，一天比一天更得她心意。这恰恰是她平生最酷爱的展示品位之道，她一直盼着有朝一日能在属于自己的贵族府邸四壁之上尽情施展这番才华。起初，她父亲因自尊心作祟而犹豫了颇久，克里斯蒂娜却劝说道：“哎呀，芝加哥又不是我们的家乡；用不了多久，我们就要远隔重洋、去到万里之外了。您明知道，我们心里根本不大在乎这儿老百姓的看法：我们只需顾全自己的体面与主见就够了。这活儿我看既不掉价，也无损大家闺秀的仪态。我几乎不必亲自动手碰任何东西，只需站在旁边发号施令罢了；在您雇的那么多人里头，总该能挑出一两双不算太笨手笨脚的手，能照着简单明白的吩咐去干活吧。一切全凭我的眼光调遣就行。咱们父女俩都是早起的人，赶在每天画店开门营业之前，整套改头换面就能大功告成。况且，”她补充道（说话时脸上露出的那副神情，分明在说将来统御那座德国古堡连同城堡的主人，于她而言也绝非难事），“这是咱们自家的体己事。您手下雇的那些人，到如今也该明白在外面嚼咱们生意的舌根既不明智、也不安全。”

略微思忖了片刻，她又一锤定音地总结道：“我真心认为，把店里每一样物件的光线、陈列与整体效果都调理得当，好让有品味的人一跨进门便赏心悦目，单这一招就能给您的营业额平白添上好几千美元；顺带也能把老施瓦茨那套死板僵化、教咱们俩都忍无可忍的臭规矩彻底打破。”

这番说辞句句正中卢多尔夫先生下怀，他欣然首肯，准许女儿放手照自己的主意大刀阔斧去办。

自此，她早晨常常随父亲一同来到画店。父亲草草巡视一圈，便走进自己的私人办公室处理往来信函；她则任凭兴致所至，随心所欲地打发时光。有时她会在某幅油画前坐上足足半个钟头；有时又会拿无比挑剔的眼光细细端详一尊大雕像或小塑像。每逢新一批乐谱到货，她便一一翻检，挑出合自己心意的曲谱带回家去。

显而易见，她在店里是个享有特权的人物，除了她父亲之外，谁也管束不住她半分举止。

===Original===

She treated all the clerks, save old Schwartz, as if they were animated machines; and by a quiet order, as if she had touched a spring, would set them in motion to do her bidding. The young men in the store were of German descent, and rather heavy and undemonstrative. Mr. Schwartz’s system of order and repression had pretty thoroughly quenched them. They were educated to the niches they filled, and seemed to have no thought beyond; therefore they were all unruffled at Miss Ludolph’s air of absolute sovereignty. Mr. Schwartz was as obsequious as the rest, but, as second to her father in power, was permitted some slight familiarity. In fact this heavy, stolid prime-minister both amused and annoyed her, and she treated him with the caprice of a child toward an elephant﻿—at times giving him the sugarplum of a compliment, and oftener pricking him with the pin of some caustic remark. To him she was the perfection of womankind﻿—her reserved, dispassionate manner, her steady, unwearied prosecution of a purpose, being just the qualities that he most honored; and he worshipped her reverently at a distance, like an old astrologer adoring some particularly bright fixed star. No whisking comets or changing satellites for old Schwartz.
As for Dennis, she treated him as she probably had treated Pat Murphy, and for several days had no occasion to notice him at all. In fact he kept out of her way, choosing at first to observe rather than be observed. She became an artistic study to him, for her every movement was grace itself, except that there was no softness or gentleness in her manner. Her face fascinated him by its beauty, though its expression troubled him﻿—it was so unlike his mother’s, so unlike what he felt a woman’s ought to be. But her eager interest in that which was becoming so dear to him﻿—art﻿—would have covered a multitude of sins in his eyes, and with a heart abounding in faith and hope, not yet diminished by hard experience, he believed that the undeveloped angel existed within her. But he remembered her frown when she had first noticed his observation of her. The shrewd Yankee youth saw that her pride would not brook even a curious glance. But while he kept at a most respectful distance he felt that there was no such wide gulf between them as she imagined.

===Chinese===

除了老施瓦茨以外，她看待店里所有伙计，简直如同看待一具具会走动的发条木偶；只要她轻声下一道指令，仿佛伸手按了一记弹簧开关，他们便得立刻转动起来，乖乖照办她的差遣。店里那几个年轻小伙子都是德国裔，性子颇为木讷呆板、不苟言笑。施瓦茨先生那套讲究死规矩与高压管束的做派，早已把他们调教得服服帖帖、毫无生机。他们被规训得严丝合缝地嵌在各自领受的那个位置上，仿佛脑子里压根儿不敢越雷池半步；因此对于卢多尔夫小姐那副唯我独尊、发号施令的霸王派头，大伙儿全都习以为常、波澜不惊。施瓦茨先生自己也跟其余人一般卑躬屈膝、唯命是从，不过因他是仅次于她父亲的二把手，倒被允许略微多一点亲近随和的余地。事实上，这位笨重呆板的首席大臣既教她觉得好笑，又常教她心烦，因此她摆弄起他来，就像小孩子逗弄一头大象般随心所欲、全凭喜怒——时而赏他一颗甜丝丝的恭维糖果，更多时候却拿几句尖酸刻薄的冷箭扎他一针。而在老施瓦茨眼里，她简直是世间女子完美的极致——她那副内敛矜持、不苟喜怒的气度，她那份沉稳坚毅、百折不挠推进目标的狠劲，恰恰都是他平生最推崇的美德；于是他从远远的地方怀着虔诚敬畏之心仰慕着她，活像一位老占星家顶礼膜拜天穹中某颗格外璀璨的恒星。老施瓦茨眼中，可容不得那些轻狂乱窜的彗星或阴晴不定的卫星。

至于丹尼斯，她对他的态度大概同从前对待帕特·墨菲一般无二，一连好几天压根儿没正眼瞧过他一回。事实上，丹尼斯自己也总是主动避开她的视线，起初宁可躲在暗处静静观察，而不愿引人注目。在她身上，他寻到了一个绝佳的艺术观察标本——因为她的一举一动无一不优雅到了极致，唯独言谈举止间找不出半点柔和与温情。她那张容颜凭着绝世之美深深迷住了他，可眉宇间流露出的神情却令他心里隐隐刺痛——那神情与他母亲是何等截然不同，与他心目中一位女子理当具备的温良神韵又是何等格格不入！然而她对艺术——那门正在他心中变得无比珍贵的事业——所怀有的热切执着，在他眼里便足以遮掩千般过失；怀着一颗尚未被残酷阅历磨灭、依旧充盈着信心与希望的赤子之心，他深信在她躯壳之内必定沉睡着一位尚未唤醒的天使。不过，他依然牢牢记着她头一回察觉自己在打量她时脸上浮现出的那道蹙眉。这位精明敏感的美国佬青年看得出，她的骄傲绝不容许旁人投去哪怕一丝好奇的窥探目光。可当他恭恭敬敬地退守在极其远的距离之外时，他心里却隐隐觉得，两人之间横亘的鸿沟，其实远没有她自以为的那般天差地别。

===Original===

By birth and education he was as truly entitled to her acquaintance as the young men who sometimes came into the store with her and whom she met in society. Position and wealth were alone wanting, and in spite of his hard experience and lowly work he felt that there must be some way for him, as for others, to win these.
He longed for the society of ladies, as every right-feeling young man does, and to one of his nature the grace and beauty of woman were peculiarly attractive. If, before she came, the lovely faces of the pictures had filled the place with a sort of witchery, and created about him an atmosphere in which his artist-soul was awakening into life and growth, how much more would it be true of this living vision of beauty that glided in and out every day!
“She does not notice me,” he at first said to himself, “any more than do these lovely shadows upon the canvas. But why need I care? I can study both them and her, and thus educate my eye, and I hope my hand, to imitate and perhaps surpass their perfections in time.”
But this cool, philosophic mood did not last long. It might answer very well in regard to the pictures on the walls, but there was a magnetism about this living, breathing woman that soon caused him to long for the privilege of being near her and speaking to her of that subject that interested them both so deeply. Though he had never seen any of her paintings to know them, he soon saw that she was no novice in such matters and that she looked at works of art with the eye of a connoisseur. In revery he had many a spirited conversation with her, and he trusted that some day his dreams would become real. He had the romantic hope that if she should discover his taste and strong love of art she might at first bestow upon him a patronizing interest which would gradually grow into respect and acknowledged equality.

===Chinese===

论出身门第与学识教养，他原与那些时常陪她来画店、或在社交场上与她周旋的年轻绅士们同样有资格结识她。他所欠缺的，唯独地位与财富而已；然而尽管眼下经历艰辛、干着卑微的粗活，他坚信既然旁人能挣来这些东西，他自己也定然寻得到一条出路。

同每一位情感健全的青年男子一样，他渴望结交淑女佳人，而以他这般重情细腻的天性，女子的风姿与美貌对他更是具有一种格外动人的魅力。倘若在克里斯蒂娜到来之前，画店里那些画布上的美人容颜便已令整座店堂笼罩在一股奇异的魔力之中、替他营造出了一方足以唤醒他艺术灵魂并使其勃发生长的天地，那么对于眼前这位每日轻盈穿梭进出、活生生的绝色丽人，这种魔力又该强烈到何等地步呢！

“她根本没有留神我，”起初他暗自宽慰自己，“正如同画布上那些迷人的倩影不会留神我一样。可我又何必介怀？我大可以一边揣摩那些名画，一边细细观察她，借此磨炼我的眼光，更但愿假以时日也能磨炼出这双手的巧技，去效法乃至超越她们的完美风华。”

然而这番冷静超然的哲学心境并没有维持太久。拿这一套去对待墙上挂着的油画倒还行得通，可这位活生生、有血有肉、呼吸吐纳的女子身上散发出的强烈磁场，很快便教他心底生出一股难以遏制的渴望——渴望能获准靠近她身旁，同她聊一聊那桩令两人同样魂牵梦萦的艺术话题。尽管他从未见过她本人所绘的画作，无从知晓她的手艺究竟如何，他却很快看出来，她在这些门道上绝非外行新手，而是以一位行家鉴赏家的挑剔眼光审视着件件艺术品。在白日梦里，他曾无数次同她展开意气风发、精彩纷呈的畅谈；他笃信终有一天，他的美梦会照进现实。他甚至怀着一个浪漫天真的幻想：倘若她哪天无意中发觉了他的审美品味与对艺术的一腔炽爱，兴许起初会赏给他几分居高临下的垂青赏识，而那份赏识日后定会一点点生长为由衷的敬重，乃至彼此平等的惺惺相惜。

## XIX What Is the Matter with Him? / 第十九章 他究竟怎么了？
===Original===

The sun was just tingeing the eastern horizon with light when Dennis sprang from his bed on the following morning. He vowed that Miss Ludolph should never have cause to complain of him again; for, great as was the luxury of being awakened by such exquisite music, it was one that he could not afford.
It must be confessed that he gave a little more care than usual that morning to his toilet; but his resources were very limited. Still, as nature had done so much for him, he could not complain. By half-past six his duties in the store were accomplished, and brushed and furbished up as far as possible, he stood outside the door awaiting his fair taskmistress. Sometimes he wondered at the strange fascination she exercised over him, but generally ended by ascribing it to her beauty and love of art.
A little after the time appointed she appeared with her father, and seemed pleased at Dennis’s readiness for work.
“I shall not have to sing you awake this morning,” she said, “and I am glad, for I am in a mood for business.”
She was attired in a close-fitting walking-dress that set off her graceful person finely. It was evident that her energetic nature would permit no statuesque repose while Dennis worked, but that she had come prepared for active measures.
She had inherited a good constitution, which, under her father’s direction, had been strengthened and confirmed by due regard to hygienic rules. Therefore she had reached the stage of early womanhood abounding in vitality and capable of great endurance. Active, graceful motion was as natural to her as it is for a swallow to be on the wing. The moment she dropped her book, palette, or pencil, she was on her feet, her healthful nature seeming like a mountain brook, that, checked for a time in its flow, soon overleaps its bounds and speeds on more swiftly than ever. But the strange part of this superabundant activity was, that she never seemed to do anything in an abrupt way, as from mere impulse. Every act glided into another smoothly and gracefully. Her lithe, willowy figure, neither slight nor stout, was peculiarly adapted to her style of movement. She delighted in the game of billiards, for the quick movements and varied attitudes permitted, and the precision required, were all suited to her taste; and she had gained such marvellous skill that even her father, with his practiced hand, was scarcely her match.

===Chinese===

次日清晨，朝阳刚刚将东方的天际线染上一抹微光，丹尼斯便翻身跃起下了床。他暗暗发誓，绝不再让卢多尔夫小姐有一丝指责自己的由头；毕竟，能被那般天籁般的乐曲唤醒固然是一种莫大的享受，却也是他万万承受不起的奢华。

平心而论，这天早晨他在仪容打理上确实比平日多花了几分心思；怎奈他手头的行头实在寒酸有限。话虽如此，老天爷既已在相貌身材上格外厚待了他，倒也教他无甚可抱怨的。六点半刚过，店里的日常杂务便已尽数料理妥当；他尽可能地把自己衣裳鞋帽刷洗掸净、收拾齐整，随即立在大门外，等候他那位貌美如花的监工女主人驾临。有时他也会暗自诧异她施加在自己身上的那种奇异魔力，但思来想去，往往归因于她的美貌与她对艺术的一腔热爱。

过了约定的时刻不多一会儿，她便同父亲一道现身了，见丹尼斯早已严阵以待准备干活，似乎颇感满意。

“今早可不用我再高歌一曲把你唱醒了，”她开口道，“这倒好，我今天正一门心思想着办正事呢。”

她身着一袭合体修身的便装长裙，将她优雅曼妙的身段衬托得恰到好处。显而易见，她那精力充沛的性子，绝不容许自己在丹尼斯忙碌时像一尊雕像般袖手旁观，而是做好了大干一场、雷厉风行的准备。

她天生禀赋了一副极好的体魄，又在父亲的督导下常年恪守卫生养生之法，练就了一身更加强健坚韧的底子。因此，正当妙龄初绽的她浑身上下洋溢着勃勃生机，极富耐力。敏捷而优雅的举止于她而言再自然不过，恰似燕子振翅凌空般浑然天成。每当她随手放下书本、调色板或画笔，转瞬便已起身立定；她那健康活泼的天性恰似一条山间清涧，纵使一时受阻滞流，转眼便会跃过堤岸，比先前更加欢快迅疾地奔涌向前。更奇特的是，这份过人的精力却从不显得毛躁唐突，绝无半点一时兴起之感；每一个动作都如同行云流水般自然滑顺地衔接到下一个动作。她那柔韧修长、不胖不瘦、如垂柳般袅娜的身材，更是与这种矫健灵动的姿态相得益彰。她极酷爱台球运动——因为打球时所允许的迅捷走位与千姿百态的身姿，以及所需的精准力道，无一不合她的脾胃；她也确实练就了出神入化的高超球技，甚至连经验老到的父亲也很难是她的对手。

As she tripped lightly up the long winding stairs to the showroom over the front door where their labors were to begin, she appeared to Dennis the very embodiment of grace and beauty. And yet she seemed so cold and self-centred, so devoid of warm human interest in the great world of love, joy, and suffering, that she repelled while she fascinated.
“If the blood should come into the cheeks of one of her father’s statues, and the white marble eyes turn to violet blue, and the snowy hair to wavy gold, and it should spring from its pedestal into just such life, it would be more like her than any woman I ever saw,” thought Dennis, as he stood for a moment or two waiting to do her bidding.
Her plans had been thoroughly matured, and she acted with decision. Pointing to the side opposite the door﻿—the side which would naturally strike the eye of the visitor first﻿—she said, “I wish all the pictures taken down from that wall and placed around the room so that I can see them.”
She began as an absolute dictator, intending to give no hint of her plans and purposes except as conveyed by clear, terse orders. But these had so intelligent and appreciative an interpreter in Dennis, that gradually her attention was drawn to him as well as to his work.
He had his stepladder ready, and with a celerity decidedly pleasing, soon placed the pictures safely on the floor, so that she could still see them and judge of their character. Though his dexterous manner and careful handling of the pictures were gratifying, it must be confessed that his supple form, the graceful and varied attitudes he unconsciously assumed in his work, pleased her more, and she secretly began to study him as an artistic subject, as he had studied her.
In her complacency she said: “So far, very well, Mr. Fleet. I congratulate myself that I have you to assist me, instead of that awkward fraud, Mr. Berder.”
“And I assure you, Miss Ludolph, that I have longed intensely for this privilege ever since I knew your purpose.”
“You may have cause to repent, like many another whose wishes have been gratified; for your privilege will involve a great deal of hard work.”
“The more the better,” said Dennis, warmly.
“How so? I should think you had more to do now than you would care about.”
“Work is no burden to one of my years and strength, provided it is suited to one’s tastes.

“若是她父亲收藏的那尊雕像双颊骤然涌上鲜活的血色，雪白的大理石眼眸化作深紫罗兰色，皑皑白发变成波浪般的金发，随即从底座上纵身一跃、化作这般鲜活的生命，只怕那也比我见过的世间任何女子都更像她！”丹尼斯站在原地静候差遣的片刻，心里暗暗涌起这样一个念头。

她早已胸有成竹，做起事来果断利落。她抬手指向正对着房门的那一面墙——也就是来客跨进屋子最先撞入眼帘的迎面墙——下令道：“我要把那面墙上的画统统摘下来，沿屋子四周摊开摆在地上，好让我逐一审看。”

起初，她摆出一副绝对独裁者的架势，除了一道道清晰简练的指令之外，压根儿不打算透露半点自己的构思与意图。然而这些指令落到丹尼斯身上，却遇上了一个如此聪慧而又心领神会的领悟者，以至于她的注意力渐渐不只停留在画作上，也悄然被引到了他本人身上。

他早已备好了折梯，动作麻利得着实赏心悦目，没多久便把画作稳稳当当地一幅幅移放到地板上，且摆放的角度恰到好处，教她既看得清画面，又便于品评高下。虽说他那手脚麻利、轻拿轻放的细致劲儿固然叫人舒心，但平心而论，真正更合她眼缘的，却是他在干活时那具柔韧矫健的身姿，以及不知不觉间流露出的种种优雅多变的体态——她竟也暗暗开始将他当作一个艺术观察对象细细揣摩起来，一如他从前揣摩她那般。

她心满意足地夸赞道：“到目前为止干得极好，弗利特先生。我真庆幸身边有你这样一位帮手，而不是那个笨手笨脚的草包骗子贝尔德先生。”

“而我敢向您担保，卢多尔夫小姐，打从我得知您的计划那一刻起，便一直热切盼望着能有这份荣幸。”

“像许多心想事成的人一样，没准你很快就要后悔了；因为你这份荣幸里头可少不了大把吃苦受累的力气活呢。”

“那再好不过，越多越好。”丹尼斯热忱地说道。

“何出此言？我还当眼下你手头要干的差事已经多得教你不胜其烦了呢。”

“对于我这般年纪和力气的人来说，只要活儿合自己心意，劳作便算不得什么负担。
